**Quick lesson:** The design separates the two interaction patterns instead of forcing one API style onto both workloads. Converse is a Bedrock Runtime API pattern that AWS positions for model-agnostic, multi-turn chat. The application must still check that the selected chat model supports that API. StartAsyncInvoke is the Bedrock Runtime API for asynchronous invocation. It accepts a model input and an output data configuration, such as Amazon S3, and returns an invocationArn. That fits the report workflow here because the scenario states that the selected report model supports asynchronous invocation with S3 output. InvokeModel is synchronous and returns one…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 30
Skipped
A company is building a customer portal that uses Amazon Bedrock models. The portal must expose one custom HTTPS API to web and mobile clients. Chat requests are multi-turn and need a single response within seconds. Report-generation requests can run for minutes. The selected report model supports Bedrock asynchronous invocation with S3 output. The API must reject malformed JSON before invoking compute.

Which design best meets these requirements?

Create an API Gateway REST API with request validation. Use Lambda to call InvokeModelWithResponseStream for chat and report jobs, then write each completed stream to S3.
Explanation
Incorrect. InvokeModelWithResponseStream is useful when the client needs streamed output, but report jobs can run for minutes and are meant for later retrieval. Keeping a Lambda invocation open to collect a long stream adds operational risk and does not use Bedrock-managed asynchronous invocation.
Create an API Gateway REST API with request validation. Use Lambda to call StartAsyncInvoke for chat and report jobs, then have clients poll each invocationArn.
Explanation
Incorrect. StartAsyncInvoke is appropriate for asynchronous work that can complete later when the selected model supports it. It is not the best fit for interactive multi-turn chat that needs a single response within seconds.
Create an API Gateway REST API with request validation. Send every request to SQS, and have Lambda call InvokeModel for each message, then write completions to S3.
Explanation
Incorrect. SQS with Lambda is a valid asynchronous application pattern, but sending every request through SQS does not meet the low-latency chat requirement. InvokeModel is synchronous, so the solution still requires workers to manage each model call.
Correct answer
Create an API Gateway REST API with request validation. Use Lambda to call Converse for chat and StartAsyncInvoke for reports with S3 output.
Explanation
Correct. API Gateway can validate the client request before Lambda runs. Converse fits model-agnostic multi-turn chat, and StartAsyncInvoke fits the report workload because the selected model supports asynchronous invocation with S3 output.
Overall explanation
The design separates the two interaction patterns instead of forcing one API style onto both workloads. Converse is a Bedrock Runtime API pattern that AWS positions for model-agnostic, multi-turn chat. The application must still check that the selected chat model supports that API.

StartAsyncInvoke is the Bedrock Runtime API for asynchronous invocation. It accepts a model input and an output data configuration, such as Amazon S3, and returns an invocationArn. That fits the report workflow here because the scenario states that the selected report model supports asynchronous invocation with S3 output.

InvokeModel is synchronous and returns one response from a model-specific request body. Streaming uses a different API, InvokeModelWithResponseStream. Streaming is not the same as a managed asynchronous job, and it does not remove the need to keep application compute active while collecting the response.

For Bedrock API selection details, see Amazon Bedrock API inference options. For the synchronous API behavior, see Run inference with InvokeModel. For asynchronous invocation, see StartAsyncInvoke API reference.

Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging is enabled in the Region.

Which approach meets these requirements with the most accurate attribution?

Correct answer
Record toolUseId, tool name, latency, and status in the tool runner; correlate with Bedrock logs by requestMetadata.
Explanation
Correct. For client-side tool use with Converse, the application executes the tool and returns a matching toolResult. The tool runner is the accurate place to measure tool latency and tool failures, while requestMetadata helps attribute model logs to a prompt variant.
Enable enableTrace on InvokeAgent requests; use callerChain, collaboratorName, and action group events to measure Converse tool use.
Explanation
Incorrect. Agent trace data applies to InvokeAgent requests for Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic. The scenario uses a Converse application with client-side tools, so InvokeAgent trace fields do not observe those tool calls.
Use Bedrock invocation logs as the tool trace source; infer each tool’s latency, status, and arguments from Converse payload records.
Explanation

Place tool names in X-Amzn-Bedrock-Request-Metadata; use Cost Explorer and cost allocation tags to baseline tool usage.
Explanation
Incorrect. For Converse, request metadata is supplied in the request body, not the InvokeModel metadata header. Request metadata is recorded for log attribution only, and it is not delivered as a cost allocation tag in Cost Explorer.
Overall explanation
In Amazon Bedrock client-side tool use, the model chooses when to request a tool, but the application runs the tool. With the Converse API, the application receives a toolUse request, runs the tool, and sends back a toolResult with the same toolUseId. See Call a tool with the Converse API.

A tool performance framework needs measurements from two places. The application tool runner should record call counts, latency, status, and tool identifiers. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs can add model-side data such as operation, model ID, identity, request metadata, and token counts. See Log Amazon Bedrock model invocation information.

requestMetadata is useful for attribution, such as a prompt variant or experiment ID. It is not a billing tag, and it does not appear in Cost Explorer. For Converse, the metadata is supplied in the request body, as described in Track costs using application inference profiles and request metadata.

Question 32
Skipped
A manufacturing company is building a GenAI assistant that creates incident-review briefs from equipment failure reports. The workflow must run a safety analysis and a repair-parts analysis concurrently. It must route the report for human review when either analysis returns a high risk score. Operations needs per-report execution history and managed retries for transient tool errors.

Which approach should the company use?

Build an Agent Squad router with Strands worker agents. Run the router in a container and write logs for each routed request and retry event.
Explanation
Incorrect. Agent Squad and Strands Agents can implement advanced routing and worker-agent patterns in application code. This approach adds custom orchestration and logging work when the scenario asks for managed retries and operational execution history.
Build a Bedrock multi-agent collaboration with a supervisor agent. Create worker agents for the analyses and use agent traces for operational review.
Explanation
Incorrect. A multi-agent collaboration can delegate work to specialized agents and can provide trace details about agent reasoning and tool use. It does not provide the same explicit workflow controls for retries and per-report state transitions as Step Functions.
Correct answer
Build an AWS Step Functions state machine with Parallel, Choice, and Retry states. Invoke Lambda tasks that call the specialist agents.
Explanation
Correct. Step Functions provides durable workflow execution, parallel branches, conditional routing, and built-in retry policies. Lambda tasks can call Amazon Bedrock or agent runtimes while Step Functions records the execution path for each report.
Build an Amazon Bedrock Flow with prompt and condition nodes. Put both analyses in the flow and branch on risk scores for the final brief.
Explanation
Incorrect. Bedrock Flows are useful for composing prompt chains and conditional GenAI logic with low operational overhead. The scenario needs workflow-level execution history and managed retry behavior across tool calls, which Step Functions fits better.
Overall explanation
AWS Step Functions is the best fit when an AI workflow needs durable orchestration, parallel branches, conditions, retries, and execution history. The workflow can use a Parallel state for the two analyses, a Choice state for the risk threshold, and Retry rules for transient tool failures.

Amazon Bedrock and agent frameworks still play an important role. Lambda tasks in the state machine can call Amazon Bedrock APIs, invoke a Bedrock agent alias, or call a Strands-based agent runtime. Step Functions provides the control plane around those calls.

Amazon Bedrock Flows are stronger when the main requirement is prompt chaining, model calls, and conditional GenAI composition. They are not the best match when operations teams need the workflow controls that state machines provide.

Agent traces and custom router logs can help developers understand agent behavior. They do not replace a managed workflow service when the scenario depends on durable state, retry policies, and auditable execution paths. For more information, see What is AWS Step Functions?, Handling errors in Step Functions workflows, and Amazon Bedrock Flows.

Skipped
A renewable energy company is building an operations assistant on Amazon Bedrock. The assistant must classify sensor alerts, summarize maintenance logs, and answer diagnostic questions. The client already sends a requestCategory value for the three task types. Evaluation results show that a small FM is accurate for classification and summaries. A larger FM is needed for diagnostic questions. Product managers must be able to inspect the routing logic and prompt chain without code deployments. The company also wants to avoid invoking multiple FMs for every request.

Which implementation will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Build an AWS Lambda router that stores routing rules in code and invokes task-specific prompts through the Bedrock runtime API.
Explanation
Incorrect. A Lambda router can implement model selection, and it is a valid pattern when the team wants full code control. The scenario requires product managers to inspect routing logic and prompt chains without code deployments, so this adds unnecessary operational overhead.
Correct answer
Build an Amazon Bedrock Flow that uses requestCategory conditions to invoke the selected task-specific prompt and FM.
Explanation
Correct. Bedrock Flows can chain prompts, models, and conditions in a managed workflow. Rule-based conditions on the existing requestCategory value avoid a separate FM router and invoke only the selected task FM.
Build a single Bedrock prompt that uses the largest approved FM for all requests and controls answer length with max tokens.
Explanation
Incorrect. A single large model can simplify implementation and may improve quality for hard questions. It ignores the evaluation result that a smaller model is sufficient for some tasks, so it does not optimize average cost.
Build a Bedrock Agent with one action group per task and instruct the agent to choose the action group from requestCategory.
Explanation
Incorrect. A Bedrock Agent can choose tools based on instructions and can use action groups for custom task logic. The scenario already has a deterministic category value, so agent orchestration adds planning overhead and is less transparent than a Flow for inspecting prompt-chain logic.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Flows is designed for managed coordination across prompts, models, and workflow steps. A flow contains nodes and connections, and condition nodes can route data to different paths. This fits the scenario because the request already includes a requestCategory value. See Amazon Bedrock Flows.

The important tradeoff is where routing happens. If an FM classifies the request inside the workflow, the application pays for that FM call before it invokes the selected task model. Here, rule-based routing on existing request metadata avoids that extra FM call.

A Bedrock Agent can route to action groups, but agents are better when the model must plan tool use from a less structured request. See Agents for Amazon Bedrock. A Lambda router can also work, but it moves the workflow into code and reduces visibility for product managers. A single large model is simple, but it wastes capacity on simple classification and summarization tasks.

Which TWO actions should the company implement to meet these traceability requirements?

Catalog approved S3 buckets in AWS Glue Data Catalog. Add collection names, object keys, and ingestion timestamps to chunk metadata.
Explanation
Incorrect. This approach creates useful source metadata and can identify the S3 object that supplied a chunk. It does not preserve the required document version for each cited claim.
Correct selection
Catalog each approved S3 data source in AWS Glue Data Catalog. Add source IDs and document versions to chunk metadata during ingestion.
Explanation
Correct. AWS Glue Data Catalog provides a managed metadata inventory for approved data sources. Propagating the same identifiers into chunk metadata lets generated summaries cite the retrieved evidence.

Run Amazon Macie discovery jobs on approved S3 buckets. Tag chunks with finding IDs, source object keys, and classification labels.

Incorrect. Macie findings can support sensitive-data governance for content in S3. Finding IDs and classification labels do not provide complete source collection, document ID, and document version lineage for generated claims.

Traceability in a GenAI application needs two different records. The application needs source lineage for the content that the model used. The platform also needs an audit trail for prompt and API activity.

AWS Glue Data Catalog is useful as the managed catalog for approved data sources and their metadata. During ingestion, the pipeline should copy stable source attributes, such as collection, document ID, and version, into the metadata for each chunk. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can use document metadata for filtering and retrieval workflows, and the application can include that metadata in citations. See AWS Glue Data Catalog and crawlers and Metadata and filtering for knowledge bases.

CloudTrail addresses the audit requirement. It records supported Amazon Bedrock API calls with details such as the caller identity and event time. These records help auditors reconstruct who used model and prompt resources. See Logging Amazon Bedrock API calls with AWS CloudTrail.

The other approaches are plausible parts of governance or traceability designs. Bucket-level catalog metadata, current S3 object metadata, and Macie findings can help in specific reviews. They do not preserve the full evidence chain required for cited claims and prompt use. The strongest design records source metadata before retrieval and preserves API activity separately for audit review.

Correct. CountTokens estimates input tokens for the same model before inference, so the team can test prompt and context changes without generation cost. Pruning retrieved context reduces input tokens, and smaller task-specific maxTokens values reduce the upfront quota reservation.
Overall explanation
Token efficiency starts with measurement before the model runs. Amazon Bedrock CountTokens returns the input token count that the same model would use for an inference request. AWS states that the call does not incur charges. See Count tokens for Amazon Bedrock model invocations.

The scenario has two separate waste sources. Too many retrieved chunks increase input tokens. A high maxTokens value increases the quota reservation at request start, even if the model later produces a short answer. AWS explains this reservation behavior in Runtime quotas for token usage.

maxTokens limits generated output tokens. It does not limit the input context window. To control output length, set a realistic value for the task and also monitor stopReason values for results such as max_tokens or model_context_window_exceeded. The inference field is described in InferenceConfiguration.

Prompt caching and CloudWatch metrics are useful, but they do not replace prompt measurement and context pruning. Caching is hit-dependent, and response fields should be checked to confirm cache reads and writes. Prompt caching for Amazon Bedrock explains these cache usage fields. The most direct first change is to estimate tokens, reduce unnecessary context, and choose output limits that match the use case.

Which implementation meets these requirements with the least custom logic?

Call ApplyGuardrail with source OUTPUT first. Route GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED to a terminal state, and set TimeoutSeconds on the state machine.
Explanation
Incorrect. The source value OUTPUT is for evaluating generated or returned content, not the initial customer text. The workflow needs to block unsafe input before policy lookup, partner calls, or model invocation starts.
Attach the guardrail to InvokeModel. Route blocked messages to a terminal state, and set timeout values on the Lambda tasks in each branch.
Explanation
Incorrect. A guardrail on InvokeModel protects the Bedrock model call, but the workflow includes tasks that run before the model call. Lambda task timeouts limit individual tasks, but they do not define one maximum duration for the whole workflow.
Correct answer
Call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT first. Route GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED to a terminal state, and set TimeoutSeconds on the state machine.
Explanation
Correct. ApplyGuardrail can evaluate text with a configured Bedrock guardrail without invoking a foundation model. A Step Functions terminal state handles the blocked path, and a state machine TimeoutSeconds value limits the whole execution.
Call a Lambda classifier before all tasks. Route unsafe results to a terminal state, and add a Wait state before model invocation.
Explanation
Incorrect. A custom classifier adds logic that duplicates a policy already defined in the Bedrock guardrail. A Wait state delays the workflow, but it does not enforce the required 2 minute maximum execution time.
Overall explanation
ApplyGuardrail is the best fit when a workflow must evaluate text before any model call or tool call happens. The independent API can assess text by using a configured Bedrock guardrail without invoking a foundation model. The request identifies whether the content is INPUT or OUTPUT, and the response includes an action such as GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED. See Use the ApplyGuardrail API.

Step Functions is the right control plane for the stopping behavior. A Choice state can send unsafe input to a terminal Fail or Succeed state. A state machine level TimeoutSeconds sets a maximum duration for the whole execution, not only for one Lambda task.

Attaching a guardrail to InvokeModel is useful for Bedrock inference, and Bedrock can discard the model inference when input evaluation intervenes. However, that does not protect earlier workflow tasks such as policy lookup or partner API calls. For model invocation guardrail details, see Use guardrails for model inference and How guardrails work.

The ApplyGuardrail API lets an application evaluate text before it calls a model, so a shared Lambda proxy can enforce one policy for all clients.

**Quick lesson:** Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases does not automatically refresh a data source by default. The default sync frequency is On-demand. After files are added, changed, or removed, the data source must be synced so the vector store reflects those changes. The important design point is that sync is incremental. Bedrock processes documents that changed since the last sync. New documents are ingested, deleted documents are removed from the vector store, and changed content is re-parsed, re-chunked, re-embedded, and re-indexed. Question 44
Skipped
A pharmaceutical company uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon S3 data source for research protocols. Scientists add, change, and delete files throughout the day. The search assistant must reflect changes within 1 hour. The team wants low operational overhead and does not want unchanged documents to be reprocessed.

Which approach will meet these requirements?

Run a scheduled workflow that recreates the knowledge base data source each hour. Start a sync after each recreation.
Explanation
Incorrect. Recreating the data source adds unnecessary operational work and risks disrupting retrieval. Amazon Bedrock already supports incremental sync for added, modified, and deleted documents.
Keep the data source at its default sync frequency. Enable S3 Versioning on the source bucket to publish changed objects.
Explanation
Incorrect. S3 Versioning helps preserve object versions, but it does not cause Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to sync automatically. The default sync frequency is on demand, so changes can remain out of the vector store.
Correct answer
Run a scheduled workflow that calls StartIngestionJob for the knowledge base data source. Track each job with GetIngestionJob.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases data source sync is incremental. A scheduled call to StartIngestionJob keeps the vector store current, and unchanged documents are skipped during sync.
Use S3 event notifications to invoke a Lambda function that updates the vector store directly after object changes.
Explanation
Incorrect. Directly updating the underlying vector store would bypass the managed Knowledge Bases sync process for this S3 data source. Bedrock also supports direct ingestion APIs, but scheduled incremental sync with StartIngestionJob is the simpler documented fit here.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases does not automatically refresh a data source by default. The default sync frequency is On-demand. After files are added, changed, or removed, the data source must be synced so the vector store reflects those changes.

The important design point is that sync is incremental. Bedrock processes documents that changed since the last sync. New documents are ingested, deleted documents are removed from the vector store, and changed content is re-parsed, re-chunked, re-embedded, and re-indexed. Unchanged documents are skipped, so a scheduled sync does not mean a full rebuild every time.

The API operation for starting a sync is StartIngestionJob. The workflow needs the knowledgeBaseId and dataSourceId. The application can use GetIngestionJob with the returned job ID to monitor progress. See Sync to ingest your data sources into the knowledge base and StartIngestionJob.

Saving a prompt updates the draft, but creating a version makes a snapshot of the prompt and its configuration for application use. That snapshot lets the team connect a regression to a specific prompt release. See Deploy prompts using Prompt management.

The caller can also supply requestMetadata, so the application can attach a release ID or prompt version reference to each call. See Log model invocation data in Amazon Bedrock.

Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Keep the REST API. Set response transfer mode to STREAM, call ConverseStream in Lambda, and pass Bedrock EventStream events unchanged.
Explanation
Incorrect. Bedrock streaming uses AWS EventStream, not browser-native SSE. The application layer must convert Bedrock stream events into the SSE format that the React client expects.
Create a WebSocket API. Keep Lambda calling ConverseStream, and push contentBlockDelta messages through the API Gateway management API.
Explanation
Incorrect. A WebSocket API can support two-way stateful communication, but the scenario already has a REST endpoint and an SSE client contract. This approach adds a larger API change than required.
Correct answer
Keep the REST API. Set response transfer mode to STREAM, call ConverseStream in Lambda, and emit SSE from contentBlockDelta events.
Explanation
Correct. API Gateway response streaming is supported for REST APIs with AWS_PROXY integrations. ConverseStream returns structured Bedrock stream events, so the Lambda function must translate relevant deltas into SSE messages.
Create an HTTP API. Keep Lambda calling ConverseStream, and emit SSE from contentBlockDelta events through the Lambda proxy integration.
Explanation
Incorrect. API Gateway response streaming is documented for REST APIs, not HTTP APIs. Using HTTP API would not meet the stated response streaming requirement through API Gateway.
Overall explanation
For this scenario, the best design keeps the existing API Gateway REST API and enables response streaming on the integration. API Gateway response streaming uses response transfer mode STREAM. It is supported for REST APIs with HTTP_PROXY or AWS_PROXY integrations, which matches a Lambda proxy integration. See Response streaming for REST APIs in API Gateway.

Amazon Bedrock ConverseStream is the streaming form of the Converse API. It emits structured events such as messageStart, contentBlockDelta, messageStop, and metadata. A Lambda function can read the stream and send only the useful text deltas to the client. See ConverseStream API reference.

Bedrock does not return native browser SSE frames. The streaming body for model-specific streaming uses AWS EventStream, and applications must translate chunks when the browser contract is SSE or WebSocket messages. This is why forwarding the Bedrock stream unchanged is not enough. See InvokeModelWithResponseStream API reference.

A WebSocket API can be a valid design when the client needs bidirectional, long-lived communication. It is not the smallest change here because the browser already expects SSE over HTTPS. An HTTP API also does not satisfy this API Gateway response streaming requirement, because the documented response transfer mode applies to REST APIs.

Which change should the developer make?

Route this provider through InvokeModel. Send the provider's documented model-specific JSON body.

Incorrect. InvokeModel supports model-specific JSON bodies and can be appropriate for provider-specific integrations. The scenario requires the shared client to continue using Converse across providers.

Incorrect. This keeps a valid Converse request shape, but it changes the provider-specific control that the team added. The scenario requires passing a model-specific request field, not replacing it with a common parameter.

Explanation
Incorrect. additionalModelResponseFieldPaths requests extra fields from the model response by using JSON Pointer paths. It does not send provider-specific request parameters to the model.
Correct answer
Put the provider-specific sampling field in additionalModelRequestFields. Keep common fields in inferenceConfig.
Explanation
Correct. Converse uses inferenceConfig for common inference parameters. Model-specific fields belong in additionalModelRequestFields, so moving the sampling field there fixes the request structure.
Overall explanation
Converse gives applications a common messages-style interface across supported Amazon Bedrock models. It separates common inference parameters from provider-specific parameters. Common parameters, such as maxTokens and temperature, go in inferenceConfig. Model-specific extensions go in additionalModelRequestFields.

The failure in this scenario is a request-shape problem. The application is using the right API family, but it placed a provider-specific sampling field in the common parameter section. Moving only that field to additionalModelRequestFields keeps the shared Converse code path and fixes the integration issue.

additionalModelResponseFieldPaths is for requesting extra fields from the model response. InvokeModel is useful when an application chooses to work directly with each model's body format, but that gives up the common Converse request contract for this path. Use API Gateway request validation with JSON Schema. Reject requests that fail field length, type, required-field, and format checks.
Explanation
This is incorrect. JSON Schema validation is useful for request shape, length, and required fields. It does not determine whether free-text content is toxic or depends on the current league risk context.
Correct selection
Attach a Bedrock guardrail to model calls. Configure content filters, denied topics, word filters, and sensitive information filters.
Explanation
This is correct. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can inspect user inputs and model outputs against managed safety policies. The guardrail can block or redact configured categories at the model invocation boundary.

Explanation
This is incorrect. AWS WAF can block requests in real time by using text matching and regular expressions. It is brittle for prompt-injection attempts and cannot apply the dynamic context and user risk scoring required in the scenario.
Correct selection
Run a Lambda validator before model calls. Start a Step Functions review workflow only for requests that match custom risk rules.
Explanation
This is correct. Lambda can run custom checks that use the current league context, user risk score, and phrase policy before invoking Amazon Bedrock. Starting Step Functions only for flagged requests avoids adding workflow latency to normal requests.

Explanation
This is incorrect. Prompt instructions help shape model behavior, but they are not a security boundary for hostile or unsafe input. A jailbreak attempt can ask the model to ignore those instructions.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provide managed safety controls for user inputs and model responses. A guardrail can use content filters, denied topics, word filters, and sensitive information filters. When a policy is matched, the guardrail can return an intervention instead of allowing unsafe content. See Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

The dynamic phrase and risk policy needs application-specific logic. A Lambda validator can apply current game context and user risk data before the Bedrock call. Step Functions can run escalation or review only for flagged requests. This keeps common safe requests on the low latency path while risky requests follow a governed workflow. Prompt wording, JSON shape validation, and AWS WAF text rules are useful controls, but they do not provide the same real-time semantic safety with dynamic business rules. See Invoke Lambda with Step Functions.

Which approach will improve retrieval relevance with the LEAST custom code?

Correct answer
Set overrideSearchType to HYBRID and add a Bedrock reranking configuration to the Knowledge Base request.
Explanation

Explanation

Overall explanation
For a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base, vectorSearchConfiguration.overrideSearchType can be set to HYBRID or SEMANTIC. HYBRID combines vector-embedding search with raw-text search. This is useful when users ask natural-language questions that also include exact identifiers.

The scenario also states that the OpenSearch Serverless vector store has a filterable raw text field. That matters because AWS documents hybrid search support for OpenSearch Serverless vector stores when the store contains a filterable text field. See Configure and test knowledge base retrieval.

Amazon Bedrock reranking can be used during Knowledge Base retrieval through Retrieve or RetrieveAndGenerate. Reranking is for textual data and can override the default Knowledge Bases ranking. See Rerank models in Amazon Bedrock.

Calling OpenSearch Serverless directly could be valid in another architecture. OpenSearch Serverless hybrid search uses a hybrid query and a search pipeline that combines scores. In this scenario, the application must keep using the Knowledge Bases API, so using the Knowledge Base retrieval configuration is the lower-code fit. See Configure neural search for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.

Which approach meets these requirements?

Correct answer
Create a bedrock-runtime interface endpoint with private DNS. Attach a custom endpoint policy. Use CloudTrail for Bedrock API audit.
Explanation
Correct. The bedrock-runtime endpoint supports native inference APIs such as Converse and InvokeModel through AWS PrivateLink. A custom endpoint policy can restrict principals, actions, and resources through the endpoint, and CloudTrail provides API request attribution.
Create a bedrock-runtime interface endpoint with private DNS. Attach a custom endpoint policy. Use invocation logs for Bedrock API audit.
Explanation
Incorrect. This uses the correct private endpoint and can enforce least privilege through the endpoint policy. Model invocation logging can capture inference inputs, outputs, and metadata, but CloudTrail is the audit source for Bedrock API activity.
Create a bedrock-runtime interface endpoint with private DNS. Use CloudTrail for Bedrock API audit. Rely on IAM policies for least privilege.
Explanation
Incorrect. This uses the correct private endpoint and the correct audit source for Bedrock API activity. However, IAM policies alone do not provide the required least-privilege control through the VPC endpoint path.
Create a bedrock interface endpoint with private DNS. Attach a custom endpoint policy. Use CloudTrail for Bedrock API audit.
Explanation
Incorrect. This uses a custom endpoint policy and the correct audit source for API activity. However, the bedrock endpoint is not the documented data-plane endpoint for native inference calls such as Converse and InvokeModel.
Overall explanation
For native Amazon Bedrock inference, the application should use the bedrock-runtime interface VPC endpoint. AWS PrivateLink lets workloads in a VPC call Bedrock without public IP addresses, NAT gateways, or internet gateways. With private DNS enabled, the application can keep using normal Regional service names.

Creating the endpoint is not enough for least privilege. The default endpoint policy allows full access through the endpoint. A custom endpoint policy is needed to restrict which principals, actions, and resources can use that network path. IAM permissions still authorize the caller, and the endpoint policy adds a separate network-path control.

CloudTrail is the correct audit source for Bedrock API activity. Model invocation logging can publish inference inputs, outputs, and metadata to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3 when enabled. That logging helps with model interaction review, but it does not replace CloudTrail for API request attribution.

It uses the bedrock-runtime endpoint through Converse or ConverseStream. It is not a universal abstraction for every model, but it matches this scenario because the models are message-capable and the assistant needs tool use and guardrails. See Carry out a conversation with the Converse API operations.

Cross-Region inference profiles are used when the design needs Bedrock to route inference across multiple Regions. The application specifies the inference profile ID or ARN in modelId for runtime calls such as Converse and InvokeModel. Application inference profiles can also be used with runtime calls, but a profile created from a single-Region model does not add cross-Region routing. See Use inference profiles in Amazon Bedrock.

The SCP detail is important for a Geographic cross-Region inference profile. A request can route to destination Regions that the account did not explicitly opt in to. If any destination Region in the profile is blocked by SCPs, the request fails. The organization must design the Region policy for every destination Region in the selected Geographic profile, not only the source Region. See Supported Regions and models for cross-Region inference.

Splitting requests across different Bedrock runtime APIs does not increase quota. Runtime quotas are shared by model and endpoint across APIs such as InvokeModel, Converse, Responses, and Chat Completions. This means API choice should be based on integration behavior, not on a belief that each API has separate capacity. See Runtime quotas for Amazon Bedrock.

Question 54
Skipped
A regional bank is building a loan assistant by using Amazon Bedrock. Users often refer to earlier answers in follow-up questions that can arrive hours later and reach different application instances. The assistant must preserve context across stateless web requests. The bank already uses Amazon Comprehend custom classification and wants a tracked clarification workflow when intent confidence is low. The solution must avoid long-running application processes.

Which design best meets these requirements?

Correct answer
Call the Converse API with recent turns from DynamoDB. Start Step Functions when Amazon Comprehend returns low intent confidence.
Explanation
Correct. The Converse API is designed for conversational interactions with Amazon Bedrock models. DynamoDB can store conversation history across stateless requests, and Step Functions can coordinate a clarification flow without holding an application process open.
Call the Converse API from Step Functions. Keep recent turns in execution input, and resume the workflow after clarification.
Explanation
Incorrect. Step Functions can coordinate workflow state and can resume work after a clarification step. However, using execution input as the only history store ties the conversation context to a workflow execution instead of a durable session record that the web tier can retrieve by conversation ID.
Call the Converse API with recent turns from DynamoDB. Return clarifying questions synchronously from the web API handler.
Explanation
Incorrect. This approach can send a clarification question and can preserve model context with DynamoDB. However, it does not create a tracked clarification workflow outside the web tier for answers that arrive later across stateless requests.
Call the Converse API with recent turns from DynamoDB. Use a Lambda router with keyword rules to ask clarification questions.
Explanation
Incorrect. DynamoDB and the Converse API address the conversation context requirement. The Lambda router does not use the existing Amazon Comprehend confidence signal, and keyword rules add custom routing logic that is less aligned with the stated low-confidence workflow.
Overall explanation
Interactive GenAI systems need separate handling for conversation context and workflow state. Conversation context helps the model understand follow-up questions. Workflow state helps the application decide whether to answer, ask for clarification, or wait for the user.

The Amazon Bedrock Converse API gives applications a consistent way to send conversational messages to supported models. The application can retrieve recent turns from DynamoDB by conversation ID and include them in the request. This works well when requests are stateless and can reach different application instances.

Amazon Comprehend custom classification can provide an intent classification signal for the application. When that signal has low confidence, AWS Step Functions can coordinate the clarification path outside the web process. This lets the application track the pending clarification without keeping a Lambda function or web handler open.

For the conversational API pattern, see Carry out a conversation with the Converse API. For workflow orchestration, see What is AWS Step Functions?. For Comprehend custom classification, see Custom classification.

Question 55
Skipped
A logistics company uses Amazon Bedrock Converse from eu-west-1 to run a dispatch assistant. The model has an EU geography-tied cross-Region inference profile. The company must keep processing within EU Regions, improve availability during Bedrock capacity issues, and continue calling a single approved source Region endpoint. SCPs currently allow Bedrock runtime calls only in eu-west-1.

Which approach meets these requirements?

Keep modelId set to the regional model ARN. Use Step Functions to open a circuit and retry later from eu-west-1.
Explanation
A circuit breaker can reduce repeated calls during a disruption, but this approach does not add Bedrock capacity across destination Regions. Bedrock cross-Region inference is invoked through inference profiles, not by choosing a different runtime behavior around a regional model ARN.
Correct answer
Use the EU geography-tied inference profile ARN as modelId. Allow bedrock:InvokeModel* in every profile destination Region.
Explanation
This approach is correct because the application can keep calling Bedrock from the approved source Region. The EU profile lets Bedrock route requests to supported EU destination Regions, and the SCPs must allow the required runtime actions in those destinations.
Use a Global inference profile ARN as modelId. Add an SCP exception that permits the selected profile for Bedrock runtime calls.
Explanation
This approach can improve resilience through an inference profile, but it does not meet the EU-only processing requirement. Global profiles can route to supported commercial Regions worldwide, and their destination Regions can change over time.
Use the EU geography-tied inference profile ARN as modelId. Allow bedrock:InvokeModel* only in the source Region.
Explanation
Using the EU profile is a good start, but the SCP configuration is not sufficient. AWS documents that blocking any destination Region in a profile can cause cross-Region inference requests to fail.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference separates the source Region from the destination Region. The application sends the request to the source Region, and Bedrock routes the request through the selected inference profile. For runtime APIs such as Converse, the application specifies the inference profile ARN in modelId.

The EU geography-tied profile is the best fit because the scenario requires EU-only processing and a single approved source Region endpoint. The SCP change is also required. If an SCP blocks any destination Region in the selected profile, the request can fail even when other destinations are allowed.

A Global profile is useful for broad resilience, but it does not satisfy strict EU processing requirements. Global profiles have special policy behavior, including aws:RequestedRegion set to unspecified for Region-agnostic authorization. For details, see Increase throughput with Global cross-Region inference.

Before writing Region controls, call GetInferenceProfile from each source Region that the application will use. Inspect the models field to identify destination Region ARNs. For more details, see Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference and Supported Regions and models for inference profiles.

Question 56
Skipped
A legal services company is building a contract review assistant. The assistant must use a ReAct loop: an FM chooses the next action, approved tools run, observations return, and the loop repeats. Some checks use an approval service that accepts a correlation value and responds minutes later. Some contract packages produce model requests larger than 256 KiB. The team wants durable orchestration without custom servers.

Which TWO design choices meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Place the full InvokeModel request in Body. Use JSONPath selectors to trim data before later state transitions.
Explanation
Incorrect. Body payloads for the optimized Bedrock InvokeModel integration are limited to 256 KiB. Trimming later state transitions does not fix a request that is already too large for Body.
Use an AgentCore InvokeHarness task. Invoke the harness with Request Response and keep approvals inside the harness.
Explanation
Incorrect. AgentCore InvokeHarness can be invoked from Step Functions by using Request Response. However, Request Response proceeds after the HTTP response and does not give Step Functions a callback wait for the delayed approval result.
Correct selection
Use a Standard Workflow. Model the reasoning step with Bedrock InvokeModel and the external step with a task token.
Explanation
Correct. A Standard Workflow can orchestrate a durable loop across model calls, tool calls, and branching logic. The task token pattern lets an external service return later by calling Step Functions with the callback result.
Use an Express Workflow. Invoke Bedrock with Request Response and poll the approval service between model steps until completion.
Explanation
Incorrect. Request Response is a valid service integration pattern for Express Workflows. However, polling is a weaker fit for an approval service that responds minutes later, and the scenario asks for durable orchestration without custom servers.
Correct selection
Store contract request artifacts in S3. Reference them through the optimized Bedrock Input field with an S3Uri.
Explanation
Correct. The optimized Bedrock InvokeModel integration supports Step Functions-specific Input and Output fields that can refer to Amazon S3. This avoids putting an oversized model payload directly into the workflow state.
Overall explanation
A ReAct style system needs orchestration that can repeat model reasoning, call tools, inspect observations, and branch. AWS Step Functions can make each step explicit in the workflow definition. The optimized Amazon Bedrock integration can call InvokeModel by using a Task resource such as arn:aws:states:::bedrock:invokeModel.

The approval service changes the integration choice. .waitForTaskToken waits until Step Functions receives SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure. Standard Workflows can support this pattern where the service integration allows it, but Express Workflows support only Request Response integrations. See Integrating services with Step Functions.

The large contract packages also change the payload design. The optimized Bedrock InvokeModel integration has a 256 KiB limit for Body payloads, and Step Functions has a separate 256 KiB state size quota. For larger payloads, use the Step Functions-specific Input or Output fields with an S3Uri. See Amazon Bedrock service integration with Step Functions.

Correct answer

For preventive control of Amazon Bedrock usage, AWS Organizations supports Amazon Bedrock policies. These policies can attach to the organization root, OUs, or accounts, but they require Region-specific guardrails and must reference a specific guardrail version.

**Quick lesson:** For a large RAG vector store on a managed Amazon OpenSearch Service domain, the team should design the index layout before loading data. AWS documents that the default layout for managed domains is five primary shards and one replica per primary shard. AWS also notes that the primary shard count is not easy to change after indexing starts. See Amazon OpenSearch Service shard strategy documentation. ### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 58
Skipped
A pharmaceutical distributor is building a RAG assistant for product support teams. The team will use managed Amazon OpenSearch Service k-NN indexes as the vector store. The corpus is 2.4 TiB across four product lines, and each query includes one product line. Growth differs by product line. The team must optimize p95 retrieval latency before indexing starts.

Which index architecture should the team choose?

Create product-line indexes, route queries with product-line filters, and target 30-50 GiB per primary shard.
Explanation
This is incorrect. Separate product-line indexes are a reasonable architecture for this workload. However, 30-50 GiB per shard is AWS guidance for write-heavy log workloads, not latency-sensitive search.
Correct answer
Create product-line indexes, route queries with a small routing index, and target 10-30 GiB per primary shard.
Explanation
This is correct. The query already includes the product line, so routing can limit retrieval to a specialized index. Targeting 10-30 GiB per primary shard aligns with AWS guidance for latency-sensitive search workloads.
Create one shared detail index, add a small routing index, and keep the default five primary shards.
Explanation
This is incorrect. A routing index does not help enough if all vectors remain in one default-sharded detail index. The design still leaves the main retrieval index with very large shards that are hard to change after indexing starts.
Create one shared index, route queries with product-line filters, and keep the default five primary shards.
Explanation
This is incorrect. Product-line filters can reduce returned results, but the shared index still creates a broad search design. The default five-primary-shard layout would make each shard too large for this latency-sensitive corpus.
Overall explanation
For a large RAG vector store on a managed Amazon OpenSearch Service domain, the team should design the index layout before loading data. AWS documents that the default layout for managed domains is five primary shards and one replica per primary shard. AWS also notes that the primary shard count is not easy to change after indexing starts. See Amazon OpenSearch Service shard strategy documentation.

The best design uses domain-specific indexes because every query already includes a product line. A small routing index can send the query to the right product-line index. This reduces search scope and lets the team tune shard counts separately as each product line grows.

For latency-sensitive search, AWS recommends 10-30 GiB per shard. The 30-50 GiB range is for write-heavy log workloads, so it is not the best target here. For k-NN indexes on managed domains, the index must also use index.knn: true and a knn_vector field, as described in k-nearest neighbor search in Amazon OpenSearch Service.

**Quick lesson:** Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases builds an index from the configured data source. When source files are added, changed, or deleted, the data source must be synced before retrieval reflects those changes. AWS documents StartIngestionJob, GetIngestionJob, and ListIngestionJobs as the APIs for starting and inspecting these jobs. See Sync to ingest your data sources into your knowledge base. The scenario points to a freshness problem, not a ranking problem. The source files were updated, but the knowledge base ingestion history has no recent jobs. An incremental ingestion job is the lowest-change fix because it updates the index without changing…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 59
Skipped
An energy utility uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for a field technician assistant. Updated safety procedures are uploaded to the same Amazon S3 prefix each night. Technicians still receive answers based on older procedures. The knowledge base ingestion history shows no recent jobs after the uploads. The team wants to restore retrieval freshness with minimal architecture changes.

Which action should the team take?

Change the chunking strategy to SEMANTIC. Recreate the knowledge base data source configuration.
Explanation
Incorrect. Semantic chunking can improve how documents are split for some retrieval patterns. It adds cost and operational change, but it does not address the missing ingestion activity shown in the scenario.
Enable reranking for retrieval. Reorder the retrieved text chunks before response generation.
Explanation
Incorrect. Reranking recalculates relevance for chunks that retrieval already returned. It cannot rank updated safety procedures that have not been indexed.
Correct answer
Run StartIngestionJob for the data source. Use GetIngestionJob until the incremental sync completes.
Explanation
Correct. Updating files in the source location does not by itself update the knowledge base index. Starting and monitoring an ingestion job refreshes the index so retrieval can use the changed content.
Increase numberOfResults for vector search. Compare more returned chunks from each technician query.
Explanation
Incorrect. Increasing the number of returned results can help when relevant indexed chunks rank too low. It does not add newly changed source content to the knowledge base index.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases builds an index from the configured data source. When source files are added, changed, or deleted, the data source must be synced before retrieval reflects those changes. AWS documents StartIngestionJob, GetIngestionJob, and ListIngestionJobs as the APIs for starting and inspecting these jobs. See Sync to ingest your data sources into your knowledge base.

The scenario points to a freshness problem, not a ranking problem. The source files were updated, but the knowledge base ingestion history has no recent jobs. An incremental ingestion job is the lowest-change fix because it updates the index without changing retrieval logic.

Increasing numberOfResults can help when the right content is indexed but not high enough in the results. Reranking can reorder retrieved textual chunks, but it works only on content that retrieval already returns. Changing to semantic chunking may improve boundaries between chunks, but it is a heavier remediation and does not directly explain why new source files are absent from retrieval.

Amazon Bedrock gives two different monitoring views. Runtime metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace show operational signals such as invocations, latency, token counts, errors, throttles, and streaming time to first token. These metrics are useful for alarms and dashboards, but they do not calculate semantic KPIs such as hallucination rate or prompt effectiveness by themselves.

Model invocation logging is the better source for detailed request and response analysis. It is disabled by default and must be configured per account and Region. It can send records to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or both, but only to destinations in the same account and Region. See Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.

The prompt version should be added through requestMetadata. Bedrock records this metadata in invocation logs when logging is enabled in the Region where the call is made. This lets the team group token usage and quality investigations by prompt version. See Track cost allocation using invocation logs.

For fleet-level alarms, the team should query InvocationClientErrors, InvocationServerErrors, and InvocationThrottles without requiring the ModelId dimension. Bedrock publishes metrics both with and without ModelId, and some failures are published only without ModelId. The Invocations metric is not a total failure counter because it excludes throttled requests and input validation rejections. See Monitor Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics.

Question 63
Skipped
A travel marketplace uses API Gateway and Lambda to run a booking assistant with Amazon Bedrock Converse. The assistant calls partner tools for tour details. User messages are English or Spanish and are under 100 KB. Partner tool results can include untrusted free text. The company must reduce PII disclosure and harmful content in both prompts and responses.

Which approach provides the MOST complete defense-in-depth protection with low operational overhead?

Mask PII found by DetectPiiEntities. Run Bedrock Guardrails in Detect mode, and call ApplyGuardrail on partner tool text.
Explanation
Incorrect. Detect mode can help teams measure detections before enforcement, but it does not take blocking or masking action. The scenario requires reducing harmful content in prompts and responses, not only reporting it.
Log PII found by DetectPiiEntities for audit. Apply Bedrock Guardrails in Converse, and call ApplyGuardrail on final responses.
Explanation
Incorrect. Logging PII detections helps with audit needs, but it does not prevent PII from reaching the model. Applying checks only to final responses also misses untrusted partner tool text before the model uses that text as context.
Mask PII found by DetectPiiEntities. Apply Bedrock Guardrails in Converse, and pass partner tool text as toolResult content.
Explanation
Incorrect. PII masking before invocation and Converse guardrails are both useful controls. However, Bedrock Guardrails content filters do not evaluate toolResult content in tool-use workloads, so untrusted partner text needs a separate check.
Correct answer
Block or mask PII found by DetectPiiEntities. Apply Bedrock Guardrails in Converse, and call ApplyGuardrail on partner tool text.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Comprehend can locate PII in the supported real-time text, and the application can block or mask that text before invocation. Bedrock Guardrails can evaluate model inputs and outputs, and ApplyGuardrail can validate untrusted tool text that normal tool-use guardrail evaluation does not cover.
Overall explanation
A strong safety design uses controls at more than one point in the request path. Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities can locate PII in supported real-time text and return offsets, types, and scores. The application must then use those results to block or mask sensitive text before it reaches the model.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can evaluate user inputs and model responses for configured policies such as content filters, denied topics, sensitive information filters, and word filters. In tool-use workloads, normal content filters do not evaluate toolResult, toolSpec, or model-generated tool-call arguments in toolUse.input. The independent ApplyGuardrail API lets a Lambda function validate untrusted tool text as INPUT or OUTPUT without invoking a foundation model.

Detect mode is useful for measuring false positives and false negatives before enforcement. It is not enough when the requirement is to reduce harmful content and PII disclosure during live use.

For the documented behavior, see DetectPiiEntities, Personally identifiable information, How Amazon Bedrock Guardrails works, Content filters, and Use the ApplyGuardrail API.

Question 64
Skipped
An insurance company uses Amazon Bedrock to answer English policy questions in an employee portal. The team tested two text models from the same model family. The smaller model works for routine questions, but the larger model gives better answers for complex questions. The company wants to reduce inference cost, keep a single invocation target, and avoid maintaining custom routing logic.

Which approach should the company use?

Create a cross-Region inference profile for the larger model. Route traffic through the profile to increase regional capacity.
Explanation
Incorrect. A cross-Region inference profile routes requests across supported Regions for a model. It does not choose between smaller and larger models based on prompt complexity.
Correct answer
Create a configured Amazon Bedrock prompt router with the two same-family models. Set the larger model as the fallback model.
Explanation
Correct. A configured prompt router can route requests between two models in the same model family. Setting the larger model as the fallback supports quality when the router does not choose the smaller model.
Create an application inference profile for both models. Use the profile identifier to route simple prompts to the smaller model.
Explanation
Incorrect. An application inference profile tracks usage and costs for a model in one or more Regions. It is not a prompt router and does not make model selection decisions.
Create a Lambda function that classifies prompts using recent application metrics. Invoke the selected Bedrock model from the function.
Explanation
Incorrect. A custom Lambda router could be built, but it adds routing code and maintenance. The scenario asks to avoid custom routing logic and keep the design operationally simple.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing is designed for this kind of cost and quality tradeoff. It gives the application one serverless invocation target and routes each request between models in the same model family. A configured router lets the team choose the models and define a fallback model. The routing criteria compare expected response quality relative to the fallback model.

Cross-Region inference profiles solve a different problem. They can route requests from a source Region to destination Regions that are part of the profile. They help with regional inference routing, not with choosing between models for routine and complex prompts. Application inference profiles also solve a different problem because they track cost and usage.

A custom Lambda router is a valid engineering pattern when the team needs application-specific decision logic. It has more operational work than the managed Bedrock routing feature. The Bedrock documentation also notes that prompt routing is optimized for English prompts and does not adjust decisions from application-specific performance data. For this scenario, those limits fit the stated workload and constraints.

For more information, see Intelligent prompt routing in Amazon Bedrock, Use inference profiles in Amazon Bedrock, and Supported Regions and models for cross-Region inference.

Users upload résumés through Amazon API Gateway, and an AWS Lambda function stores each file in Amazon S3 before calling an Amazon Bedrock foundation model. The company also must mask any missed PII in responses and delete uploaded files after 30 days.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Invoke Bedrock with the uploaded text and enable a Bedrock guardrail for PII masking. Store the response in S3, and expire S3 objects after 30 days.
Explanation
Incorrect. Amazon Bedrock guardrails can evaluate prompts and responses for sensitive information. However, this approach still sends the raw uploaded text to Amazon Bedrock, which violates the stated internal policy.

Explanation
Incorrect. Post-processing can reduce PII exposure in responses, but it does not protect the request sent to Amazon Bedrock. Macie alerts can support governance over S3 data, but alerts do not redact prompts.
Correct answer
Call Amazon Comprehend from Lambda to redact PII before invoking Bedrock. Attach a Bedrock guardrail for PII masking, and expire S3 objects after 30 days.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Comprehend can detect PII in text before Lambda sends the request to Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock guardrails can add response-side PII masking, and S3 Lifecycle expiration can enforce the 30-day retention rule.
Overall explanation
The deciding point is where the organization requires redaction to happen. Amazon Comprehend can detect PII entities in text, so the Lambda function can replace sensitive values before it sends any request to Amazon Bedrock.

Amazon Bedrock guardrails can apply sensitive information filters to both user inputs and model responses. In this scenario, guardrails are still useful as defense in depth for missed PII in responses. They do not satisfy the policy by themselves because the raw prompt would still be sent to the Amazon Bedrock service.

Amazon Macie is a governance service for discovering sensitive data in Amazon S3. It is not designed as a low-latency inline redaction step for every model request. S3 Lifecycle rules are the managed way to expire uploaded files after the required retention period.

Question 66
Skipped
A pharmaceutical company is building an Amazon Bedrock assistant for adverse-event intake. The application uses the Converse API with tool use to retrieve case notes from an internal system. Compliance requires runtime filtering for toxic or violent language in user text, retrieved note text, and final responses. The team does not want to replace the model or build a custom classifier.

Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Run Bedrock model evaluation jobs for toxicity before release, and allow production calls only from approved prompts.
Explanation
Incorrect. Model evaluations can help assess behavior before deployment, but they do not provide runtime blocking for new user text or retrieved note text. Approved prompts also do not control harmful content that arrives from tools at runtime.
Correct answer
Attach the guardrail to each Converse call, and call ApplyGuardrail on tool-returned note text before reusing it.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can filter user inputs and model text responses during supported inference. The ApplyGuardrail API can also evaluate text independently, which covers retrieved note text before the application sends it back to the model.
Use word filters for the prohibited terms, and add denied topics for each harmful-content policy category.
Explanation
Incorrect. Word filters are exact-match filters, so they are not a complete safety framework for toxic or violent language. Denied topics can help with specific subjects, but they do not replace content filters for broad harmful-content categories.
Attach the guardrail only to each Converse call, and pass tool-returned note text through the normal toolResult field.
Explanation
Incorrect. Guardrail content filters evaluate user messages, system prompts, and model text responses. In tool-use workloads, content filters do not evaluate toolResult fields, so retrieved note text can be outside the guardrail evaluation path.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are designed for runtime safeguards on model inputs and model responses. They include content filters for categories such as Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, Misconduct, and Prompt Attack. See Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

Tool-use applications need extra care. Guardrail content filters evaluate user messages, system prompts, and model text responses, but they do not evaluate toolResult, toolSpec, or model-generated tool call arguments in toolUse.input. The best design applies the guardrail to the model call and also uses ApplyGuardrail to check retrieved text before the application gives that text back to the model. See Content filters.

ApplyGuardrail is useful because it can evaluate content without invoking a foundation model. That makes it a good fit for screening text from tools, search results, or other application components. Word filters and denied topics can be part of a policy, but they are not enough for broad runtime moderation of toxic or violent language.

Question 67
Skipped
A medical device manufacturer uses Amazon Bedrock to draft service bulletins from technician notes. Regulations require a certified engineer to approve or reject each draft before publication. Reviewers use an existing internal web portal that can call an HTTPS endpoint when a reviewer acts. The portal already writes each decision to DynamoDB for analysis. The company wants orchestration to wait for the reviewer without polling.

Which implementation will meet these requirements with the least custom orchestration?

Correct answer
Orchestrate the workflow in AWS Step Functions with a callback task token. Use API Gateway and Lambda to submit the reviewer decision.
Explanation
Correct. The callback pattern lets a Step Functions task pause until an external system returns the task token. API Gateway and Lambda provide a managed HTTPS path from the review portal back to the workflow.
Publish each review event to EventBridge and process approvals with Lambda. Use DynamoDB status records to resume publication logic.
Explanation
Incorrect. This design can support asynchronous approval events, but it requires custom state management for approval and publication. It does not provide the managed wait and resume behavior that Step Functions callbacks provide.
Start a second Step Functions workflow from the portal decision. Use DynamoDB records to correlate the approval with the draft.
Explanation
Incorrect. This design is event driven, but it splits the review process across workflows. It requires custom correlation logic and does not preserve the approval wait inside one managed workflow state.
Expose the draft through API Gateway and invoke Amazon Bedrock from Lambda. Store approval feedback after the response returns to the portal.
Explanation
Incorrect. This design collects feedback but does not provide a managed workflow that waits for approval before publication. Long human review steps do not fit a single synchronous API and Lambda request path.
Overall explanation
Human augmentation patterns separate model work from human judgment. In this scenario, Amazon Bedrock can create the draft, but publication must wait for a certified engineer. AWS Step Functions supports this with the callback task token pattern. The workflow pauses at a task and resumes only when an external system returns the token by calling SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure.

API Gateway is a good front door for the existing review portal. Lambda can validate the request and call the Step Functions API. This avoids polling and keeps the workflow state in a managed service. A separate workflow, EventBridge plus Lambda, or a direct synchronous API design can be useful in other workloads, but each adds custom coordination or cannot hold a long human review step cleanly. See the AWS documentation for Service integration patterns in Step Functions and the tutorial for creating a human approval workflow.

Question 68
Skipped
A logistics company is building a GenAI control tower assistant. Browser users ask long operational questions. The assistant must start returning tokens quickly, and some responses can exceed 10 MB. The team does not need request streaming or response mapping templates.

Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Use a REST API with Lambda proxy integration in STREAM mode. Have Lambda use ConverseStream and log integrationLatency for first-token alarms.
Explanation
Incorrect. This uses the right API Gateway and Bedrock streaming path. However, for streamed integrations, integrationLatency measures until the response stream is complete, so it is not the correct time-to-first-content signal.
Use a REST API with Lambda proxy integration in STREAM mode. Have Lambda use InvokeModelWithResponseStream and log timeToFirstContent.
Explanation
Incorrect. This can stream Bedrock output through a supported API Gateway pattern. However, InvokeModelWithResponseStream uses a model-specific request body, which does not meet the requirement for one message-based request format across chat models.
Correct answer
Use a REST API with Lambda proxy integration in STREAM mode. Have Lambda use ConverseStream and log timeToFirstContent.
Explanation
Correct. API Gateway response streaming is supported for REST APIs with proxy integrations when the response transfer mode is STREAM. ConverseStream provides a consistent messages-style API across supported Bedrock models, and API Gateway provides a time-to-first-content access log variable for streamed responses.
Use a REST API with Lambda proxy integration in STREAM mode. Have Lambda use ConverseStream and enable endpoint caching.
Explanation
Incorrect. This uses the required REST API and Lambda proxy integration pattern. However, API Gateway endpoint caching is not supported when response streaming is enabled because caching requires full response buffering.
Overall explanation
For this GenAI API, API Gateway response streaming fits the need to reduce time to first content and handle responses larger than the normal buffered payload limit. AWS documents response streaming for REST APIs with HTTP_PROXY or AWS_PROXY integrations. For the Lambda proxy integration in this scenario, the integration must use responseTransferMode set to STREAM. See Set up response streaming for REST APIs in API Gateway.

Lambda also needs a streaming-enabled handler path. For Node.js managed runtimes, the handler uses awslambda.streamifyResponse() and writes to a writable response stream. Lambda function URLs have their own RESPONSE_STREAM mode, but that changes the integration pattern. Endpoint caching is not available for streamed API Gateway integrations because caching requires full response buffering.

On the Bedrock side, ConverseStream is the best fit when the application needs one messages-style interface across supported Bedrock models. InvokeModelWithResponseStream also streams, but it uses a model-specific request body. For either streaming API, the team should call GetFoundationModel and check responseStreamingSupported. See InvokeModelWithResponseStream.

For observability, API Gateway has separate variables for streamed integrations. $context.integration.timeToFirstContent measures when content first starts returning. $context.integration.latency or $context.integrationLatency measures until the stream is complete, so it is not a first-token metric. See Troubleshoot response streaming for REST APIs in API Gateway.

Converse is still flexible. The middleware can pass common inference fields through the standard request shape and can include model-specific inference parameters when a model needs them. That is useful when an enterprise integration must hide most model differences but cannot remove all model-specific controls.

Calling Converse on the control-plane endpoint fails because Converse is a runtime operation. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can use the RetrieveAndGenerate operation. The response structure includes citation information for generated output. See the official RetrieveAndGenerate API Reference.

For operational transparency, the application should publish its own confidence and grounding scores as CloudWatch custom metrics. CloudWatch metrics are designed for dashboards, alarms, and trend analysis. The AWS documentation explains how applications publish metrics with PutMetricData in Publish custom metrics.

CloudWatch Logs and metric filters can be useful when values exist only in logs, but the scenario says the application already computes the scores. Agent traces help inspect agent behavior, but they add an agent workflow and do not replace direct score metrics. Generated source summaries can add explanation text, but service citations provide a more direct link to retrieved evidence.

Explanation
Incorrect. On-demand evaluations are useful for selected spans or traces. The scenario needs recurring offline evaluation across many labeled sessions with built-in aggregate and per-session results.
Correct answer
Run Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations as a batch job from CloudWatch Logs with session-level goal and trajectory evaluators.
Explanation
Correct. Batch evaluations run asynchronously across multiple sessions from a CloudWatch Logs location. Session-level goal and trajectory evaluators match the need to score expected outcomes and expected tool sequences.

Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations assesses agent and tool performance by using telemetry and traces. It can evaluate agents that run in AgentCore Runtime and agents that run outside AgentCore. The service uses conversation content, model prompts, model completions, tool inputs, and tool outputs to reconstruct sessions.

The decisive requirement is the need for recurring offline reports across many labeled sessions. Batch evaluation runs asynchronously over multiple sessions from a CloudWatch Logs location. It returns aggregate and per-session results, which fits a held-out evaluation set. See Evaluation types for AgentCore Evaluations.

Session-level evaluators are the right granularity for this workload. The documented ground-truth mappings include Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with session-level assertions and trajectory evaluators with expectedTrajectory. Trajectory evaluators can check whether the agent used the expected tools in an exact order, in order with extra tools, or in any order. See Ground truth evaluations.

Trace-level correctness and tool-call evaluations can be useful for narrower questions. They do not match the labeled session set when the team must score both outcomes and tool sequences. On-demand evaluation is useful for targeted investigation, but batch evaluation better fits recurring offline reporting at scale. See Create an evaluator.

Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging is the right audit source for supported runtime calls such as Converse. CloudWatch metrics and alarms are still useful for operations. The AWS/Bedrock namespace includes invocation volume, latency, token counts, errors, throttles, and log delivery metrics. Metrics do not provide prompt and response records or guardrail evaluation audit events. See Monitor Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics.

A logistics company is building an AI assistant for shipment exception handling. Operations analysts must change the prompt sequence and routing logic every week. The analysts are not developers. Which approach will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Create an Amazon Bedrock Flow with prompt nodes and conditional connections. Invoke the flow from the web application.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock Flows provides a visual interface for editing workflow nodes and connections. The web application can invoke the flow without embedding the workflow logic in custom application code.

Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Flows is designed for multi-step generative AI workflows. A flow uses nodes and connections to define how data moves through prompts, models, conditions, and other supported components. This provides a visual interface for editing workflow nodes and connections, while developers can still invoke the finished flow from an application.

An OpenAPI contract with API Gateway is useful for API-first integration. It does not solve visual maintenance for prompt routing if the logic remains in Lambda. AWS Amplify is useful for fast front-end development, but client-side workflow logic is harder to govern and update safely. AWS Step Functions can orchestrate workflows, but it adds more custom integration work for prompt-specific logic.
