Which approach should the developer implement?

Correct answer
Configure an OpenSearch remote-inference connector in the search account to assume an AI account role. Grant the role bedrock:InvokeModel.
Explanation
Correct. The OpenSearch domain can keep ownership of the indexed wiki data and call a remote Bedrock embedding model. The role that the connector uses must have permission to invoke the model in the account that controls Bedrock access.
Create a Bedrock Knowledge Base in the AI account. Use an OpenSearch Serverless collection there as the vector store for the existing wiki index.
Explanation
Incorrect. A Bedrock Knowledge Base is a good managed choice when it owns ingestion into a supported vector store. This approach creates a second vector store instead of using the existing OpenSearch Service domain in the search account.
Create an OpenSearch remote-inference connector in the AI account. Grant it cross-account read access to the search domain for neural search workflows.

Explanation
Incorrect. OpenSearch can use external embedding endpoints, so this is a plausible design in other cases. This approach does not use Amazon Bedrock embedding models and adds model-hosting operations.
Overall explanation
For semantic search with OpenSearch, the retrieval workflow belongs close to the OpenSearch index. OpenSearch can use a remote-inference connector to call an embedding model, including an Amazon Bedrock model. This lets OpenSearch generate embeddings during ingestion or query processing without moving document content to a new vector store.

In this scenario, the search account owns the wiki index and the AI account owns Bedrock model access. A cross-account connector preserves both boundaries. The IAM role used by the connector needs permission such as bedrock:InvokeModel on the target model.

A Bedrock Knowledge Base is useful when the managed service ingests sources into a supported vector store. It is not the best fit when the application must use an existing OpenSearch Service domain and avoid a second vector store. A SageMaker endpoint could provide embeddings, but it does not meet the stated requirement to use Bedrock embedding models.

Overall explanation
For Amazon Bedrock native inference, IAM permissions are tied to the underlying inference action. The Converse API requires bedrock:InvokeModel. The ConverseStream API requires bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream.

The secure design is to grant bedrock:InvokeModel only on the approved model ARNs. That allows the non-streaming application path and keeps model selection under IAM control. Not granting bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream prevents streaming inference through ConverseStream and InvokeModelWithResponseStream.

Question 56
Skipped
An insurance carrier uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon S3 data source for policy documents. The documents are PDFs. Compliance labels and access-control attributes change several times per day, but the PDF text changes only monthly. The search assistant must reflect label changes quickly. The team wants to minimize reprocessing of unchanged content.

Which maintenance design will meet these requirements with the LEAST reprocessing?

Rewrite the PDF files with updated metadata fields, keep the same S3 keys, and run a Knowledge Bases data source sync.
Explanation
Incorrect. Changing the content files causes Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to treat the documents as changed content. Changed content is re-parsed, re-chunked, re-embedded, and re-indexed during sync.
Convert each PDF to CSV with adjacent metadata files, update the metadata files, and run a Knowledge Bases data source sync.
Explanation
Incorrect. CSV files are always re-ingested when their metadata files change. This would not use the metadata-only optimization that can apply to non-CSV content files.
Correct answer
Update the PDF .metadata.json files, omit a custom transformation Lambda, and run a Knowledge Bases data source sync.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can optimize a sync when only .metadata.json files change for non-CSV content. This approach updates retrieval metadata without forcing the PDF content to be parsed, chunked, embedded, and indexed again.
Attach a custom transformation Lambda to enrich chunk metadata, update the metadata files, and run a Knowledge Bases sync.
Explanation
Incorrect. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases cannot use the metadata-only optimization when a custom transformation Lambda is used. This adds flexibility, but it does not minimize reprocessing for metadata-only changes.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases data source sync is change-based. A sync processes documents that were added, changed, or deleted since the last sync. Unchanged documents are skipped, and deleted documents are removed from the vector store.

For S3 data sources, Bedrock can use a metadata-only optimization in a narrow case. Only the .metadata.json files must change. The associated content files must not be CSV files, and the data source must not use a custom transformation Lambda.

This design fits the scenario because the PDFs stay unchanged, while compliance labels and access attributes change often. Updating only the metadata files and running a sync keeps retrieval filters current with less embedding work.

Rewriting the PDFs changes the content files, so Bedrock must process the documents again. Converting to CSV removes the optimization benefit because CSV content is always re-ingested when metadata changes. A custom transformation Lambda also prevents the metadata-only optimization. For details, see Sync to ingest your data sources into your knowledge base.

A logistics company is building a RAG assistant with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The source content is unstructured customs guidance stored in Amazon S3. The current configuration retrieves short passages that match the query, but responses often miss nearby exceptions in the same section. The company wants better context without building a custom preprocessing pipeline.

Which approach should the developer use?

Correct answer
Configure hierarchical chunking with smaller child chunks and broader parent chunks in the knowledge base.
Explanation
Correct. Hierarchical chunking lets Bedrock retrieve precise child chunks first and then use the broader parent chunks for context. This improves answers that need nearby supporting text without requiring a custom chunking pipeline.
Configure semantic chunking with an FM and return the original chunk boundaries from the knowledge base.
Explanation
Incorrect. Semantic chunking can improve boundaries by splitting content by meaning instead of fixed length. It does not retrieve smaller chunks and then replace them with broader parent chunks for added context.
Configure fixed-size chunking with larger chunks and a higher overlap percentage in the knowledge base.
Explanation
Incorrect. Larger fixed chunks can add context, but they also reduce retrieval precision and can include unrelated text. Higher overlap can help at boundaries, but it does not provide parent-child retrieval behavior.
Configure no chunking and store each full document as one chunk with document-level metadata filters.
Explanation
Incorrect. Storing each full document as one chunk can provide context, but it makes retrieval less precise for clause-level questions. Metadata filters can narrow documents, but they do not solve the need for precise retrieval plus broader local context.
Overall explanation
Hierarchical chunking is designed for cases where the application needs both precise retrieval and enough surrounding context. Amazon Bedrock first retrieves smaller child chunks. It then replaces those child chunks with their broader parent chunks before the response generation step.

This design is different from simply making every chunk larger. Larger fixed chunks can include more context, but they can also reduce the quality of semantic matching. Hierarchical chunking keeps the search focused on smaller units while giving the model a larger passage to read.

Bedrock Knowledge Bases uses embeddings and a vector store for unstructured sources such as Amazon S3. For chunking behavior, see Chunking options for Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases. For how unstructured data sources are embedded for retrieval, see Data sources for Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock.

SageMaker Model Cards provide a managed place to document governance information for model deployments. A model card can include intended use, risk rating, training details, evaluation results, observations, considerations, recommendations, and custom information. See Amazon SageMaker Model Cards.

The important design point is how versioning works. Edits to a model card create additional versions, except for approval-status updates. That makes the model card content the right place for release evidence, and the approval status the right place for review workflow movement.

Exporting a model card to PDF is useful for sharing or audit packages, but it should not replace the managed model card record. Tags can support attribution, but tags are not a substitute for structured model governance documentation.

Use a SageMaker batch transform job that starts on a fixed schedule and reads pending S3 objects.

The service accepts requests, stores inputs in Amazon S3, queues the work, and writes outputs to Amazon S3. This pattern is useful for large payloads, long processing times, and bursty traffic.

For this scenario, the important resource allocation point is scaling on queue pressure, not on simple request count. SageMaker provides backlog metrics such as ApproximateBacklogSizePerInstance. For scale from zero, the HasBacklogWithoutCapacity metric can help start capacity when requests are waiting. See Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference and Automatically scale an asynchronous endpoint.

A real-time endpoint is optimized for synchronous low-latency inference, but it usually keeps capacity available. Batch transform is strong for planned offline jobs, but it is less responsive to ad hoc request bursts. Serverless Inference reduces idle management for some models, but it is not the right choice for a GPU-required FM workload.

AWS WA Tool uses lenses to measure a workload against best practices. Which combination of actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

Create an OpenSearch Serverless vector collection. Use Lambda to ingest PDF chunks and run filtered vector queries.
Explanation
Incorrect. OpenSearch Serverless vector collections can support semantic vector search. This approach still requires custom ingestion and retrieval logic, which adds operational overhead compared with a managed knowledge base.
Configure an OpenSearch Service domain with the neural plugin. Build pipelines that call Bedrock for embeddings and queries.
Explanation
Incorrect. The OpenSearch neural plugin can integrate embedding generation into OpenSearch workflows. However, managing an OpenSearch Service domain and custom pipelines creates more operational work than the stated requirement allows.
Correct selection
Create an Amazon Bedrock managed knowledge base from the S3 documents. Use a supported embedding model.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock managed knowledge bases reduce the work needed to build and operate RAG retrieval. Bedrock manages the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval infrastructure for the knowledge base.
Build an Aurora PostgreSQL pgvector table. Use Lambda to chunk documents, create embeddings, and run filtered similarity queries.

Add site, product, and document type metadata. Apply metadata filters in knowledge base retrieval calls.
Explanation
Correct. Metadata filters help restrict retrieved chunks before the model receives context. This supports the requirement to keep retrieval within the user’s site and product line.

Amazon Bedrock managed knowledge bases are designed to reduce the work needed to build RAG applications. Bedrock manages the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval infrastructure. The team still selects a data source and a supported embedding model. See Knowledge bases for Amazon Bedrock.

Metadata filters are also important because the assistant must retrieve only content for the user’s site and product line. The application should pass those filters during retrieval, so unrelated chunks are not added to the prompt context.

Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, OpenSearch Service with the neural plugin, and OpenSearch Serverless vector collections can support semantic vector retrieval. A health benefits company uses a standard Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for a member benefits assistant. The application currently invokes a foundation model after custom code selects policy snippets. Auditors now require each response to include source evidence that reviewers can check before release. The team wants to minimize custom orchestration and must not treat retrieval relevance as proof of factual accuracy.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

Migrate the content to a managed knowledge base. Call Retrieve with managedSearchConfiguration and generate citations in code.
Explanation
Incorrect. Managed knowledge bases use different retrieval configuration semantics and do not require this existing standard knowledge base to be migrated. This approach adds migration work and custom citation generation.
Correct answer
Call RetrieveAndGenerate for the knowledge base. Return the generated answer with its citations to source chunks.
Explanation
Correct. RetrieveAndGenerate combines retrieval from the knowledge base with model generation. The response includes citations to specific source chunks, which supports review of the answer against evidence.
Call Retrieve for the knowledge base. Apply Guardrails contextual grounding with the returned chunks as references.
Explanation
Incorrect. Contextual grounding can help detect whether a response aligns with provided reference content. This approach still needs custom orchestration and does not provide the built-in generated answer with citations.
Call Retrieve for the knowledge base. Invoke the model with returned chunks and store chunk identifiers as citations.
Explanation
Incorrect. Retrieve can return relevant source chunks that an application can pass to a model. This approach requires custom generation and citation handling, so it does not minimize custom orchestration.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases has two separate paths. Retrieve returns relevant source chunks or images, while RetrieveAndGenerate performs retrieval and model generation and includes citations to source chunks, as described in Query a knowledge base and generate responses.

That built-in path fits a standard knowledge base when reviewers need evidence and the team wants less custom orchestration. A retrieval score can help rank chunks, but the KnowledgeBaseRetrievalResult API reference describes it as relevance to the query, not factuality.

Retrieve plus a custom verification step or Guardrails contextual grounding can be useful when an application needs more control over verification. Those approaches still require application code to invoke the model, attach evidence, or interpret grounding results.

Managed knowledge bases use different retrieval configuration semantics, and the RetrieveAndGenerate API reference states that the operation cannot be used with managed knowledge bases. Migrating an existing standard knowledge base would add work without meeting the stated need more directly; see Test retrieval from a managed knowledge base.

AWS CDK stacks are promoted by CodePipeline. The applications run in several VPCs. Security requires that calls to the gateway and to Bedrock Runtime do not use public internet paths. Security also requires endpoint-based access control for approved application VPC endpoints.

Which gateway design should the developer deploy?

Expose a private API Gateway REST API. Allow any execute-api VPC endpoint and call Bedrock Runtime through an interface endpoint.
Explanation
Incorrect. This design keeps the gateway and model invocation paths private. It does not meet the endpoint-based access control requirement because it does not restrict invocation to approved application VPC endpoints.
Expose an internal Application Load Balancer to the proxy. Share the ALB through application VPC routing and call Bedrock Runtime through an interface endpoint.
Explanation
Incorrect. This design can keep traffic on private network paths when the routing is configured correctly. It does not provide the requested endpoint-based access control with approved execute-api VPC endpoints for a centralized API gateway.
Correct answer
Expose a private API Gateway REST API. Allow approved execute-api VPC endpoints and call Bedrock Runtime through an interface endpoint.
Explanation
Correct. A private REST API in API Gateway is reachable through interface VPC endpoints for API Gateway. A resource policy can restrict access to approved VPC endpoint IDs, and a Bedrock Runtime interface endpoint keeps model invocation traffic on AWS PrivateLink.
Expose a private API Gateway REST API. Allow approved execute-api VPC endpoints and run the Lambda proxy only in private subnets.
Explanation
Incorrect. Private subnets do not create private connectivity to Amazon Bedrock Runtime by themselves. The Lambda proxy still needs a Bedrock Runtime interface endpoint to invoke the model without a public service path.
Overall explanation
A private enterprise GenAI gateway must control both ingress and egress. For ingress, a private API Gateway REST API is invoked through interface VPC endpoints for execute-api. A resource policy can restrict calls to approved VPC endpoint IDs, VPCs, accounts, or other supported conditions. See Private REST APIs in API Gateway.

For egress to Amazon Bedrock, the Lambda proxy should use an interface VPC endpoint for Bedrock Runtime. This uses AWS PrivateLink and avoids sending model invocation traffic to public service endpoints. Placing Lambda in private subnets is not enough by itself. The VPC still needs a private path to the AWS service. See Use Amazon Bedrock with interface VPC endpoints.

Internal load balancers, VPC routing, and private backends are useful in many enterprise systems. They do not match this requirement as closely as a private API Gateway design with approved execute-api endpoints. CodePipeline and AWS CDK can promote the same gateway pattern across environments while automated checks verify resource policies, endpoint configuration, and Bedrock Runtime access before release.

Question 66
Skipped
A manufacturing company already operates a production workflow on Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic. The workflow uses multi-agent collaboration and action groups to answer parts inventory questions. Operators see intermittent slowdowns and tool failures. The final answer text does not show which collaborator or action group caused each issue. The company wants per-request observability with minimal changes to the agent design.

Which approach should the company use?

Instrument each action group target to emit CloudWatch metrics with session and invocation IDs.
Explanation
Incorrect. Custom metrics can help show tool-level latency and errors for action group targets. This approach requires more changes and does not provide the built-in multi-agent trace path with callerChain and collaboratorName.
Correct answer
Set enableTrace to true on InvokeAgent requests. Store trace data for callerChain, collaboratorName, and action group events.
Explanation
Correct. InvokeAgent supports trace data when enableTrace is set to true for the request. The trace can show agent reasoning, actions, failure details, and multi-agent coordination fields such as callerChain and collaboratorName.
Enable model invocation logging for bedrock-runtime calls. Analyze operation, modelId, requestMetadata, and token count fields.
Explanation
Incorrect. Model invocation logging is useful for supported bedrock-runtime calls such as Converse and InvokeModel. It does not provide the structured trace for an agent-runtime InvokeAgent request or show the action group path.
Parse InvokeAgent response chunks and action group logs. Correlate final text with Lambda request IDs and timestamps.
Explanation
Incorrect. InvokeAgent response chunks provide the generated response content, but they do not replace trace data. Correlating logs by time and request IDs adds operational work and does not show the built-in multi-agent path.
Overall explanation
For an existing Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic workload, the most useful telemetry is the agent trace for the specific request. The InvokeAgent API can include trace data when the request sets enableTrace to true, and the response can include chunk and trace attributes. Trace data can show actions, processed information, failure reasons, and multi-agent coordination details such as callerChain and collaboratorName. See InvokeAgent.

Model invocation logging is a different mechanism for documented bedrock-runtime calls. It records model-level fields such as operation, model ID, identity, request metadata, and token counts. It does not replace agent tracing for an InvokeAgent path; see Log model invocation data. Parsing response chunks or action group logs can add partial evidence, but it does not give the built-in trace path for collaborator handoffs. The practical framework is to use agent traces for tool and collaborator behavior, and runtime invocation logs for model-level usage signals.

Question 67
Skipped
A media archive company is building a RAG search service for transcripts and captions. The embedding model produces 12,288-dimension vectors. Search requests must combine semantic similarity with keyword terms and nested rights metadata. New documents must be searchable within 30 seconds. The team wants to minimize index-engine tuning and shard management.

Which TWO architecture choices meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Create a Classic Serverless vector collection and rely on its default refresh interval for new documents.
Explanation
Incorrect. Classic Serverless vector collections can be suitable for some vector search workloads. In this scenario, the documented 60-second refresh interval does not meet the 30-second freshness requirement.
Correct selection
Create an OpenSearch Serverless NextGen vector search collection for the embedding indexes.
Explanation
Correct. OpenSearch Serverless vector collections can support vectors with up to 16,000 dimensions. NextGen vector collections also have a 10-second refresh latency, which meets the freshness requirement.
Create a managed OpenSearch Service domain with knn_vector fields and tune primary shards for low-latency search.
Explanation
Incorrect. This is a valid design pattern for many managed-domain k-NN workloads. In this scenario, the 12,288-dimension embeddings exceed the documented 10,000-float limit for managed-domain knn_vector fields.
Correct selection
Run vector retrieval with full-text clauses and nested rights filters in the same Serverless vector collection.
Explanation
Correct. OpenSearch Serverless vector search supports full-text search, filtering, and nested queries alongside vector retrieval. This meets the requirement to combine semantic search with keyword terms and nested rights metadata.
Create separate managed k-NN indexes for transcripts, captions, and rights metadata with application-side result merging.
Explanation
Incorrect. Separate indexes can be useful when domains need different tuning or isolation. In this scenario, this approach adds result-merging logic and does not avoid the managed-domain vector dimension constraint.
Overall explanation
OpenSearch has two related but different paths for vector search. A managed OpenSearch Service domain uses k-NN indexes that require index.knn: true and a knn_vector field. AWS documents knn_vector in managed domains as supporting a single list of up to 10,000 floats, as described in k-nearest neighbor search in Amazon OpenSearch Service.

OpenSearch Serverless vector search collections are a better match for this scenario. AWS documents support for up to 16,000 dimensions, plus Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, and dot product similarity. The same collection type also supports full-text search, filtering, aggregations, geospatial queries, and nested queries alongside vector retrieval. See Vector search collections in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.

The generation of the Serverless vector collection also matters. NextGen vector collections have a documented 10-second refresh_interval, while Classic vector collections have a 60-second interval. NextGen collections also simplify mappings by not requiring engine or mode parameters, which fits a requirement to reduce engine tuning.

Question 68
Skipped
A travel company is building an assistant that reviews refund disputes. Each high-risk dispute must receive independent risk scores from three specialized Amazon Bedrock prompts. The company must combine the scores by using business weights and deterministic tie rules. The workflow must keep a durable execution history for each dispute and avoid custom code for orchestration.

Which TWO actions should the company take? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Use a Step Functions Standard workflow with a Parallel state for the prompt calls.
Explanation
Correct. A Step Functions Standard workflow provides durable workflow execution history. A Parallel state can run the independent prompt branches at the same time and then continue after all branches finish.
Build a Lambda fan-out coordinator that invokes all prompts and aggregates scores in one function.
Explanation
Incorrect. A Lambda-only coordinator could invoke multiple prompts and apply scoring logic. However, it puts orchestration, retries, and branch tracking into custom code instead of using a durable workflow service.
Use an agent orchestrator with three tool calls and a synthesis prompt for the final score.
Explanation
Incorrect. An agent can plan tool use and combine information from multiple calls. A synthesis prompt is not the best fit for deterministic weighted voting and auditable tie rules.
Coordinate the prompt calls in Bedrock Flows and route branches with Flow conditions.
Explanation
Incorrect. Bedrock Flows can coordinate generative AI steps, prompts, and conditions. The scenario needs durable workflow orchestration and deterministic aggregation, which fits Step Functions and Lambda more directly.
Correct selection
Add a Lambda task that applies weighted voting and tie rules to the model outputs.
Explanation
Correct. Lambda is a good fit for deterministic aggregation after the model calls finish. The function can apply business weights and tie rules without training a new model.
Overall explanation
The scenario calls for a runtime ensemble with independent model judgments. A Step Functions Parallel state is designed for fan-out and fan-in workflows. In a Standard workflow, Step Functions also keeps a durable execution history. That history helps the company inspect which branch ran and what happened for each high-risk dispute.

The weighted vote belongs in deterministic application logic. AWS Lambda can apply business weights, handle ties, and return one final decision. This keeps the aggregation rule explicit and auditable. It also avoids training or fine-tuning a separate model only to implement a policy rule.

Bedrock Flows is useful for chaining prompts, models, and conditional logic in generative AI workflows. It is less direct here because the scenario emphasizes durable workflow orchestration and deterministic scoring. A Lambda-only fan-out can work for simple cases, but it moves orchestration and retry behavior into custom code. An agent orchestrator can choose tools and synthesize results, but a synthesis prompt is not the right control point for fixed voting rules. See AWS Step Functions Parallel state, Standard and Express workflows, What is AWS Lambda?, and Amazon Bedrock Flows.

The team needs to monitor a sampled subset of live traffic, score tool choice and parameter quality, and apply a company-specific safety rubric. Live requests do not include reference answers.

Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Create a custom TOOL_CALL evaluator without ground-truth placeholders by using Lambda or an LLM-as-a-judge rubric.
Explanation
Correct. A TOOL_CALL evaluator can score tool selection and parameter quality at the right level of detail. A custom evaluator can implement a company-specific rubric by using Lambda code or an LLM-as-a-judge configuration.
Create a custom online evaluator that uses ground-truth placeholders for expected responses and tool trajectories.
Explanation
Incorrect. Custom evaluators that use ground-truth placeholders cannot be used in online evaluation configurations. Online evaluations process live production traffic, where ground-truth values are not available.
Run a batch evaluation from CloudWatch Logs with expected trajectories and compare aggregate results after traffic is stored.
Explanation
Incorrect. Batch evaluation is useful for offline analysis across stored sessions. The scenario requires sampled live monitoring and states that live requests do not include reference answers.
Modify a built-in evaluator such as Builtin.Helpfulness by changing its model and prompt template for the safety rubric.
Explanation
Incorrect. Built-in evaluators can be used across evaluation types, but their evaluator model and prompt template configurations cannot be changed. A custom evaluator is needed for a company-specific safety rubric.
Correct selection
Configure an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations online evaluation with filters and a sampling rate for production traces.
Explanation
Correct. Online evaluations are designed to monitor live production traffic. Filters and sampling help control cost while still evaluating real agent behavior from telemetry.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations supports online, on-demand, and batch evaluation types. Online evaluation is the right fit when a team needs continuous monitoring of live production traffic with filters and sampling. The evaluation is based on agent telemetry and traces, not only the final response.

Tool quality should be measured at the TOOL_CALL level when the team needs to score tool choice and parameter quality. For a company-specific rubric, the team can create a custom evaluator. AWS supports LLM-as-a-judge evaluators and code-based evaluators that use an AWS Lambda function ARN.

Ground-truth values are not available for ordinary live requests. AWS therefore does not allow custom evaluators with ground-truth placeholders in online evaluation configurations. Built-in evaluators such as Builtin.Helpfulness are useful, but their model and prompt template settings are not editable.

For more information, see Evaluation types, Create evaluators, and Built-in evaluators overview.

Run nightly work as Bedrock batch inference jobs. Submit the jobs against the provisioned model ARN to reuse purchased capacity.
Explanation

Correct selection
Run nightly work as Bedrock batch inference jobs. Store JSONL input files in S3 with modelInput and a recordId for each request.
Explanation

Correct selection
Purchase Bedrock Provisioned Throughput for the real-time model. Pass the provisioned model ARN as modelId in Converse calls.

Use on-demand bedrock-runtime for the real-time assistant. Add a work queue, bounded concurrency, and retries for transient capacity errors.
Explanation

Overall explanation
The real-time workload and the overnight workload have different throughput needs. Provisioned Throughput is the better fit for the real-time assistant because it buys model-specific capacity measured in Model Units. The application must call the supported runtime API and pass the provisioned model ARN as modelId. Using the base model ID would use on-demand capacity instead. See Invoke a model with Provisioned Throughput and Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput.

The overnight workload can use Bedrock batch inference because it can wait for completion and does not need unsupported batch features such as tool calling or structured output using response_format. Batch inference reads JSONL input from Amazon S3. Each record includes modelInput, and adding recordId makes result matching reliable because output order is not guaranteed. See Run batch inference and Prepare data for batch inference.

On-demand runtime with queues and retries is useful, but it is not the same as reserved capacity. AWS documents that quotas are upper bounds, and on-demand requests can still receive transient capacity errors under high demand. The bedrock-mantle endpoint is also not appropriate here because batch inference and Provisioned Throughput are available only through bedrock-runtime. See Amazon Bedrock throughput best practices.

A telecommunications provider operates a field-support assistant by using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. The source documents mix prose troubleshooting steps with exact alarm IDs and router model numbers. Documents are indexed with product family and firmware version metadata, and the support session provides both values at query time. Vector-only retrieval often returns similar symptoms but misses the exact alarm ID. Raising retrieved chunks improves recall but exceeds the retrieval latency and context budget.

Which change should the developer make?

Keep SEMANTIC search and increase the number of retrieved results. Add a Bedrock reranker before generation.
Explanation
Incorrect. A reranker can improve the order of returned passages, but it cannot rank a passage that retrieval did not return. Increasing the result count also conflicts with the latency and context budget in the scenario.
Correct answer
Set the knowledge base retrieval to HYBRID search. Add metadata filters for product family and firmware version.
Explanation
Correct. Hybrid search combines semantic matching with keyword matching, which helps when queries contain exact identifiers. Metadata filters reduce the search space and help keep retrieval latency and context size under control.
Use only text search over alarm IDs and model numbers. Disable semantic retrieval for field-support queries.
Explanation
Incorrect. Text search is useful for exact IDs, but it loses the semantic matching needed for symptom descriptions and troubleshooting prose. The documents contain both exact terms and natural language, so a combined retrieval strategy fits better.
Keep SEMANTIC search and rebuild chunks around full procedures. Store fewer, larger chunks in the vector index.
Explanation
Incorrect. Larger chunks can preserve procedure context, but they usually add more tokens to the prompt. This does not address the exact alarm ID matching problem and can worsen the context budget issue.
Overall explanation
When a RAG corpus contains both natural language and exact identifiers, hybrid retrieval is often the best retrieval pattern. Semantic search finds passages with similar meaning. Keyword search finds literal terms such as alarm IDs, product codes, and model numbers. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can use a search type such as HYBRID when the underlying vector store supports it.

Metadata filters are useful when the fields are indexed and the values are known at query time. Filtering by product family and firmware version narrows the candidate set before the model receives context. This reduces irrelevant chunks and helps control token use. A reranker is useful after retrieval, but it cannot fix a retrieval step that failed to return the exact-ID passage. See Configure and customize queries and response generation and Vector search with Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.

Question 72
Skipped
A live sports company is adding a GenAI assistant for camera crews at stadiums. Operators connect over 5G from venues in several countries. Regulators require raw video frames and speaker identifiers to stay at a telecom edge location in the country. The company may send anonymized text metadata to an approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint in the parent AWS Region. Preprocessing must add less than 10 ms of network latency, and the company does not want to install hardware at venues.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

Deploy preprocessing services on AWS Outposts racks in in-country carrier colocation sites. Keep raw media on rack storage. Send anonymized metadata to Amazon Bedrock in the parent Region.
Explanation
Incorrect. AWS Outposts can support in-country processing and storage in a facility that the company controls or uses. It is not the best fit because the requirement focuses on 5G carrier-edge placement without deploying dedicated hardware for this workload.
Deploy preprocessing services on carrier-managed edge nodes in each country. Use Direct Connect and a VPC endpoint to send anonymized metadata to Amazon Bedrock.
Explanation
Incorrect. Carrier-managed edge compute can appear to satisfy residency and latency needs. It does not provide the managed AWS VPC extension at the 5G edge that Wavelength provides, and it adds custom platform integration work.
Correct answer
Deploy preprocessing services in AWS Wavelength Zones in each required country. Keep raw media in the Wavelength Zone. Send anonymized metadata to Amazon Bedrock.
Explanation
Correct. AWS Wavelength places AWS compute and storage services at the 5G carrier edge. This supports low-latency preprocessing near the operators while sending only approved metadata to a regional Bedrock endpoint.
Deploy preprocessing services in AWS Wavelength Zones in each country. Archive raw media to Outposts rack storage in carrier colocation. Send anonymized metadata to Amazon Bedrock.
Explanation
Incorrect. This approach uses Wavelength for the latency-sensitive preprocessing step. The extra Outposts storage tier adds hardware, cost, and operational work without improving the required FM access pattern.
Overall explanation
AWS Wavelength extends an Amazon VPC to the edge of a communications service provider network. It is designed for applications that need very low latency from 5G devices or users. You can run edge preprocessing on services such as Amazon EC2 in a Wavelength Zone, then use the parent Region for regional services.

In this scenario, the important split is between raw regulated data and approved derived data. Raw video frames and speaker identifiers stay at the telecom edge in the country. The application sends only anonymized text metadata to Amazon Bedrock in the approved parent Region. That pattern enables FM access without moving prohibited raw data into the Region.

AWS Outposts is a strong choice when a company needs AWS-managed infrastructure in its own data center or colocation facility. It is less suitable here because it requires dedicated hardware placement and does not automatically provide the same carrier 5G edge integration as Wavelength. A carrier-managed edge platform can also keep data close to users, but it adds custom integration and does not extend the AWS VPC into the carrier edge in the same managed way.

For more information, see What is AWS Wavelength?, What is AWS Outposts?, and What is Amazon Bedrock?.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 73
Skipped
A media company is building a script-analysis assistant. A Step Functions Standard workflow implements a ReAct loop. One Task calls an Amazon Bedrock model to choose the next action, and Lambda tools return observations to the loop. The workflow validates the client request before it starts. The workflow then builds the provider-specific InvokeModel Body from prompt templates and tool observations. The model request is about 40 KiB. During releases, malformed model-specific JSON in the InvokeModel payload causes runtime failures.

Which change should the developer make?

Correct answer
Add a Lambda validation task immediately before the optimized Bedrock InvokeModel task. Pass the checked request in Body.
Explanation
Correct. This validates the exact payload that the workflow built for the model call. Step Functions does not validate model-specific content inside Body, and the 40 KiB payload is small enough to use Body.
Run an AppConfig-controlled Lambda validator when the workflow starts. Validate the execution input against the release schema.
Explanation
Incorrect. AppConfig can help manage configuration such as schema versions. Validating only the execution input is too early because the workflow later assembles the model-specific request body.
Add Retry and Catch to the optimized Bedrock InvokeModel task. Send Bedrock invocation errors to a release rollback path.
Explanation
Incorrect. Retry and Catch can make failures easier to handle after the model invocation fails. They do not prevent malformed model-specific JSON from reaching the InvokeModel task.
Add an API Gateway request validator before StartExecution. Reject client requests that fail the public JSON schema.
Explanation
Incorrect. API Gateway request validation can protect the workflow input. The malformed payload is created later inside the workflow, so this does not validate the final InvokeModel Body.
Overall explanation
A ReAct workflow often repeats a pattern: call a model, inspect the model output, run a tool, and pass the observation into the next model call. Step Functions can call Amazon Bedrock by using the optimized InvokeModel integration, such as arn:aws:states:::bedrock:invokeModel.

The deciding detail is where the malformed JSON appears. The workflow builds the provider-specific Body after the client request is already validated. Therefore, validation must check the final request immediately before the Bedrock task.

Step Functions does not validate the model-specific content inside Body. A Lambda task can enforce the expected JSON structure and fail the workflow before the model invocation. The 40 KiB payload is also below the documented 256 KiB limit for Body, so the workflow does not need to use Input with an S3 URI for size reasons.

API Gateway validation and validation at workflow start are useful in other designs. They are not sufficient when the payload is changed later by prompt templates and tool observations. Retry and Catch are still useful for resiliency, but they handle errors after the call reaches Bedrock. For the documented integration behavior, see Call Amazon Bedrock with Step Functions.

Question 74
Skipped
A supply chain company uses Amazon Bedrock Prompt management for a purchasing assistant. An AWS Step Functions QA workflow runs edge-case prompts against each candidate prompt version. Each run calls a Lambda validator that checks the response contract and writes JSON results to CloudWatch Logs. The team wants CloudWatch alarms for new regression failures with minimal custom code. The team does not need old log events converted into metrics.

Which approach will meet these requirements?

Write QA logs to a newly created Infrequent Access log group. Create a metric filter before the QA run and alarm on that metric.
Explanation
This approach is technically possible for storing new QA logs in a lower-cost log class. It does not meet the metric filter requirement because metric filters are supported only for log groups in the Standard log class.
Use AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics for the QA run. Filter by ModelId and alarm on invocation error metrics.
Explanation
Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics are useful for service errors, latency, invocations, and token counts. They do not contain the Lambda validator's semantic pass or fail result for each prompt test.
Schedule a Lambda function to run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query. Publish matching failures as a custom metric and alarm on that metric.
Explanation
This approach can analyze log data and publish a custom metric for alarms. It adds custom code and scheduled-query operations, so it does not meet the minimal custom code requirement for new failures.
Correct answer
Keep the log group in the Standard log class. Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter before the QA run and alarm on that metric.
Explanation
This is correct because CloudWatch Logs metric filters can convert matching validation log events into CloudWatch metrics. The filter must exist before the events arrive, and metric filters require the Standard log class.
Overall explanation
For a QA system, log the semantic result of each prompt test and turn failure events into an operational signal. CloudWatch Logs metric filters can publish metrics from matching log events. CloudWatch alarms can then act on those metrics.

The important tradeoff is timing and log class. Metric filters only publish datapoints for events that arrive after the filter exists. They also require a log group in the Standard log class. See Creating metrics from log events using filters.

A scheduled query with Lambda can work when a team needs custom aggregation or historical analysis. In this scenario, the team needs alarms for new failures and wants minimal custom code, so a metric filter is the simpler fit. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in AWS/Bedrock are useful for service health, latency, and token usage. They do not represent the Lambda validator's content quality decision. See Monitor Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 75
Skipped
A retail bank is implementing a generative AI chat feature for authenticated customers. API Gateway starts a Step Functions workflow for audit logging and stopping conditions. A streaming-capable application component calls Amazon Bedrock and forwards response chunks to the client. Auditors require the approved Bedrock guardrail to check both customer prompts and generated responses. Unsafe prompts must not reach the model. Allowed responses must continue to stream to the client.

Which implementation best meets these requirements with the least custom policy code?

Call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT before inference. Call InvokeModelWithResponseStream without a guardrail for allowed prompts.
Explanation
Incorrect. This approach can stop unsafe input before model inference. However, it does not use the approved Bedrock guardrail to evaluate generated responses during the Bedrock inference call.
Correct answer
Call InvokeModelWithResponseStream with the approved guardrail. Include the required headers and JSON body configuration.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to InvokeModelWithResponseStream, so the guardrail evaluates the user input and the model response in the streaming path. If input evaluation intervenes, Bedrock returns the configured blocked message and does not run model inference.
Call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT before inference. Check streamed chunks with source OUTPUT after generation completes.
Explanation
Incorrect. This approach separates output checking from the streaming inference path. It can allow response text to be delivered before the Bedrock guardrail has assessed the complete generated output.
Call InvokeModelWithResponseStream with the guardrail identifier only. Omit the guardrail version and body configuration.
Explanation
Incorrect. Bedrock documents required guardrail request settings for InvokeModelWithResponseStream. An incomplete guardrail configuration can cause request errors instead of enforcing the approved policy.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can run as part of model inference. When a guardrail is attached to an inference request, Bedrock evaluates the input and the output. If input evaluation intervenes, Bedrock returns the configured blocked message and discards the foundation model inference. If output evaluation intervenes, Bedrock overrides or masks the response according to the guardrail configuration. See How guardrails work.

For a streaming chat path, the most direct control point is the streaming Bedrock inference API. InvokeModelWithResponseStream supports guardrails when the request includes the required guardrail information and uses the required JSON configuration. This keeps the policy enforcement inside Bedrock and avoids a separate policy engine in Lambda. The independent ApplyGuardrail API is useful when you need to assess text outside an FM invocation, but using it before or after a separate streaming call does not provide the same in-path response enforcement. See Use a guardrail with model inference and Use the ApplyGuardrail API.

This avoids…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 1
Skipped
An industrial equipment manufacturer uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store to retrieve maintenance procedures. The application finds relevant documents, but technicians often find the most useful procedures below less relevant results. Queries frequently combine descriptive symptoms with exact equipment identifiers and fault codes.

The company wants to improve retrieval relevance and prioritize the procedures that best address each query. The existing vector index includes a filterable text field.

Which combination of changes meets these requirements with MINIMAL operational overhead? (Select two)

Move document embeddings to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector. Develop a ranking algorithm that combines vector distances, equipment metadata, and document attributes

Increase the number of retrieved passages and expand the generation model's context window. Pass every retrieved passage to the model in its original order so that the model can identify the most relevant procedures

Correct selection
Configure a managed Amazon Bedrock reranker in the knowledge base retrieval configuration to reorder candidate passages by their relevance to each query

Correct selection
Enable hybrid search for the knowledge base to combine semantic similarity with keyword matching against the OpenSearch Serverless vector store

Deploy an OpenSearch Service domain with Learning to Rank. Train a relevance model on labeled maintenance queries and integrate its scores into the application's retrieval workflow

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Configure a managed Amazon Bedrock reranker in the knowledge base retrieval configuration to reorder candidate passages by their relevance to each query

A reranker evaluates the relationship between the query and the candidate passages returned by initial retrieval. It directly addresses the reported problem: useful procedures already appear in the results, but their positions do not adequately reflect their relevance.

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports managed reranking through its retrieval configuration. The developer can select a supported reranker model and configure how many reranked results to return. This avoids deploying a separate inference endpoint or building a custom ranking service.

For example, a reranker can prioritize a procedure that directly addresses the reported equipment failure over a passage that merely discusses similar machinery. The company should evaluate ranking quality on representative technician queries and balance the candidate count against reranking latency and cost. Reranking can reorder retrieved candidates but cannot recover passages that initial retrieval never selected.

Enable hybrid search for the knowledge base to combine semantic similarity with keyword matching against the OpenSearch Serverless vector store

Hybrid search combines vector-based semantic matching with keyword matching. This suits technician queries that contain both descriptions of symptoms and exact equipment identifiers or fault codes.

Semantic search helps retrieve passages that describe the same failure using different wording. Keyword matching contributes evidence from specific identifiers that similarity search alone might undervalue. The existing OpenSearch Serverless index includes the filterable text field required for the supported hybrid search configuration.

The developer can request HYBRID search through the knowledge base retrieval configuration without implementing a separate search pipeline. Hybrid retrieval and managed reranking address complementary stages: candidate selection and final ordering. The company should validate their combined effect against representative queries rather than assume that every query will improve.

Incorrect options:

Deploy an OpenSearch Service domain with Learning to Rank. Train a relevance model on labeled maintenance queries and integrate its scores into the application's retrieval workflow - OpenSearch Learning to Rank can improve relevance by applying a trained ranking model. It requires preparation of relevance judgments, feature definitions, and training data, followed by model training outside OpenSearch Service.

Introducing a separate domain and integrating a custom ranking workflow adds development and operational responsibilities. Managed Bedrock reranking addresses the ranking problem without requiring the company to maintain that additional infrastructure and model lifecycle.

Move document embeddings to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector. Develop a ranking algorithm that combines vector distances, equipment metadata, and document attributes - Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector can support vector similarity searches, and a custom scoring algorithm can incorporate document metadata. This architecture can provide substantial control over relevance calculations.

The company already has a functioning vector store and retrieves relevant procedures. Migrating embeddings and developing a ranking algorithm introduces unnecessary work compared with enabling the existing knowledge base's managed retrieval capabilities.

Increase the number of retrieved passages and expand the generation model's context window. Pass every retrieved passage to the model in its original order so that the model can identify the most relevant procedures - Increasing the retrieval count can improve candidate coverage when the relevant passage is absent from a smaller result set. Expanding the context window can also allow the generation model to consume more source material.

Neither change directly improves the ordering of retrieved results. Passing more passages in their existing order can increase inference cost and introduce distracting context while leaving the reported ranking issue unresolved.

Engineers then cannot invoke any other model in any account, regardless of the permissions in their…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 2
Skipped
A global engineering firm uses an organization in AWS Organizations with all features enabled to manage 40 AWS accounts. Engineers use Amazon Bedrock across many of these accounts. The firm must prevent specific topics, such as unreleased product designs and pending acquisitions, and proprietary information, such as internal project code names, from being included in prompts to Amazon Bedrock models. The firm must also ensure that engineers can use only approved Amazon Bedrock models. The firm centrally manages the IAM roles that engineers use.

Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select two)

Attach a permissions boundary to each engineer's IAM role that requires the approved Amazon Bedrock guardrail identifier for every model invocation. Create an SCP that allows engineers to use only approved models

Correct selection
Use AWS CloudFormation to create a custom Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a block filtering policy. Deploy the guardrail to every account in the organization by using stack sets

Correct selection
Create an SCP that allows engineers to use only approved models and that requires engineers to specify the approved guardrail identifier in every call to invoke an approved model

Create AWS Config custom rules that detect Amazon Bedrock invocations that do not use a guardrail and notify the security team about each noncompliant invocation

Create an SCP that denies model invocation when a call does not specify the centrally deployed guardrail identifier. Attach a permissions boundary to each engineer's IAM role that allows the engineer to invoke only approved models

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Create an SCP that allows engineers to use only approved models and that requires engineers to specify the approved guardrail identifier in every call to invoke an approved model

Service control policies (SCPs) set the maximum permissions for every IAM principal in the member accounts where they apply, and account administrators cannot modify or remove them. A single SCP can restrict model invocation actions, such as bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, to the ARNs of approved foundation models. Engineers then cannot invoke any other model in any account, regardless of the permissions in their identity-based policies.

The same SCP can use the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key to require that every invocation references the approved guardrail. Requests that omit the guardrail, or that reference a different guardrail such as a permissive one an engineer created, are denied. Because SCPs support the full IAM policy language, including conditions and specific resource ARNs, the firm can express both controls in one policy. Targeted Deny statements are the recommended way to keep each control enforceable.

Applying both controls through one SCP gives the firm central, consistent enforcement across all 40 accounts with a single policy to maintain. Unlike controls attached to individual roles, the SCP also covers principals that are created later or outside the central role management process. No principal can bypass the model or guardrail requirements.

Use AWS CloudFormation to create a custom Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a block filtering policy. Deploy the guardrail to every account in the organization by using stack sets

The firm needs a guardrail that actually stops restricted content from reaching the models. A guardrail with a block filtering policy uses denied topics to detect discussions of subjects such as unreleased product designs and pending acquisitions. It uses word filters or sensitive information filters to detect proprietary terms such as internal project code names. When the guardrail detects this content in a prompt, it blocks the request and returns a predefined message instead of sending the prompt to the model.

Denied topics support only a block action, so a block filtering policy is required to meet the topic requirement. Blocking also ensures that proprietary terms are never processed by the model, which directly satisfies the requirement to prevent this information from being included in prompts.

AWS CloudFormation StackSets deploys the same guardrail definition to every account in the organization from a central location. The firm gets consistent controls in all 40 accounts and can update the guardrail centrally as restricted topics change. Because each account receives its own copy of the guardrail, the SCP condition lists the guardrail identifiers that the stack set deploys.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/amazon-bedrock-guardrails-announces-iam-policy-based-enforcement-to-deliver-safe-ai-interactions/

Incorrect options:

Attach a permissions boundary to each engineer's IAM role that requires the approved Amazon Bedrock guardrail identifier for every model invocation. Create an SCP that allows engineers to use only approved models - A permissions boundary applies only to the IAM roles it is attached to. Enforcing the guardrail requirement through boundaries means that any principal without the boundary, such as a role created later by an account administrator or a role outside the central management process, can invoke models without the guardrail. That leaves a path for proprietary information to reach the models.

The guardrail requirement is the most security-sensitive control in this scenario, so it belongs in an SCP that applies to every principal and that member accounts cannot change. Splitting the controls across boundaries and an SCP also adds policies to manage without improving protection compared with a single SCP.

Create an SCP that denies model invocation when a call does not specify the centrally deployed guardrail identifier. Attach a permissions boundary to each engineer's IAM role that allows the engineer to invoke only approved models - The SCP portion of this option enforces the guardrail requirement correctly. However, restricting models through permissions boundaries depends on attaching the boundary to every engineer role. Any principal without the boundary could invoke unapproved models, so the firm cannot guarantee that engineers use only approved models across all accounts.

Managing boundaries on many roles in 40 accounts also adds administrative overhead and risk of drift. A single SCP enforces both the approved model list and the guardrail requirement for every principal, which makes it the more reliable and simpler control.

Create AWS Config custom rules that detect Amazon Bedrock invocations that do not use a guardrail and notify the security team about each noncompliant invocation - AWS Config evaluates the configuration state of AWS resources. It does not inspect individual API calls, such as model invocations, to see whether they include a guardrail. Custom rules could not reliably detect each noncompliant invocation.

Even if detection were possible, notifications occur after the prompt has already reached the model. This is a detective control, not a preventive control, so it cannot stop restricted content from being sent to models or restrict engineers to approved models.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/unlock-new-possibilities-aws-organizations-service-control-policy-now-supports-full-iam-language

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/amazon-bedrock-guardrails-announces-iam-policy-based-enforcement-to-deliver-safe-ai-interactions/

Question 3
Skipped
A generative AI platform exposes a public endpoint that accepts free-form user prompts and forwards them to a foundation model. During load testing, engineers observe that some requests fail unpredictably when users submit very long prompts or request verbose outputs. These failures cause retries at the client layer and increase overall latency. The development team wants to introduce controls so that requests exceeding safe limits are handled consistently before reaching the model. The solution must protect downstream services, provide predictable behavior for clients, and avoid embedding complex logic into application code.

What do you recommend as the MOST operationally efficient solution for this workload?

Use Amazon API Gateway to forward all requests to the backend and rely on the foundation model to return token limit errors. Capture those errors in AWS Lambda and retry the request with reduced parameters. Return the retried response to the client

Use Amazon API Gateway to enforce payload size limits and additionally implement custom token counting logic in Lambda to dynamically rewrite prompts and outputs, truncate content when limits are exceeded, and retry requests automatically until they succeed, while logging all adjustments for audit purposes.

Correct answer
Use Amazon API Gateway request validation and mapping templates to enforce maximum input size and estimated token limits before invoking the backend. Reject requests that exceed configured thresholds with clear error responses. Forward only validated requests to the model invocation layer

Use AWS Lambda to calculate token usage for every request after it passes through the API layer. Truncate inputs and outputs dynamically based on remaining context window size. Allow the API to accept all requests without validation to maximize flexibility

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon API Gateway request validation and mapping templates to enforce maximum input size and estimated token limits before invoking the backend. Reject requests that exceed configured thresholds with clear error responses. Forward only validated requests to the model invocation layer

Enforcing limits at the API boundary prevents oversized requests from reaching downstream services. By using request validation and mapping templates, the API layer can reject requests that exceed safe input size or estimated token thresholds before invoking the model. This creates predictable and fast failure behavior for clients.

Handling token related constraints at the API level reduces unnecessary load on the backend and avoids wasted inference calls. Clients receive immediate feedback and can adjust requests without triggering retries or timeouts. This improves overall system stability and user experience.

This approach keeps token management logic centralized and declarative. It avoids embedding complex truncation or retry logic in application code while aligning with best practices for protecting backend services.

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon API Gateway to forward all requests to the backend and rely on the foundation model to return token limit errors. Capture those errors in AWS Lambda and retry the request with reduced parameters. Return the retried response to the client - Relying on the model to surface token limit errors shifts control too far downstream. Failed invocations still consume latency and compute before errors are returned. Retrying requests after failure increases response time and operational cost. This design also creates inconsistent behavior under load. Clients may experience unpredictable delays due to retries rather than receiving immediate feedback.

Use Amazon API Gateway to enforce payload size limits and additionally implement custom token counting logic in Lambda to dynamically rewrite prompts and outputs, truncate content when limits are exceeded, and retry requests automatically until they succeed, while logging all adjustments for audit purposes. - Although this option attempts to manage limits, it introduces excessive complexity into the backend. Dynamically rewriting prompts and retrying requests obscures original user intent and makes behavior harder to reason about. Automatic retries can also mask genuine client side issues. Managing token limits is more effective when enforced early. This approach over engineers the solution instead of preventing invalid requests at the boundary.

Use AWS Lambda to calculate token usage for every request after it passes through the API layer. Truncate inputs and outputs dynamically based on remaining context window size. Allow the API to accept all requests without validation to maximize flexibility - Allowing all requests through the API layer removes an important control point. Token calculation and truncation in Lambda occur only after the request has already consumed resources. This increases cost and failure rates under heavy usage. Truncating inputs silently can also lead to incomplete or misleading model outputs. Clients are not clearly informed that their requests exceeded limits.

A home design media company wants to build an application that analyzes interior design trends. The application must analyze videos and photos from public design exhibitions and international furniture fairs to identify style elements such as color palettes, materials, furniture shapes, and decor themes. The solution must store the extracted information and must provide a dashboard that summarizes the design trends for the company's editors.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Use an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock to analyze text descriptions of the exhibition videos and photos and use Stable Diffusion for image analysis. Store the results in Amazon OpenSearch Service and create a dashboard in Amazon Managed Grafana with OpenSearch visualizations

Use Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels to train a custom model for design trend analysis. Store the results in Amazon DynamoDB and create a dashboard in Amazon Managed Grafana with custom plugins for design trend analytics

Correct answer
Use AWS Step Functions to process the videos and photos with multimodal foundation models (FMs) in Amazon Bedrock. Store the analysis results in Amazon S3 and visualize the trends in an Amazon QuickSight dashboard

Use the Amazon Rekognition DetectLabels API with its default label set to tag objects in the videos and photos. Store the labels in Amazon S3 and visualize them in an Amazon QuickSight dashboard

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use AWS Step Functions to process the videos and photos with multimodal foundation models (FMs) in Amazon Bedrock. Store the analysis results in Amazon S3 and visualize the trends in an Amazon QuickSight dashboard

Multimodal foundation models in Amazon Bedrock accept images, and some models also accept video, as direct input. They can describe nuanced visual concepts such as color palettes, materials, furniture silhouettes, and overall decor themes. With a well-designed prompt, the model returns structured output, such as JSON with fields for each style attribute. No model training or labeled dataset is required, so the company can start analyzing exhibition media immediately and adjust the attributes it extracts by changing the prompt.

AWS Step Functions orchestrates the processing workflow without servers to manage. A state machine can retrieve each photo or video, extract frames when a model accepts only images, invoke the Amazon Bedrock model through the native service integration, handle retries and errors, and write the structured results to Amazon S3. Map states let the workflow process large batches of exhibition media in parallel.

Amazon S3 provides durable, low-cost storage for the extracted attributes. Amazon QuickSight can query the results through Amazon Athena and present interactive dashboards that show how styles, colors, and materials change across exhibitions and seasons. Every component is fully managed and serverless, so this solution delivers the analysis, storage, and dashboard requirements with the least operational overhead.

The model would miss visual details that are not described in text.

Stable Diffusion is an image generation model, not an image analysis model, so it cannot extract style elements from photos. Managing Amazon OpenSearch Service and Amazon Managed Grafana for this workload also adds operational overhead compared with Amazon S3 and Amazon QuickSight.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 5
Skipped
A pharmaceutical research company is developing a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application to help drug safety scientists investigate complex relationships among chemical compounds, protein targets, clinical trials, adverse event reports, and regulatory approvals across multiple countries. The dataset contains highly interconnected entities with multi-hop relationships. For example, a compound connects to a protein target, which connects to a different trial, which connects to a regulatory finding. The scientists must be able to examine these relationships holistically to make accurate safety assessments.

The application must deliver comprehensive answers that capture indirect relationships between entities and must return responses in less than 2.5 seconds.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Use an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector database with k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) searches and implement manual relationship mapping in an application layer that runs in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store, increase the number of retrieved results to 100 chunks for each query, and apply a reranking model to the results

Correct answer
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with GraphRAG and store the data in Amazon Neptune Analytics. Analyze the multi-hop relationships between entities and automatically identify related information across documents

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector store and implement custom relationship identification logic with AWS Lambda functions that query multiple vector embeddings in sequence

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with GraphRAG and store the data in Amazon Neptune Analytics. Analyze the multi-hop relationships between entities and automatically identify related information across documents

Standard vector search retrieves chunks that are semantically similar to a question, but it does not follow connections between entities that appear in different documents. A question about how a compound might relate to a regulatory finding through an intermediate protein target and trial requires multi-hop reasoning across those links. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with GraphRAG addresses this by combining vector search with a knowledge graph that represents the entities and their relationships explicitly.

During ingestion, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases automatically extracts entities and relationships from the source documents and builds a graph in Amazon Neptune Analytics alongside the vector embeddings. At query time, the knowledge base first finds relevant chunks through vector similarity. It then traverses the graph to collect connected entities and related content from other documents. This provides the model with context that captures indirect relationships, which produces comprehensive answers that a vector-only approach would miss.

Neptune Analytics is a memory-optimized graph analytics engine that runs fast graph traversals, which helps keep responses under 2.5 seconds. The company does not need to design a graph schema, write extraction pipelines, or maintain traversal queries, because the knowledge base manages graph construction and retrieval. Both services are fully managed, so this solution delivers multi-hop reasoning with the least operational overhead.

Incorrect options: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector store and implement custom relationship identification logic with AWS Lambda functions that query multiple vector embeddings in sequence - A vector store retrieves chunks by semantic similarity and does not store explicit relationships between entities. Custom Lambda logic that runs several vector queries in sequence would need to infer connections, decide which entities to follow, and repeat searches. That approach is complex to build and maintain, and it is likely to miss indirect relationships.

Running many sequential queries for each question also adds latency, which makes the 2.5-second target difficult to meet. This design carries more operational overhead than a managed GraphRAG solution.

Use an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector database with k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) searches and implement manual relationship mapping in an application layer that runs in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group - k-NN search in OpenSearch Serverless finds semantically similar content but cannot traverse relationships between entities. Manual relationship mapping in an application layer requires the company to define, store, and update every relationship as the research data changes, which is a large ongoing effort.

Running the mapping logic on an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group adds infrastructure that the company must patch, scale, and monitor. This option has high operational overhead and does not reliably capture multi-hop relationships.

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store, increase the number of retrieved results to 100 chunks for each query, and apply a reranking model to the results - Retrieving 100 chunks for each query increases the chance that some related content appears in the results, but vector similarity alone still cannot identify which chunks are connected through intermediate entities. A reranker improves the ordering of results by relevance to the question, not by relationship paths between entities.

Large result sets also increase the number of input tokens and the processing time for each response, which threatens the 2.5-second latency target. This option adds cost without delivering true multi-hop reasoning.
