Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use AWS AppConfig feature flags to store routing rules that map user segments to specific Amazon Bedrock models and retrieve the configuration at runtime inside the application. Implement AppConfig deployment strategies with gradual rollout and CloudWatch alarms so product managers can shift traffic safely without redeploying code

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/using-aws-appconfig-feature-flags/

Using AWS AppConfig feature flags provides a structured and safe mechanism for controlling model routing logic without redeploying application code. AppConfig enables you to store configuration values such as model IDs, user segment mappings, and routing percentages, all of which can be retrieved dynamically at runtime by the application. This separation of routing logic from code allows business stakeholders to make controlled changes while keeping the application stable.

AppConfig deployment strategies offer gradual rollout, bake times, metric monitors, and automatic rollback triggers. This protects the platform from sudden configuration errors or unexpected spikes in model latency or cost, since changes are introduced incrementally and monitored through CloudWatch alarms. Because routing decisions are pulled from AppConfig at runtime, traffic can be shifted to different models for specific user segments such as premium users, power users, or experimental cohorts with zero downtime.

This approach aligns with best practices for configuration based dynamic routing, minimizes risk by using staged deployments, and provides strong operational safety. It also supports product teams by giving them a controlled mechanism to test new model configurations before widening rollout.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/best-practices-for-validating-aws-appconfig-feature-flags-and-configuration-data/

Incorrect options:

Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to store JSON objects that contain model routing rules and fetch them at runtime, but update these parameters manually without deployment strategies or rollout controls. Rely on the application to immediately adopt any parameter change without guardrails, validation, or monitoring - Storing routing rules in Parameter Store is functional but lacks the operational safety features required for gradual rollout. Updating parameters manually forces the application to adopt new routing values immediately, which can break user experience if a configuration error or performance regression occurs. Without deployment strategies, validation, or monitoring, product managers have no guardrails or rollback automation, which violates the requirement for safe rollouts. Parameter Store can support configuration storage, but AppConfig is the recommended service for progressive delivery.

Write routing rules into an Amazon DynamoDB table and update the table directly whenever product managers want to shift traffic between models. Fetch the DynamoDB configuration values on every request and bypass any staged rollout or configuration validation mechanisms - Using DynamoDB to store routing rules creates unnecessary operational complexity and lacks mechanisms for gradual rollout, automatic rollback, or configuration validation. Directly updating the DynamoDB table exposes the system to immediate configuration changes that may cause traffic shifts without safety controls. This architecture places all responsibility for configuration safety on the application logic rather than using built in tools like AppConfig deployment strategies. It also introduces additional costs and does not provide built in integration with CloudWatch alarms for monitoring configuration health.

Embed routing flags in Amazon S3 objects and instruct the application to periodically poll the bucket for changes to determine which model to call. Allow product managers to upload new objects to modify routing behavior without using versioning, deployment guards, or real time monitoring - Storing routing flags in S3 objects and polling for changes lacks structured deployment controls, validation, and monitoring. S3 does not provide staged configuration rollout, so any file update can immediately alter routing behavior with no gradual deployment or rollback protections. This approach can also introduce delays or inconsistencies due to polling intervals and has no automation for detecting or recovering from misconfigurations. It fails the requirement for controlled feature flag based routing with fast but safe updates.

With Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), each shopper request first retrieves the catalog entries that are most relevant to the request, and the model generates…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 21
Skipped
An online home furnishings retailer is building a generative AI (GenAI) solution that uses Amazon Bedrock with an Anthropic Claude model to recommend furniture and decor items to shoppers. Shoppers report that some recommended items are discontinued or unavailable on the website, and that other recommended items do not match their needs. Shoppers also report that some recommendations take a long time to appear.

The retailer investigates and finds that nearly every shopper interaction with the recommendation solution is unique. The retailer also confirms that the solution recommends items that do not exist in the retailer's product catalog. The retailer must resolve these issues.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Store the product catalog data in Amazon OpenSearch Service and validate each product recommendation against the catalog after generation. Use Amazon DynamoDB to cache responses

Use prompt engineering to restrict the model responses to relevant products. Use streaming with the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API to reduce the latency that shoppers perceive

Switch to a larger Anthropic Claude model with a bigger context window, insert the complete product catalog into every prompt so that the model can see all available items, and enable prompt caching on the catalog section

Correct answer
Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for the product catalog and implement Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Set the latency parameter in the performance configuration to optimized

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for the product catalog and implement Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Set the latency parameter in the performance configuration to optimized

The model recommends items that are not in the catalog because it relies on general knowledge from its training data instead of the retailer's actual inventory. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base ingests the product catalog, creates embeddings, and stores them in a vector index. With Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), each shopper request first retrieves the catalog entries that are most relevant to the request, and the model generates recommendations from those retrieved items. The model only sees real, current products in its context, which addresses both the nonexistent items and the irrelevant recommendations.

The knowledge base stays aligned with the catalog through data source syncs. When the retailer adds new items or removes discontinued items, a sync updates the index, and recommendations reflect the change immediately. Metadata filtering can restrict retrieval to items that are currently in stock or within a shopper's chosen category. This further improves relevance without changes to the model.

Latency-optimized inference in Amazon Bedrock runs supported models on optimized infrastructure that reduces response time. The retailer enables it by setting the latency parameter in the performance configuration to optimized, including within the generation configuration of knowledge base requests. Because nearly every interaction is unique, caching would rarely help. Reducing the actual inference time for each request is the effective way to resolve the slow recommendations.

Incorrect options:

Switch to a larger Anthropic Claude model with a bigger context window, insert the complete product catalog into every prompt so that the model can see all available items, and enable prompt caching on the catalog section - A full product catalog for a retailer is typically far too large to fit in a model's context window, and including it in every prompt would dramatically increase input tokens and cost. Larger models also generate responses more slowly, which makes the latency problem worse.

Prompt caching reduces the cost and processing time of repeated prompt prefixes, but every catalog update changes the prefix and invalidates the cache. Very long contexts can also reduce the model's ability to focus on the most relevant items. RAG retrieves only the relevant products and is the scalable approach.

Use prompt engineering to restrict the model responses to relevant products. Use streaming with the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API to reduce the latency that shoppers perceive - Prompt instructions can ask the model to recommend only available products, but the model does not know which products the retailer sells. Without retrieved catalog data in the context, the model continues to generate plausible but nonexistent items regardless of the instructions.

Streaming with InvokeModelWithResponseStream shows output sooner, which improves perceived responsiveness, but the total generation time does not change. This option treats the symptoms without addressing why the model recommends items outside the catalog.

Store the product catalog data in Amazon OpenSearch Service and validate each product recommendation against the catalog after generation. Use Amazon DynamoDB to cache responses - Validating recommendations after generation detects nonexistent items, but it does not stop the model from producing them. The application would need to discard invalid results and possibly regenerate them, which adds more latency to an already slow experience.

Response caching in Amazon DynamoDB helps only when requests repeat. The retailer found that nearly every interaction is unique, so the cache hit rate would be very low and the caching layer would add cost and complexity without reducing latency.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 22
Skipped
A global advertising agency must use Amazon Bedrock to establish a strong governance process for AI-generated campaign content. The agency needs to manage more than 400 prompt templates. Nine creative teams use the templates across four AWS Regions to generate advertising copy. The solution must provide version control with approval workflows that notify reviewers about pending approvals. The solution must also provide detailed audit trails that record prompt activity and must enforce consistent prompt parameterization to maintain quality standards.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Configure prompt templates in Amazon Bedrock Studio and build Amazon CloudWatch dashboards that display prompt usage metrics. Store the content approval status in Amazon DynamoDB and use AWS Lambda functions to enforce approvals

Correct answer
Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management for version control and configure AWS CloudTrail for audit logging. Control approval permissions with IAM policies and create parameterized prompt templates that define variables

Deploy Amazon SageMaker Canvas with prompt templates that are stored in Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudFormation for version control and use AWS Config to enforce approval policies

Store every prompt template as a separate AWS Secrets Manager secret, replicate the secrets to each Region, use secret version staging labels to represent draft and approved states, and configure Amazon SNS topics that subscribe to Secrets Manager rotation events to notify reviewers about pending approvals

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management for version control and configure AWS CloudTrail for audit logging. Control approval permissions with IAM policies and create parameterized prompt templates that define variables

Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management is the native Amazon Bedrock feature for creating, storing, and governing prompt templates. Authors work on a draft prompt and create immutable, numbered versions when the prompt is ready for release. Applications reference a specific version by its ARN, so production workloads use only an approved snapshot while authors continue to iterate on the draft. This gives the agency clear, reliable version control across hundreds of templates without building a custom repository.

Prompt Management supports variables in double curly braces within each template. Teams must supply defined inputs, such as the brand name, target audience, or campaign channel, instead of writing free-form prompts. This enforces consistent parameterization and quality standards across all nine teams. IAM policies separate duties by granting authors permission to edit drafts and restricting actions such as bedrock:CreatePromptVersion to designated approvers. That establishes an approval gate before a prompt version can be used in production.

AWS CloudTrail records Prompt Management API activity as management events. These events include who created, updated, versioned, or deleted each prompt, along with when and from where the action occurred. This creates the detailed audit trail the agency requires. The agency can also create Amazon EventBridge rules that match these CloudTrail events and send notifications to reviewers through Amazon SNS when a draft is ready for approval. Because every component is a managed AWS capability, the agency meets its governance requirements with minimal custom development.

Incorrect options:

Store every prompt template as a separate AWS Secrets Manager secret, replicate the secrets to each Region, use secret version staging labels to represent draft and approved states, and configure Amazon SNS topics that subscribe to Secrets Manager rotation events to notify reviewers about pending approvals - AWS Secrets Manager is designed to store and rotate credentials, API keys, and other secrets. Using it for hundreds of prompt templates misuses the service, adds per-secret costs, and provides no support for prompt variables or Amazon Bedrock integration. Version staging labels are meant for credential rotation, not editorial approval.

Secrets Manager rotation events occur when a secret rotates, not when a prompt author submits a draft for review. Notifications based on those events would not match the approval workflow. This design adds cost and complexity without meeting the governance requirements.

Deploy Amazon SageMaker Canvas with prompt templates that are stored in Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudFormation for version control and use AWS Config to enforce approval policies - Amazon SageMaker Canvas is a no-code machine learning tool for building models and generating predictions. It is not a governance platform for managing Amazon Bedrock prompt templates. Storing prompts in Amazon S3 again provides no native parameterization or prompt versioning.

AWS CloudFormation manages infrastructure as code and is not designed to version individual prompt templates that change frequently. AWS Config evaluates resource configurations against rules, but it does not provide human approval workflows. This design misapplies each service and does not meet the requirements.

Configure prompt templates in Amazon Bedrock Studio and build Amazon CloudWatch dashboards that display prompt usage metrics. Store the content approval status in Amazon DynamoDB and use AWS Lambda functions to enforce approvals - Amazon Bedrock Studio was a web interface for building GenAI prototypes, and its capabilities have moved to Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio. It does not provide the version control and approval gates that the agency needs to govern prompts centrally across teams and Regions.

Amazon CloudWatch dashboards show usage metrics but do not create an audit trail of who changed each prompt. Storing approval status in Amazon DynamoDB and enforcing it with AWS Lambda functions requires custom code that the agency must build and maintain. The design lacks native versioning and auditability.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 23
Skipped
A manufacturing company uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize equipment inspection reports. During production shifts, the application processes approximately 12,000 requests each hour and requires predictable inference throughput. The company purchases sufficient provisioned throughput by using CreateProvisionedModelThroughput and confirms that its status is InService. Amazon CloudWatch metrics show no utilization of the provisioned capacity, while the application continues to encounter on-demand throttling.

The application invokes the model with the following Python code. The base_model_id variable contains the foundation model's on-demand model ID.

response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(
    modelId=base_model_id,
    contentType="application/json",
    body=json.dumps(payload)
)
Which change will direct requests to the purchased capacity and resolve the identified throttling issue?

Configure exponential backoff with jitter to retry requests that encounter on-demand throttling

Correct answer
Set modelId to the provisionedModelArn value returned by CreateProvisionedModelThroughput when invoking the model

Purchase additional model units for the foundation model to increase the available provisioned capacity

Replace the model ID with the foundation model ARN from the same AWS Region as the provisioned capacity to route requests through that capacity

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Set modelId to the provisionedModelArn value returned by CreateProvisionedModelThroughput when invoking the model

The modelId parameter determines which model resource or throughput resource Amazon Bedrock invokes. Supplying the foundation model's on-demand ID directs requests to on-demand inference. Purchasing provisioned throughput does not automatically redirect those requests, which explains why the purchased capacity remains unused.

CreateProvisionedModelThroughput returns a provisionedModelArn value that identifies the provisioned resource. The application must pass this ARN as modelId in its InvokeModel requests. The same resource-selection principle applies when using supported streaming or Converse operations.

The scenario confirms that the provisioned resource is InService and that the company purchased sufficient capacity. Changing the invocation target therefore addresses the identified cause of throttling. Provisioned throughput still has capacity limits, so the company should continue monitoring utilization after correcting the configuration.

Incorrect options:

Purchase additional model units for the foundation model to increase the available provisioned capacity - Additional model units increase purchased inference capacity, but the metrics show that the application does not use its existing provisioned capacity. This indicates an invocation configuration problem rather than insufficient provisioned capacity.

Purchasing more capacity does not change the modelId value that the application sends. Requests would continue to use on-demand inference, leaving the additional provisioned capacity unused and increasing unnecessary expenditure.

Configure exponential backoff with jitter to retry requests that encounter on-demand throttling - Exponential backoff with jitter can help applications recover from transient throttling. It spreads retries over time and reduces the likelihood that multiple clients repeatedly retry together.

The application would still submit those retries to the on-demand model ID. Retry logic neither selects the provisioned resource nor consumes the purchased capacity, so it does not correct the underlying configuration error.

Replace the model ID with the foundation model ARN from the same AWS Region as the provisioned capacity to route requests through that capacity - A foundation model ARN identifies the underlying foundation model. Although it provides a fully qualified identifier, it does not identify the company's separate provisioned throughput resource.

Using the same AWS Region does not create an automatic association between an invocation and available provisioned capacity. The application must select the ARN containing the provisioned-model resource type, rather than the foundation-model ARN.

A nonprofit education foundation is using Amazon Bedrock to build an application that helps schoolteachers write funding proposals for classroom projects. The application uses an Amazon Nova Lite foundation model (FM). The application has five required inputs and must return responses in a consistent text format. The foundation wants to receive a notification in Amazon Bedrock when a response contains demeaning or bullying language. However, the foundation does not want to block every flagged response.

The foundation creates an Amazon Bedrock flow that accepts an input prompt and sends it to the Amazon Nova Lite FM, which returns a response.

Which additional steps must the foundation take to meet these requirements? (Select two)

Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that uses the insults content filter with the filter action set to block, and configure a custom blocked response message that alerts the foundation. Attach the guardrail to the prompt node of the flow

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to define the required inputs as variables, select the Amazon Nova Lite FM, and specify the response output format. Add the prompt to the prompt node of the flow

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to define the required inputs as variables, select the Amazon Nova Lite FM, and specify the response output format. Add the prompt to the prompt node of the flow

Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management lets the foundation define a reusable prompt that declares each required input as a variable in double curly braces, such as the project title, grade level, budget, learning objectives, and timeline. When the flow runs, the prompt node receives values for all five variables, so every request supplies the same structured information. This enforces the required inputs without custom validation code.

A managed prompt also stores the model selection and the inference configuration. The foundation selects the Amazon Nova Lite FM in the prompt and writes explicit output formatting instructions into the template, such as required section headings and their order. Because every invocation uses the same template and settings, the application returns responses in a consistent text format.

Amazon Bedrock Flows supports prompt nodes that reference a prompt from Prompt Management. After the foundation adds the managed prompt to the prompt node, the flow maps the input node data to the prompt variables and sends the rendered prompt to the model. This approach also gives the foundation versioning, so it can refine the template and publish new versions without rebuilding the flow.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/streamline-generative-ai-development-in-amazon-bedrock-with-prompt-management-and-prompt-flows-preview/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/streamline-generative-ai-development-in-amazon-bedrock-with-prompt-management-and-prompt-flows-preview/

Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that uses the insults content filter with the filter action set to detect. Attach the guardrail to the prompt node of the flow

The insults content filter in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails detects language that is demeaning, humiliating, mocking, insulting, or belittling, which includes bullying language. The hate filter targets attacks based on identity attributes such as race, religion, or gender. The insults filter is therefore the correct category for this requirement.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails supports a detect action in addition to block. With the detect action, the guardrail evaluates the content and records the finding in the guardrail trace and assessment. It does not take action on the content, so the response still reaches the teacher. This matches the requirement to receive a notification about bullying language without blocking every flagged response.

Amazon Bedrock Flows lets the foundation attach a guardrail directly to a prompt node. The guardrail evaluates the model response each time the node runs, and the flow trace surfaces the detection results in Amazon Bedrock. This gives the foundation visibility into flagged content without adding custom code or extra nodes to the flow.

Incorrect options:

Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that uses the hate content filter with the filter action set to block. Attach the guardrail to the prompt node of the flow - The hate content filter targets content that discriminates against or attacks people based on identity attributes such as race, ethnicity, religion, gender, or sexual orientation. Bullying and demeaning language falls under the insults category, so the hate filter would not reliably detect the content the foundation cares about.

Setting the filter action to block also stops every flagged response from reaching the user. The foundation explicitly does not want to block all flagged responses. This option fails both the category requirement and the action requirement.

Create an Amazon Bedrock prompt router that specifies the Amazon Nova Lite FM. Add the required inputs as variables to the input node, add the prompt router to the prompt node, and add the output format to the output node of the flow - An Amazon Bedrock prompt router selects between models in the same model family based on predicted response quality and cost for each request. It does not define prompt variables or output formatting instructions. The foundation needs one specific model, so a router adds no value here.

A flow's input node passes data into the flow, and its output node returns the final result. Neither node enforces prompt templates or response formatting. This design does not produce the consistent, structured prompt that the foundation requires.

Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that uses the insults content filter with the filter action set to block, and configure a custom blocked response message that alerts the foundation. Attach the guardrail to the prompt node of the flow - The insults content filter is the correct category for bullying language. However, the block action stops every flagged response from reaching the user. That violates the requirement not to block all flagged responses.

A custom blocked message only changes the text that replaces the blocked content. It does not send a notification to the foundation, and teachers would still lose the entire response. The detect action is the correct setting for this scenario.

Invoke the model through a regional endpoint and allow Bedrock to handle failover transparently at runtime. Monitor latency and error rates using Amazon CloudWatch to validate resilience during peak traffic windows

Amazon Bedrock cross Region inference is designed to improve availability for models that have limited regional presence. It allows inference requests to be automatically routed to another supported Region when the primary Region experiences capacity constraints or disruptions. This routing happens transparently without requiring application code changes.

By invoking the model through a regional endpoint, the application benefits from built in resilience while keeping the architecture simple. Bedrock manages the complexity of cross Region routing, which reduces operational overhead and lowers the risk of misconfigured failover logic. This is especially effective for predictable peak usage patterns across geographies.

From a cost perspective, cross Region inference avoids the need to provision and pay for dedicated throughput in every Region. The team achieves high availability and resilience while respecting the constraint of a limited budget.

Maintain separate configuration for each geography to control routing behavior - While this approach uses cross Region inference, setting up fallback logic in application code introduces operational complexity and maintenance risk. Increase provisioned throughput for the existing Bedrock model in the primary Region to absorb peak traffic spikes. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to detect saturation and trigger auto scaling policies. Leverage higher baseline capacity instead of cross Region failover to maintain application availability - Increasing provisioned throughput raises baseline costs and does not protect against Regional service disruptions. If the primary Region becomes unavailable, higher capacity does not improve availability. This approach addresses load but not resilience. The scenario explicitly mandates not to reserve excess capacity. This option fails to meet both the cost and availability requirements.

Question 26
Skipped
A consumer electronics manufacturer is building a customer support application that must handle 15,000 queries each day about devices, repairs, and warranty claims. The application must answer questions from 70,000 support articles that the manufacturer updates every day. The application must integrate with a repair management API to check the status of repairs and to help customers start new repair requests. The application must maintain context across multi-turn conversations with customers. The manufacturer must also capture complete audit trails for every response the application provides.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Build a custom orchestration service on Amazon ECS that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with tool definitions for the repair management API, store document embeddings in a self-managed vector database on Amazon EC2, keep conversation history in Amazon ElastiCache, and write every model request and response to Amazon S3 through custom logging middleware

Create a custom model in Amazon Bedrock through continued pre-training on all support articles. Set up an Amazon API Gateway REST API that uses AWS Lambda functions to connect the model to the repair management API

Correct answer
Create an Amazon Bedrock agent with action groups that integrate with the repair management API. Associate an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the agent to search the support articles by using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Enable trace events to capture audit trails

Deploy a fine-tuned Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock for each product category. Create AWS Lambda functions that connect each model to the repair management API and store the conversation history in Amazon DynamoDB

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Create an Amazon Bedrock agent with action groups that integrate with the repair management API. Associate an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the agent to search the support articles by using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Enable trace events to capture audit trails

Amazon Bedrock Agents provides managed orchestration for conversational applications that need to reason, retrieve information, and take actions. Action groups define the operations the agent can perform, such as checking repair status or starting a repair request, through an OpenAPI schema or function definitions. The agent determines when to call an action from the conversation, collects any missing parameters from the customer, and invokes an AWS Lambda function that calls the repair management API. The manufacturer does not need to write its own orchestration logic.

An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base associated with the agent provides managed RAG over the 70,000 support articles. The manufacturer syncs the data source each day, and the knowledge base updates its index incrementally. Answers then reflect the latest article content without any model retraining. The agent decides when a question requires knowledge base retrieval and when it requires an API action, and it can combine both in a single response.

Agents maintain conversation context within a session through a session ID, so customers can ask follow-up questions without repeating details. Trace events record each step of the agent's processing, including preprocessing, orchestration reasoning, knowledge base queries, action group invocations, and the final response. Combined with model invocation logging and AWS CloudTrail, the trace data provides complete audit trails. Every capability is managed, so this solution has the least operational overhead.

Incorrect options: Deploy a fine-tuned Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock for each product category. Create AWS Lambda functions that connect each model to the repair management API and store the conversation history in Amazon DynamoDB - Fine-tuning a separate model for each product category creates many custom models that the manufacturer must train, evaluate, and host. Each one requires Provisioned Throughput, which significantly increases cost. Because support articles change every day, the models would quickly become outdated unless they were retrained continually.

Connecting each model to the repair management API with custom Lambda functions and storing history in Amazon DynamoDB means the manufacturer must build its own orchestration and context management. This design has no built-in audit trail of reasoning steps and carries far more operational overhead.

Create a custom model in Amazon Bedrock through continued pre-training on all support articles. Set up an Amazon API Gateway REST API that uses AWS Lambda functions to connect the model to the repair management API - Continued pre-training adapts a model to a domain by training it on large amounts of unlabeled text. It does not give the model reliable, up-to-date recall of specific article content. Articles that change every day would require repeated training jobs to keep the model current, which is costly and slow.

A custom API Gateway and Lambda integration also requires the manufacturer to build its own orchestration, conversation memory, and audit logging. This option does not address multi-turn context or audit trails, and it adds significant operational work.

Build a custom orchestration service on Amazon ECS that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with tool definitions for the repair management API, store document embeddings in a self-managed vector database on Amazon EC2, keep conversation history in Amazon ElastiCache, and write every model request and response to Amazon S3 through custom logging middleware - A custom orchestration service with tool definitions can technically meet the requirements, but the manufacturer must build and operate every component. These include the orchestration loop, the ECS service, a self-managed vector database, a cache cluster for conversation history, and custom logging middleware.

Each component needs scaling, patching, monitoring, and failure handling. Amazon Bedrock Agents with a knowledge base provides the same capabilities as managed features, so this design has far more operational overhead than necessary.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 27
Skipped
A travel booking company is using Amazon Bedrock to build a generative AI (GenAI) application that produces detailed destination guides. The application uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a multi-agent workflow. The workflow has three sequential states: an itinerary drafter, a travel advisory validator, and an editorial style reviewer. Each state generates intermediate reasoning traces and outputs that it passes to the next state. The application uses an Amazon S3 bucket for process storage and final outputs.

During load testing, approximately 30% of workflow executions fail because the data passed between Step Functions states exceeds the 256 KB payload quota. A GenAI developer must revise the application architecture to handle the Step Functions 256 KB payload quota efficiently and to maintain workflow observability. The revised architecture must preserve the existing multi-agent reasoning and acting (ReAct) pattern.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Convert the Standard workflow to an Express workflow to gain higher throughput, enable Amazon CloudWatch Logs at the ALL log level with execution data included for observability, and split each agent's reasoning trace into several smaller output fields so that no individual field exceeds 256 KB

Store the intermediate outputs in Amazon DynamoDB and pass only item references between states. Add a Map state that retrieves the complete data from DynamoDB whenever each agent step needs it

Add AWS Lambda functions that compress the outputs to less than 256 KB before each agent state. Configure each agent task to decompress its input before processing and to compress its results before passing them to the next state

Correct answer
Configure the Amazon Bedrock service integration in Step Functions to use S3 bucket URIs in the input and output parameters for large payloads. Use the ResultSelector and ResultPath fields to pass the S3 references between the agent states and preserve the sequential validation workflow

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure the Amazon Bedrock service integration in Step Functions to use S3 bucket URIs in the input and output parameters for large payloads. Use the ResultSelector and ResultPath fields to pass the S3 references between the agent states and preserve the sequential validation workflow

Step Functions provides an optimized service integration for Amazon Bedrock that supports large payloads through Amazon S3. In the InvokeModel task, the developer can specify an S3 URI as the input source instead of passing the full prompt in the state input. The developer can also specify an S3 URI as the output destination so that Amazon Bedrock writes the full model response, including the reasoning traces, directly to Amazon S3. The large content never travels through the state payload, so the 256 KB quota no longer constrains the workflow. The application already uses an S3 bucket for process storage, so no new data store is required.

The ResultSelector field extracts only the fields the workflow needs from the task result, such as the S3 location of the output. The ResultPath field places that reference in the state output without discarding the original input. Each downstream agent state receives a compact reference and passes it to its own Amazon Bedrock integration as the input URI. The itinerary drafter, travel advisory validator, and editorial style reviewer therefore keep their sequential order and their ReAct behavior, each reasoning over the full output of the previous agent.

This design maintains observability. The Step Functions execution history still records every state transition, input, output, and error, and each state output shows the exact S3 object that the agent produced. The developer can open any intermediate reasoning trace in Amazon S3 to diagnose issues. Because the solution uses native Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock capabilities without extra functions or services, it has the least operational overhead.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/build-generative-ai-apps-using-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-bedrock/

Incorrect options:

Store the intermediate outputs in Amazon DynamoDB and pass only item references between states. Add a Map state that retrieves the complete data from DynamoDB whenever each agent step needs it - Amazon DynamoDB limits each item to 400 KB, and detailed reasoning traces from multiple agents can exceed that size. That would reintroduce a size constraint and require chunking logic. The design also adds a new data store to provision, secure, and maintain, even though the application already has an S3 bucket for process storage.

A Map state runs the same steps for each element of an input array. It is not a data retrieval mechanism. Retrieving data from DynamoDB for each agent requires additional task states or custom code, which increases operational overhead compared with the native S3 input and output support of the Amazon Bedrock integration.

Add AWS Lambda functions that compress the outputs to less than 256 KB before each agent state. Configure each agent task to decompress its input before processing and to compress its results before passing them to the next state - Compression does not guarantee that payloads stay under 256 KB. As guides and reasoning traces grow, compressed outputs can still exceed the quota and cause the same failures. The approach adds compression and decompression Lambda functions around every agent step, which increases latency, cost, and code to maintain.

Compressed payloads also appear in the execution history as unreadable encoded data. Developers can no longer inspect intermediate outputs directly in the Step Functions console, which reduces workflow observability instead of preserving it.

Convert the Standard workflow to an Express workflow to gain higher throughput, enable Amazon CloudWatch Logs at the ALL log level with execution data included for observability, and split each agent's reasoning trace into several smaller output fields so that no individual field exceeds 256 KB - Express workflows have the same 256 KB payload limit as Standard workflows. Converting the workflow type does not change how much data the states can pass. Splitting a reasoning trace into several fields also does not help, because the limit applies to the total state payload, not to individual fields.

Express workflows also do not keep a built-in execution history in the Step Functions console. The developer must rely on CloudWatch Logs, which reduces the observability that Standard workflows provide for long-running multi-agent processes. This option adds changes without solving the payload problem.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 28
Skipped
An aviation maintenance provider is building a generative AI (GenAI) application that uses Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to give technicians answers from approved aircraft maintenance manuals and service bulletins. The application uses Amazon OpenSearch Service to retrieve vector embeddings. Technicians report that searches often miss documents that contain exact part numbers, fault codes, and aviation acronyms. Technicians also report that searches return many documents that are semantically similar but not relevant to the task.

The provider needs to improve retrieval quality and keep response latency low for technicians as the document collection grows to 12 million documents.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Increase the dimensions of the vector embeddings from 768 to 3,072 and use an AWS Lambda function to remove irrelevant results after retrieval

Increase the number of nearest neighbors that each k-NN query returns and raise the ef_search value of the HNSW index to broaden the candidate results

Implement a two-stage retrieval architecture that uses a machine learning model hosted on Amazon SageMaker AI to rerank the initial vector search results

Correct answer
Configure hybrid search that combines vector similarity search with keyword matching to capture both semantic meaning and exact terms and acronyms

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure hybrid search that combines vector similarity search with keyword matching to capture both semantic meaning and exact terms and acronyms

Dense vector embeddings capture the general meaning of text well, but they often represent exact tokens such as part numbers, fault codes, and acronyms weakly. Two documents can have nearly identical embeddings even when one contains the exact part number a technician needs and the other does not. That explains both symptoms in this scenario. Searches miss exact term matches and return semantically similar but irrelevant documents.

Hybrid search in Amazon OpenSearch Service combines lexical keyword search, based on the BM25 algorithm, with k-NN vector search in a single query. A search pipeline with a normalization processor scales the scores from both methods to a common range and combines them with configurable weights. Documents that match exact terms such as a fault code receive strong lexical scores. Documents that match the intent of the question receive strong semantic scores. The final ranking rewards results that satisfy both.

Hybrid search is a native OpenSearch Service capability, so the provider adds no new services, models, or infrastructure to manage. The provider enables it through query and search pipeline configuration on the existing domain. OpenSearch Service runs both searches efficiently and scales to millions of documents with low latency. This solution improves retrieval quality with the least operational overhead.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/hybrid-search-with-amazon-opensearch-service/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/hybrid-search-with-amazon-opensearch-service/

Incorrect options:

Increase the dimensions of the vector embeddings from 768 to 3,072 and use an AWS Lambda function to remove irrelevant results after retrieval - Increasing embedding dimensions from 768 to 3,072 does not fix the core weakness of dense vectors with exact tokens such as part numbers and acronyms. Larger vectors capture more semantic detail, but they still do not guarantee exact term matching. The change also requires re-embedding all 12 million documents and rebuilding the index.

Larger vectors increase index size, memory consumption, and query latency, which conflicts with the low-latency requirement. A post-processing AWS Lambda function can only remove results after retrieval. It cannot recover relevant documents that the vector search never returned, and it adds custom code to maintain.

Implement a two-stage retrieval architecture that uses a machine learning model hosted on Amazon SageMaker AI to rerank the initial vector search results - A reranking model can improve the ordering of retrieved results, but it can only reorder the candidates that the first-stage vector search returns. If the vector search misses documents with exact part numbers or fault codes, the reranker never sees those documents and cannot fix the recall problem.

Hosting a reranking model on Amazon SageMaker AI adds an endpoint that the provider must deploy, scale, monitor, and pay for. The extra inference step also increases end-to-end latency. This design carries more operational overhead than native hybrid search.

Increase the number of nearest neighbors that each k-NN query returns and raise the ef_search value of the HNSW index to broaden the candidate results - Returning more nearest neighbors and raising the ef_search value makes the approximate k-NN search more thorough within the vector space. However, it still ranks results only by semantic similarity. The additional candidates are likely to be more semantically similar but irrelevant documents, which worsens the reported problem.

Higher ef_search values and larger result sets also increase query latency and compute consumption. As the collection grows to 12 million documents, the latency impact becomes more pronounced. This conflicts with the requirement to keep response latency low.

Correct option:

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows to define a multi step workflow that applies standardized pre processing to inputs and post processing to outputs. Run A/B evaluations by comparing different flow variants and capture metrics automatically. Use the flow structure to ensure consistent handling across all evaluations

Prompt Flows are designed to orchestrate end to end prompt execution with explicit stages. They allow teams to apply consistent pre processing steps before the model invocation and standardized post processing steps after generation. This ensures that every evaluation applies the same transformations in a repeatable way. By defining different flow variants, teams can run controlled comparisons and A B tests without changing application code. The flow itself becomes the unit of experimentation, which simplifies governance and reduces the risk of inconsistent handling. Metrics can be collected uniformly across runs.

This approach directly supports fairness evaluations because it enforces identical handling across groups while allowing controlled variation where needed. It scales well as workflows grow more complex and evaluation requirements expand.

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows to orchestrate model calls, but embed all pre processing and post processing logic inside application code before invoking the flow. Use the flow to route requests and capture outputs. Compare results by toggling code paths during tests - Although Prompt Flows are used, pushing transformation logic into application code undermines their purpose. This splits responsibility across layers and increases the chance of inconsistent behavior between environments or test runs. It also makes experimentation harder to audit. Fairness evaluation benefits from centralized, declarative workflows. Distributing logic into code paths reduces transparency and repeatability.

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to maintain multiple prompt versions, attach metadata for fairness experiments, and leverage downstream systems to interpret and adjust outputs. Coordinate evaluations by switching prompts and correlating results manually across test runs - Prompt Management supports prompt lifecycle control but does not enforce execution order or transformation steps. Relying on downstream systems to adjust outputs introduces variability that is outside the evaluation framework. Manual correlation of results is error prone. This approach does not provide a systematic way to apply identical pre and post processing across experiments. As a result, fairness conclusions may be unreliable.

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to version prompts and manually apply input normalization and output rewriting inside the prompt text. Switch prompt versions during testing to compare results across groups. Log outputs externally for later fairness analysis - Prompt Management focuses on versioning and organizing prompts, not on orchestrating multi step processing. Embedding normalization and rewriting logic directly into prompt text makes behavior harder to reason about and less consistent across evaluations. Manual comparisons also increase the risk of bias in analysis. This approach lacks a structured way to enforce uniform pre processing and post processing. It becomes difficult to guarantee that all test runs apply identical handling.

Which configuration provides the MOST detailed analysis of guardrail decision-making for content filtering?

Correct answer
Enable guardrail tracing by setting {"trace": "enabled"} in the guardrailConfig parameter. Monitor the InvocationsIntervened metric filtered by the GuardrailPolicyType dimension values ContentPolicy, TopicPolicy, and SensitiveInformationPolicy

Run Amazon Bedrock automated model evaluation jobs that include guardrail assessment metrics and test prompt injection resistance with airline-specific test cases. Use the evaluation dashboard to analyze which guardrail policies block malicious content most effectively while preserving legitimate queries

Enable guardrail tracing by setting {"trace": "enabled"} in the guardrailConfig parameter. Monitor the InvocationsIntervened metric filtered by the GuardrailContentSource dimension to identify whether input prompts or output responses triggered each intervention

Create a separate guardrail for each policy type, send every member query through each guardrail in sequence with separate API calls, and infer which policy blocked the query by checking which call returned an intervention, then record the results in a spreadsheet for manual review each week

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Enable guardrail tracing by setting {"trace": "enabled"} in the guardrailConfig parameter. Monitor the InvocationsIntervened metric filtered by the GuardrailPolicyType dimension values ContentPolicy, TopicPolicy, and SensitiveInformationPolicy

When guardrail tracing is enabled in the guardrailConfig parameter of a Converse or InvokeModel request, the response includes a trace with the full guardrail assessment for that request. The trace identifies each policy that evaluated the content and what it found. For content filters, it shows the filter type, such as PROMPT_ATTACK, along with the detection confidence and the action taken. For denied topics, it shows which topic matched. For sensitive information filters, it shows the entity type that was detected, such as an email address or a loyalty number pattern, and whether the content was blocked or masked.

This request-level detail is what the developer needs to tune the guardrail. For example, if legitimate questions about baggage fees are blocked by a denied topic, the trace shows exactly which topic definition matched so that the developer can refine the definition or sample phrases. If genuine member questions trigger the prompt attack filter with low confidence, the developer can adjust the filter strength. The developer can also distinguish real attacks, which usually show high-confidence prompt attack detections, from false positives.

The InvocationsIntervened metric with the GuardrailPolicyType dimension adds an aggregate view across all traffic. It shows how many interventions come from the content policy, the topic policy, and the sensitive information policy, so the developer can see which policy blocks the most requests and whether a configuration change shifts the pattern. Combining detailed request traces with metrics for each policy type gives the most complete analysis of guardrail decision-making.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/safeguard-your-generative-ai-workloads-from-prompt-injections/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/safeguard-your-generative-ai-workloads-from-prompt-injections/

Incorrect options:

Run Amazon Bedrock automated model evaluation jobs that include guardrail assessment metrics and test prompt injection resistance with airline-specific test cases. Use the evaluation dashboard to analyze which guardrail policies block malicious content most effectively while preserving legitimate queries - Automated model evaluation jobs assess model and guardrail performance against a prepared test dataset at a point in time. They are useful for testing configurations before release, but they do not explain why a specific production query from a member was blocked.

Evaluation results summarize performance across test cases rather than providing the decision details for each blocked request. The developer would still lack the request-level policy, detection, and confidence information needed to analyze real interventions.

Create a separate guardrail for each policy type, send every member query through each guardrail in sequence with separate API calls, and infer which policy blocked the query by checking which call returned an intervention, then record the results in a spreadsheet for manual review each week - Running every query through several separate guardrails multiplies API calls, latency, and cost. It also changes how the guardrail is applied in production, so the results might not reflect the behavior of the combined guardrail.

Inferring the cause from which call returned an intervention reveals only the policy type, not the specific topic, entity, or detection confidence. Manual weekly review in a spreadsheet is slow and error prone compared with built-in tracing and metrics.

Enable guardrail tracing by setting {"trace": "enabled"} in the guardrailConfig parameter. Monitor the InvocationsIntervened metric filtered by the GuardrailContentSource dimension to identify whether input prompts or output responses triggered each intervention - Enabling guardrail tracing provides detailed assessments for each request, which is valuable. However, filtering metrics by the GuardrailContentSource dimension shows only whether interventions came from inputs or outputs, not which policy type caused them.

The developer needs to see how interventions are distributed across the policy types to prioritize tuning. The GuardrailPolicyType dimension provides that breakdown, so this option gives a less detailed aggregate view than the correct option.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 31
Skipped
An academic publishing platform is building an application that summarizes submitted research manuscripts at scale. Authors submit manuscripts through an API that is backed by AWS Lambda, and the API writes each incoming manuscript to an Amazon S3 bucket.

The platform wants to use a pretrained foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to summarize each manuscript. The platform must store the summaries in Amazon S3 and make them available through the API. Authors can wait up to 48 hours to receive their summaries. Submission volume fluctuates, with large bursts of traffic before major conference deadlines. The application must be scalable and fault tolerant.

Which approach will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

Deploy the FM on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that runs on GPU instances, configure automatic scaling with a minimum capacity large enough to absorb conference deadline bursts, and invoke the endpoint from the ingestion Lambda function for every manuscript as soon as the manuscript arrives

Configure the ingestion Lambda function to start an AWS Step Functions workflow that runs parallel Lambda tasks. Configure each task to invoke the Amazon Bedrock API to summarize one manuscript and write the summary to Amazon S3, and configure the workflow to retry failed tasks

Configure the ingestion Lambda function to invoke the Amazon Bedrock API immediately for each request and return the summary directly to the author. Store the summaries in Amazon S3

Correct answer
Modify the ingestion Lambda function to send each manuscript to an Amazon SQS queue. Use a Lambda function with a batch window to poll the queue and submit the accumulated manuscripts to the Amazon Bedrock batch inference API

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Modify the ingestion Lambda function to send each manuscript to an Amazon SQS queue. Use a Lambda function with a batch window to poll the queue and submit the accumulated manuscripts to the Amazon Bedrock batch inference API

Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes many prompts from a single JSON Lines file in Amazon S3 and writes the results back to Amazon S3. For select foundation models, batch inference is priced 50% lower than on-demand inference, and a typical job completes within 24 hours. Authors can wait up to 48 hours, so the platform gives up nothing it needs by trading real-time responses for this discount, which makes batch inference the most cost-effective way to run the summarization workload.

Amazon SQS provides a durable buffer between manuscript submission and processing. During bursts before conference deadlines, messages accumulate safely in the queue instead of overwhelming downstream components, and messages that cannot be processed can move to a dead-letter queue for investigation. The polling Lambda function uses a batch window to collect many messages at once, writes the corresponding prompts to a JSON Lines input file in Amazon S3, and calls the CreateModelInvocationJob API to start a batch job.

Accumulating manuscripts before submission also matters because each model enforces a minimum number of records for each batch job, often 100. The batch window and queue let the function wait until enough manuscripts are ready, even during quiet periods. When the job completes, Amazon Bedrock writes the summaries to an output location in Amazon S3 that the API can serve. Every component is serverless and scales automatically, so the design is scalable, fault tolerant, and the lowest-cost option.

Incorrect options:

Configure the ingestion Lambda function to invoke the Amazon Bedrock API immediately for each request and return the summary directly to the author. Store the summaries in Amazon S3 - Invoking Amazon Bedrock synchronously for every request uses on-demand pricing, which costs about twice as much as batch inference for supported models. During bursts, the many simultaneous calls can also exceed on-demand quotas and cause throttling errors.

This design has no queue to buffer traffic and no retry mechanism, so failed requests are lost unless the author resubmits them. Long manuscripts can also push synchronous Lambda invocations toward their timeout. The approach is less fault tolerant and more expensive than necessary.

Deploy the FM on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that runs on GPU instances, configure automatic scaling with a minimum capacity large enough to absorb conference deadline bursts, and invoke the endpoint from the ingestion Lambda function for every manuscript as soon as the manuscript arrives - Running a GPU-based SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with a minimum capacity large enough for bursts means paying for GPU instances continuously, even when submission volume is low. The platform must also manage the endpoint, scaling policies, and model updates.

Real-time inference is unnecessary when authors can wait up to 48 hours. This option adds infrastructure cost and operational effort compared with Amazon Bedrock batch inference.

Configure the ingestion Lambda function to start an AWS Step Functions workflow that runs parallel Lambda tasks. Configure each task to invoke the Amazon Bedrock API to summarize one manuscript and write the summary to Amazon S3, and configure the workflow to retry failed tasks - Step Functions can orchestrate parallel tasks with retries, but each Lambda task invokes Amazon Bedrock with on-demand pricing. Step Functions Standard workflows also charge for each state transition, which adds cost at scale.

Without a buffering queue, sudden bursts can start many parallel executions that compete for on-demand model capacity and trigger throttling. This option is more complex and more expensive than batch inference.

Question 32

A ride sharing company is developing a Driver Risk Assistant that evaluates structured telemetry data, such as speed readings, acceleration patterns, braking events, and categorical driver ratings, to generate short natural language risk insights. The system should need minimum infrastructure management and must respond in under 400 milliseconds as well as scale to millions of requests per day while ensuring very low inference cost. It must also minimize hallucinations because risk insights feed into regulatory reporting and insurance calculations. The output must follow a strict JSON schema so that downstream safety analytics systems can reliably parse and aggregate the results.

Which solution should the architect choose to meet all these requirements?

Correct answer
Use a Titan Text Lite model configured with JSON mode or function calling so that outputs follow a predefined schema, and integrate response streaming via Amazon Bedrock Converse API to reduce token first latency

Use an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base to embed telemetry events and perform semantic searches for similar historical driving patterns, then generate a risk summary using a Titan text model. Aggregate retrieved examples and form the final structured JSON output from the model response

Deploy a large fine tuned transformer model on Amazon SageMaker GPU instances and scale it with automatic instance count adjustments. Train the model specifically on telemetry data to improve risk reasoning accuracy while maintaining a consistent schema through custom post processing code in the inference container

Use a Claude 3 Sonnet configuration to generate risk insights, and rely on prompt engineering to enforce schema rules. Adjust temperature and top p values to reduce hallucinations and improve consistency across high traffic scenarios

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use a Titan Text Lite model configured with JSON mode or function calling so that outputs follow a predefined schema, and integrate response streaming via Amazon Bedrock Converse API to reduce token first latency

Titan Text Lite is designed for low latency and cost efficient inference, which makes it ideal for workloads that require sub 400 millisecond responses at very high scale. When JSON mode or function calling is enabled, the model produces deterministic and machine readable outputs that conform to the required schema. This eliminates the need for fragile post processing logic and ensures that risk scoring pipelines downstream can trust the structure of the model generated content.

Because the telemetry inputs are short and mostly structured, Titan Text Lite can process them quickly and predictably without the overhead of a larger reasoning oriented model. The use of streaming in the Amazon Bedrock Converse API further reduces first token latency, helping meet the strict performance boundary. This combination meets the company’s needs for predictability, speed, low hallucination risk, and cost efficiency, all while maintaining a stable schema controlled output for downstream analytics systems.

Incorrect options:

Use a Claude 3 Sonnet configuration to generate risk insights, and rely on prompt engineering to enforce schema rules. Adjust temperature and top p values to reduce hallucinations and improve consistency across high traffic scenarios - Claude 3 Sonnet is more capable but has a higher latency and cost profile, which makes it less suitable for a system that must consistently respond in under 400 milliseconds at massive scale. Relying on prompt engineering alone to enforce a schema also introduces variability in structural accuracy because schema correctness is not guaranteed by the model without JSON mode or function calling.

Deploy a large fine tuned transformer model on Amazon SageMaker GPU instances and scale it with automatic instance count adjustments. Train the model specifically on telemetry data to improve risk reasoning accuracy while maintaining a consistent schema through custom post processing code in the inference container - Hosting a custom fine tuned model on SageMaker requires managing GPU instances, autoscaling settings, container logic, and schema enforcement code. This introduces significant operational overhead that contradicts the need for minimal infrastructure management. It also increases cost and latency due to the overhead of maintaining and running a large transformer model.

Use an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base to embed telemetry events and perform semantic searches for similar historical driving patterns, then generate a risk summary using a Titan text model. Aggregate retrieved examples and form the final structured JSON output from the model response - Knowledge Bases are intended for retrieval augmented generation and rely on embedding vectors to fetch relevant context. Telemetry data consisting of numeric readings, timestamped events, and categorical values is not an appropriate match for semantic retrieval. It also introduces unnecessary retrieval latency which would violate the sub 400 millisecond requirement.

An airline is building a generative AI (GenAI) application for its contact centers. The application analyzes live customer calls and generates suggested responses for human agents in real time. The application must handle 300,000 concurrent calls during peak travel periods and must deliver each suggestion with less than 150 ms of end-to-end latency. The airline already has an architecture that transcribes the call audio streams. The application must stay within a fixed quarterly compute budget and must support automatic scaling.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Deploy a low-latency model that is optimized for real-time inference on Amazon Bedrock. Purchase Provisioned Throughput and configure automatic scaling policies

Package a small open-source language model in an AWS Lambda container image, configure provisioned concurrency that covers the full 300,000-call peak at all times to avoid cold starts, and run inference on the Lambda CPUs so that the airline pays only for the compute that each suggestion consumes

Deploy a large, complex reasoning model on Amazon Bedrock. Purchase Provisioned Throughput and optimize the application for batch processing

Deploy a large language model (LLM) on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that runs on dedicated GPU instances

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Deploy a low-latency model that is optimized for real-time inference on Amazon Bedrock. Purchase Provisioned Throughput and configure automatic scaling policies

A latency budget of 150 ms for each suggestion leaves very little time for model inference. Smaller models that are optimized for real-time inference generate short outputs, such as a suggested agent reply, much faster than large reasoning models. Amazon Bedrock also offers latency-optimized inference for supported models, which reduces time to first token and overall response time. Choosing a fast, right-sized model is the most important decision for meeting a strict latency target at high concurrency.

Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated model capacity, measured in model units, for the airline's workload. With reserved capacity, requests during peak travel periods are not throttled by shared on-demand quotas, and latency stays consistent at 300,000 concurrent calls. Provisioned Throughput also has predictable pricing, which lets the airline plan capacity against its fixed quarterly compute budget instead of absorbing variable on-demand charges during peaks.

Automatic scaling policies adjust capacity to match demand. The airline can use Amazon CloudWatch metrics, such as invocations and latency, to trigger capacity changes. It can add capacity ahead of known peak travel periods and reduce it during quieter periods so that it does not pay for idle capacity. Combining a real-time optimized model, reserved throughput, and scaling policies meets the latency, concurrency, budget, and scaling requirements with a managed service.

Optimizing AI responsiveness: A practical guide to Amazon Bedrock latency-optimized inference:

Incorrect options:

Deploy a large, complex reasoning model on Amazon Bedrock. Purchase Provisioned Throughput and optimize the application for batch processing - Large, complex reasoning models are designed for multistep analysis and often generate long intermediate reasoning before they answer. That processing typically takes seconds, not milliseconds, so these models cannot meet a 150 ms latency requirement for each suggestion.

Batch processing groups requests and processes them together, which increases the time before any individual result is available. Real-time agent assistance requires an immediate response for each call. This option conflicts with the latency requirement and increases cost for capacity the use case does not need.

Deploy a large language model (LLM) on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that runs on dedicated GPU instances - Hosting an LLM on dedicated GPU instances can deliver low latency for individual requests, but supporting 300,000 concurrent calls would require a very large fleet of GPU instances. The cost of that fleet would likely exceed the fixed quarterly compute budget, especially for peak capacity that sits idle outside travel periods.

The option also does not configure auto scaling, and the airline would need to manage instance selection, model optimization, scaling, and endpoint operations itself. A large LLM is also slower than a model optimized for real-time inference, which makes the 150 ms target harder to meet.

Package a small open-source language model in an AWS Lambda container image, configure provisioned concurrency that covers the full 300,000-call peak at all times to avoid cold starts, and run inference on the Lambda CPUs so that the airline pays only for the compute that each suggestion consumes - Running language model inference on Lambda CPUs is far slower than GPU-backed or managed FM inference, so each suggestion would take much longer than 150 ms. Lambda also has concurrency limits for each account and Region, and supporting 300,000 concurrent executions would require large quota increases.

Provisioned concurrency that covers the full peak at all times charges for that capacity continuously, including outside peak travel periods. That contradicts the goal of paying only for consumed compute and threatens the fixed quarterly budget. This option fails the latency requirement and the cost requirement.

Question 34
Skipped
A telecommunications company is using Amazon Bedrock to build a customer-facing AI assistant that handles sensitive account requests, such as billing disputes and SIM card replacement inquiries. The company must implement defense-in-depth safety controls that block sophisticated prompt injection and jailbreak attempts. The company must retain audit logs of every safety intervention. The AI assistant must also provide cross-Region failover capabilities.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Create Amazon Bedrock guardrail denied topics that describe common prompt injection techniques, deploy identical guardrails in a secondary Region by using AWS CloudFormation StackSets, configure Amazon Route 53 health checks to fail over the application endpoint, and rely on AWS CloudTrail management events to record each guardrail intervention

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with content filters set to HIGH to protect against prompt injection attacks. Use AWS WAF to block suspicious inputs and use AWS CloudTrail to log API calls for audits

Correct answer
Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with the prompt attack content filter set to HIGH to block prompt injection attacks. Use a guardrail profile to enable cross-Region guardrail inference, and capture detailed guardrail intervention events in Amazon CloudWatch Logs with custom metrics

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with custom content filters set to HIGH to protect against harmful content and add word filters for known attack patterns. Configure cross-Region guardrail replication for failover and store the logs in AWS CloudTrail for compliance audits

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with the prompt attack content filter set to HIGH to block prompt injection attacks. Use a guardrail profile to enable cross-Region guardrail inference, and capture detailed guardrail intervention events in Amazon CloudWatch Logs with custom metrics

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails includes a prompt attack filter in its content filter policies. It detects jailbreak attempts, which try to bypass the model's safety behavior, and prompt injection attacks, which embed instructions that override the developer's system instructions. Setting the filter strength to HIGH applies the most aggressive detection. The guardrail evaluates every input before it reaches the model and evaluates outputs before they reach the customer. Combined with the other guardrail policies, such as content filters and sensitive information filters, this creates layered controls around the model rather than relying on any single protection.

A guardrail profile enables cross-Region inference for guardrails. With a guardrail profile, Amazon Bedrock can distribute guardrail evaluation across multiple Regions within a geographic area, which improves throughput and keeps guardrail processing available during capacity constraints or disruptions in a single Region. Using a guardrail profile is also a prerequisite for the Standard safeguard tier, which provides more robust prompt attack detection. This meets the cross-Region failover requirement for the safety layer without the company building its own replication.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails publishes metrics such as InvocationsIntervened to Amazon CloudWatch, and model invocation logging can deliver the guardrail trace and assessment details to CloudWatch Logs. The logs record which policy intervened, what action was taken, and when. Custom metrics derived from these logs let the security team track attack trends and alert on spikes. The retained log groups provide the durable audit trail of every safety intervention that the company requires.

Incorrect options:

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with content filters set to HIGH to protect against prompt injection attacks. Use AWS WAF to block suspicious inputs and use AWS CloudTrail to log API calls for audits - AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests for patterns such as SQL injection or malicious IP addresses. It does not understand the meaning of natural language prompts, so it cannot reliably detect sophisticated prompt injection or jailbreak attempts that use ordinary language. Adding WAF provides little additional protection for this threat.

AWS CloudTrail records API calls, such as who invoked a model and when. It does not capture the details of guardrail interventions, such as which policy blocked a prompt. This option also provides no cross-Region failover capability, so it fails two of the three requirements.

Create Amazon Bedrock guardrail denied topics that describe common prompt injection techniques, deploy identical guardrails in a secondary Region by using AWS CloudFormation StackSets, configure Amazon Route 53 health checks to fail over the application endpoint, and rely on AWS CloudTrail management events to record each guardrail intervention - Denied topics block conversations about subject areas that the company defines, such as investment advice. They are not designed to detect the structural techniques of prompt injection and jailbreak attacks, which can target any topic. The prompt attack filter is the purpose-built control.

Maintaining duplicate guardrails across Regions with AWS CloudFormation StackSets and Route 53 health checks adds operational work that guardrail profiles avoid. AWS CloudTrail management events record configuration changes, not individual guardrail interventions during inference. The audit requirement would therefore remain unmet.

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with custom content filters set to HIGH to protect against harmful content and add word filters for known attack patterns. Configure cross-Region guardrail replication for failover and store the logs in AWS CloudTrail for compliance audits - Custom content filters and word filters focus on harmful content categories and exact matches. Word filters can block known phrases, but sophisticated prompt injection attacks vary their wording to avoid exact matches. This option does not enable the prompt attack filter, which is the guardrail feature designed for these attacks.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails does not offer a cross-Region guardrail replication feature. Cross-Region resilience for guardrails comes from guardrail profiles. AWS CloudTrail also does not store detailed records of guardrail interventions. This option relies on a capability that does not exist and an inappropriate logging service.

EventBridge rules provide an event driven mechanism to detect small document updates and trigger Lambda functions for lightweight embedding refresh operations. S3 or application level events can trigger Lambda for urgent corrections, enabling immediate updates that propagate quickly through the vector index.
