This workflow ensures long term consistency, handles embedding drift, and resets index fragmentation. It complements incremental updates and creates a predictable maintenance cycle.

Incorrect options:

Use an hourly AWS Batch job to reprocess all documents and regenerate embeddings, with manual triggers for urgent updates - Reprocessing all documents every hour is inefficient and does not meet the need for lightweight incremental updates or immediate urgent corrections. Manual intervention also introduces operational delays and risk.

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service ingestion pipelines for all changes and rely on scheduled cron based reprocessing for full index replacement - Batch reprocessing on a schedule is not sufficient for urgent corrections and does not provide incremental update efficiency. This method applies uniform processing instead of combining real-time, incremental, and quarterly refresh workflows.

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a quarterly document sync job for full index rebuild - The option is incorrect because it replaces the existing vector store with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases instead of providing a maintenance architecture that supports incremental updates, real-time urgent corrections, and quarterly rebuilds for the current vector index.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 36
Skipped
A food delivery platform runs a generative AI (GenAI) support assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock to answer customer questions in real time. During the evening dinner rush, the platform sees intermittent failures in API calls to the foundation models (FMs), including throttling exceptions and temporary service errors.

The platform needs a solution that handles transient errors and provides detailed observability into FM performance. The solution must prevent cascading failures during throttling events and must provide distributed tracing across service boundaries to identify the components that contribute to latency. The solution must also make it possible to correlate performance issues with specific FM characteristics, such as the model ID and the prompt size.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Implement a custom retry mechanism with a fixed delay of 2 seconds between retries. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor the application error rates and latency metrics

Correct answer
Configure the AWS SDK to use standard retry mode with exponential backoff and jitter. Use AWS X-Ray tracing with annotations to identify and filter service components

Configure the AWS SDK to use adaptive retry mode and use AWS CloudTrail distributed tracing to monitor throttling events

Increase the maximum number of retry attempts in the AWS SDK to 20 and remove the delay between retries so that failed requests are resent immediately

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure the AWS SDK to use standard retry mode with exponential backoff and jitter. Use AWS X-Ray tracing with annotations to identify and filter service components

Throttling exceptions and temporary service errors are transient, so a well-designed retry strategy can recover from them automatically. Standard retry mode in the AWS SDK retries these errors with exponential backoff, which increases the wait time after each failed attempt. Jitter adds randomness to each wait time, so thousands of clients that fail at the same moment do not retry in synchronized waves that overwhelm the service again.

Standard retry mode also includes a retry quota that limits how many retries a client can make when failures increase. When the quota is exhausted, the client stops retrying and fails fast instead of adding more load to a struggling service. Together, backoff, jitter, and the retry quota prevent retry storms and the cascading failures that occur when retries amplify throttling during peak demand.

AWS X-Ray traces each request as it flows across service boundaries, such as from Amazon API Gateway to AWS Lambda to Amazon Bedrock. Its service map and trace timelines show which components contribute the most latency. Annotations are indexed key-value pairs that the application adds to traces, such as the model ID, prompt token count, and inference configuration. Engineers can use filter expressions on these annotations to find slow or failed traces for a specific model or prompt size, which correlates performance issues with specific FM characteristics.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/

Incorrect options:

Implement a custom retry mechanism with a fixed delay of 2 seconds between retries. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor the application error rates and latency metrics - A fixed delay between retries causes clients that fail at the same time to retry at the same time, which creates synchronized bursts that can trigger more throttling. Without exponential backoff, jitter, or a retry limit based on failure rates, this approach can amplify load during peak periods and contribute to cascading failures.

CloudWatch alarms on error rates and latency show that problems exist, but they do not provide distributed tracing across service boundaries. They also cannot correlate latency with specific FM characteristics, so this option fails the observability requirements.

Increase the maximum number of retry attempts in the AWS SDK to 20 and remove the delay between retries so that failed requests are resent immediately - Removing the delay between retries causes failed requests to be resent instantly. During throttling, this floods the service with additional requests, which increases throttling and can cause cascading failures across the application.

Raising the retry limit to 20 makes the problem worse, because each failed request can generate many more calls. This option also provides no distributed tracing or correlation of performance issues with FM characteristics.

Configure the AWS SDK to use adaptive retry mode and use AWS CloudTrail distributed tracing to monitor throttling events - Adaptive retry mode adds client-side rate limiting on top of standard retry behavior, which can help in some throttling scenarios. However, AWS CloudTrail does not provide distributed tracing. CloudTrail records API activity for auditing, such as who called which API and when, but it does not trace requests across services or measure latency within each component.

Without a tracing service, the platform cannot identify the components that contribute to latency or correlate performance issues with FM characteristics. This option fails the observability requirements.

An insurance company is building a GenAI workflow that processes claims descriptions in multiple languages and varying complexity and uses different specialized models for triage, summarization, and risk classification. The company wants to select the appropriate model based on language, token length, and content category and also evolve routing rules over time using performance metrics such as latency, cost, and human quality scores stored in an operational metrics store. You are responsible for designing an orchestration workflow that can apply content based routing, use metric driven rules for model selection, and support confidence based cascading between models.

Which two approaches should you implement to design this intelligent routing workflow so that it can adapt to content characteristics and observed model performance? (Select two)

Correct selection
Use Step Functions with a Lambda pre processing task to compute language, token length, and content attributes and pass them to Choice states for routing to the triage, summarization, or risk classification model. Store performance metrics in DynamoDB and have a Lambda task read these metrics at runtime to adjust routing thresholds dynamically

Implement a single Lambda function with hardcoded if else rules to select models based on language and token length and store metrics only as CloudWatch Logs. Rely on manual review of CloudWatch dashboards to determine when to update or redeploy routing rules

Use Step Functions with a Lambda pre processing task that computes language and token length, then call a metrics evaluation Lambda function to read latency and quality data from DynamoDB before routing to a Bedrock model. Apply Choice states only after the model inference step so the workflow can examine the generated output and decide whether to invoke a backup model

Use Step Functions Choice states with routing rules fixed by values stored in Parameter Store and update thresholds manually through configuration changes. Write latency and quality metrics to DynamoDB but use them only for offline dashboards rather than feeding them into the real time routing logic

Correct selection
Use Step Functions Map or Parallel states to branch decisions and insert a metrics evaluation Lambda task that reads historical performance data to compute confidence scores before selecting the model. Implement a cascading workflow that invokes a primary model first and conditionally calls a backup model when confidence or quality thresholds from the metrics store are not met

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Use Step Functions with a Lambda pre processing task to compute language, token length, and content attributes and pass them to Choice states for routing to the triage, summarization, or risk classification model. Store performance metrics in DynamoDB and have a Lambda task read these metrics at runtime to adjust routing thresholds dynamically

Step Functions is well suited for orchestrating GenAI workflows that need clear state transitions, branching logic, and structured routing. A Lambda pre processing task can determine language, token length, and content features and feed them into Choice states that map cleanly to selection of triage, summarization, or risk classification models. This pattern maintains readability, auditability, and compliance while keeping routing logic declarative.

Creating workflows with Step Functions:  via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/welcome.html

Using DynamoDB as a metrics store allows runtime access to key performance data such as latency trends, cost changes, or quality score drift. A metrics evaluation task inside the state machine can read these values to adjust routing dynamically without redeploying code, enabling adaptive systems that respond to real usage data.

This architecture ensures that model selection adapts to both content complexities and real time or historical performance signals. It also supports controlled evolution of routing policies and integrates cleanly with confidence based fallback behavior.

Use Step Functions Map or Parallel states to branch decisions and insert a metrics evaluation Lambda task that reads historical performance data to compute confidence scores before selecting the model. Implement a cascading workflow that invokes a primary model first and conditionally calls a backup model when confidence or quality thresholds from the metrics store are not met

Using Step Functions Map or Parallel states provides a flexible structure for building multi stage workflows that can evaluate metrics, compute confidence, and then route requests accordingly. A metrics evaluation Lambda function can retrieve historical performance values such as latency percentiles or quality scores and apply formulas to compute confidence levels, which informs whether to invoke the primary or secondary model. This supports iterative improvement and continuous learning from live traffic.

A cascading pattern allows the workflow to invoke a primary model first and check the output quality or confidence against thresholds informed by the metrics store. When thresholds are not met, Step Functions can branch to call a backup model, enabling safety nets for high risk decisions and improving accuracy without dramatically increasing complexity.

This approach combines dynamic routing, metrics informed logic, and a fallback mechanism tailored to the business domain. It enables routing selection to adapt over time as models improve, degrade, or vary by content category.

Incorrect options:

Use Step Functions Choice states with routing rules fixed by values stored in Parameter Store and update thresholds manually through configuration changes. Write latency and quality metrics to DynamoDB but use them only for offline dashboards rather than feeding them into the real time routing logic - Using Parameter Store to supply static routing rules limits adaptability because routing thresholds cannot change in real time based on model performance. Even though metrics are written to DynamoDB, they are never used by the routing logic, so the workflow cannot evolve with real world latency, cost, or quality patterns. This creates a system that behaves exactly the same regardless of how models perform, which breaks the requirement for metric driven routing. The architecture also prevents confidence based cascading because performance data is not consulted during model selection.

Implement a single Lambda function with hardcoded if else rules to select models based on language and token length and store metrics only as CloudWatch Logs. Rely on manual review of CloudWatch dashboards to determine when to update or redeploy routing rules - Hardcoding model routing logic directly inside a Lambda function makes the workflow rigid and difficult to evolve because any change in thresholds requires manual code changes and redeployment. Writing metrics only to CloudWatch Logs instead of a structured store prevents automated routing based on performance signals. The lack of orchestration or dynamic evaluation prevents adaptive behavior, and the workflow cannot support multi stage or cascading logic. There is no mechanism for using runtime data to alter routing decisions based on content type or model performance.

Use Step Functions with a Lambda pre processing task that computes language and token length, then call a metrics evaluation Lambda function to read latency and quality data from DynamoDB before routing to a Bedrock model. Apply Choice states only after the model inference step so the workflow can examine the generated output and decide whether to invoke a backup model - Placing the Choice state after the initial model invocation breaks the requirement to route based on content characteristics before inference, which wastes model capacity and increases latency because every request is forced through at least one model call. Even though the workflow appears to incorporate metrics, the routing logic is reactive rather than proactive, making it impossible to select the correct model upfront based on language, token length, category, or performance thresholds. The architecture also prevents true confidence based cascading because the first model is always invoked regardless of content type or performance metrics, which defeats the purpose of adaptive routing. This approach increases unnecessary model usage and does not satisfy the need for dynamic model selection prior to invoking specialized models.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 38
Skipped
An energy utility is using Amazon Bedrock to build an AI advisory application that recommends home energy efficiency upgrades to residential customers. The application must explain its reasoning and cite the specific sources behind its data. The application must retrieve information from the utility's internal data sources, such as rebate program guides and tariff schedules, and must show step-by-step reasoning for each recommendation. The application must also link each data claim to its source document and keep response latency under 2.5 seconds.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Fine-tune an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock on the utility's rebate guides and tariff schedules so that the model learns the content and cites the source documents from memory

Correct answer
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with source attribution enabled. Call an Anthropic Claude model through the Messages API with RAG and apply high relevance thresholds to the source documents. Store the reasoning and citations in Amazon S3 for auditing

Configure Amazon SageMaker AI to host a custom Anthropic Claude model and use the model's reasoning parameter. Use AWS Lambda to process the responses and add source citations from a separate Amazon RDS database

Use Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic Claude models and extended thinking. Configure a 6,000-token thinking budget and store the reasoning traces and citations in Amazon DynamoDB for auditing

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with source attribution enabled. Call an Anthropic Claude model through the Messages API with RAG and apply high relevance thresholds to the source documents. Store the reasoning and citations in Amazon S3 for auditing

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) workflow over the utility's internal data sources. The knowledge base ingests, chunks, embeds, and indexes the rebate program guides and tariff schedules, and it retrieves the most relevant passages for each customer question. The utility does not need to build or operate its own retrieval pipeline, which keeps operational overhead low.

Source attribution is built into the knowledge base response. The RetrieveAndGenerate API returns citations that map each portion of the generated text to the specific retrieved chunks and their source document locations. That directly links every data claim to its source document. Applying high relevance thresholds to retrieval limits the context to strongly matching passages. This improves citation accuracy and keeps the prompt small, which helps the response stay within the 2.5-second latency target.

The utility can customize the knowledge base prompt template to instruct the Claude model to present concise step-by-step reasoning that explains how each recommendation follows from the cited sources. Storing the reasoning and citations in Amazon S3 provides a durable, low-cost audit trail. Writing to S3 happens outside the response path, so it does not add latency for customers. This design meets the explainability, attribution, retrieval, and latency requirements with managed services.

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic Claude models and extended thinking. Configure a 6,000-token thinking budget and store the reasoning traces and citations in Amazon DynamoDB for auditing - Extended thinking lets a Claude model reason internally before it answers, but a 6,000-token thinking budget adds substantial generation time to every request. That processing makes it very unlikely that responses stay under the 2.5-second latency requirement.

Extended thinking also does not retrieve information from the utility's data sources or link claims to source documents. Without a retrieval layer and built-in source attribution, the application cannot cite specific documents reliably. This design fails both the latency and the attribution requirements.

Configure Amazon SageMaker AI to host a custom Anthropic Claude model and use the model's reasoning parameter. Use AWS Lambda to process the responses and add source citations from a separate Amazon RDS database - Anthropic Claude models are available through Amazon Bedrock as a managed service, not as custom models that a customer hosts on Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints. Hosting and scaling a custom model, even if possible, adds infrastructure that the utility must manage, patch, and monitor.

Adding citations from a separate Amazon RDS database after generation requires custom logic to match claims to sources. That logic is prone to errors and adds latency. This design has far more operational overhead than a managed knowledge base with built-in source attribution.

Fine-tune an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock on the utility's rebate guides and tariff schedules so that the model learns the content and cites the source documents from memory - Fine-tuning changes a model's weights so that it absorbs patterns from training data, but the model does not retain reliable links to specific source documents. A fine-tuned model can produce confident but unverifiable references, which fails the requirement to link each data claim to its source document.

Rebate programs and tariff schedules change over time, so the utility would need to retrain the model repeatedly to keep it current. Fine-tuned models also require Provisioned Throughput to run. This approach adds cost and operational overhead compared with RAG.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 39
Skipped
A pharmaceutical manufacturer is building an internal generative AI (GenAI) assistant on Amazon Bedrock to summarize corporate documents for several departments. Every response from the assistant must follow the same structure: an executive summary, a rating of compliance risks, and a list of clauses that require further review. The assistant must adjust the tone of each response to match the requesting employee's department, such as regulatory affairs, procurement, or clinical operations. The assistant must block harassment, prohibited topics, and sensitive information such as patient medical record numbers.

The manufacturer needs a solution to centrally manage prompt variants for 14 departments and their teams. The manufacturer wants to minimize ongoing orchestration work and the maintenance of post-processing logic. The manufacturer also wants the ability to refine the assistant's content moderation criteria over time.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST maintenance overhead?

Correct answer
Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to create reusable prompt templates with a variant for each department. Attach Amazon Bedrock guardrails that use content filter categories and sensitive term lists to block prohibited content

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to define base prompt templates and enforce department-specific tone through system prompt variables. Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to apply audience-based threshold tuning and manage the guardrails through an internal administration API

Inject department-specific instructions into each Amazon Bedrock API call and store the response formatting rules in Amazon DynamoDB. Use AWS Step Functions to validate each response and use Amazon Comprehend to filter content after the assistant generates each response

Create a separate Amazon Bedrock agent for each department with department-specific instructions, attach an action group that calls an AWS Lambda function to reformat every response into the required structure, and configure Amazon Macie to scan the agent outputs that are stored in Amazon S3 for sensitive data before employees can view the summaries

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to create reusable prompt templates with a variant for each department. Attach Amazon Bedrock guardrails that use content filter categories and sensitive term lists to block prohibited content

Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management provides a central, fully managed repository for prompt templates. The manufacturer can define one template that fixes the required output structure of an executive summary, a compliance risk rating, and a list of clauses for review. It can then create a variant for each department that adjusts the tone for regulatory affairs, procurement, clinical operations, and the other groups. Prompt Management supports versioning, variables, and side-by-side comparison of variants. Teams can refine prompts and publish new versions without building or maintaining their own prompt storage and selection logic.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforces content moderation as a managed policy layer instead of custom post-processing code. Content filters block harmful categories such as hate, insults, and misconduct. Denied topics block prohibited subject areas, word filters block specific terms, and sensitive information filters detect or mask personally identifiable information and custom patterns, such as patient medical record numbers. The guardrail evaluates both prompts and responses, so the manufacturer does not need separate validation or filtering pipelines.

This combination directly supports the requirement to refine moderation criteria over time. Administrators can adjust filter strengths, add denied topics, or extend sensitive term lists, and then publish a new guardrail version. The prompts and application code do not need to change. Because both Prompt Management and Guardrails are native Amazon Bedrock features, the manufacturer avoids orchestration workflows, custom databases, and post-processing functions. This design has the least maintenance overhead.

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to define base prompt templates and enforce department-specific tone through system prompt variables. Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to apply audience-based threshold tuning and manage the guardrails through an internal administration API - Amazon Bedrock Guardrails does not provide an audience-based threshold tuning feature that changes filter behavior based on the requesting department. To approximate this behavior, the manufacturer would need to create and select among multiple guardrails through custom application logic.

Managing the guardrails through an internal administration API also adds a custom component that the manufacturer must build, secure, and maintain. Relying only on system prompt variables for tone, instead of managed variants, gives up the versioning and comparison benefits of Prompt Management. This design adds maintenance overhead instead of reducing it.

Inject department-specific instructions into each Amazon Bedrock API call and store the response formatting rules in Amazon DynamoDB. Use AWS Step Functions to validate each response and use Amazon Comprehend to filter content after the assistant generates each response - Injecting instructions into every API call and storing formatting rules in Amazon DynamoDB spreads prompt logic across application code and a custom data store. The manufacturer must maintain the injection code, the rule schema, and the synchronization between them, which works against the goal of central prompt management.

AWS Step Functions validation workflows and Amazon Comprehend post-generation filtering create exactly the orchestration and post-processing logic the manufacturer wants to avoid. Filtering only after generation also leaves user inputs unchecked. Every change to the moderation criteria requires updates to custom workflow code.

Create a separate Amazon Bedrock agent for each department with department-specific instructions, attach an action group that calls an AWS Lambda function to reformat every response into the required structure, and configure Amazon Macie to scan the agent outputs that are stored in Amazon S3 for sensitive data before employees can view the summaries - Amazon Bedrock Agents is designed to orchestrate multistep tasks with tools and knowledge bases. Using it only to apply department-specific instructions to a summarization prompt adds unnecessary orchestration. A separate agent for each department multiplies the resources the manufacturer must configure and maintain, and the Lambda-based reformatting step is custom post-processing code.

Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3 objects for data security and posture management. It is not an inline content moderation control for GenAI responses. It does not block harassment or prohibited topics, and scanning stored outputs adds delay and storage steps that a guardrail avoids entirely.

A multinational online travel marketplace runs an itinerary generation service that must switch among several foundation models (FMs) in Amazon Bedrock based on data residency regulations, cost targets, and response quality goals. The marketplace must enforce custom controls that come from proprietary business logic. These controls include dynamic spending limits, compliance rules that differ by AWS Region, and live A/B experiments across multiple FMs. The service must be able to change the FM it uses without deploying new code.

The service must route each traveler request based on detailed rules that consider the traveler's loyalty tier, the booking value, the traveler's regulatory jurisdiction, and live token cost data. The cost data changes every 30 minutes, and each change must take effect immediately across more than 25,000 concurrent requests.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Store the routing rules and Amazon Bedrock FM IDs as environment variables in an AWS Lambda function. Update the environment variables in the Lambda console when business requirements change. Configure an Amazon API Gateway REST API to read request parameters and make the routing decisions to choose the appropriate FM

Configure AWS Lambda authorizers on an Amazon API Gateway REST API to evaluate routing rules that are stored in AWS AppConfig. Return authorization context values based on the business logic and route each request to a dedicated Lambda function for each Amazon Bedrock FM

Correct answer
Configure an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the routing configuration from the AWS AppConfig Agent for every traveler request. Run the business logic in the Lambda function to choose the appropriate FM for each request. Expose the service through a single Amazon API Gateway REST API endpoint

Configure Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing with a prompt router that spans the candidate FMs and send every traveler request to the prompt router ARN

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the routing configuration from the AWS AppConfig Agent for every traveler request. Run the business logic in the Lambda function to choose the appropriate FM for each request. Expose the service through a single Amazon API Gateway REST API endpoint

AWS AppConfig is built to manage dynamic application configuration and feature flags separately from application code. The marketplace can store its routing rules in an AppConfig configuration profile, including tier mappings, booking value bands, jurisdiction rules, spending limits, and A/B allocation percentages. Engineers or automated processes can update the rules without changing or redeploying the Lambda function. AppConfig validators can check each new configuration against a JSON schema or a Lambda validator before deployment, which protects the service from malformed rules.

The AWS AppConfig Agent runs as a Lambda extension alongside the function. It retrieves the latest configuration, caches it locally, and refreshes it in the background at a configurable polling interval. The function reads the configuration from a local endpoint on every request, so lookups add almost no latency and do not overload the AppConfig service at 25,000 concurrent requests. When the cost data changes every 30 minutes, the marketplace can deploy the new configuration with an immediate deployment strategy. Every running function picks up the change on its next poll without a cold start or a new deployment.

Running the routing logic inside the Lambda function gives the marketplace full programming flexibility to combine loyalty tier, booking value, jurisdiction, and live cost data in any way the business requires. The function can call the selected FM through the Amazon Bedrock runtime API by using the model ID from the configuration. A single Amazon API Gateway endpoint keeps the client contract stable while the model choice changes behind it. AppConfig also supports multi-variant feature flags and automatic rollback on Amazon CloudWatch alarms, which supports safe A/B experiments across FMs.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/using-aws-appconfig-feature-flags/

Incorrect options:

Configure Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing with a prompt router that spans the candidate FMs and send every traveler request to the prompt router ARN - Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing chooses between models within the same model family. It routes based on the predicted response quality and cost for each prompt. The routing criteria are internal to the service and cannot be extended with proprietary business rules.

The prompt router cannot consider the traveler's loyalty tier, the booking value, the regulatory jurisdiction, or custom spending limits. It also does not support controlled A/B experiments with allocations that the marketplace defines. It cannot meet the requirement for custom routing controls.

Configure AWS Lambda authorizers on an Amazon API Gateway REST API to evaluate routing rules that are stored in AWS AppConfig. Return authorization context values based on the business logic and route each request to a dedicated Lambda function for each Amazon Bedrock FM - Lambda authorizers are designed to authenticate and authorize API callers, not to make model routing decisions. API Gateway can cache authorizer results for up to 1 hour, which means cached routing decisions could keep sending traffic to an outdated FM after the cost data changes. This conflicts with the requirement for immediate propagation.

Dedicated Lambda functions for each FM also mean that adding a new model requires a new function, a new integration, and a new route. Those changes are code and infrastructure deployments, which violates the requirement to switch FMs without deploying new code. The design also duplicates logic across many functions and increases the maintenance burden.

Store the routing rules and Amazon Bedrock FM IDs as environment variables in an AWS Lambda function. Update the environment variables in the Lambda console when business requirements change. Configure an Amazon API Gateway REST API to read request parameters and make the routing decisions to choose the appropriate FM - Lambda environment variables are static values that are set in the function configuration. Every change requires a configuration update to the function, which forces new execution environments and cold starts. Environment variables also have a total size limit of 4 KB, which constrains complex rule sets, and manual console updates provide no validation, staged rollout, or automatic rollback.

This design cannot propagate cost changes every 30 minutes in a controlled and reliable way across thousands of concurrent requests. Having API Gateway read request parameters also cannot apply the combined business logic that the marketplace requires. The solution does not meet the dynamic routing requirements.

Question 41

A global tax advisory firm is building an AI assistant that uses Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to help clients understand their tax obligations. The firm wants the assistant to deliver near real-time, low-latency responses. The assistant must serve clients in North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. Clients will use the assistant with their confidential financial records, and these records must not leave the client's own geographic area.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Deploy one Amazon Bedrock knowledge base in a single AWS Region and invoke the model through a global cross-Region inference profile so that requests from every geographic area can use capacity in any Region

Deploy an AWS Outposts rack in each AWS Region where the firm operates and create Amazon S3 buckets that store the knowledge bases in each Region. Deploy Amazon RDS as a vector database on each Outpost and deploy an Amazon Bedrock model with a cross-Region inference profile in a central Region

Correct answer
Deploy an Amazon Bedrock model in each AWS Region where the firm operates and configure a geographic cross-Region inference profile. Configure a vector database by using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases and store the knowledge base data in Amazon S3 in each Region where the firm operates

Deploy an Amazon Bedrock model with a cross-Region inference profile and create Amazon S3 buckets that store a knowledge base in each AWS Region where the firm operates. In each Region, configure Amazon Kendra to interact with the knowledge base and configure an AWS Lambda function that uses Amazon Kendra and Amazon Bedrock to process the assistant prompts

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Deploy an Amazon Bedrock model in each AWS Region where the firm operates and configure a geographic cross-Region inference profile. Configure a vector database by using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases and store the knowledge base data in Amazon S3 in each Region where the firm operates

Deploying the assistant in each AWS Region where the firm operates places model inference and retrieval close to clients, which minimizes network latency and supports near real-time responses. A client in Europe interacts with the European deployment, a client in Asia Pacific with the Asia Pacific deployment, and so on. Each deployment processes requests locally instead of sending them to a distant central Region.

A geographic cross-Region inference profile, such as a profile for the EU or the US, distributes inference requests across multiple Regions within the same geographic area. This increases throughput and absorbs traffic peaks while ensuring that requests and data are processed only in Regions inside that geography. Clients get the performance benefits of cross-Region capacity without their confidential financial records leaving their geographic area.

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides a managed vector store and RAG workflow in each Region. Storing the source data in Amazon S3 buckets within each Region keeps confidential records at rest inside the client's geographic area. Retrieval happens against the local knowledge base, so data residency is maintained throughout ingestion, retrieval, and generation. The design meets the latency, multi-geography, and residency requirements with managed services.

Incorrect options:

Deploy an Amazon Bedrock model with a cross-Region inference profile and create Amazon S3 buckets that store a knowledge base in each AWS Region where the firm operates. In each Region, configure Amazon Kendra to interact with the knowledge base and configure an AWS Lambda function that uses Amazon Kendra and Amazon Bedrock to process the assistant prompts - Amazon Kendra is available in fewer AWS Regions than Amazon Bedrock, so the firm might not be able to deploy it in every Region where clients need service. Using Amazon Kendra alongside a knowledge base also duplicates retrieval capabilities and adds an extra search layer that increases latency and cost.

The custom AWS Lambda orchestration that combines Amazon Kendra and Amazon Bedrock adds code that the firm must build and maintain in every Region. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases already provides integrated retrieval and generation, so this design adds complexity without meeting the requirements more effectively.

Deploy an AWS Outposts rack in each AWS Region where the firm operates and create Amazon S3 buckets that store the knowledge bases in each Region. Deploy Amazon RDS as a vector database on each Outpost and deploy an Amazon Bedrock model with a cross-Region inference profile in a central Region - AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure to customer data centers and on-premises locations. It is not deployed inside AWS Regions, so the design misapplies the service. Amazon Bedrock models also do not run on Outposts.

Running inference in a central Region sends prompts that contain confidential financial records from every geographic area to that one Region. That violates the requirement that client data must not leave its geographic area. It also adds latency for clients located far from the central Region.

Deploy one Amazon Bedrock knowledge base in a single AWS Region and invoke the model through a global cross-Region inference profile so that requests from every geographic area can use capacity in any Region - A global cross-Region inference profile can route requests to Regions in any geographic area. That violates the requirement that confidential records must not leave the client's geographic area, because a European client's prompt could be processed in another part of the world.

A single knowledge base in one Region also stores and retrieves all client data in one location, which breaks residency for clients in other geographic areas. Distant clients would also experience higher latency for every request.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 42
Skipped
A GenAI developer deployed a fine-tuned code-completion large language model (LLM) to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The developer used the Large Model Inference (LMI) container with Deep Java Library (DJL) Serving and kept the default serving configuration for continuous batching. The model runs on GPU-based Amazon EC2 instances that each have 8 GPUs. As traffic grows in production, the developer finds that the endpoint needs many instances to meet demand, and the developer wants to avoid the rising cost of this inefficient capacity.

An analysis of the logs shows that the longest combined input and output sequence in real requests is 8 times shorter than the maximum sequence length that the model was configured to handle. The current number of concurrent requests that each instance serves is also low. Profiling shows that the model's weights and activations fit entirely within 4 GPUs.

Which combination of steps should the developer take to improve resource utilization? (Select two)

Move the model to a SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint so that the endpoint scales capacity automatically with traffic

Use a tensor parallelism degree of 8 to split the model across all 8 GPUs and improve memory efficiency

Enable speculative decoding to reduce the response latency of each request

Correct selection
Reduce the model's maximum sequence length so that each GPU can support a larger rolling batch size

Correct selection
Use a tensor parallelism degree of 4 to deploy two model replicas on each instance

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Use a tensor parallelism degree of 4 to deploy two model replicas on each instance

Tensor parallelism splits a model's layers across multiple GPUs so that a model too large for one GPU can run. The degree of tensor parallelism should match what the model actually needs. Profiling shows that the model fits within 4 GPUs, so splitting it across all 8 GPUs wastes capacity and adds communication overhead between GPUs on every forward pass.

With a tensor parallelism degree of 4, each 8-GPU instance can host two independent model replicas, each using 4 GPUs. The developer can configure this through the LMI tensor parallel degree setting together with SageMaker AI inference components or multiple model workers on each instance. Each replica serves requests in parallel, which roughly doubles the throughput that each instance can deliver.

Doubling throughput per instance means the endpoint needs fewer instances to serve the same traffic. Smaller tensor parallel groups also reduce cross-GPU synchronization, which improves the efficiency of each replica. This step directly addresses the low utilization and the high instance count.

Reduce the model's maximum sequence length so that each GPU can support a larger rolling batch size

LMI serving backends reserve GPU memory for the key-value (KV) cache based on the configured maximum sequence length. When the maximum length is far larger than real requests need, the container reserves memory for sequences that never occur. That limits how many requests the rolling batch can hold at the same time and explains the low concurrency on each instance.

Logs show that real sequences are 8 times shorter than the configured maximum. Reducing the maximum sequence length to fit actual traffic, with a reasonable safety margin, frees a large portion of GPU memory. The serving backend can then fit many more concurrent sequences into the rolling batch, so each GPU processes more requests at once.

A larger rolling batch size increases throughput for each GPU without adding hardware. Combined with running two replicas on each instance, this step lets the endpoint serve the same traffic with far fewer instances, which directly reduces cost.

Incorrect options:

Use a tensor parallelism degree of 8 to split the model across all 8 GPUs and improve memory efficiency - The model already fits within 4 GPUs, so splitting it across 8 GPUs does not improve memory efficiency in a useful way. It allows only one replica on each instance and increases communication overhead between GPUs, which can reduce performance for each request.

This configuration keeps throughput for each instance low, so the endpoint still needs many instances. It works against the goal of improving resource utilization.

Move the model to a SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint so that the endpoint scales capacity automatically with traffic - SageMaker AI Serverless Inference does not support GPU instances and has limited memory for each endpoint. An LLM that needs 4 GPUs cannot run on a serverless endpoint.

Serverless endpoints also introduce cold starts that are unsuitable for interactive code completion. This option cannot host the model and does not address the utilization problem.

Enable speculative decoding to reduce the response latency of each request - Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to propose tokens that the main model verifies, which can reduce latency for each request. However, it consumes extra GPU memory and compute for the draft model, which can reduce the memory available for batching concurrent requests.

The core problems are memory over-allocation for long sequences and inefficient use of GPUs across replicas. Speculative decoding does not address either problem and does not reduce the number of instances needed.

Question 43

A national healthcare network uses multiple foundation models (FMs) through Amazon Bedrock for its generative AI (GenAI) applications. To comply with a new internal AI governance policy for GenAI workloads that handle patient data, the network needs a token management solution. The token management solution must proactively alert when applications approach the token limits of each specific model. The solution must also process more than 8,000 requests each minute and must maintain token usage metrics to allocate costs across six hospital departments.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Implement Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with token quota policies and capture metrics on rejected requests. Configure Amazon EventBridge rules to send notifications based on the guardrail metrics and use Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to visualize token usage trends across models

Request service quota increases for the tokens-per-minute quota of every model, enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to an Amazon S3 bucket, run a daily Amazon Athena query that totals the input and output tokens for each department from the logs, and email the results to department managers so that they can review consumption and request more quota whenever their applications return throttling errors

Correct answer
Build model-specific tokenizers in an AWS Lambda function that estimates the token usage of each request before the request is sent to Amazon Bedrock. Configure the function to publish token metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and to trigger alarms when requests approach model limits. Store detailed token usage records in Amazon DynamoDB for cost reporting

Use Amazon API Gateway as a proxy for all Amazon Bedrock API calls. Configure request throttling with custom usage plans that define token quotas and configure API Gateway to reject requests that would exceed the token limits

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Build model-specific tokenizers in an AWS Lambda function that estimates the token usage of each request before the request is sent to Amazon Bedrock. Configure the function to publish token metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and to trigger alarms when requests approach model limits. Store detailed token usage records in Amazon DynamoDB for cost reporting

Each FM in Amazon Bedrock has its own tokenizer, context window, and maximum output tokens, so the same text produces different token counts on different models. Model-specific tokenizers in an AWS Lambda function calculate an accurate token estimate for each request before the function sends the request to Amazon Bedrock. For supported models, the function can also use the Amazon Bedrock CountTokens API. Because the estimate happens before invocation, the solution can warn about, trim, or route requests that are close to a model's limits instead of discovering the problem only after a request fails.

The Lambda function publishes custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch with dimensions for the model, the application, and the hospital department. CloudWatch alarms watch these metrics and alert the operations team when token counts approach a defined percentage of each model's limits, such as 80% of the context window or a tokens-per-minute quota. This provides the proactive alerting that the governance policy requires. Lambda scales automatically to handle more than 8,000 requests each minute.

Amazon DynamoDB stores a detailed record of each request, including the department, model, estimated tokens, and actual input and output token counts from the Amazon Bedrock response. DynamoDB on-demand capacity absorbs high write volumes without capacity planning. The network can query these records to allocate costs accurately across the six hospital departments and to produce audit evidence for the governance policy.

Incorrect options:

Implement Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with token quota policies and capture metrics on rejected requests. Configure Amazon EventBridge rules to send notifications based on the guardrail metrics and use Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to visualize token usage trends across models - Amazon Bedrock Guardrails evaluates content for safety and policy compliance, such as harmful content, denied topics, and sensitive information. It does not provide token quota policies, so this option relies on a capability that does not exist.

Metrics about rejected requests are also reactive. They report problems after requests fail rather than warning when applications approach limits. This option does not track token usage by department for cost allocation.

Request service quota increases for the tokens-per-minute quota of every model, enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to an Amazon S3 bucket, run a daily Amazon Athena query that totals the input and output tokens for each department from the logs, and email the results to department managers so that they can review consumption and request more quota whenever their applications return throttling errors - Raising quotas changes the limits but does not alert anyone when applications approach them. A daily Athena report identifies usage a day after it occurs, and managers learn about problems only after their applications return throttling errors. This is reactive and does not meet the requirement for proactive alerts.

Email reports also do not provide continuous metrics or automated alarms. Although the logs can support daily cost summaries, the design lacks real-time monitoring of token usage against model-specific limits.

Use Amazon API Gateway as a proxy for all Amazon Bedrock API calls. Configure request throttling with custom usage plans that define token quotas and configure API Gateway to reject requests that would exceed the token limits - API Gateway usage plans throttle and limit requests based on request counts and rates for each API key. They do not count model tokens, which vary by model and by prompt. API Gateway has no built-in way to determine how many tokens a request will consume, so it cannot reject requests based on token limits.

Rejecting requests at the gateway also blocks work instead of providing early warnings. This option offers no token usage metrics by department for cost allocation.

The platform team suspects they could reduce costs by splitting the workflow into cheaper classification steps and only invoking the more capable model when necessary.

As a GenAI engineer, how should you implement a solution to optimize cost while preserving output quality for complex workloads?

Precompute simple labels for all images offline using a SageMaker training job and store them in Amazon DynamoDB, but still invoke the large multimodal model online for every incoming request to maintain a consistent experience. Use the stored labels only as metadata in responses rather than as a decision point for bypassing the multimodal model

Correct answer
Configure an Amazon SageMaker inference pipeline where a first, cheaper model hosted on SageMaker performs image or text classification and confidence scoring, and only call an Amazon Bedrock multimodal model in a later stage when the request requires detailed reasoning or the classifier has low confidence. Use routing logic in the pipeline container to short circuit the workflow and return early for simple label requests so that the multimodal model is invoked only when needed

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure an Amazon SageMaker inference pipeline where a first, cheaper model hosted on SageMaker performs image or text classification and confidence scoring, and only call an Amazon Bedrock multimodal model in a later stage when the request requires detailed reasoning or the classifier has low confidence. Use routing logic in the pipeline container to short circuit the workflow and return early for simple label requests so that the multimodal model is invoked only when needed

A staged or cascaded pattern that uses a cheaper model as a first filter aligns directly with multi model routing and serial inference best practices on AWS. SageMaker inference pipelines let you chain multiple containers on the same endpoint and run them in sequence, which is well suited to architectures where a lightweight classifier handles simple tasks and a more capable multimodal model is reserved for complex requests. By computing a confidence score or checking the requested output type, the pipeline can decide to return the classifier result immediately for simple label use cases and only forward the request to the Bedrock multimodal model when richer reasoning or description is needed.

This approach reduces cost in two ways. First, a significant portion of traffic never reaches the expensive multimodal model if the classifier result is sufficient. Second, the heavy model is invoked only for the subset of cases that genuinely require detailed explanations, which aligns with AWS guidance on routing queries to different models based on complexity and cost characteristics. Multi LLM routing patterns emphasize using smaller models for simpler tasks and escalating to larger models only when necessary, which is exactly what this cascade achieves.

From an operational perspective, inference pipelines simplify deployment because the models share the same underlying infrastructure and endpoint. This reduces integration overhead and allows you to monitor end to end performance and cost by stage, while keeping latency low since the containers run on the same instance. You can further tune routing thresholds over time using production metrics to balance cost and quality for the image and text analysis workload.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/part-4-model-hosting-patterns-in-amazon-sagemaker-design-patterns-for-serial-inference-on-amazon-sagemaker/

Incorrect options:

Migrate the large multimodal model to a larger instance type on SageMaker and enable Provisioned Throughput on Amazon Bedrock so that all requests continue to call the same model with lower latency. Rely on the increased capacity to absorb traffic without introducing additional routing or staged inference logic - Upsizing the multimodal model infrastructure and enabling provisioned throughput improves latency and peak capacity, but it does not address the underlying cost problem because every request still calls the most expensive model. The pattern ignores the opportunity to differentiate between simple and complex tasks and fails to use cheaper models for straightforward label predictions, which contradicts AWS guidance on cost aware routing and cascaded inference. Without a staged decision point, token and compute usage remain high across all requests, including trivial ones that a small classifier could easily handle. The result is higher steady state spend and suboptimal resource utilization compared to a cascaded architecture that gates calls to the large multimodal foundation model.

Precompute simple labels for all images offline using a SageMaker training job and store them in Amazon DynamoDB, but still invoke the large multimodal model online for every incoming request to maintain a consistent experience. Use the stored labels only as metadata in responses rather than as a decision point for bypassing the multimodal model - Precomputing labels offline and storing them in DynamoDB can be useful for metadata enrichment, but the design as stated still invokes the expensive multimodal model for every request, which eliminates the cost benefit of a cascade. The offline labels do not influence routing or gating logic, so the system does not skip the multimodal model even when a simple label would have been sufficient. This pattern also introduces additional complexity in the data pipeline without delivering proportional savings in inference costs. AWS guidance on cascading emphasizes using early models to filter or fully answer simple queries, which is not happening here because the multimodal model remains the mandatory final step for all traffic.

Set up an Amazon SageMaker inference pipeline where a lightweight classifier runs first and forwards its prediction to the multimodal model so that both models contribute to the final answer. Always invoke the multimodal model to confirm or refine the classifier output to maintain consistent response quality - Although this option appears to follow a cascaded design, it still invokes the large multimodal model for every request, which eliminates the cost and throughput benefits that cascaded inference is meant to achieve. AWS guidance on multi model routing and inference pipelines makes it clear that the smaller model must act as a gate, returning results directly when confidence is high and escalating to a more capable model only when needed. By always forwarding requests to the multimodal model, the workflow becomes a serial enrichment pipeline rather than a conditional cascade, resulting in nearly the same compute cost, token usage, and latency as the original single model architecture.

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon API Gateway to route all inference requests to an AWS Lambda function that reads model and provider selection from AWS AppConfig at runtime. Update routing rules and configuration values in AppConfig to change models or providers without redeploying code. Control rollout and rollback by using AppConfig deployment strategies and validators

This approach cleanly separates configuration from code by externalizing model and provider selection into a managed configuration service. By using AWS AppConfig, the application can dynamically read which model or provider to invoke at runtime, enabling changes without any code modification or redeployment. This directly supports flexible architecture patterns required for fast experimentation and operational agility.

The use of deployment strategies in AppConfig allows gradual rollouts, such as canary or percentage based releases, which is critical when testing new models or providers. Validators add safety by automatically rolling back changes if errors or unhealthy conditions are detected. This design aligns with best practices for controlled configuration changes in production systems.

Because the routing logic remains stable in AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway, teams can switch models or providers quickly in response to cost, performance, or quality considerations. This makes the architecture resilient, adaptable, and well suited for evolving generative AI workloads.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/creating-asynchronous-ai-agents-with-amazon-bedrock/

Incorrect options:

Store the selected model and provider as environment variables in AWS Lambda and update them whenever a switch is required. Redeploy the Lambda function to propagate the new configuration to all environments. Use Lambda versions and aliases to manage traffic shifting between configurations - This design couples configuration changes to code deployments by relying on Lambda environment variables. Even though Lambda versions and aliases support traffic shifting, every model or provider change still requires a redeployment, which increases operational overhead and risk. This does not satisfy the requirement to switch dynamically without code changes. Additionally, environment variables lack advanced rollout controls such as validators or automatic rollback based on health metrics. This makes rapid experimentation and safe provider switching more difficult in production environments.

Implement an abstraction layer in AWS Lambda that reads model selection rules from AWS AppConfig. Configure provider endpoints by leveraging the Lambda function code. Update AppConfig to toggle feature flags while keeping provider specific logic fixed in code. Redeploy the function when switching providers to ensure consistency - While this option introduces AWS AppConfig, it undermines flexibility by hardcoding provider specific logic inside the Lambda function. Any change in provider still requires a code update and redeployment, which defeats the goal of provider switching without modifying code. AppConfig becomes limited to simple feature toggles rather than full routing control. This partial abstraction can lead to brittle designs where configuration and code drift over time. It also increases maintenance complexity as the number of supported providers grows.

Configure Amazon API Gateway with static stage variables that define the model and provider to invoke. Manually update the stage variables during a release window to switch models for all users at once. Rely on API Gateway caching to minimize latency during changes - Static stage variables in Amazon API Gateway provide limited flexibility and are better suited for coarse grained configuration. Updating them typically affects all users at once and does not support gradual rollouts or automated rollback mechanisms. This increases the blast radius of changes and operational risk. Relying on API Gateway caching does not address the core requirement of dynamic and safe model or provider switching. This approach also lacks fine grained control and observability during experimentation.

Question 46

A multinational logistics company is developing a generative AI (GenAI) application on Amazon Bedrock that analyzes patterns and relationships in shipment and customer data. The application will process tens of millions of new data points each day across AWS Regions in Europe, South America, and Asia Pacific before storing the data in Amazon S3.

The application must comply with local data protection and data storage regulations, and both data residency and data processing must remain on the same continent where the data originates. The application must also maintain audit trails of its decision-making processes and must provide data classification capabilities.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Process the data points in each Region, use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy all processed data to a global analytics account in a single Region for centralized reporting, use Amazon Comprehend PII detection to classify the replicated data, and keep the application logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs with a 30-day retention period

Deploy the application in each Region with local IAM policies and use Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference to distribute the workload. Use Amazon CloudWatch to log the AI decision-making processes and data processing activities, and track compliance certifications across Regions manually

Correct answer
Use Amazon S3 Object Lock with Region-specific S3 bucket policies. Preprocess the data points within the Region that matches their geographic origin before sending them to Amazon Bedrock. Use Amazon Macie to classify the data and use AWS CloudTrail immutable logs to audit the decision-making processes

Create a separate AWS account for each Region with its own compliance framework. Use Amazon SageMaker AI with custom monitoring to track model performance and compliance with data residency requirements, and create manual reports for each regulatory jurisdiction

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon S3 Object Lock with Region-specific S3 bucket policies. Preprocess the data points within the Region that matches their geographic origin before sending them to Amazon Bedrock. Use Amazon Macie to classify the data and use AWS CloudTrail immutable logs to audit the decision-making processes

Data residency starts with where data is processed and stored. Preprocessing each data point in the Region that matches its geographic origin, and invoking Amazon Bedrock from that same Region, keeps processing on the originating continent. Region-specific S3 bucket policies control which principals and services can access each bucket. They can deny requests that do not meet residency conditions, such as replication or access from outside approved locations. Together, these controls keep both processing and storage within the required continent.

Amazon S3 Object Lock applies write-once-read-many (WORM) protection to stored objects. In compliance mode, no user, including the root user, can delete or overwrite protected objects until the retention period ends. This supports regulations that require data and records to be retained unchanged. Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and classify sensitive data in Amazon S3, such as personal information and financial data. It provides the data classification capability that the regulations require, with findings for each bucket and object.

AWS CloudTrail records the API activity that makes up the application's decision-making processes, such as which principal invoked which model, with which inputs, and when. CloudTrail log file integrity validation lets auditors verify that logs were not altered, and storing the logs in an S3 bucket protected by Object Lock makes them immutable. This produces a tamper-evident audit trail that satisfies the audit requirement across all three continents.

Incorrect options:

Deploy the application in each Region with local IAM policies and use Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference to distribute the workload. Use Amazon CloudWatch to log the AI decision-making processes and data processing activities, and track compliance certifications across Regions manually - Cross-Region inference distributes requests across multiple Regions. Unless it is strictly limited to a geographic profile within one continent, it can process data outside the continent of origin. This option does not specify that constraint, so it risks violating the residency requirement.

Amazon CloudWatch logs can be modified or deleted by users with sufficient permissions and do not provide an immutable audit trail on their own. Tracking compliance certifications manually is error prone and does not scale. This option also provides no data classification capability.

Process the data points in each Region, use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy all processed data to a global analytics account in a single Region for centralized reporting, use Amazon Comprehend PII detection to classify the replicated data, and keep the application logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs with a 30-day retention period - Replicating all processed data to a single global analytics Region moves data off its originating continent, which violates the residency requirement even though initial processing happens locally. Classifying the replicated data in the central Region compounds the violation.

CloudWatch Logs with a 30-day retention period deletes records quickly and does not provide an immutable, long-term audit trail. This option fails both the residency requirement and the audit requirement.

Create a separate AWS account for each Region with its own compliance framework. Use Amazon SageMaker AI with custom monitoring to track model performance and compliance with data residency requirements, and create manual reports for each regulatory jurisdiction - Separate accounts can isolate workloads, but custom monitoring in Amazon SageMaker AI and manual reports require substantial effort to build and maintain. Manual reporting is error prone and does not produce reliable, immutable audit trails of decision-making processes.

This option also moves the workload away from Amazon Bedrock to SageMaker AI without a clear benefit and provides no automated data classification capability. It fails the classification requirement and adds operational overhead.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Configure AWS CloudTrail Insights to analyze API call patterns across accounts and detect anomalous activity in Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon S3, and AWS KMS. Correct answer
Use IAM attribute-based access control (ABAC) to map departments to specific permissions and configure VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock model API calls. Use IAM condition keys to enforce specific GuardrailIdentifier and ModelId values. Configure AWS CloudTrail to capture management events, data events for S3 objects, and AWS KMS key usage activity, and enable S3 server access logging for file-level interactions with the video archive. Send all CloudTrail logs to AWS CloudTrail Lake and create Amazon CloudWatch alarms that alert on unexpected activity

Configure VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock model API calls and use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful or unauthorized content in prompts and responses. Use Amazon Bedrock trace events to track all agent and model invocations and export the traces to Amazon CloudWatch Logs as an audit record of model usage. Store all prompts and outputs in Amazon S3 with server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use IAM attribute-based access control (ABAC) to map departments to specific permissions and configure VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock model API calls. Use IAM condition keys to enforce specific GuardrailIdentifier and ModelId values. Configure AWS CloudTrail to capture management events, data events for S3 objects, and AWS KMS key usage activity, and enable S3 server access logging for file-level interactions with the video archive. Send all CloudTrail logs to AWS CloudTrail Lake and create Amazon CloudWatch alarms that alert on unexpected activity

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) grants permissions based on tags, such as a department tag on an IAM role and a matching tag on resources. The broadcaster can map teams such as editorial, analytics, and compliance to specific permissions without writing separate policies for every combination of user and resource. IAM condition keys add precise control over FM access patterns. Policies can require a specific guardrail through the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier key and restrict invocations to approved model IDs, so every request uses an approved model with the required privacy protections applied.

VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock use AWS PrivateLink to keep model API traffic on the AWS network. Prompts that describe sensitive footage and the generated outputs never traverse the public internet, which secures model inputs and outputs in transit. Combined with encryption at rest through AWS KMS, this design protects model data throughout its lifecycle and supports the company's privacy standards.

AWS CloudTrail records who called which API and when. That includes management events for Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Rekognition, data events for object-level access to the video archive in Amazon S3, and AWS KMS key usage. S3 server access logging adds detailed records of file-level requests. AWS CloudTrail Lake stores these events in an immutable, queryable data store, so auditors can run SQL queries to answer questions such as which users accessed specific footage or used a particular KMS key. CloudWatch alarms detect unexpected activity across the services and alert the security team quickly.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction_attribute-based-access-control.html

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction_attribute-based-access-control.html

Incorrect options:

Configure VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock model API calls and use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful or unauthorized content in prompts and responses. Use Amazon Bedrock trace events to track all agent and model invocations and export the traces to Amazon CloudWatch Logs as an audit record of model usage. Store all prompts and outputs in Amazon S3 with server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) - VPC endpoints and guardrails help secure model traffic and content, but this option does not define who can access which models or enforce access patterns through identity-based policies. Without IAM controls such as condition keys for approved models and guardrails, users could invoke any model or call models without the guardrail.

Amazon Bedrock trace events describe the reasoning and processing steps of agents and guardrails for debugging. They are not a comprehensive identity audit of who accessed which resources across services. The option also does not record access to the video archive in Amazon S3 or the use of AWS KMS keys, so it fails the audit requirement.

Create an individual IAM user with long-term access keys for each analyst, store the keys in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation every 90 days, attach the AmazonBedrockFullAccess and AmazonRekognitionFullAccess managed policies to every analyst so that work is never blocked, route all model traffic through a NAT gateway in a shared VPC, enable Amazon GuardDuty for threat detection across all accounts, and store the prompts and model outputs in an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode so that no user can change the records during audits - Long-term access keys for individual IAM users increase the risk of credential exposure and contradict AWS best practices, which favor temporary credentials through IAM roles and federation. Attaching full-access managed policies to every analyst removes any control over which models and guardrails users can use.

Routing model traffic through a NAT gateway sends requests to public service endpoints instead of keeping them on private connectivity. Amazon GuardDuty and S3 Object Lock provide threat detection and immutable storage, but they do not record who accessed which resources and when. This design fails the access control and secure I/O requirements and provides an incomplete audit trail.

Configure AWS CloudTrail Insights to analyze API call patterns across accounts and detect anomalous activity in Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon S3, and AWS KMS. Use Amazon Macie to scan and classify the video archive, encrypt all stored data with SSE-KMS, and capture KMS API usage events with CloudTrail. Process the Insights anomalies and Macie findings with Amazon EventBridge rules and use Amazon CloudWatch alarms to send notifications and start automated security responses - CloudTrail Insights detects unusual patterns in API call volume and error rates, but it is an anomaly detection feature rather than a complete audit trail. This design also does not control FM access patterns with identity policies or secure model traffic with VPC endpoints.

Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in text-based content in Amazon S3, such as documents and structured data files. It does not analyze video content, so it cannot classify the footage archive. This option relies mostly on detective controls and does not provide the preventive access controls and secure model I/O that the platform requires.
