A large enterprise is preparing to deploy an advanced language model that is several hundred gigabytes in size so that all inference happens entirely within its private network boundary. Initial tests show that the model files and tokenizer components take a long time to download and load into GPU memory, causing container startup to fail and preventing the system from becoming ready. The operations team also needs reliable and predictable health checks so that deployments do not roll back during long initialization periods.

How would you configure the hosting environment, container behavior, and initialization timeouts to ensure that this very large model can load successfully and serve real time traffic?

Correct answer
Use SageMaker AI real time inference with large GPU instances such as ml.p4d or ml.g5 and configure extended container startup and health check timeouts to allow long model loading periods. Increase model loading quotas and adjust container health checks so that the endpoint becomes ready only after the model is fully downloaded and initialized

Use SageMaker AI real time inference with large GPU instances such as ml.g5 and keep default container startup and health check timeouts unchanged. Rely on automatic retries during deployment to allow the model to finish loading without adjusting the initialization window

Deploy the model on SageMaker AI multi model endpoints that automatically load models on demand to reduce initialization time. Let the container evict and reload model files dynamically to optimize for throughput and faster startup

Use SageMaker AI real time inference with medium sized GPU instances and shorten container startup timeouts so that failed containers restart quickly. Rely on repeated restarts to eventually complete the model load when the infrastructure is under low utilization

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use SageMaker AI real time inference with large GPU instances such as ml.p4d or ml.g5 and configure extended container startup and health check timeouts to allow long model loading periods. Increase model loading quotas and adjust container health checks so that the endpoint becomes ready only after the model is fully downloaded and initialized

Large language models often require extended download and initialization times, and SageMaker AI allows increasing container startup and health check timeouts so that endpoints do not fail during long loading phases. Selecting large GPU instances such as ml.p4d or ml.g5 families provides the memory and compute capacity necessary for multi hundred gigabyte models to load successfully. Configuring extended health checks ensures that the endpoint transitions to InService only after the model is fully ready. This combination of sufficient GPU resources and expanded initialization windows allows stable real time inference for very large models.

Incorrect options:

Use SageMaker AI real time inference with medium sized GPU instances and shorten container startup timeouts so that failed containers restart quickly. Rely on repeated restarts to eventually complete the model load when the infrastructure is under low utilization - Using smaller GPU instances and shortening timeouts increases the likelihood of container crashes and repeated restarts. Restart cycles do not solve the root cause because the model still cannot fit comfortably within the available memory or initialize within an artificially shortened window.

Deploy the model on SageMaker AI multi model endpoints that automatically load models on demand to reduce initialization time. Let the container evict and reload model files dynamically to optimize for throughput and faster startup - Multi model endpoints are designed for hosting many smaller models and load models dynamically, which introduces additional latency and is not suitable for multi hundred gigabyte LLMs. Evicting and reloading large model files repeatedly significantly degrades performance and increases failure rates.

Use SageMaker AI real time inference with large GPU instances such as ml.g5 and keep default container startup and health check timeouts unchanged. Rely on automatic retries during deployment to allow the model to finish loading without adjusting the initialization window - Leaving default timeout settings unchanged does not provide enough initialization time for multi hundred gigabyte models to download and load into GPU memory. Even with large GPU instances, the endpoint will transition to a failed state because the default container health check thresholds are not sufficient for long loading cycles.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 49
Skipped
A health insurance company runs a generative AI (GenAI) claims summarization application in a workload AWS account. The application uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize approximately 50,000 claim files each day. The application architecture includes an Amazon API Gateway REST API that sends requests to AWS Lambda functions that run in private VPC subnets. The claim files contain sensitive member information and reside in a governed data lake in a central data account. The central data account uses Amazon S3, Amazon Athena, and AWS Glue.

The company must ensure that all calls from the application to Amazon Bedrock travel only over private connectivity between the workload VPC and Amazon Bedrock. The data lake must enforce fine-grained, column-level access controls across the company's AWS accounts.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
In the workload account, create interface VPC endpoints for the Amazon Bedrock runtime and run the Lambda functions in private subnets. Add IAM conditions to the inference and data-plane policies to allow calls only through approved endpoints and roles. In the central data account, use AWS Lake Formation LF-tag-based access control to create cross-account table-level and column-level grants

Create a VPC peering connection between the workload VPC and a VPC in the central data account, create the Amazon Bedrock runtime interface VPC endpoint only in the central data account VPC, route all Lambda traffic to Amazon Bedrock across the peering connection, and create Amazon S3 Access Points with prefix-based access policies for each consuming account so that each account can read only the approved columns of the claim data in the data lake

Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 only in the workload account and invoke Amazon Bedrock through its public endpoints. Manage data access with database-level grants in AWS Lake Formation and stream AWS CloudTrail logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs without metric filters or alarms

Use VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock and Amazon S3 in the workload account and manage data lake access only with IAM path-based policies. Send AWS CloudTrail logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, build dashboards periodically, and allow public fallback for cross-Region reads to shorten setup time

Overall explanation
Correct option:

In the workload account, create interface VPC endpoints for the Amazon Bedrock runtime and run the Lambda functions in private subnets. Add IAM conditions to the inference and data-plane policies to allow calls only through approved endpoints and roles. In the central data account, use AWS Lake Formation LF-tag-based access control to create cross-account table-level and column-level grants

Interface VPC endpoints for the Amazon Bedrock runtime use AWS PrivateLink to create elastic network interfaces with private IP addresses inside the workload VPC. When the Lambda functions run in private subnets and private DNS is enabled on the endpoint, every InvokeModel or Converse call resolves to the endpoint and travels over the AWS network. No traffic crosses the public internet, and the private subnets do not need a NAT gateway or an internet gateway to reach Amazon Bedrock.

IAM conditions enforce the private path instead of relying only on network design. The company can add the aws:SourceVpce condition key to the policies attached to the Lambda execution roles so that Amazon Bedrock and data-plane calls succeed only when they arrive through approved VPC endpoints. The company can also attach endpoint policies that restrict which principals and actions can use each endpoint. Together, these controls ensure that even valid credentials cannot call Amazon Bedrock over a public path.

In the central data account, AWS Lake Formation provides fine-grained access control over tables that are cataloged in AWS Glue and queried through Amazon Athena. LF-tag-based access control (LF-TBAC) lets the company tag sensitive columns, such as member identifiers and diagnosis codes, and grant permissions on tag expressions instead of individual resources. Lake Formation shares these grants across accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager, so the workload account receives table-level and column-level access to exactly the data it needs. This approach scales well as new tables and accounts are added.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/use-aws-privatelink-to-set-up-private-access-to-amazon-bedrock/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/use-aws-privatelink-to-set-up-private-access-to-amazon-bedrock/

Incorrect options:

Create a VPC peering connection between the workload VPC and a VPC in the central data account, create the Amazon Bedrock runtime interface VPC endpoint only in the central data account VPC, route all Lambda traffic to Amazon Bedrock across the peering connection, and create Amazon S3 Access Points with prefix-based access policies for each consuming account so that each account can read only the approved columns of the claim data in the data lake - Placing the Amazon Bedrock endpoint in a different account's VPC and routing Lambda traffic over VPC peering adds cross-account networking complexity and DNS configuration without any benefit. The workload account can create its own interface endpoint and keep inference traffic local to its VPC. This design also concentrates a dependency for the workload account's inference path in the central data account.

Amazon S3 Access Points with prefix-based policies control access to objects and prefixes, not to columns inside those objects. A caller that can read an object can read every column in it. This design cannot deliver the fine-grained column-level access that AWS Lake Formation provides for Athena and AWS Glue tables.

Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 only in the workload account and invoke Amazon Bedrock through its public endpoints. Manage data access with database-level grants in AWS Lake Formation and stream AWS CloudTrail logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs without metric filters or alarms - A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 keeps only S3 traffic private. Invoking Amazon Bedrock through its public endpoints sends inference requests and sensitive claim content over a public path, which violates the private connectivity requirement.

Database-level grants in AWS Lake Formation give access to every table and column in a database. They cannot provide the fine-grained column-level control the company requires. Streaming CloudTrail logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs without metric filters or alarms adds visibility but no enforcement or alerting.

Use VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock and Amazon S3 in the workload account and manage data lake access only with IAM path-based policies. Send AWS CloudTrail logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, build dashboards periodically, and allow public fallback for cross-Region reads to shorten setup time - Allowing public fallback for cross-Region reads creates a path in which traffic can leave private connectivity. That undermines the private networking controls the company requires and introduces an uncontrolled data exposure risk.

IAM path-based policies can restrict access to S3 prefixes and objects, but they cannot enforce column-level permissions within a table. Periodic dashboards are a reporting activity that does not prevent unauthorized access. This design meets neither requirement.

Question 50
Skipped
A market research firm is building a generative AI (GenAI) application that produces industry briefings from several internal and external data sources. These sources include internal survey databases, licensed third-party datasets, and public economic data feeds. The firm must ensure that every generated briefing is fully traceable to its sources. The application must support data source registration and must use metadata tagging to attribute content to its original source. The application must also maintain audit logs of data access and usage across the entire pipeline.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Maintain a source registry in Amazon DynamoDB and attach source identifiers to AWS X-Ray traces. Use sampled traces to document data access across ingestion, retrieval, and generation

Correct answer
Register all data sources in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and apply metadata tags that attribute content to each data source. Use AWS CloudTrail to log access and activity across services

Store the data in Amazon S3 and use S3 object tagging for attribution. Use the AWS Glue Data Catalog to manage schema information and use AWS CloudTrail to log access to the S3 buckets

Use AWS Lake Formation to catalog the data sources and control access. Apply metadata tags directly to the objects in Amazon S3 and use AWS CloudTrail to monitor API activity

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Register all data sources in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and apply metadata tags that attribute content to each data source. Use AWS CloudTrail to log access and activity across services

The AWS Glue Data Catalog provides a central, persistent metadata repository for data sources of many types. It can register Amazon S3 datasets, JDBC databases such as the internal survey databases, and other sources through crawlers and connections. Registering every source in one catalog gives the firm a single inventory of where each dataset lives, its schema, and when it changed. That inventory forms the foundation of a traceable GenAI pipeline.

Metadata tags and table properties in the Data Catalog let the firm record attribution details for each source, such as the provider, license type, acquisition date, and data owner. When the application retrieves data to generate a briefing, it can carry these identifiers into its prompts, retrieved context, and outputs. Each statement in a briefing can then be traced back to the registered source it came from. Because the tags live with the catalog entries, attribution stays consistent across every source type, not only data stored in Amazon S3.

AWS CloudTrail records API activity across AWS services, including AWS Glue catalog operations, Amazon S3 data events, AWS Lake Formation permission checks, and Amazon Bedrock model invocations. A trail that captures management and data events gives the firm a tamper-resistant audit log that shows who accessed which data and when. It also shows how data moved through ingestion, retrieval, and generation. Together, the Data Catalog and CloudTrail meet the registration, attribution, and audit requirements.

Incorrect options:

Maintain a source registry in Amazon DynamoDB and attach source identifiers to AWS X-Ray traces. Use sampled traces to document data access across ingestion, retrieval, and generation - A DynamoDB registry can hold custom source metadata, and X-Ray traces can help correlate processing across sources. Building and maintaining that registry would require application-specific implementation.

Sampled traces omit requests by design and do not automatically capture every relevant briefing. They are useful diagnostic evidence but cannot serve as the complete persistent audit required here.

Use AWS Lake Formation to catalog the data sources and control access. Apply metadata tags directly to the objects in Amazon S3 and use AWS CloudTrail to monitor API activity - AWS Lake Formation provides fine-grained access control and uses the AWS Glue Data Catalog for metadata. However, applying attribution tags directly to S3 objects covers only data stored in Amazon S3. Sources such as internal databases and external feeds that are accessed through connections would have no attribution tags.

Splitting attribution between object tags and the catalog also creates two places to maintain metadata, which leads to inconsistencies. Tags applied within the Data Catalog keep attribution together with source registration for every source type.

Store the data in Amazon S3 and use S3 object tagging for attribution. Use the AWS Glue Data Catalog to manage schema information and use AWS CloudTrail to log access to the S3 buckets - S3 object tagging works only for objects in Amazon S3, so attribution would not cover the internal survey databases or other sources that are not stored in S3. Using the AWS Glue Data Catalog only for schema information also leaves out the registration and attribution metadata that traceability requires.

Logging access only to the S3 buckets misses activity in other parts of the pipeline, such as catalog changes, database queries through connections, and Amazon Bedrock invocations. The audit trail would be incomplete for an end-to-end pipeline.

Use Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluations to measure context relevance, correctness, and faithfulness

A hybrid evaluation approach combines scalable automated assessment with targeted expert judgment. The evaluator can screen routine responses, while engineers investigate flagged outputs and ambiguous cases. This reduces the volume of manual reviews without making an automated judge the sole authority for difficult technical decisions.

Amazon Bedrock provides context relevance for evaluating retrieved passages and correctness and faithfulness for evaluating generated answers. Faithfulness assesses whether the answer stays grounded in the retrieved text. These metrics help distinguish retrieval problems from unsupported generation, although an automated score does not guarantee factual accuracy.

SageMaker Feature Store can maintain structured evaluation records in its offline store. Expert findings can inform subsequent evaluation datasets and improvements to the RAG application.

Confidence in recognizing an entity does not establish that the retrieved maintenance procedure applies to the fault or that the generated recommendation follows the evidence.

Step Functions can coordinate processing, and CloudWatch can track the resulting scores. Neither changes what those scores measure. An entity confidence threshold therefore cannot serve as a reliable threshold for retrieval accuracy or hallucination detection.

Fine-tune an evaluator LLM on equipment maintenance content and use it as the sole reviewer for all responses. Parallelize assessments with AWS Lambda. Publish relevance and factual accuracy scores to Amazon CloudWatch A domain-adapted evaluator can provide useful automated assessments, and parallel execution can improve evaluation throughput. Domain-specific training does not eliminate evaluator errors, particularly when records conflict or unusual equipment failures require expert interpretation.

This option makes the evaluator the sole reviewer and provides no escalation path for ambiguous cases. It also does not explicitly evaluate the retrieved evidence separately from the generated response. Targeted expert review and dedicated retrieval metrics provide a more complete evaluation approach.

Configure the generation model to return a confidence score and supporting citations with every troubleshooting response. Store these results in Amazon DynamoDB and use AWS Lambda to verify that each cited document exists. Send low-confidence responses to engineers and accept high-confidence responses whenever their cited documents appear in the knowledge base A generation model's self-reported confidence is not an independently validated measure of correctness. The model can express high confidence while misinterpreting a maintenance record or inventing a procedural step.

Verifying that a cited document exists establishes only that the reference points to available material. It does not establish that the document supports the associated claim. This approach can accept confident hallucinations and provides no substantive assessment of retrieval relevance or evidence support.

They must choose an approach that minimizes end user latency without over engineering the frontend integration.

What is the MOST operationally efficient way to improve responsiveness for time sensitive interactions?

Correct answer
Use Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithStreaming to stream tokens as they are generated by the foundation model. Forward the streamed output through Amazon API Gateway REST API response streaming so clients receive partial responses over HTTP immediately. Avoid buffering responses in the backend to minimize time to first token

Use Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithStreaming and push tokens to clients using Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API connections. Maintain persistent bidirectional connections and manage connection state for each client. Close the connection after the full response is generated

Use Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithStreaming to stream tokens as they are generated by the foundation model. Forward the streamed output through Amazon API Gateway HTTP API so clients receive partial responses over HTTP immediately. Optimize performance by reducing payload size and using faster HTTP integrations

Use Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel to generate the full response and return it through Amazon API Gateway HTTP API. Optimize performance by reducing payload size and using faster HTTP integrations. Leverage client side loading indicators to manage perceived latency

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithStreaming to stream tokens as they are generated by the foundation model. Forward the streamed output through Amazon API Gateway REST API response streaming so clients receive partial responses over HTTP immediately. Avoid buffering responses in the backend to minimize time to first token

InvokeModelWithStreaming enables the foundation model to emit tokens incrementally as they are generated, which significantly reduces time to first token. By forwarding these tokens directly through Amazon API Gateway REST API response streaming, the application can deliver partial responses over standard HTTP connections. This directly improves perceived responsiveness for interactive workloads. REST API response streaming avoids the need for persistent connections or specialized client protocols. Clients begin receiving output as soon as generation starts, even for long responses, which aligns with user expectations in chat style interfaces. This keeps the architecture simple while delivering real time feedback.

By avoiding backend buffering, this design preserves the benefits of model level streaming. It provides a balanced solution that optimizes user experience without introducing unnecessary operational complexity.

Building responsive APIs with Amazon API Gateway response streaming:  via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/building-responsive-apis-with-amazon-api-gateway-response-streaming/

Exam Alert -

When evaluating latency optimization and streaming patterns on the exam, pay close attention to what is being streamed and why.

REST API response streaming is the preferred choice when a foundation model streams output incrementally and clients only need to receive data over standard HTTP. It supports progressive delivery, improves time to first token, and avoids the operational overhead of managing persistent connections.

WebSocket APIs are designed for bidirectional, event driven communication where the server and client continuously exchange messages. They introduce additional complexity and are rarely the BEST choice when the use case only requires streaming responses from the backend to the client.

HTTP APIs are optimized for cost and simple request response patterns, but they do not provide native response streaming for incremental payload delivery. Switching from REST API to HTTP API alone does not reduce model generation latency or improve perceived responsiveness.

Key take-away: If the scenario emphasizes fast first output, partial responses, or streaming tokens, look first for InvokeModelWithStreaming combined with REST API response streaming. Choose WebSockets only when the question explicitly requires bidirectional or event driven communication.

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithStreaming and push tokens to clients using Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API connections. Maintain persistent bidirectional connections and manage connection state for each client. Close the connection after the full response is generated - WebSocket APIs support real time bidirectional communication, but they introduce additional complexity that is unnecessary for simple response streaming. Managing persistent connections and connection state increases operational overhead. This approach is more appropriate for event driven or collaborative scenarios. Using WebSockets does not inherently improve time to first token beyond what REST response streaming already provides. For standard request response chat interactions, this design over engineers the solution.

Use Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel to generate the full response and return it through Amazon API Gateway HTTP API. Optimize performance by reducing payload size and using faster HTTP integrations. Leverage client side loading indicators to manage perceived latency - InvokeModel waits for the full response to be generated before returning any output. Transport level optimizations cannot compensate for generation latency at the model layer. This approach does not meet the requirement to deliver partial responses early.

Use Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithStreaming to stream tokens as they are generated by the foundation model. Forward the streamed output through Amazon API Gateway HTTP API so clients receive partial responses over HTTP immediately. Optimize performance by reducing payload size and using faster HTTP integrations - InvokeModelWithStreaming does stream tokens from the foundation model as they are generated. That part of the option is correct. However, Amazon API Gateway HTTP API does not support response streaming. HTTP APIs always buffer the full backend response and return it only after completion. As a result, even if Lambda receives tokens incrementally from Bedrock, the client will not see any partial output until the entire response finishes.

As a GenAI engineer, how should you troubleshoot and optimize the vector search configuration so that retrieval performance and relevance remain consistent as the system scales? (Select two)

Resize and rebalance OpenSearch shards so that vector data and query load are distributed evenly across the cluster. Use OpenSearch dashboards to monitor hot shards and reindex when necessary to eliminate load concentration

Increase the top K value for all vector queries and pass the larger candidate list to Amazon Bedrock for re ranking. Allow autoscaling to trigger based solely on CPU utilization to handle traffic surges

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Tune the OpenSearch Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) index by adjusting efSearch, efConstruction, and M settings to balance recall and latency for large vector workloads. Validate improvements by using OpenSearch Trace Analytics and query level metrics during peak traffic periods

Tuning HNSW parameters such as efSearch, efConstruction, and M allows you to directly control the balance between accuracy and latency. Larger HNSW graphs with higher ef values improve recall but require more compute, so finding the right balance is essential for predictable performance. Adjusting these parameters helps the system respond more efficiently as the corpus size grows.

Vector search clusters experience different behavior during peak traffic, so evaluating changes under real conditions is important. OpenSearch Trace Analytics provides query level visibility, allowing you to confirm whether the tuning reduces latencies. This type of monitoring shows which parameters have the greatest performance impact.

Iterative tuning is necessary because vector workloads shift over time as new content is added. By continuously validating performance and relevance, you ensure that search results remain accurate and the system can handle seasonal surges without latency spikes.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/choose-the-k-nn-algorithm-for-your-billion-scale-use-case-with-opensearch/

Resize and rebalance OpenSearch shards so that vector data and query load are distributed evenly across the cluster. Use OpenSearch dashboards to monitor hot shards and reindex when necessary to eliminate load concentration

Shard size and distribution have a major effect on vector search performance because heavy traffic can overload certain shards. Even distribution of vectors across the cluster ensures that no single shard becomes a bottleneck. This reduces tail latency and improves overall throughput during busy periods.

Monitoring shard behavior through OpenSearch dashboards helps identify hotspots. If certain shards receive too many queries or contain too many vectors, rebalancing or resizing them becomes necessary. The goal is to remove imbalances before they create user-facing delays.

As datasets grow into tens of millions of vectors, initial shard settings often become outdated. Reindexing, changing shard counts, or increasing node capacity helps maintain stability. Proper shard tuning keeps the vector index responsive and ensures relevance does not degrade during traffic spikes.

Incorrect options:

Switch the vector index to Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) mode but keep the current shard count and default Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) parameters unchanged. Use CloudWatch metrics at the cluster level instead of examining query level latencies or relevance metrics - Switching to HNSW without tuning its parameters or fixing shard imbalance does not solve the core issues. The default ANN settings may not suit large scale workloads, so performance problems and relevance inconsistencies will continue. Relying only on cluster level CloudWatch metrics hides the detailed insights needed to fix the root cause. Vector search optimization requires examining query level metrics, tail latency, index distribution, and ANN configuration. Without this deeper analysis, you cannot address inconsistent performance or poor retrieval quality.

Increase the top K value for all vector queries and pass the larger candidate list to Amazon Bedrock for re ranking. Allow autoscaling to trigger based solely on CPU utilization to handle traffic surges - Increasing top K makes queries more expensive and usually slows down vector search during traffic spikes. Adding a Bedrock re ranking step further increases overall latency and does not fix underlying index inefficiencies. This approach only shifts the problem rather than resolving it. Autoscaling based only on CPU misses the fact that vector workloads fail for reasons unrelated to compute limits. Shard imbalance, poor ANN configuration, and graph construction issues require tuning at the search layer, not reactive scaling.

Consolidate the vector index into a single high memory OpenSearch node to reduce cross shard communication. Use S3 snapshots as the primary method for ensuring consistent retrieval behavior - Consolidating the index onto a single node removes horizontal scalability and introduces a major bottleneck. Large vector workloads require distributed search to handle high query volume, and a single node cannot provide this. Traffic spikes would quickly overwhelm the system. S3 snapshots are useful for backup and recovery, but they do not affect search latency, relevance, or index performance. They do nothing to address the real cause of stale or slow results.

Custom CloudWatch metrics allow you to track specific fairness dimensions such as sentiment deltas, tone divergence, stereotype indicators, or content asymmetry. Dashboards allow policy stakeholders to visualize fairness trends over time and understand how specific groups are affected. This approach supports data driven fairness governance by providing monitoring, alerting, and auditing capabilities that scale with model usage.

This approach relies heavily on human review, which does not scale for multilingual generative workloads. Manual processes cannot provide the real time fairness monitoring required for public sector communication governance. Without automated metrics or group segmentation, fairness deviations may remain undetected until long after outputs have been delivered.

Use S3 Metadata, which introduces live inventory tables that work with familiar SQL based tools, to query these attributes efficiently at scale. Filter matching objects using SQL queries before retrieving content for foundation model context

Store document attributes as Amazon S3 object metadata and object tags, and additionally generate embeddings for each document to support semantic ranking across the dataset. Index both metadata and embeddings in Amazon OpenSearch Service and rerank results before sending them to the model. Maintain periodic re indexing workflows to keep vector representations synchronized with metadata updates

Generate vector embeddings for all documents and encode timestamps and authorship into the embedding input. Store embeddings in a vector database and retrieve documents using similarity search only. Use prompt logic to infer metadata relevance instead of explicit filtering

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Store document attributes such as creation date, author, and domain as Amazon S3 object metadata and object tags at upload time. Use S3 Metadata, which introduces live inventory tables that work with familiar SQL based tools, to query these attributes efficiently at scale. Filter matching objects using SQL queries before retrieving content for foundation model context

Storing timestamps, authorship, and domain attributes as Amazon S3 object metadata enables fast, deterministic filtering without scanning document content. S3 Metadata introduces live inventory tables that work with familiar SQL based tools, allowing teams to query object level attributes efficiently even when managing millions of objects. This design significantly improves retrieval speed and precision. Because metadata queries execute independently of document content, the system avoids unnecessary reads and scales predictably as the dataset grows. Filtering objects before retrieval ensures that only contextually valid documents are passed to the foundation model, improving grounding quality and reducing noise.

This approach avoids the cost and operational complexity of embedding generation and vector indexing. It aligns well with use cases where users rely on explicit attributes such as time ranges, ownership, and domain classification to locate relevant context.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-s3-metadata-now-supports-metadata-for-all-your-s3-objects/

Incorrect options:

Store document attributes as Amazon S3 object metadata and object tags, and additionally generate embeddings for each document to support semantic ranking across the dataset. Index both metadata and embeddings in Amazon OpenSearch Service and rerank results before sending them to the model. Maintain periodic re indexing workflows to keep vector representations synchronized with metadata updates - Although this design uses object metadata, generating embeddings introduces unnecessary cost and complexity for a retrieval pattern driven by structured attributes. Maintaining embedding pipelines for millions of objects increases latency and operational overhead. Vector based reranking provides limited value when users explicitly filter by timestamps and authorship. The additional infrastructure does not materially improve precision for metadata driven queries.

Store document attributes inside the document body and rely on full text search to extract timestamps and authorship during retrieval. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service keyword queries to scan document content across the repository. Increase shard count and replica settings to handle scale - Embedding metadata inside document content forces full text scans during retrieval, which does not scale efficiently for large object counts. Keyword search is not optimized for extracting structured attributes such as timestamps or ownership at query time. Increasing shard count improves throughput but does not reduce query complexity. This approach increases cost while still delivering inconsistent retrieval performance.

Generate vector embeddings for all documents and encode timestamps and authorship into the embedding input. Store embeddings in a vector database and retrieve documents using similarity search only. Use prompt logic to infer metadata relevance instead of explicit filtering - Vector embeddings are not suitable for precise filtering on structured attributes like dates or authorship. Encoding metadata into embeddings reduces interpretability and makes retrieval behavior harder to control. This also increases compute and storage costs significantly. Using similarity search alone ignores native object metadata capabilities that are purpose built for fast attribute based filtering. This design does not meet the performance or cost requirements of the scenario.

An equipment financing provider uses Amazon Bedrock to assess lease applications from scanned financial forms. The application must extract structured fields, remove personally identifiable information (PII) before foundation model inference, and generate approval recommendations. Human reviewers must work from the corresponding approved geographic jurisdiction. The provider's Regional queueing and orchestration layer already supports 32,000 applications daily and a 99.95% availability target. The provider must add document processing, privacy controls, and auditable storage. All required services and a model supporting in-Region inference are available in each approved Region.

Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select three)

Use Regional Textract extraction and send the complete extracted records to Amazon Bedrock with instructions to omit personal identifiers from recommendations. Apply sensitive-information filters to model outputs, store only sanitized recommendations, and send responses that trigger a filter to locally based human reviewers instead of reviewing extraction confidence

Correct selection
Store original forms, processing results, and review records in approved Regional S3 buckets. Restrict access to those buckets, prevent cross-Region replication, and retain CloudTrail management events and S3 data events alongside application audit records in the same Region

Correct selection
Use Amazon Textract with Amazon A2I in each applicant's approved Region. Route low-confidence extraction results to a private work team whose reviewers operate from the corresponding approved jurisdiction

Validate extracted fields with AWS Glue Data Quality. Use Step Functions to route failed checks to reviewers and transform validated records into optimized prompts before invoking Amazon Bedrock

Correct selection
Use Lambda with Regional Amazon Comprehend PII detection to redact extracted text before Bedrock inference. Apply Bedrock Guardrails to outputs. Enforce approved resources and Regions through IAM and SCPs, and restrict model and guardrail processing to in-Region operation

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Use Amazon Textract with Amazon A2I in each applicant's approved Region. Route low-confidence extraction results to a private work team whose reviewers operate from the corresponding approved jurisdiction

Amazon Textract extracts text and structured information from scanned forms and supplies confidence scores. Amazon A2I supports human review conditions for Textract results, including low-confidence form fields. This directly addresses the need to review uncertain extraction before downstream assessment.

The Textract integration requires the A2I resources to use the same AWS Region as the AnalyzeDocument request. Deploying the processing and review resources in the applicant's approved Region supports the Regional architecture.

A Regional A2I deployment does not establish where reviewers physically work. The provider must select and manage a private team that meets the jurisdiction requirement. Review results should return to the workflow before redaction and inference continue.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/process-mortgage-documents-with-intelligent-document-processing-using-amazon-textract-and-amazon-comprehend/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/process-mortgage-documents-with-intelligent-document-processing-using-amazon-textract-and-amazon-comprehend/

Store original forms, processing results, and review records in approved Regional S3 buckets. Restrict access to those buckets, prevent cross-Region replication, and retain CloudTrail management events and S3 data events alongside application audit records in the same Region

Separate Regional S3 storage locations provide explicit destinations for original documents and processing artifacts. Resource-scoped permissions restrict the application to approved buckets, while preventing cross-Region replication avoids copying these records outside the permitted boundary.

CloudTrail management events record relevant administrative activity, and S3 data events record selected object-level operations. Application audit records add information that infrastructure logs do not fully describe, such as extraction confidence, reviewer corrections, model identifiers, and approval recommendations.

Retaining these records in the approved Region supports investigation without exporting sensitive evidence. Object metadata and tags can help correlate artifacts, but they do not replace event logs or application decision records.

Use Lambda with Regional Amazon Comprehend PII detection to redact extracted text before Bedrock inference. Apply Bedrock Guardrails to outputs. Enforce approved resources and Regions through IAM and SCPs, and restrict model and guardrail processing to in-Region operation

Lambda can call Amazon Comprehend PII detection and use the returned text offsets to redact sensitive values before constructing the Bedrock request. The workflow must submit only the sanitized content to the foundation model and prevent unredacted documents from entering the inference payload.

Bedrock Guardrails provide additional output controls, but output filtering does not substitute for preprocessing. Redaction quality must match the provider's document types and sensitive fields, and processing failures must not bypass the privacy step.

IAM and SCP restrictions must enforce access to approved resources and Regional operations. IAM roles themselves are not Regional resources. Selecting in-Region model inference and avoiding cross-Region guardrail processing preserves the single-Region boundary while using the existing scalable orchestration layer.

Incorrect options:

Index uploaded financial forms with Amazon Kendra and Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use semantic search results to populate structured application fields and use relevance scores to determine whether extraction requires human review - Kendra and OpenSearch Service provide search capabilities. Semantic relevance scores indicate how well indexed content matches a query; they are not confidence scores for extracting individual fields from scanned forms.

The option also lacks PII redaction and the required extraction-review mechanism. Search can complement a document application, but it does not replace the specified extraction and privacy controls.

Validate extracted fields with AWS Glue Data Quality. Use Step Functions to route failed checks to reviewers and transform validated records into optimized prompts before invoking Amazon Bedrock - Glue Data Quality can validate structured records against rules such as completeness and valid ranges. Step Functions can orchestrate review, but those checks do not inherently identify uncertain OCR or form extraction.

Prompt optimization also does not remove PII or enforce Regional processing. These services could complement the architecture, but this option does not provide the required privacy and extraction-confidence controls.

Use Regional Textract extraction and send the complete extracted records to Amazon Bedrock with instructions to omit personal identifiers from recommendations. Apply sensitive-information filters to model outputs, store only sanitized recommendations, and send responses that trigger a filter to locally based human reviewers instead of reviewing extraction confidence - Sending complete extracted records to Bedrock exposes their PII to the foundation model before output filtering occurs. Instructions to omit identifiers and sanitized storage cannot satisfy a requirement to redact before inference.

Sensitive-information filter interventions also measure a different condition from extraction confidence. A misread financial field can require review without triggering a PII filter, so this workflow would miss required review cases.

A pharmaceutical company uses AWS Control Tower to govern its research accounts. Sensitive research data must remain within the European Union. Developers must submit Amazon Bedrock requests through the AWS Region, eu-central-1. The company permits Amazon Nova Pro inference only through the eu.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 cross-Region inference profile, including processing in that profile's EU destination Regions.

The company's existing SCPs deny Regional operations outside eu-central-1. Developer IAM roles have broad Amazon Bedrock permissions. When a developer invokes Nova Pro through the Bedrock Chat/Text playground in eu-central-1, the request fails with this error:

User: arn:aws:sts::482761935028:assumed-role/ResearchGenAIRole/AnalystSession
Action: bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream
Resource: arn:aws:bedrock:eu-north-1::foundation-model/amazon.nova-pro-v1:0
Context: A service control policy explicitly denies the action
The company must enable the approved inference profile while retaining its restrictions on other models, request-origin Regions, and unrelated AWS operations.

Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select two)

Enable Amazon Nova Pro model access in eu-north-1 and retry the request while retaining the existing SCP restrictions

Configure the Bedrock Runtime client to use the eu-central-1 endpoint and invoke the approved EU profile. Keep the SCP denies for other Regions and rely on the selected endpoint to restrict all inference processing to eu-central-1

Correct selection
Update the SCPs to permit Nova Pro inference only through the approved profile. Use bedrock:InferenceProfileArn to scope the destination-Region exception to that profile's ARN in eu-central-1

Modify the Regional SCP restriction to exempt Amazon Bedrock inference through every profile whose identifier begins with eu.

Verify that the developer roles allow the required inference actions on the approved profile and Nova Pro model resources in eu-central-1 and every destination Region listed in the profile

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Update the SCPs to permit Nova Pro inference only through the approved profile. Use bedrock:InferenceProfileArn to scope the destination-Region exception to that profile's ARN in eu-central-1

The error identifies an explicit SCP denial on a Nova Pro model resource in eu-north-1. Although the developer submits the request in eu-central-1, cross-Region inference requires authorization for the profile's destination model resources. The existing restriction blocks that authorization.

The bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key allows administrators to distinguish foundation model access through the approved profile from other access. A narrowly scoped exception referencing the profile ARN in eu-central-1 permits the required destination evaluations without opening those Regions to unrelated operations. The SCP configuration must also preserve the requirement to invoke Nova Pro only through the approved profile.

The originating request remains subject to the source-Region restriction because Bedrock separately evaluates access to the inference profile resource. This approach preserves eu-central-1 as the request origin while permitting processing in the profile's EU destinations. Administrators must ensure that no other applicable SCP continues to deny the required inference operations.

Enable Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference in multi-account environments:

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/enable-amazon-bedrock-cross-region-inference-in-multi-account-environments/

The reported request requires bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream. Applications that also perform non-streaming inference need bedrock:InvokeModel. Verifying the complete destination list avoids checking only eu-central-1 or the single Region named in the error.

This check complements the SCP adjustment. The developer roles' broad Bedrock permissions might already provide the necessary identity-based permissions, but the administrator must verify that coverage. IAM permissions authorize the request, and the SCPs determine whether organizational policy permits those permissions to take effect.

Incorrect options:

Configure the Bedrock Runtime client to use the eu-central-1 endpoint and invoke the approved EU profile. Keep the SCP denies for other Regions and rely on the selected endpoint to restrict all inference processing to eu-central-1 The Regional client endpoint determines where the request enters Amazon Bedrock. It does not force a cross-Region inference profile to perform all processing in that same Region.

The approved profile can route processing to its other EU destinations. Retaining destination-Region denies without an appropriate exception preserves the authorization failure.

Enable Amazon Nova Pro model access in eu-north-1 and retry the request while retaining the existing SCP restrictions Model access configuration does not remove an organizational policy denial. The error specifically identifies the SCP as the blocking control.

Addressing only eu-north-1 also overlooks authorization for the profile's other destinations. The company must correct the applicable SCP restriction and verify permissions across the complete resource set.

Modify the Regional SCP restriction to exempt Amazon Bedrock inference through every profile whose identifier begins with eu. An exception covering every eu. profile would extend access beyond the approved Nova Pro profile. Other models could benefit from the same exception.

Keeping inference within the EU satisfies the geographic boundary but does not satisfy the company's model-specific restriction. The exception must identify the approved profile precisely.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 58
Skipped
An industrial equipment manufacturer operates a maintenance assistant through a React application hosted with AWS Amplify. The application uses an AWS AppSync GraphQL API with an AWS Lambda resolver configured for RequestResponse invocation. The resolver calls the Amazon Bedrock RetrieveAndGenerate API to answer questions from a knowledge base of equipment manuals.

Technicians report that detailed troubleshooting questions frequently time out. Application traces show that retrieval completes quickly, but generating longer answers can take 45 seconds. The manufacturer needs to eliminate the synchronous request bottleneck, preserve access to the maintenance knowledge base, and display answer text progressively.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Increase the resolver's Lambda function timeout to 180 seconds and configure the React application to retry failed GraphQL requests with exponential backoff

Configure provisioned concurrency for the resolver's Lambda function and enable AppSync resolver caching with a cache key that includes the user identity and question text. Retain RequestResponse invocation and RetrieveAndGenerate for cache misses. Increase the browser request timeout to 180 seconds and display a loading indicator until the resolver returns the complete answer

Correct answer
Implement an AWS Amplify AI Kit conversation route with a tool that retrieves maintenance knowledge base content. Deliver generated response chunks through AppSync subscriptions and use the useAIConversation React hook to update the interface progressively

Replace RetrieveAndGenerate with InvokeModelWithResponseStream and send the user's question directly to the foundation model. Deliver generated text through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Implement an AWS Amplify AI Kit conversation route with a tool that retrieves maintenance knowledge base content. Deliver generated response chunks through AppSync subscriptions and use the useAIConversation React hook to update the interface progressively

An Amplify AI Kit conversation route supports streaming interactions through AppSync. The backend receives generated response chunks from Amazon Bedrock and publishes updates that subscribed clients receive. This separates delivery of the answer from the original synchronous GraphQL request, addressing the bottleneck that causes longer generations to exceed the request execution limit.

The conversation route can access the existing knowledge base through a retrieval tool. Amplify documents an integration that exposes a custom AppSync query backed by the Bedrock Retrieve operation. The model uses the retrieved passages as context when generating its answer. This preserves access to the maintenance manuals while replacing the original synchronous RetrieveAndGenerate interaction.

The useAIConversation React hook manages subscription updates and exposes conversation messages as React state as chunks arrive. Technicians can begin reading an answer before generation finishes. Streaming improves time to the first visible answer text and avoids holding the initial request open for the entire generation, although it does not inherently reduce the model's total generation time.

Incorrect options:

Increase the resolver's Lambda function timeout to 180 seconds and configure the React application to retry failed GraphQL requests with exponential backoff - The Lambda function timeout and the AppSync request execution limit are separate constraints. AppSync has a maximum request execution time of 30 seconds. Increasing the Lambda timeout to 180 seconds does not allow a synchronous GraphQL request to wait for a 45-second generation.

Exponential backoff helps with transient failures such as throttling, but it does not remove this duration mismatch. Retrying a long-running generation can repeat the same timeout and incur additional inference work. The client also continues to receive no answer text until a request completes successfully.

Replace RetrieveAndGenerate with InvokeModelWithResponseStream and send the user's question directly to the foundation model. Deliver generated text through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API - InvokeModelWithResponseStream supports streaming foundation model output, and an API Gateway WebSocket API can support a custom delivery architecture. The issue is that direct model invocation does not perform knowledge base retrieval. Sending only the user's question omits the maintenance passages that the original RetrieveAndGenerate operation supplied.

The manufacturer explicitly requires continued access to its maintenance knowledge base. This option would require an additional retrieval and context-assembly step to meet that requirement. Streaming alone does not preserve the retrieval-augmented generation behavior of the original application.

Configure provisioned concurrency for the resolver's Lambda function and enable AppSync resolver caching with a cache key that includes the user identity and question text. Retain RequestResponse invocation and RetrieveAndGenerate for cache misses. Increase the browser request timeout to 180 seconds and display a loading indicator until the resolver returns the complete answer - Provisioned concurrency reduces Lambda initialization delays, and resolver caching can accelerate requests that reuse cached results. The traces identify extended model generation as the problem. New troubleshooting questions that miss the cache still require the synchronous resolver to wait for the full answer.

Increasing the browser timeout does not change the AppSync request execution limit. A loading indicator provides status feedback but does not deliver answer text progressively. These optimizations can help other latency conditions, but they do not resolve the failure described in the scenario.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 59
Skipped
A global vacation rental marketplace helps travelers around the world find places to stay. The marketplace has 40 million monthly active users. The company wants to implement semantic search across a database that contains 18 million property listings and 180 million guest reviews. The company currently stores this data in a PostgreSQL database.

The solution must support complex natural language queries, such as "quiet cabin near hiking trails with a fast internet connection." The solution must return results for at least 95% of queries within 400 ms. Listing details, such as availability and nightly rates, change every 30 minutes, and the solution must keep search results current with those changes. The solution must also scale cost-effectively during peak travel seasons.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

Migrate the listing data to Amazon OpenSearch Service and implement keyword-based search rules with custom analyzers and relevance tuning to match listings on attributes such as property type, amenities, and location. Create Amazon API Gateway HTTP API endpoints that convert user queries into structured search parameters

Keep the data in PostgreSQL and use SQL filters to select candidate properties. Send the candidates and their reviews to a Bedrock language model for ranking on every request, and calculate amenity facets in Lambda

Correct answer
Migrate the listing data to Amazon OpenSearch Service and use a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from listing descriptions, reviews, and amenities. Convert each natural language query to an embedding with the same FM and run k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) searches to find semantically similar results

Keep the listing data in PostgreSQL and install the pgvector extension. Use a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from the listing data and store the embeddings in PostgreSQL. Create an AWS Lambda function that converts natural language queries into vectors with the same FM and runs similarity searches in the database

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Migrate the listing data to Amazon OpenSearch Service and use a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from listing descriptions, reviews, and amenities. Convert each natural language query to an embedding with the same FM and run k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) searches to find semantically similar results

Semantic search requires the system to match the meaning of a query, not only its keywords. An embeddings model in Amazon Bedrock, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, converts listing descriptions, reviews, and amenities into vectors that capture meaning. It converts each traveler's query into a vector in the same embedding space. Because the model supports many languages, travelers around the world can search in their own language and still match relevant listings. Calling a managed embeddings API removes any need to train or host an embeddings model.

Amazon OpenSearch Service includes a vector engine that performs approximate k-NN search with algorithms such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). This approach is designed to search hundreds of millions of vectors with low latency, which supports the requirement to return 95% of queries within 400 ms. OpenSearch also combines vector similarity with filters on structured fields, such as location, dates, and price. Travelers get results that match both the meaning of the query and their practical constraints.

To keep results current, the application re-embeds only the listings that changed in each 30-minute window and updates them with the OpenSearch bulk API. The index never needs a full rebuild. For cost-effective scaling, the company can use Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector collections, which adjust capacity automatically with demand, or size managed domains with vector compression to reduce memory costs. Because the solution relies on managed services for both embeddings and vector search, it requires the least development effort.

Amazon OpenSearch Service’s vector database capabilities explained:

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/amazon-opensearch-services-vector-database-capabilities-explained/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/amazon-opensearch-services-vector-database-capabilities-explained/

Incorrect options:

Keep the data in PostgreSQL and use SQL filters to select candidate properties. Send the candidates and their reviews to a Bedrock language model for ranking on every request, and calculate amenity facets in Lambda A language model can compare candidate properties against a user's preferences. This approach nevertheless requires the application to assemble, transmit, and rank potentially large collections of listing and review text for every request.

It does not use a precomputed semantic index to narrow the candidate set efficiently. Repeated generation work, custom ranking orchestration, and database-side candidate retrieval make it a poor fit for the latency, independent scaling, and development-effort requirements.

Migrate the listing data to Amazon OpenSearch Service and implement keyword-based search rules with custom analyzers and relevance tuning to match listings on attributes such as property type, amenities, and location. Create Amazon API Gateway HTTP API endpoints that convert user queries into structured search parameters - Keyword-based search with custom analyzers matches terms, not meaning. A query such as "quiet cabin near hiking trails" might miss relevant listings that describe a "secluded lodge close to mountain paths." Keyword rules cannot reliably interpret complex natural language intent.

Building API Gateway endpoints to convert free-form queries into structured parameters also requires substantial custom parsing logic that must be maintained as user phrasing changes. This design does not deliver semantic search and increases development effort.

Keep the listing data in PostgreSQL and install the pgvector extension. Use a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from the listing data and store the embeddings in PostgreSQL. Create an AWS Lambda function that converts natural language queries into vectors with the same FM and runs similarity searches in the database - The pgvector extension adds vector search to PostgreSQL, but indexing and querying approximately 198 million vectors in the same database that serves transactional workloads creates heavy memory and compute demands. Vector queries during peak seasons would compete with application traffic, which makes the 400 ms target difficult to achieve consistently.

Scaling a PostgreSQL database to handle this vector workload typically requires large instances and read replicas, which is not cost-effective. The company must also build and maintain the Lambda function, the embedding workflow, and the query logic itself, which adds development effort.

Question 60
Skipped
An insurance company uses Amazon Bedrock to run an application that generates summaries of property damage claim reports for adjusters. The application produces inconsistent summary quality and occasionally includes factual hallucinations. The application's monthly costs are 35% higher than the company's budget forecast.

A GenAI developer must implement a near real-time monitoring solution that detects hallucinations, identifies unusual token consumption, and provides early warnings of cost anomalies. The solution must require minimal custom development and maintenance overhead.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Run Amazon Bedrock evaluation jobs that use LLM-based judgments to detect hallucinations and use Amazon CloudWatch to track token usage. Build an AWS Lambda function that processes the CloudWatch metrics and sends notifications about usage patterns

Correct answer
Turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to an Amazon S3 bucket with text output logging enabled. Use Amazon Bedrock guardrails with contextual grounding checks to detect hallucinations, and create Amazon CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms on the token usage metrics

Use AWS CloudTrail to log every Amazon Bedrock API call and build a custom Amazon QuickSight dashboard to visualize token usage patterns. Use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to detect quality drift in the generated summaries

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with every content filter category set to HIGH strength to catch hallucinated statements, stream the model invocation logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, schedule hourly CloudWatch Logs Insights queries that calculate token totals, and invoke an AWS Lambda function that compares the totals with a static daily budget and sends Amazon SNS notifications

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to an Amazon S3 bucket with text output logging enabled. Use Amazon Bedrock guardrails with contextual grounding checks to detect hallucinations, and create Amazon CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms on the token usage metrics

The contextual grounding check in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails detects hallucinations at inference time. For a summarization workload, the application passes the original claim report as the grounding source. The guardrail scores each summary for grounding, which measures whether the content is supported by the source, and for relevance to the query. Summaries that score below the configured thresholds are flagged or blocked immediately. That gives the company near real-time hallucination detection on every request without building a custom evaluation pipeline.

Amazon Bedrock publishes runtime metrics such as InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, and Invocations to Amazon CloudWatch automatically. CloudWatch anomaly detection applies machine learning to each metric's history to build a model of expected values, including daily and weekly patterns. An anomaly detection alarm fires when token consumption moves outside the expected band. This provides early warning of runaway prompts, unexpectedly long outputs, or traffic spikes that drive cost overruns. The alarms need no manually tuned static thresholds and adapt as normal usage changes.

Model invocation logging with text output enabled captures the full prompts and generated summaries in Amazon S3. When an alarm fires or a guardrail flags a summary, the developer can inspect the exact inputs and outputs to find the root cause, such as oversized claim reports or prompts that invite speculation. Every component in this design is a managed Amazon Bedrock or CloudWatch feature, so the solution meets all three monitoring goals with minimal custom development and maintenance.

Incorrect options:

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with every content filter category set to HIGH strength to catch hallucinated statements, stream the model invocation logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, schedule hourly CloudWatch Logs Insights queries that calculate token totals, and invoke an AWS Lambda function that compares the totals with a static daily budget and sends Amazon SNS notifications - Content filters in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails detect harmful content categories such as hate, insults, sexual content, violence, misconduct, and prompt attacks. They do not assess whether a summary is factually supported by the source document. Setting every filter to HIGH strength increases false positives without detecting hallucinations.

Hourly CloudWatch Logs Insights queries, a custom AWS Lambda function, and a static daily budget create custom components that the developer must maintain. Static thresholds also miss unusual patterns that stay under the daily total. CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms deliver faster and more accurate warnings with no custom code.

Run Amazon Bedrock evaluation jobs that use LLM-based judgments to detect hallucinations and use Amazon CloudWatch to track token usage. Build an AWS Lambda function that processes the CloudWatch metrics and sends notifications about usage patterns - Amazon Bedrock evaluation jobs run on demand against prompt datasets and produce reports after each job completes. They are useful for periodic quality assessment before deployment, but they do not evaluate every production response in near real time. Hallucinations that occur between evaluation runs go undetected until the next job.

The custom AWS Lambda function adds code that the developer must build and maintain to process metrics and send notifications. CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms provide this capability natively. This design adds custom work while leaving gaps in real-time detection.

Use AWS CloudTrail to log every Amazon Bedrock API call and build a custom Amazon QuickSight dashboard to visualize token usage patterns. Use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to detect quality drift in the generated summaries - AWS CloudTrail records API activity for auditing, such as who invoked which model and when. It does not capture token counts or response content in a form suitable for usage anomaly detection. Building a custom Amazon QuickSight dashboard also provides visualization only, with no automated alerting on cost anomalies.

Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor is designed for models hosted on SageMaker endpoints. It cannot directly monitor summaries generated by Amazon Bedrock foundation models. Even with custom data capture, its drift statistics do not detect hallucinations in individual summaries.

Question 61
Skipped
A logistics company uses an Amazon Bedrock foundation model (FM) to generate shipment exception summaries. The company wants to evaluate a candidate model before replacing its production model. The candidate must demonstrate better relevance, factual accuracy, and fluency across routine and unusual shipment scenarios. The company requires a sequential validation process with human review and approval after every stage. Automated quality gates must assess the completed model comparison against predefined acceptance thresholds before the team prepares its final evaluation report.

Consider the following steps:

1. Analyze the evaluation results and prepare a comprehensive report
2. Conduct controlled A/B testing between the candidate and production models
3. Build a representative test dataset that includes common scenarios and edge cases
4. Define evaluation metrics and acceptance thresholds for relevance, factual accuracy, and fluency
5. Implement automated quality gates in AWS Step Functions to assess the comparison results
Which option places all five steps in the correct order?

Perform steps 3, 4, 2, 5, and 1 in that order

Perform steps 4, 3, 2, 1, and 5 in that order

Correct answer
Perform steps 4, 3, 2, 5, and 1 in that order

Perform steps 3, 2, 4, 5, and 1 in that order

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Perform steps 4, 3, 2, 5, and 1 in that order

First define the evaluation metrics and acceptance thresholds so that the team agrees on what constitutes an improvement. Then build a representative dataset with routine shipment scenarios, difficult exceptions, and reference responses where appropriate. Reviewers approve these artifacts before the model comparison begins.

Next conduct controlled A/B testing under comparable conditions and collect scores for both models. Implement automated quality gates in AWS Step Functions to assess those completed comparison results against the predefined thresholds. Choice states can evaluate scores supplied by evaluation tasks and route passing or failing results appropriately. Automated threshold checks complement the required human approvals.

Finally, analyze the model scores and quality gate outcomes to prepare the comprehensive evaluation report. Document improvements, regressions, edge-case performance, and whether the candidate satisfies the acceptance criteria. Reviewers use this evidence to decide whether to approve the production replacement.

Incorrect options:

Perform steps 3, 4, 2, 5, and 1 in that order - This sequence builds the dataset before defining the evaluation criteria. It reverses the intended dependency between deciding what to measure and constructing test cases that support those measurements.

Existing examples can inform planning, but this systematic process establishes the metrics and thresholds first. The team then selects scenarios and reference responses that provide suitable coverage for the approved criteria.

Perform steps 3, 2, 4, 5, and 1 in that order - This sequence builds the dataset and conducts A/B testing before defining the evaluation metrics. The comparison therefore begins without an agreed scoring framework or predefined acceptance thresholds.

Selecting success criteria after observing model responses can bias the replacement decision. Defining metrics first gives both models a consistent evaluation standard and guides dataset construction.

Perform steps 4, 3, 2, 1, and 5 in that order - This sequence prepares the final evaluation report before applying the automated quality gates. It omits the gate outcomes from the evidence available when the team produces that report.

The company requires automated assessment of the comparison results before final reporting. Preliminary analysis can occur earlier, but the comprehensive report must incorporate both the measured performance and the acceptance decisions.
