A media company wants to add a conversational assistant into its existing customer portal serving both web and mobile clients. The solution must return real-time responses, support GraphQL queries that fetch and update domain data alongside foundation model outputs, and convert incoming GraphQL requests into structured prompts for the foundation model while keeping latency low and hiding model API details from client applications.

Which solution would you implement to address these requirements?

Correct answer
Use AWS AppSync with direct Lambda resolvers to process GraphQL queries and transform them into foundation model prompts. Implement the inference logic inside the Lambda function and return structured outputs to clients while keeping model details hidden

Use an API Gateway HTTP API fronting a Lambda function that parses GraphQL payloads and invokes the foundation model endpoint. Cache responses in API Gateway to reduce model invocations and expose the HTTP API directly to web and mobile clients

Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate GraphQL parsing and foundation model calls and return results through Amazon EventBridge. Integrate the customer portal with EventBridge to fetch conversational responses from subscribed event targets

Use AWS AppSync with pipeline resolvers that invoke a Velocity Template Language (VTL) template to forward GraphQL requests directly to the foundation model endpoint. Rely on AppSync caching to reduce latency and expose the model output to clients without using Lambda for prompt transformation

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use AWS AppSync with direct Lambda resolvers to process GraphQL queries and transform them into foundation model prompts. Implement the inference logic inside the Lambda function and return structured outputs to clients while keeping model details hidden

AppSync provides a managed GraphQL service that can combine domain data access and foundation model inference within a single API while maintaining low latency. Direct Lambda resolvers allow the system to transform GraphQL requests into structured prompts, invoke the model, and merge the results with application data in real time.

This approach keeps client applications unaware of the underlying model APIs, centralizes prompt transformation logic, and supports both web and mobile clients through a unified GraphQL interface. AppSync also provides efficient data fetching and caching features that further reduce latency and round trips.

Incorrect options:

Use an API Gateway HTTP API fronting a Lambda function that parses GraphQL payloads and invokes the foundation model endpoint. Cache responses in API Gateway to reduce model invocations and expose the HTTP API directly to web and mobile clients - API Gateway HTTP APIs do not provide built-in GraphQL support or resolver level data fetching and therefore require custom parsing and stitching logic that increases latency and complexity. Caching GraphQL responses is unreliable because conversational outputs and domain data often change per request, and exposing HTTP APIs directly to clients does not offer the unified GraphQL interface required.

Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate GraphQL parsing and foundation model calls and return results through Amazon EventBridge. Integrate the customer portal with EventBridge to fetch conversational responses from subscribed event targets - Step Functions is designed for long running or orchestrated workflows and cannot deliver the low latency, synchronous response model required for conversational assistants. EventBridge is also not suitable for direct client integration because it lacks native mechanisms for request response flows or real-time communication with user applications.

Use AWS AppSync with pipeline resolvers that invoke a Velocity Template Language (VTL) template to forward GraphQL requests directly to the foundation model endpoint. Rely on AppSync caching to reduce latency and expose the model output to clients without using Lambda for prompt transformation - This option forwards GraphQL requests directly to the model endpoint, which does not allow the required prompt transformation, input shaping, or structured orchestration that Lambda resolvers provide. AppSync caching is not suitable for dynamic conversational outputs because each request produces unique responses, and bypassing Lambda prevents centralizing model integration logic.

What is the most effective way to redesign the document processing and chunking strategy?

Use a Lambda function to split each PDF into fixed size text chunks and then let Amazon Titan Text Embeddings handle semantic interpretation. Then rely on the foundation model to reconstruct missing definitions and logical structure during inference

Convert PDFs to structured formats such as HTML and upload them directly to Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Leverage default ingestion pipeline to automatically infer hierarchical boundaries and generate Titan embeddings from the processed text

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Convert PDFs into structured formats such as HTML and extract headings, subheadings, and table boundaries before ingestion. Then configure Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with hierarchical chunking rules and metadata mapping so that it creates structurally aligned segments for Titan embeddings and retrieval

Using structured preprocessing combined with hierarchical chunking inside Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases creates well aligned segments that reflect the true structure of regulatory documents. Converting PDFs into HTML or similar structured formats allows the system to extract document landmarks such as headings, subheadings, paragraph blocks, and footnotes, enabling precise segmentation before ingestion. Configuring Bedrock Knowledge Bases with hierarchical boundaries ensures that its ingestion engine produces coherent chunks that preserve the relationships between definitions and their surrounding context.

Hierarchical chunking organizes your data into a hierarchical structure, allowing for more granular and efficient retrieval based on the inherent relationships within your data:  via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/amazon-bedrock-knowledge-bases-now-supports-advanced-parsing-chunking-and-query-reformulation-giving-greater-control-of-accuracy-in-rag-based-applications/

Once these segments are passed through Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, the Knowledge Base stores both embeddings and metadata in a manner optimized for semantic retrieval. This setup significantly improves retrieval quality because the assistant can reference complete, context rich sections instead of partial or disconnected clauses.

Incorrect options:

Use a Lambda function to split each PDF into fixed size text chunks and then let Amazon Titan Text Embeddings handle semantic interpretation. Then rely on the foundation model to reconstruct missing definitions and logical structure during inference - Fixed size chunking ignores headings, definitions, and logical boundaries, which often causes embeddings to lose context or mix unrelated concepts. Relying on the foundation model to reconstruct missing structure leads to inconsistent retrieval for compliance focused content.

Upload entire documents directly into Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases without any preprocessing and leverage the default ingestion pipeline to identify chunk boundaries. Set up the Knowledge Base to automatically recover the logical relationships within the documents - Default Knowledge Base chunking works for simple documents but does not reliably detect complex hierarchical boundaries within regulatory PDFs. Without preprocessing, the ingestion pipeline may produce inconsistent or incomplete segments that reduce retrieval precision.

Convert PDFs to structured formats such as HTML and upload them directly to Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Leverage default ingestion pipeline to automatically infer hierarchical boundaries and generate Titan embeddings from the processed text - This option seems correct because it uses structured preprocessing and Bedrock Knowledge Bases. However, it is incorrect because default KB ingestion does not guarantee preservation of hierarchical boundaries, especially in complex PDFs with nested definitions, long clauses, or multi level regulatory structures. Failing to configure custom hierarchical chunking rules results in inconsistent segmentation and lower retrieval precision.

Use Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking to programmatically create artifacts for datasets, preprocessing jobs, training jobs, and model packages, and associate them through actions and contexts into a directed acyclic graph. The solution uses Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking to model datasets, preprocessing jobs, training jobs, and model artifacts as first class lineage entities and connects them via actions and contexts into a directed acyclic graph. By integrating these API calls into training, preprocessing, and deployment workflows across accounts, the solution produces a complete, queryable lineage view that shows how every production endpoint was derived from upstream inputs.

Cross account support through AddAssociation and properly scoped IAM roles allows experimentation accounts to link their artifacts to central production endpoints while maintaining security boundaries. Auditors can then query the lineage graph to reconstruct the full history of any model version, which is critical for traceability over sensitive clinical and imaging workloads. Use Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking to record training jobs and model packages as artifacts in the production account, and capture dataset and preprocessing job information in tags and CloudWatch Logs. Use a separate reporting script that combines lineage APIs, tags, and logs to build lineage graphs when needed - Recording only training jobs and model packages in SageMaker Lineage while leaving datasets and preprocessing jobs in tags and logs creates an incomplete lineage graph that breaks end to end traceability. Auditors would still need to piece together critical parts of the model history from unstructured sources, which defeats the goal of having a single, consistent lineage system built entirely on artifacts, actions, and contexts.

Question 33

A global retailer wants to build a GenAI customer support assistant that responds to users in real time through a web and mobile app. The assistant must answer natural language questions, call internal APIs to fetch order status or refund eligibility, and sometimes trigger workflows to update CRM records. The engineering team wants a managed orchestration approach that can maintain conversation context and return responses within a few seconds.

Which orchestration approach should the solutions architect recommend to coordinate the GenAI model, tools, and downstream actions for this real time assistant?

Send each chat message into EventBridge and start a Step Functions Standard workflow that fans out to Lambda tasks calling Bedrock and internal APIs. Clients poll another API to retrieve the final aggregated response after the workflow completes

Orchestrate each user request using a Step Functions Express workflow that is triggered by API Gateway. Load conversation history in the workflow and call Bedrock as well as internal APIs through Lambda. Return the response after the state machine finishes

Call the Bedrock model directly from a Lambda function and manually embed order and CRM data into prompts. Use a Lambda function to store and reload conversation history from DynamoDB and construct all logic without any agent or tool orchestration

Correct answer
Provision an agent using Amazon Bedrock Agents and define action groups that call Lambda functions wrapping internal order and CRM APIs. Expose the agent through API Gateway so the assistant can maintain conversation context, and respond in real time

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Provision an agent using Amazon Bedrock Agents and define action groups that call Lambda functions wrapping internal order and CRM APIs. Expose the agent through API Gateway so the assistant can maintain conversation context, and respond in real time

This option uses Amazon Bedrock Agents as the managed orchestration layer that coordinates the foundation model, tool calls, and conversation context. Agents in Bedrock can maintain multi turn conversations, automatically decide when to call tools, and orchestrate interactions with downstream systems through action groups. You define action groups that map to Lambda functions or HTTP endpoints which wrap internal order status APIs, refund logic, or CRM workflows. The agent uses these action groups to autonomously call tools when user queries require actions, then combines tool responses with model reasoning to produce a final natural language answer.

Exposing the agent through Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda gives web and mobile clients a low latency, stateless interface while keeping orchestration inside Bedrock Agents. API Gateway can front a REST or WebSocket API for interactive applications, while the agent core runtime remains serverless and managed. This pattern matches AWS guidance for using Bedrock to build agents that integrate with tools and business systems, and it aligns with the need for near real time responses for conversational assistants.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

Incorrect options:

Orchestrate each user request using a Step Functions Express workflow that is triggered by API Gateway. Load conversation history in the workflow and call Bedrock as well as internal APIs through Lambda. Return the response after the state machine finishes - This option uses AWS Step Functions Express Workflows as the primary orchestrator for each conversational request. Express workflows support high throughput and relatively low latency, and they integrate well with Lambda, Bedrock, and other AWS services. However, Step Functions focuses on workflow state transitions rather than fine grained conversational tool use and agentic reasoning. The architect would need to manually implement conversation state handling, tool selection, and multi step reasoning logic inside the state machine and Lambda tasks, which adds complexity for an interactive assistant that must respond in a few seconds. In addition, Step Functions introduces extra overhead compared to calling an agent directly, which works against the strict latency requirements for real time chat.

Call the Bedrock model directly from a Lambda function and manually embed order and CRM data into prompts. Use a Lambda function to store and reload conversation history from DynamoDB and construct all logic without any agent or tool orchestration - This option builds a custom orchestration layer entirely inside a single Lambda function and treats Amazon Bedrock as a basic text generation API. While this approach can work for very simple use cases, it ignores the managed tool calling and agent features that Bedrock provides. The developer must write custom code to parse user intent, decide which internal APIs to call, manage prompt construction, and stitch together model responses with tool outputs. This manual orchestration increases complexity and reduces flexibility compared to using Bedrock Agents, which are designed to integrate tools and handle multi turn interactions with less custom glue logic.

Send each chat message into EventBridge and start a Step Functions Standard workflow that fans out to Lambda tasks calling Bedrock and internal APIs. Clients poll another API to retrieve the final aggregated response after the workflow completes - This option uses Amazon EventBridge and Step Functions Standard Workflows with a polling pattern, which fits asynchronous event processing much better than low latency conversational flows. Standard workflows introduce higher startup latency and are optimized for long running or durable processes instead of sub second or few second interactive responses. Persisting intermediate data in S3 and asking clients to poll for results increases end to end latency and complicates the client experience, which conflicts directly with the requirement for real time responses in a chat interface. The event driven pattern and batch style orchestration do not match the primary skill area of designing low latency GenAI workflows for interactive assistants.

A compliance team needs to process tens of thousands of PDF reports each night and generate concise GenAI summaries for auditors. The reports are uploaded to Amazon S3 throughout the day, and the summaries must be ready by the next morning. The team wants to avoid long synchronous API calls, handle failures for individual documents, and automatically retry only failed items without reprocessing the whole batch.

How should the solutions architect orchestrate this large scale, batch GenAI summarization workflow?

Build an AWS Glue job that runs each night, crawls the S3 bucket for new PDFs, and calls Bedrock from within a single Spark driver script that loops over all documents. The script writes summaries back to S3 and reruns the entire Glue job if any error appears in the nightly logs

Configure S3 event notifications to trigger a Lambda function for every new PDF and have the function call Bedrock synchronously to generate a summary and store it in S3

Create a nightly Step Functions Express workflow that uses a single Lambda task to scan S3 for all new PDFs, call Bedrock in large batches, and write all summaries back to S3. The workflow uses a Retry policy on that Lambda task so any error causes the entire batch job to rerun from the beginning.

Correct answer
Configure Amazon S3 to send document upload events to SQS and use an EventBridge schedule to start a Step Functions Standard workflow that consumes the queue each night with a Map state over document identifiers. Each Map item invokes Lambda to fetch the PDF from S3, calls Amazon Bedrock for summarization, writes the summary back to S3, and applies per item retry policies so only failed documents run again

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure Amazon S3 to send document upload events to SQS and use an EventBridge schedule to start a Step Functions Standard workflow that consumes the queue each night with a Map state over document identifiers. Each Map item invokes Lambda to fetch the PDF from S3, calls Amazon Bedrock for summarization, writes the summary back to S3, and applies per item retry policies so only failed documents run again

This solution uses Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon EventBridge, AWS Step Functions Standard, AWS Lambda, and Amazon Bedrock in a coordinated batch architecture that fits the requirements. S3 event notifications send object created events into SQS, which decouples document ingestion from processing and smooths spiky upload patterns throughout the day. An EventBridge scheduled rule triggers a Step Functions Standard state machine at night, which reads identifiers from SQS or a manifest and uses a Map state to fan out thousands of parallel branches, one per document. Each branch calls a Lambda function that fetches a specific PDF from S3, invokes Bedrock to generate a summary, and stores the result back in S3 for auditors to consume the next morning.

Step Functions Map state supports item level retry and error handling, which ensures that only failed documents are retried without reprocessing the successful ones. This pattern provides clear visibility into per document status, integrates well with SQS for decoupling and buffering, and uses Bedrock asynchronously through Lambda while avoiding long running synchronous calls from clients. It also leverages the durability and orchestration guarantees of Step Functions Standard workflows, which are designed for long running, high fan out batch processing with strong observability.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-map.html

Incorrect options:

Create a nightly Step Functions Express workflow that uses a single Lambda task to scan S3 for all new PDFs, call Bedrock in large batches, and write all summaries back to S3. The workflow uses a Retry policy on that Lambda task so any error causes the entire batch job to rerun from the beginning. - This option uses a Step Functions Express workflow but processes all documents inside a single Lambda task that scans S3 and calls Bedrock in bulk. While Express workflows can handle high throughput, a single task that batches tens of thousands of documents ties the fate of the entire job to one function and one retry policy; any failure forces a rerun of the whole batch instead of retrying only the problematic items. It does not exploit the per item parallelization and fine grained retry capabilities that a Map state in a Standard workflow can provide for large nightly batches.

Configure S3 event notifications to trigger a Lambda function for every new PDF and have the function call Bedrock synchronously to generate a summary and store it in S3 - This option triggers a Lambda per document on every S3 upload and calls Bedrock synchronously, which effectively makes each summarization a small, isolated operation without any centralized orchestration for the nightly batch. It can quickly run into concurrency management challenges, offers limited per item observability across tens of thousands of functions, and does not give the team a straightforward way to coordinate retries for only failed documents in the context of a scheduled nightly run.

Build an AWS Glue job that runs each night, crawls the S3 bucket for new PDFs, and calls Bedrock from within a single Spark driver script that loops over all documents. The script writes summaries back to S3 and reruns the entire Glue job if any error appears in the nightly logs - This option centralizes all work inside a single AWS Glue job that loops over every PDF and calls Bedrock from one script, which creates a monolithic nightly batch. If any document triggers an exception and the Glue job fails, the team must rerun the entire job, which reprocesses already completed documents and wastes time and compute. It does not offer fine grained, per document retry semantics or a clean parallel orchestration model for tens of thousands of independent summarization tasks.

A supply chain organization has built a graph of suppliers, warehouses, routes, and risk scores and is now adding textual reports, incident summaries, and audit findings to help a foundation model answer risk related questions. The team wants the assistant to consider both the graph structure and the semantic similarity of text when retrieving context for questions like "Which suppliers are at highest risk of disruption over the next quarter, and why?" As the GenAI specialist, you must design a retrieval mechanism that can perform vector based top K searches over graph attached text while still respecting relationships in the graph.

What is the most effective approach to design this graph aware retrieval strategy for FM augmentation?

Store the graph in a separate database and export all node and edge data into a vector store so the system can run a global vector search across all content. Then attach graph metadata to the top K vector results to approximate graph awareness during post processing

Convert the entire graph to flattened documents and generate embeddings for each combined record so the assistant can perform a single vector similarity search. Then rely on the foundation model to infer supply chain relationships directly from the flattened text

Run vector similarity searches in a stand alone vector database and then filter the top results by querying the graph database separately. Then merge both results client side before sending them to the foundation model to provide contextual answers

Correct answer
Integrate the graph database with a vector capable analytics engine that supports top K similarity search on embedded text stored as node or edge properties. Then run vector similarity queries inside the graph engine so the retrieval respects graph relationships before passing results to the foundation model

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Integrate the graph database with a vector capable analytics engine that supports top K similarity search on embedded text stored as node or edge properties. Then run vector similarity queries inside the graph engine so the retrieval respects graph relationships before passing results to the foundation model

This solution uses a graph analytics engine that natively supports vector based top K queries on embedded text. This approach allows the system to perform semantic similarity search while still honoring graph relationships such as supplier to route or supplier to warehouse connectivity, which preserves the intent of the graph aware retrieval design. Running vector queries within the graph layer avoids the inconsistency that occurs when vector stores and graph stores operate independently. It ensures context retrieval uses both semantic signals and graph topology before the FM call.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/find-and-link-similar-entities-in-a-knowledge-graph-using-amazon-neptune-part-2-vector-similarity-search/

Incorrect options:

Store the graph in a separate database and export all node and edge data into a vector store so the system can run a global vector search across all content. Then attach graph metadata to the top K vector results to approximate graph awareness during post processing - Exporting graph data into a stand alone vector store loses graph connectivity and forces the system to approximate relationships using metadata. This reduces precision for risk analysis because the retrieval process no longer uses native graph traversal or topology.

Convert the entire graph to flattened documents and generate embeddings for each combined record so the assistant can perform a single vector similarity search. Then rely on the foundation model to infer supply chain relationships directly from the flattened text - Flattening graph structures into plain text breaks natural graph relationships and weakens retrieval accuracy for topological questions like supplier risk propagation. The FM cannot reliably reconstruct multi hop graph relationships from flattened embeddings.

Run vector similarity searches in a stand alone vector database and then filter the top results by querying the graph database separately. Then merge both results client side before sending them to the foundation model to provide contextual answers - Running vector search and graph queries in separate systems and merging results client side produces inconsistent retrieval sets and adds coordination overhead. The retrieval layer loses the ability to rank results using combined semantic and graph features.

Question 38
Skipped
A customer support application intermittently returns generic “model invocation failed” errors when sending structured JSON prompts to a foundation model API. Initial checks reveal that some requests include optional fields in unexpected formats and unescaped characters that were not present during earlier testing.

How should you design request validation and error handling so that malformed inputs are detected early and failures are easier to diagnose?

Send all requests directly to the model endpoint and customize the foundation model itself to reject malformed fields. Enable CloudWatch metric filters to alert developers whenever the model responds with an invocation error

Configure Amazon API Gateway to perform basic request passthrough and add a Lambda function that escapes special characters before invoking the foundation model API. Log the preprocessing results in CloudWatch Logs to help identify faulty payloads during troubleshooting

Correct answer
Implement schema validation in Amazon API Gateway using request models to enforce strict JSON structure and run a Lambda preprocessor that sanitizes and escapes user supplied fields before calling the foundation model. Capture detailed validation failures and preprocessing errors in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to provide clear diagnostics for debugging issues

Implement an Amazon SQS buffering layer that queues all incoming requests and use an Amazon Lambda consumer to normalize field names before invoking the model API. Depend on SQS dead letter queues to capture malformed payloads that cannot be processed successfully

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Implement schema validation in Amazon API Gateway using request models to enforce strict JSON structure and run a Lambda preprocessor that sanitizes and escapes user supplied fields before calling the foundation model. Capture detailed validation failures and preprocessing errors in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to provide clear diagnostics for debugging issues

Performing schema validation at Amazon API Gateway ensures malformed JSON is rejected before it reaches the model, which prevents non actionable “model invocation failed” errors. Adding a Lambda preprocessing layer allows you to sanitize user content, escape invalid characters, and enforce stricter formatting rules before calling the foundation model. This reduces model side errors and preserves clear operational boundaries.

Capturing validation and preprocessing errors in CloudWatch Logs provides actionable diagnostics for developers and enables quick issue resolution. This approach lowers noise, prevents invalid model calls, and greatly improves the reliability of model integrations in customer facing systems.

Incorrect options:

Implement an Amazon SQS buffering layer that queues all incoming requests and use an Amazon Lambda consumer to normalize field names before invoking the model API. Depend on SQS dead letter queues to capture malformed payloads that cannot be processed successfully - Using SQS with Lambda adds buffering and retries but does not enforce schema correctness or detect malformed structures before the model call. Normalizing field names without validating nested JSON formatting still allows invalid structures and unescaped characters to reach the model, resulting in the same nondeterministic failures. Dead letter queues provide after the fact insight but do not prevent malformed inputs from causing invocation errors.

Configure Amazon API Gateway to perform basic request passthrough and add a Lambda function that escapes special characters before invoking the foundation model API. Log the preprocessing results in CloudWatch Logs to help identify faulty payloads during troubleshooting - Escaping characters alone does not guarantee structural correctness because malformed optional fields, incorrect nesting, and invalid types still bypass inspection. With API Gateway running in passthrough mode, the system relies solely on Lambda for lightweight sanitation rather than full JSON schema validation, which allows problematic payloads to reach the model. While CloudWatch logging helps with diagnostics, the approach does not prevent invalid requests from generating invocation failures.

Send all requests directly to the model endpoint and customize the foundation model itself to reject malformed fields. Enable CloudWatch metric filters to alert developers whenever the model responds with an invocation error - Relying on the model to reject malformed inputs produces inconsistent behavior because foundation models do not guarantee strict schema validation. The system continues to generate generic errors and provides limited visibility into the root cause, which slows down debugging and creates noisy alarms.

Question 39
Skipped
A large healthcare provider is introducing an AI system that helps generate clinical summaries by reviewing doctor notes, patient history, and recent interactions. These summaries must be produced reliably because they support real clinical decision making, but the compliance and operations teams are concerned about potential risks. They worry that the AI could enter repetitive reasoning cycles, continue processing far longer than intended, or fail unpredictably if supporting systems become unavailable during execution. They want a tightly controlled workflow that can automatically stop when necessary and prevent cascading failures during periods of instability.

What do you recommend?

Build a workflow using Amazon Bedrock Agents and configure long agent session windows to accommodate extended reasoning cycles. Rely on agent driven retry mechanisms to handle unavailable downstream systems without implementing a centralized circuit breaker or stopping conditions

Correct answer
Design a safeguarded workflow using AWS Step Functions with explicit stopping conditions and state timeouts, apply strict Lambda function timeouts, enforce least privilege IAM policies, and configure a circuit breaker pattern using CloudWatch alarms that halts the workflow when error thresholds are exceeded. Implement logic that stops execution immediately if downstream systems fail or responses become unreliable

Use Step Functions with a single global timeout for the entire workflow and rely on CloudWatch metrics for monitoring. Allow downstream API calls to continue retrying within the state machine without any stopping conditions

Design a safeguarded workflow using AWS Step Functions with state timeouts and Lambda functions that include retry logic, and configure CloudWatch alarms to send notifications when error rates rise. Allow the workflow to continue running while alarms are active and rely on SNS notifications instead of halting execution

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Design a safeguarded workflow using AWS Step Functions with explicit stopping conditions and state timeouts, apply strict Lambda function timeouts, enforce least privilege IAM policies, and configure a circuit breaker pattern using CloudWatch alarms that halts the workflow when error thresholds are exceeded. Implement logic that stops execution immediately if downstream systems fail or responses become unreliable

This solution uses a comprehensive safeguard strategy that protects the workflow at every layer. Step Functions stopping conditions and state timeouts ensure that the AI never enters uncontrolled loops or runs longer than allowed. Lambda timeouts prevent individual tasks from consuming excessive compute or blocking workflow progress. Least privilege IAM policies restrict what the AI can access, limiting compliance risk and reducing the chance of unintended actions.

CloudWatch alarms combined with circuit breaker logic provide a final layer of defense by stopping the workflow entirely when error rates spike or downstream systems become unstable. This multi layer safety model produces predictable behavior, protects against cascading failures, and aligns with healthcare compliance requirements.

Circuit breaker pattern implementation using AWS services:  via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/circuit-breaker.html

Incorrect options:

Build a workflow using Amazon Bedrock Agents and configure long agent session windows to accommodate extended reasoning cycles. Rely on agent driven retry mechanisms to handle unavailable downstream systems without implementing a centralized circuit breaker or stopping conditions - Extending agent sessions and relying on agent level retries does not address risks related to infinite loops, runaway execution, or cascading failures. Without workflow level stopping conditions, circuit breakers, and timeouts, failures in downstream systems can cause unpredictable behavior.

Use Step Functions with a single global timeout for the entire workflow and rely on CloudWatch metrics for monitoring. Allow downstream API calls to continue retrying within the state machine without any stopping conditions - A single global timeout does not prevent iterative retry loops or protect the workflow from repeated downstream failures. Without explicit stopping conditions and automated circuit breaker enforcement, the system cannot safely halt execution during an outage.

Design a safeguarded workflow using AWS Step Functions with state timeouts and Lambda functions that include retry logic, and configure CloudWatch alarms to send notifications when error rates rise. Allow the workflow to continue running while alarms are active and rely on SNS notifications instead of halting execution - This option does not implement a circuit breaker that actually stops execution when downstream systems fail. Allowing the workflow to continue running during high error periods exposes the system to cascading failures and does not meet the requirement for automatic workflow termination.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/circuit-breaker.html

Use Amazon Athena to query sample objects from S3 and rely on pattern matching queries to estimate which files might contain regulated fields. IAM rules cannot identify or classify PII, and pushing datasets to staging buckets may still expose regulated data to model training workflows.

Question 41

A global retailer is building a retrieval augmented assistant that uses a foundation model over a knowledge base enriched with data from multiple SaaS systems, including CRM, ticketing, and product catalogs. The GenAI team must synchronize only the required subsets of records, handle continuous updates and deletes without performing full reloads, enforce encryption in transit and at rest, and prevent duplicate ingestion when updating the knowledge base.

Which data integration solution do you recommend to meet these requirements?

Use Amazon S3 event notifications to detect when SaaS platforms export new files and trigger Lambda functions that write directly to the knowledge base. Rely on the knowledge base to deduplicate records and ignore outdated entries

Correct answer
Use Amazon AppFlow to pull filtered subsets of SaaS data and enable field level mappings with enforced encryption in transit and at rest. Configure AWS Glue incremental jobs with job bookmarks to process only new and changed data and prevent duplicate loads into the knowledge base

Use AWS Glue to run full extract jobs on a fixed schedule and rely on Glue triggers to orchestrate periodic loads. Apply encryption with AWS KMS and configure a DynamoDB table to track which records have been processed

Use Amazon AppFlow to perform scheduled bulk transfers from SaaS systems and store all incoming data in Amazon S3 with server side encryption enabled. Configure AWS Glue crawlers to scan the full datasets and run transformation jobs that overwrite the knowledge base on each load

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon AppFlow to pull filtered subsets of SaaS data and enable field level mappings with enforced encryption in transit and at rest. Configure AWS Glue incremental jobs with job bookmarks to process only new and changed data and prevent duplicate loads into the knowledge base

AppFlow supports secure, bidirectional integration with SaaS applications and allows filtering and mapping to pull only relevant subsets of data while enforcing encryption at all stages of data movement. This ensures that unnecessary records and sensitive attributes never reach the knowledge base.

Glue job bookmarks track processed data and ensure that only incremental updates, including additions, modifications, and deletes, are ingested into downstream systems. This design prevents duplicate ingestion, reduces processing overhead, and keeps the knowledge base aligned with the latest SaaS changes without performing full reloads.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appflow/latest/userguide/what-is-appflow.html

Incorrect options:

Use AWS Glue to run full extract jobs on a fixed schedule and rely on Glue triggers to orchestrate periodic loads. Apply encryption with AWS KMS and configure a DynamoDB table to track which records have been processed - Running scheduled full extract jobs increases cost and processing time and fails to meet the requirement to avoid full dataset reprocessing. Tracking processed records manually in DynamoDB adds unnecessary operational complexity and does not integrate as cleanly with SaaS source systems as AppFlow's built in incremental capabilities.

Use Amazon S3 event notifications to detect when SaaS platforms export new files and trigger Lambda functions that write directly to the knowledge base. Rely on the knowledge base to deduplicate records and ignore outdated entries - Relying on SaaS exports and S3 event notifications does not provide fine grained filtering or selective synchronization, and offloading deduplication to the knowledge base risks inconsistent data quality. This approach also lacks a mechanism to capture deletes and incremental updates in real time.

Use Amazon AppFlow to perform scheduled bulk transfers from SaaS systems and store all incoming data in Amazon S3 with server side encryption enabled. Configure AWS Glue crawlers to scan the full datasets and run transformation jobs that overwrite the knowledge base on each load - This option performs bulk transfers rather than filtered or incremental loads and does not prevent duplicate ingestion. Glue crawlers and overwrite based transformations reprocess full datasets on every run and fail to meet the requirement for efficient incremental updates, delete handling, or selective synchronization.

References:

Using a Lambda function to transform or redact each detected entity ensures that only sanitized text is delivered to the model, meeting compliance requirements and operationalizing a repeatable privacy control.

Logging redaction details and maintaining audit visibility allows compliance teams to verify how specific pieces of personal information were handled before summarization. This architecture ensures that sensitive data is never exposed to the foundation model while preserving enough context for support agents to use the summaries effectively.

Implement a data masking process using CloudWatch Logs Insights that scans stored support tickets and replaces sensitive values after the content has already been processed by the model. Store the redaction metadata separately and rely on downstream systems to mask sensitive fields after the model completes its output - Tagging PII without redacting it allows the original sensitive data to flow directly into the foundation model, which violates the requirement that no raw personal information should reach the model. Even though Comprehend identifies sensitive content, delaying masking until after model processing fails to enforce privacy controls at the point of ingestion.

Use Amazon Bedrock as the primary interface and call SageMaker AI endpoints only when Bedrock models fail or return low quality output. Depend on application retries to manage routing decisions and rely on default monitoring for tracking all model interactions

The routing service runs inside a VPC and connects privately to both Bedrock and SageMaker using VPC endpoints, while IAM roles restrict which models can be invoked. Expose separate APIs for Bedrock and SageMaker AI models and instruct application teams to choose the correct backend for each workload. Without unified routing and centralized monitoring, the architecture becomes fragmented and cannot meet compliance or observability expectations.

A scientific research organization is building an advanced GenAI workspace that allows researchers to perform two very different categories of computations. Some tasks involve quick, stateless operations such as running small mathematical calculations or looking up reference values, while other tasks require submitting long running simulation jobs that need high performance compute resources and containerized environments. The organization wants a unified framework that allows its foundation models to access both types of tools in a consistent way, while ensuring that lightweight tasks run with minimal latency and heavy simulation workloads run in scalable, dedicated compute environments.

Which options can be combined to provide an efficient and extensible tool framework for both lightweight and heavy computational workloads? (Select two)

Correct selection
Deploy Lambda based Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to host stateless tool functions such as lightweight calculations and quick data lookups. Expose these Lambda based tools through MCP compliant interfaces

Deploy Lambda based Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for lightweight tools and use API Gateway endpoints to trigger simulations running on Amazon ECS. Configure the foundation model to use MCP only for quick utilities while calling API Gateway separately for simulation workloads

Correct selection
Provision Amazon ECS based Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to host containerized simulation tools that require GPU acceleration or long running compute. Configure the foundation model to invoke these ECS based MCP servers through the same MCP interface used for lightweight tools to maintain consistency

Use a single Amazon ECS cluster to run Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for both quick calculations and GPU intensive simulations. Configure all requests to be processed through the same set of containerized tools regardless of workload size

Deploy Lambda functions to execute both lightweight tools and simulation workloads and increase memory and timeout limits for simulation tasks. Configure the foundation model to invoke Lambda directly for all operations without differentiating workload types

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Deploy Lambda based Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to host stateless tool functions such as lightweight calculations and quick data lookups. Expose these Lambda based tools through MCP compliant interfaces

Using Lambda based MCP servers for lightweight tools provides the lowest latency and operationally simplest environment for fast calculations, lookup operations, and other stateless functions. Lambda is designed for rapid, event driven execution without the need for container orchestration or compute provisioning. This makes it ideal for tools that must respond instantly to model requests and perform tasks that finish within short execution windows. Exposing these Lambda functions as MCP compliant servers creates a standardized interface the foundation model can use without needing to know how or where each tool is hosted.

This design enables a clean separation of tool responsibilities since Lambda automatically scales with request volume, handles concurrency for small workloads, and keeps cost proportional to actual usage. By integrating Lambda based MCP servers into the model extension framework, the system supports efficient invocations, minimal overhead, and rapid response times for all lightweight tasks. This ensures the GenAI workspace remains responsive and cost effective for functions that do not require heavy compute.

AWS Serverless MCP Server:  via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/introducing-aws-serverless-mcp-server-ai-powered-development-for-modern-applications/

Provision Amazon ECS based Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to host containerized simulation tools that require GPU acceleration or long running compute. Configure the foundation model to invoke these ECS based MCP servers through the same MCP interface used for lightweight tools to maintain consistency

ECS based MCP servers provide an ideal environment for resource intensive simulation workflows that require GPU acceleration, long processing times, custom libraries, or specialized containerized dependencies. By using Amazon ECS, you can run tools inside tailored container images that include the simulations, frameworks, and scientific libraries needed by researchers. ECS tasks can be configured to run on GPU instances, scale horizontally for distributed workloads, and execute for extended durations that would exceed Lambda service limits. Exposing these simulation tools as MCP compliant endpoints ensures that they appear identical to the foundation model, even though they run in a much heavier compute environment.

This unified MCP interface eliminates the need for the model to manage separate invocation patterns and encourages the development of additional tools without modifying the application logic. The foundation model can issue complex requests through the same protocol while ECS handles compute intensive processing behind the scenes. This approach delivers a scalable, extensible, and operationally robust simulation framework aligned with the demands of scientific research environments.

Incorrect options:

Use a single Amazon ECS cluster to run Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for both quick calculations and GPU intensive simulations. Configure all requests to be processed through the same set of containerized tools regardless of workload size - Running all MCP servers on a single ECS cluster forces lightweight tasks to incur container startup times, higher latency, and unnecessary cost. It also loses the elasticity and rapid response that Lambda provides for stateless operations and wastes GPU or CPU capacity on tasks that do not need it.

Deploy Lambda functions to execute both lightweight tools and simulation workloads and increase memory and timeout limits for simulation tasks. Configure the foundation model to invoke Lambda directly for all operations without differentiating workload types - Simulations cannot run efficiently on Lambda because of time limits, lack of GPU support, and container constraints. Increasing memory or timeout values does not resolve the need for specialized hardware and long running workloads.

Deploy Lambda based Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for lightweight tools and use API Gateway endpoints to trigger simulations running on Amazon ECS. Configure the foundation model to use MCP only for quick utilities while calling API Gateway separately for simulation workloads - Splitting interfaces by using MCP for lightweight tools and API Gateway for simulations creates an inconsistent access model for the foundation model. This breaks the unified tool invocation requirement and forces the model to treat simulation tasks differently, increasing complexity.

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Leverage Amazon Bedrock’s native privacy guarantees, which ensure that none of the customer provided data is used to train or improve foundation models, while grounding responses exclusively from the customer’s isolated knowledge base

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases support strict isolation through per resource access controls and separate storage locations for embeddings and source content. Using separate knowledge bases for each customer ensures that retrieval never crosses tenant boundaries, while resource based policies and IAM constraints prevent any unauthorized access to another entity’s data.

Amazon Bedrock also guarantees that customer provided documents are never used to train or improve the underlying foundation models. By grounding responses solely from each customer’s isolated knowledge base, the provider can deliver personalized and secure assistance without violating legal or privacy requirements.

Application layer filtering is insufficient because the retrieval call itself may already expose embeddings or documents from other customers before the filter is applied.

Provide each customer’s documents directly to the model at runtime and control exposure by encrypting the files with a customer specific KMS key. Allow the foundation model to generate grounded answers by reading unprocessed documents and leverage output postprocessing to ensure private data is not leaked - Providing raw customer documents directly to the model bypasses the structured safeguards of knowledge bases and increases the risk of accidental exposure. Encryption alone does not prevent unintended use of private content once decrypted at inference time, and output filtering cannot guarantee complete protection of sensitive material.

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to store and index customer documents in separate logical indexes while allowing all indexes to share a single underlying storage location and unified access policy for simplified management. Leverage Amazon Bedrock’s privacy guarantees to ensure that customer data is not used to train models and depend on application side routing to direct retrieval queries to the correct customer context - Sharing a common storage layer and unified access policy undermines the required tenant level isolation because a single misconfiguration or retrieval request can expose content across customers. Application side routing cannot enforce strong access boundaries, and retrieval level separation must be enforced at the resource and policy layers within Bedrock Knowledge Bases to prevent cross tenant leakage.

A financial services company is building an internal GenAI assistant on Amazon Bedrock that will process highly sensitive transaction narratives and dispute descriptions. The security team requires that all Bedrock traffic stays entirely within their AWS network and that only specific application subnets can call the Bedrock APIs, with no exposure to the public internet.

How should you design the network architecture to meet these isolation requirements while still allowing the assistant to scale across multiple Availability Zones?

Create interface VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock and attach security groups that allow access from all subnets in the VPC for simplified management. Deploy the assistant across multiple Availability Zones and rely on default VPC routing to maintain private connectivity

Correct answer
Configure interface VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock using AWS PrivateLink and attach tightly scoped security groups that allow only approved application subnets to connect. Deploy the GenAI assistant across multiple Availability Zones to ensure scalable and private connectivity without any public internet access

Use a NAT gateway for all outbound Bedrock API calls and restrict NAT access to only the application subnets. Enable cross Availability Zone failover by attaching additional route table entries that direct Bedrock traffic through the NAT infrastructure

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure interface VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock using AWS PrivateLink and attach tightly scoped security groups that allow only approved application subnets to connect. Deploy the GenAI assistant across multiple Availability Zones to ensure scalable and private connectivity without any public internet access

An interface VPC endpoint is an entry point inside your VPC that allows your VPC resources to privately connect to AWS managed services such as Amazon Bedrock. Using interface VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock ensures that all traffic to the service stays within the AWS network and never traverses the public internet. Security groups attached to the endpoint can allow only specific application subnets to initiate Bedrock API calls, meeting strict financial services isolation requirements.

Deploying the assistant across multiple Availability Zones ensures high availability and elasticity while still keeping all traffic private. AWS PrivateLink automatically scales with the VPC endpoint, providing consistent connectivity without exposing any component to public networks.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/use-aws-privatelink-to-set-up-private-access-to-amazon-bedrock/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/use-aws-privatelink-to-set-up-private-access-to-amazon-bedrock/

Create a VPC endpoint service for the application and attach security groups that restrict which subnets can connect while routing Bedrock traffic through the service. Configure the assistant to access Bedrock using internal DNS rules so that traffic does not require direct public connectivity - Using a NAT gateway still exposes traffic paths that depend on public network infrastructure and does not meet the requirement of fully private connectivity to Amazon Bedrock. NAT cannot restrict access to specific models or endpoints at the network layer, and it introduces unnecessary cost and operational overhead for cross AZ scaling.

Use a NAT gateway for all outbound Bedrock API calls and restrict NAT access to only the application subnets. Enable cross Availability Zone failover by attaching additional route table entries that direct Bedrock traffic through the NAT infrastructure - A VPC endpoint service is used when you are the service provider, not the consumer. You create a VPC endpoint service so that other VPCs can privately connect to your application using PrivateLink. A VPC endpoint service cannot front Amazon Bedrock because Bedrock is a managed AWS service that requires an interface VPC endpoint, not a custom VPC endpoint service. Routing through internal DNS rules would not provide the guaranteed private connectivity path required for regulated workloads and does not satisfy the requirement to keep traffic fully inside the AWS network.

Create interface VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock and attach security groups that allow access from all subnets in the VPC for simplified management. Deploy the assistant across multiple Availability Zones and rely on default VPC routing to maintain private connectivity - Although interface VPC endpoints are the correct mechanism for enabling private connectivity to Amazon Bedrock, using overly permissive security groups does not satisfy the requirement that only designated application subnets may call the Bedrock APIs. Allowing all subnets to access the endpoint violates the principle of least privilege and fails to meet the financial institution's strict isolation controls, even though traffic stays inside the VPC.

A retail analytics company operates a recommendation API that relies on Amazon OpenSearch Service to provide real-time product suggestions. The system stores more than 8 million vector embeddings and processes thousands of concurrent queries during peak shopping periods. Recently, the development team has observed significant query latency and inconsistent response times due to index size, suboptimal shard configurations, and insufficient optimization of approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search parameters.

Which optimization strategy should the team adopt? (Select two)

Replace ANN based search with exact k-NN search on the existing single index and increase cluster storage capacity

Correct selection
Segment the dataset into multiple specialized indices based on product category and apply ANN tuning and shard resizing per index

Reduce the number of shards to a single global shard and disable replicas to consolidate compute resources onto fewer nodes

Correct selection
Reconfigure the OpenSearch cluster with additional shards, optimized replica counts, and suitable instance types, and tune ANN parameters such as ef_search and ef_construction

Overall explanation
Correct options:

Reconfigure the OpenSearch cluster with additional shards, optimized replica counts, and suitable instance types, and tune ANN parameters such as ef_search and ef_construction

Tuning shard counts and replica configurations helps distribute vector search workloads across the cluster, improving concurrency and reducing hot shard issues. Selecting larger or more appropriate instance types increases CPU and memory capacity, which is particularly important for ANN based vector search workloads.

Optimizing ANN parameters such as ef_search and ef_construction improves recall and latency trade offs, allowing teams to balance performance and accuracy based on API requirements. This combination directly aligns with the need to optimize performance at scale for high concurrency vector workloads.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/amazon-opensearch-services-vector-database-capabilities-explained/

Segment the dataset into multiple specialized indices based on product category and apply ANN tuning and shard resizing per index

Splitting the dataset into category based indices reduces the size of each index and limits the search scope, which significantly improves query performance. Each index can then be tuned independently for shard count, replicas, and ANN parameters, which gives the team granular control over performance.

Incorrect options:

Replace ANN based search with exact k-NN search on the existing single index and increase cluster storage capacity - This option is incorrect because replacing ANN with exact k-NN significantly increases computational cost and query latency for an 8-million-vector index under high concurrency. Exact k-NN does not scale efficiently at this dataset size and removes the ability to tune ANN parameters such as ef_search or ef_construction, which are critical for optimizing performance. Simply increasing storage does not address CPU, memory, or shard-level bottlenecks, so this approach fails to resolve the underlying latency issues in the recommendation API.

Reduce the number of shards to a single global shard and disable replicas to consolidate compute resources onto fewer nodes - Using a single shard with no replicas concentrates all search traffic on one node, which severely restricts concurrency and increases latency. This approach also reduces resilience and fails to meet performance needs for high traffic recommendation APIs.

Migrate all vector embeddings to Bedrock Knowledge Bases and use managed retrieval to replace the OpenSearch index - Although Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides a managed vector store, using it to replace OpenSearch does not solve the need to optimize the existing operational vector index. So, this option is incorrect.

Configure WebSocket keep alive pings every 30 to 60 seconds and implement mid stream retry logic that reconnects transparently and falls back to full response mode if the stream fails repeatedly

A WebSocket backend that integrates directly with Amazon Bedrock streaming APIs provides the lowest latency interaction model for real time chat. Buffering streamed chunks and flushing based on size or time boundaries ensures smooth rendering while avoiding excessive network calls on unreliable mobile networks. WebSocket keep alive intervals between 30 and 60 seconds prevent idle disconnects, and implementing reconnection plus fallback behavior ensures the chat assistant continues to function even when mid stream failures occur. This combination meets all UX requirements including typing indicators and progressive token display.

Incorrect options:

Relying on client side retries instead of server side recovery patterns leads to duplicated or missing tokens, and disabling fallback modes breaks the assistant during mid stream failures.

Use synchronous Amazon Bedrock invocations behind Amazon API Gateway with chunked transfer encoding to simulate streaming and depend on client polling to detect partial outputs. Rely on HTTP keep alive settings instead of WebSocket keep alives to handle unstable mobile connections - Synchronous Bedrock invocations cannot deliver real time token level streaming, and chunked transfer encoding cannot replicate true incremental generation for chat based workloads. Depending solely on HTTP keep alives provides insufficient resilience for mobile network instability and fails to support typing indicators or mid stream recovery.

Use an Amazon SQS queue to stream each generated token from Amazon Bedrock and let clients consume tokens with long polling to render partial responses. Handle connection interruptions by restarting the entire model invocation and discarding any previously streamed tokens - Amazon SQS is not designed for token level streaming because message delivery latency and ordering cannot support real time chat rendering. Restarting the entire inference on failure and dropping partial progress degrades the user experience and increases model invocation cost unnecessarily.

Question 52
Skipped
A generative AI application retrieves documents from an internal knowledge repository to supply context to a foundation model before generating responses. The repository contains a mix of unstructured text, structured attributes such as document classification and ownership, and technical terminology that varies across teams. Users often phrase queries differently even when referring to the same concepts. During evaluation, the team observes inconsistent retrieval behavior across different query types. Some searches return documents that are conceptually related but not operationally appropriate, while other searches fail to retrieve useful context when exact terminology is not used. The team wants to redesign the retrieval layer to improve overall relevance and consistency of results passed to the model.

Which option is the MOST effective way to design the retrieval solution?

Correct answer
Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to index documents with both text fields and vector embeddings, and execute a single query that evaluates similarity and structured attributes together. Combine vector similarity scoring with keyword matching and metadata filters inside the search engine. Adjust scoring weights to balance semantic relevance and exact matches

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to prioritize keyword and metadata search for all queries and fall back to vector similarity when no results are returned. Enforce strict metadata filtering to maintain consistency across searches. Avoid blending relevance signals to simplify ranking behavior

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to run vector similarity queries and keyword searches as separate operations. Merge and de duplicate the two result sets in the application layer before selecting documents for the model. Tune each retrieval method independently to improve overall coverage

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to index document embeddings and execute vector similarity queries for all searches. Increase the number of retrieved results to compensate for variation in phrasing. Leverage post retrieval filtering in application logic to remove unsuitable documents

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to index documents with both text fields and vector embeddings, and execute a single query that evaluates similarity and structured attributes together. Combine vector similarity scoring with keyword matching and metadata filters inside the search engine. Adjust scoring weights to balance semantic relevance and exact matches

This approach evaluates semantic similarity and structured constraints within the same query execution. By allowing the search engine to consider both vector relevance and keyword or metadata matches at once, ranking remains consistent and reflects multiple relevance signals. This produces more balanced results across diverse query styles.

Running hybrid evaluation inside Amazon OpenSearch Service enables efficient scoring and ranking without shifting responsibility to the application layer. Weighting allows fine tuning how much influence each signal has, which helps handle both conceptual similarity and strict operational requirements. This improves the quality of context provided to the foundation model. Designing retrieval this way reduces missed results and limits the inclusion of unsuitable documents. It provides a robust foundation for retrieval augmented generation workflows operating on complex enterprise datasets.

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/hybrid-search-with-amazon-opensearch-service/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/hybrid-search-with-amazon-opensearch-service/

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to index document embeddings and execute vector similarity queries for all searches. Increase the number of retrieved results to compensate for variation in phrasing. Leverage post retrieval filtering in application logic to remove unsuitable documents - Vector similarity alone does not account for structured constraints such as document classification or ownership. Increasing the number of retrieved results raises recall but also increases noise, which can negatively impact model grounding. Filtering after retrieval does not correct ranking inaccuracies introduced earlier. Shifting relevance decisions to application code adds complexity and reduces the effectiveness of search engine scoring. This approach can lead to inconsistent behavior as query patterns change.

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to run vector similarity queries and keyword searches as separate operations. Merge and de duplicate the two result sets in the application layer before selecting documents for the model. Tune each retrieval method independently to improve overall coverage - Running separate retrieval paths introduces coordination and ranking challenges. Merging results outside the search engine prevents unified scoring across semantic and keyword signals. This can lead to unpredictable ordering and difficulty tuning relevance. Maintaining multiple retrieval pipelines also increases operational overhead. The approach relies on application logic to resolve relevance rather than using native search capabilities.

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to prioritize keyword and metadata search for all queries and fall back to vector similarity when no results are returned. Enforce strict metadata filtering to maintain consistency across searches. Avoid blending relevance signals to simplify ranking behavior - Prioritizing keyword search and treating semantic retrieval as a fallback restricts relevance to exact matches. This reduces recall when users express intent using varied phrasing or synonyms. Avoiding blended scoring limits adaptability across different query types. Strict metadata filtering improves precision but can exclude useful context. This approach does not fully address inconsistent retrieval across diverse queries.

Question 53
Skipped
A global automotive manufacturer is developing a unified “Product Intelligence Assistant” that can help engineering, marketing, and field-service teams search across product manuals, assembly-line videos, test-drive transcripts, and CAD-annotation metadata. The assistant must support multimodal retrieval, provide streaming conversational responses with grounded citations, and route requests to different foundation models depending on the requesting business unit. Additionally, the company must strictly separate pre-release and public content and wants to avoid the operational burden of building custom multimodal ingestion pipelines or hosting models directly.

What do you recommend?

Correct answer
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to ingest multimodal text, transcripts, and image-derived embeddings into separate knowledge bases for public and pre-release content. Then use Amazon Bedrock Flows to orchestrate model-specific routing based on the requesting business unit, combine the retrieval output with Titan or Claude models, and stream responses to applications through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API

Deploy custom multimodal models on Amazon SageMaker, create a Step Functions workflow to handle text/image/video processing, and implement conditional branches for each business unit

Use an Application Load Balancer with ECS services that host model adapters. Implement a custom retrieval engine using OpenSearch and a global router using API Gateway and Lambda. Enable per-unit isolation with IAM condition keys

Use a single Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock and configure a Lambda function to classify business-unit requests. Pass all multimodal content as pre-processed text to the model and store semantic metadata inside DynamoDB

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to ingest multimodal text, transcripts, and image-derived embeddings into separate knowledge bases for public and pre-release content. Then use Amazon Bedrock Flows to orchestrate model-specific routing based on the requesting business unit, combine the retrieval output with Titan or Claude models, and stream responses to applications through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API

This architecture most accurately satisfies the requirement for multimodal ingestion, retrieval, routing, and response streaming with the lowest operational overhead. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases natively handle the ingestion of mixed data formats, including long-form text, transcripts derived from videos, and extracted image features, removing the need to build custom pipelines. Because the company must keep pre-release and public data strictly separated, maintaining two independent knowledge bases is the most reliable and operationally efficient design.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

Furthermore, Amazon Bedrock Flows allow the organization to implement a fully managed orchestration layer that can route requests to separate Titan or Claude models based on department, retrieve relevant vector matches, and compose the final answer in a controlled and auditable manner. When combined with response streaming via the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, this pattern delivers low-latency conversational responses with grounded context. This solution precisely matches the company's goal to avoid custom model hosting or ingestion pipelines while achieving a robust enterprise-grade assistant.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows.html

Incorrect options:

Use a single Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock and configure a Lambda function to classify business-unit requests. Pass all multimodal content as pre-processed text to the model and store semantic metadata inside DynamoDB - This approach relies entirely on Lambda to implement multimodal routing and requires DynamoDB as a manual store for vector semantics, which is not optimized for vector search or multimodal retrieval. It also forces the organization to perform multimodal extraction outside of a managed service. This increases operational burden and does not provide native grounding or separation across pre-release and public data sources.

Deploy custom multimodal models on Amazon SageMaker, create a Step Functions workflow to handle text/image/video processing, and implement conditional branches for each business unit - Hosting custom multimodal models in SageMaker and orchestrating steps via Step Functions significantly increases infrastructure responsibility. The requirement explicitly states minimizing hosting effort, and this approach introduces maintenance of containers and monitoring pipelines, making it unsuitable compared to Bedrock's managed orchestration.

Use an Application Load Balancer with ECS services that host model adapters. Implement a custom retrieval engine using OpenSearch and a global router using API Gateway and Lambda. Enable per-unit isolation with IAM condition keys - Using ECS with ALB introduces high infrastructure overhead with no direct support for retrieval, multimodal ingestion, or model orchestration. All guardrails, inputs, routing, and logging must be implemented manually, contradicting the requirement to avoid heavy custom hosting and ingestion complexity.

Configure Lake Formation with column level, row level, and cell level permissions on the clinical datasets and grant fine grained access only to the compliance group for sensitive diagnosis codes and patient identifiers. Allow the data science team to access de-identified columns and aggregated rows while enabling the Bedrock Knowledge Base to query only the permitted views

Overall explanation

Allow the data science team to access de-identified columns and aggregated rows while enabling the Bedrock Knowledge Base to query only the permitted views

Lake Formation provides granular governance controls for structured and semi structured data that can restrict access at the table, column, row, and cell levels. Applying these permissions to diagnosis codes, identifiers, and other sensitive fields ensures that only the compliance group can access regulated data while maintaining full audit visibility.

Creating separate access paths for aggregated or de-identified columns allows the general data science team to use the retrieval system without compromising patient privacy. The Bedrock Knowledge Base will only query the permitted views, ensuring that the GenAI assistant operates within the proper compliance boundaries.

Highly recommend the following deep-dive on implementing cell-level and row-level security using AWS Lake Formation:

SQL level masking is not a substitute for Lake Formation column, row, or cell level controls and cannot guarantee compliance for sensitive clinical data.

Store the clinical datasets in S3 with default bucket level permissions and use IAM identity policies to restrict access to sensitive diagnosis codes. Allow the Bedrock Knowledge Base to retrieve data directly from S3 objects while relying on IAM to enforce data visibility rules at runtime - Relying on IAM alone cannot enforce fine grained controls such as column level or row level permissions for regulated healthcare datasets. S3 bucket permissions are too coarse and do not support the required granular filtering needed before ingestion into a Bedrock Knowledge Base.

Configure Lake Formation with table level access grants and create two Data Catalog entries that separate sensitive and non sensitive clinical fields. Allow the compliance group to query both catalogs while exposing only the non sensitive catalog to the data science team. Leverage Bedrock Knowledge Bases to automatically filter restricted cells during retrieval - Creating separate Data Catalog entries does not provide true column level, row level, or cell level enforcement because users with table level permission can still access full datasets unless fine grained Lake Formation controls are applied. Bedrock Knowledge Bases cannot filter restricted cells on behalf of Lake Formation, so sensitive diagnosis codes and identifiers may still be exposed if the underlying datasets are not governed at the required granularity.

Budget enforcement logic at the gateway or Lambda layer ensures that experimental workloads remain constrained while mission critical workloads are governed through approved exceptions.

Relying on retrospective reviews does not provide the operational guardrails needed for large multi team GenAI systems.

A global enterprise operates a customer support assistant used across mobile and web platforms. Correct answer
Use Amazon Bedrock provisioned throughput to provide dedicated model capacity for peak demand and configure tokens per second allocation based on expected surge patterns. Monitor utilization with CloudWatch and adjust provisioned units to maintain for fast responses during traffic spikes

Configure Lambda functions to invoke Bedrock on-demand APIs for all requests and reserve high Lambda memory sizes to optimize throughput. Depend on AWS Lambda scaling to absorb burst traffic instead of adjusting model capacity

Use Amazon Bedrock on-demand APIs and set high retry and timeout values to smooth out throttling during peak traffic periods. Enable CloudWatch alarms on latency and continue increasing memory in application clients to improve response predictability
