Use Amazon Bedrock provisioned throughput to provide dedicated model capacity for peak demand and configure tokens per second allocation based on expected surge patterns. Monitor utilization with CloudWatch and adjust provisioned units to maintain for fast responses during traffic spikes

Provisioned throughput in Amazon Bedrock offers dedicated capacity with predictable cost, which eliminates throttling during large traffic bursts. Because capacity is reserved, the system can maintain fast responses even when demand increases unexpectedly. Configuring tokens per second capacity based on known traffic patterns gives both finance and product teams predictable behavior. Deploy the model on SageMaker AI real time endpoints with a minimal instance size and rely on auto scaling to handle all peak loads. Increase concurrent invocation limits on the application side to let the endpoint scale reactively during seasonal promotions - Using a minimal instance size for large workloads will create latency issues and slow startup times, and auto scaling alone cannot guarantee consistent fast responses during sudden spikes. Scaling decisions occur after load increases, which causes delays and throttling when demand rises quickly.

Configure Lambda functions to invoke Bedrock on-demand APIs for all requests and reserve high Lambda memory sizes to optimize throughput. Depend on AWS Lambda scaling to absorb burst traffic instead of adjusting model capacity - Placing Lambda in front of on-demand model invocations does not eliminate throttling at the model layer and can lead to higher costs without improving predictability. Lambda scales quickly but does not influence shared capacity limitations in on-demand FM invocation.

The operations team would have to maintain and implement all compliance workflows manually, creating an error prone and fragmented governance system. DynamoDB serves as a storage engine rather than a lifecycle management tool, so it does not meet the bank’s need for an auditable and managed configuration promotion process.

Which evaluation approach is most suitable for these requirements?

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation to automatically score multiple model candidates against a curated evaluation dataset

Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation provides a managed, automatic, and repeatable evaluation framework that compares multiple foundation model candidates using consistent datasets and scoring methodologies. It allows the legal tech team to measure accuracy, robustness and reasoning quality through structured evaluation tasks. The service supports custom evaluation datasets, enabling the team to incorporate legal domain specific prompts and reference answers for precise scoring.

Because the evaluation runs in a controlled and repeatable environment, the platform gains clear and measurable insights into model performance differences. Bedrock Model Evaluation also produces quantitative scores and ranking information, making it easier to determine whether a model meets production thresholds for legal accuracy and reliability. This is essential for high stakes environments where hallucinations or factual inconsistencies can lead to compliance issues. The automated nature of the service ensures that every model candidate goes through the same rigorous evaluation pipeline before deployment.

Human evaluation also does not scale efficiently when the team must assess multiple models or large numbers of prompts.

A SaaS provider exposes a text analysis API to hundreds of external customers that internally calls Amazon Bedrock for classification and sentiment analysis. Some customers send prompts that exceed model token limits or omit required fields, while others generate sudden traffic spikes that overload the downstream model endpoint. The provider wants to enforce strict schema validation for request bodies and parameters and apply tiered throttling per customer plan before any request reaches Bedrock.

Which options do you recommend? (Select two)

Place an Application Load Balancer in front of the text analysis service and attach AWS WAF with rate based rules to block high request rates from abusive clients. Rely on the downstream Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock to handle JSON parsing, required field checks, and token limit enforcement for all customers

Correct selection
Use API keys and usage plans in API Gateway to define per customer throttling limits for each subscription tier so that traffic is controlled before it reaches the downstream model endpoint

Implement throttling with Lambda reserved concurrency so that burst traffic is absorbed by the function

Use Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda integration that performs all request validation inside the function code and relies on CloudWatch alarms to detect customers who exceed token limits or send malformed payloads

Correct selection
Configure Amazon API Gateway with request validators and models that use JSON Schema to enforce required fields and token limit constraints on the text analysis API before invoking an AWS Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure Amazon API Gateway with request validators and models that use JSON Schema to enforce required fields and token limit constraints on the text analysis API before invoking an AWS Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock

Using API Gateway request validators and models with JSON Schema allows the SaaS provider to reject malformed payloads and enforce limits on fields such as token counts before any integration code runs. This ensures that only well formed requests with the required fields and acceptable sizes are passed to the Lambda function that invokes Amazon Bedrock, which protects the downstream model and simplifies error handling.

Use API keys and usage plans in API Gateway to define per customer throttling limits for each subscription tier so that traffic is controlled before it reaches the downstream model endpoint

API keys and usage plans in API Gateway are designed to implement tenant aware throttling and quotas, so the provider can define different request rates and burst limits for each customer plan and enforce them at the edge. This combination gives fine grained control over both schema validation and traffic shaping directly at the API layer, which aligns exactly with the requirement to protect Bedrock from invalid input and sudden spikes.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-api-usage-plans.html

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda integration that performs all request validation inside the function code and relies on CloudWatch alarms to detect customers who exceed token limits or send malformed payloads - Pushing all validation into the Lambda function means invalid requests still consume compute resources and can reach the integration layer, which is less efficient than rejecting them at the API Gateway edge with request validation. CloudWatch alarms only detect issues after they occur and cannot block malformed or oversized requests before they reach Lambda or Bedrock. They do not provide per customer throttling or enforce JSON schema validation, so they cannot satisfy the requirement for pre invocation protection at the API boundary.

Place an Application Load Balancer in front of the text analysis service and attach AWS WAF with rate based rules to block high request rates from abusive clients. Rely on the downstream Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock to handle JSON parsing, required field checks, and token limit enforcement for all customers - An Application Load Balancer with AWS WAF rate based rules can mitigate abusive traffic patterns, but it does not provide built in JSON Schema based validation of request bodies or per tenant usage plans. Leaving all field validation and token limit checks to the downstream Lambda function means malformed or oversized requests can still pass through the edge and waste backend capacity.

Implement throttling with Lambda reserved concurrency so that burst traffic is absorbed by the function - Relying on Lambda concurrency settings instead of API Gateway usage plans does not provide per customer throttling or tiered rate limits, so the provider cannot easily enforce different limits for each subscription plan.

A research group uses a GenAI assistant to answer questions over large technical reports that frequently exceed the context limits of the chosen foundation model. The current design forwards entire report sections into the prompt, which drives up token usage, increases latency, and often truncates important contextual clauses. The group wants to redesign the context assembly and prompt construction so that the system optimizes context window usage through pruning and compression while preserving the most relevant content?

What do you recommend?

Use Amazon Textract to extract all text from the documents and store complete sections in Amazon S3. Feed these full sections into Amazon Bedrock by increasing the model's maximum token setting and rely on the model to handle truncation efficiently

Correct answer
Implement a retrieval pipeline that ranks passages using Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, then apply prompt compression techniques to summarize selected passages before injecting them into Amazon Bedrock for final inference. Use dynamic context pruning so only the highest relevance spans enter the final prompt

Implement a retrieval pipeline with Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and forward all retrieved passages directly to Amazon Bedrock without applying any summarization or compression. Use a static relevance threshold so that all passages above the threshold are always included in the prompt for broader context coverage

Adopt Amazon Comprehend to classify document sections and send all sections belonging to matching categories directly to Amazon Bedrock. Avoid additional chunking logic because category level grouping ensures that the model receives broad thematic context

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Implement a retrieval pipeline that ranks passages using Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, then apply prompt compression techniques to summarize selected passages before injecting them into Amazon Bedrock for final inference. Use dynamic context pruning so only the highest relevance spans enter the final prompt

The most effective approach is to retrieve only the most relevant document spans and reduce their token footprint using structured summarization or prompt compression. This lowers the total tokens entering the prompt, reduces latency, and ensures that only high value content reaches the model. Combining retrieval ranking with compression preserves semantic fidelity without exceeding the model's context limit.

Dynamic pruning ensures that the prompt adapts to the query and context load in real time, which avoids unnecessary tokens and prevents truncation of important clauses. This approach maximizes both quality and efficiency, especially for workloads involving large technical documents and strict context window limits.

Incorrect options:

Implement a retrieval pipeline with Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and forward all retrieved passages directly to Amazon Bedrock without applying any summarization or compression. Use a static relevance threshold so that all passages above the threshold are always included in the prompt for broader context coverage - Relying only on retrieval and passing all matched spans without compression does not control token growth or prevent context overflow. A static threshold cannot adapt to different query lengths or content density, which leads to excessive tokens, higher latency, and a greater chance of prompt truncation. This approach fails to optimize context window usage because it does not reduce text size before inference.

Adopt Amazon Comprehend to classify document sections and send all sections belonging to matching categories directly to Amazon Bedrock. Avoid additional chunking logic because category level grouping ensures that the model receives broad thematic context - Classifying document sections and forwarding all category matched content does not solve the context limit problem and still sends large amounts of text to the model. Category based grouping is not a substitute for granular retrieval or compression and will continue to inflate token usage. This approach offers minimal improvements in efficiency or precision.

Use Amazon Textract to extract all text from the documents and store complete sections in Amazon S3. Feed these full sections into Amazon Bedrock by increasing the model's maximum token setting and rely on the model to handle truncation efficiently - Increasing the model's input token allowance is not feasible because foundation models have fixed context windows. Passing unfiltered full sections leads to high latency, unnecessary token costs, and a high risk of truncation. This approach results in lower relevance and poor performance.

A global legal consultancy is developing an AI driven clause drafting system that must route every generated clause through mandatory human review. The firm wants attorneys to evaluate each draft, provide structured feedback, and either approve or request revisions. The firm also wants to capture feedback metadata so it can analyze common revision categories, reviewer patterns, and long term trends that influence model improvement. To achieve this, the system must coordinate automated drafting steps, route human review tasks, trigger downstream processing, and store structured review data in a repository suitable for long term analysis.

What do you suggest?

Use Amazon Bedrock Agents to manage the drafting and review process and configure Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) only to notify attorneys by email when a clause is ready for review. Store each reviewer comment as a separate S3 object for later analysis

Correct answer
Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate clause generation and route cases to Amazon Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) for human review, configure A2I to send structured reviewer feedback to an Amazon EventBridge bus, and write downstream consumers that store the feedback in DynamoDB with secondary indexes for long term analysis. Implement separate event patterns to handle approvals, rejections, and revision requests

Use AWS Step Functions to draft clauses and immediately send them to attorneys via an SNS topic without involving Amazon Augmented AI (A2I). Store lawyer feedback in a single S3 prefix and periodically run Athena queries to detect revision patterns

Use Amazon Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) to manage both AI drafting and human review and configure A2I to store feedback only in its managed output buckets. Rely on manual exports from the A2I console to perform long term trend analysis

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate clause generation and route cases to Amazon Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) for human review, configure A2I to send structured reviewer feedback to an Amazon EventBridge bus, and write downstream consumers that store the feedback in DynamoDB with secondary indexes for long term analysis. Implement separate event patterns to handle approvals, rejections, and revision requests

This solution uses Step Functions to orchestrate a complete, stateful drafting workflow while delegating human review tasks to Amazon A2I, which is purpose built for integrating human decisions into AI processes. A2I ensures that reviewers submit structured, consistent feedback, and EventBridge provides an event driven routing layer for processing this feedback asynchronously. This model allows the system to remain responsive, scalable, and well structured.

Routing A2I outputs into EventBridge enables the creation of multiple consumers that handle approvals, rejections, revision requests, and analytics independently. Storing review data in DynamoDB with secondary indexes provides the firm with fast and flexible querying patterns to support trend reporting, reviewer behavior insights, and continuous improvement of the drafting model.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/circuit-breaker.html

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon Bedrock Agents to manage the drafting and review process and configure Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) only to notify attorneys by email when a clause is ready for review. Store each reviewer comment as a separate S3 object for later analysis - Using Bedrock Agents to manage the entire review flow bypasses structured human review capabilities provided by A2I. Storing reviewer feedback in S3 creates unstructured data that does not support attribute level indexing or efficient trend analysis, which the firm requires for long term insights.

Use Amazon Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) to manage both AI drafting and human review and configure A2I to store feedback only in its managed output buckets. Rely on manual exports from the A2I console to perform long term trend analysis - A2I output buckets are not optimized for analytical querying and require significant manual handling. Without an event driven or indexed storage design, the workflow cannot support automated feedback processing or long term trend reporting.

Use AWS Step Functions to draft clauses and immediately send them to attorneys via an SNS topic without involving Amazon Augmented AI (A2I). Store lawyer feedback in a single S3 prefix and periodically run Athena queries to detect revision patterns - SNS notifications do not provide structured feedback capture or task tracking and cannot ensure that required human reviews occur before clauses are approved. Storing unstructured inputs in S3 and relying on Athena queries creates operational overhead and does not support real time analytical workflows.

A media moderation system runs hourly batch jobs that send tens of thousands of content snippets through a foundation model to detect policy violations. The team currently issues one inference request per item, which leads to underutilized GPU instances, high costs, and jobs that occasionally miss their completion windows during traffic spikes.

How should you redesign the workload using batching strategies and high throughput inference configurations to maximize utilization and throughput?

Use Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs to distribute the moderation workload across multiple nodes and have each node call the foundation model endpoint in parallel. Rely on the distributed processing cluster to finish the workload faster without changing the per item invocation pattern

Increase the number of GPU instances on the existing real time endpoint and scale them to the maximum size available. Rely on the additional capacity to absorb hourly traffic spikes without modifying the request pattern or batching behavior

Configure a SageMaker real time endpoint with larger instance types and enable request level parallelism by submitting multiple concurrent mini batches across several threads. Rely on endpoint invocation concurrency to simulate high throughput behavior without adopting full batch transform or asynchronous inference

Correct answer
Configure a high throughput inference setup using Amazon SageMaker batch transform or SageMaker asynchronous inference and submit large batches that group multiple records per request. Use auto scaling rules on the model endpoint to match peak batch volumes and ensure that GPU instances remain fully utilized

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Configure a high throughput inference setup using Amazon SageMaker batch transform or SageMaker asynchronous inference and submit large batches that group multiple records per request. Use auto scaling rules on the model endpoint to match peak batch volumes and ensure that GPU instances remain fully utilized

High throughput inference is achieved by batching multiple content snippets into a single inference request so that each GPU processes larger workloads instead of many small requests. SageMaker batch transform and SageMaker asynchronous inference are purpose built for large scale batch workloads and can distribute large datasets across multiple instances efficiently.

Auto scaling ensures that the system scales proactively based on queued jobs or volume indicators, which maintains predictable throughput while controlling cost. These batching and scaling mechanisms together ensure that the hourly moderation job completes reliably within its window.

Here is a deep-dive on batch inference at scale with Amazon SageMaker:  via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/batch-inference-at-scale-with-amazon-sagemaker/

Incorrect options:

Increase the number of GPU instances on the existing real time endpoint and scale them to the maximum size available. Rely on the additional capacity to absorb hourly traffic spikes without modifying the request pattern or batching behavior - Adding more GPU instances without changing the inference pattern leaves the core inefficiency unchanged because each record still generates its own request. This increases cost substantially while retaining the overhead of small payload real time inference.

Use Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs to distribute the moderation workload across multiple nodes and have each node call the foundation model endpoint in parallel. Rely on the distributed processing cluster to finish the workload faster without changing the per item invocation pattern - Distributing work across more nodes only increases parallelism, not throughput at the model level, because inference still occurs one item at a time. The model endpoint becomes the bottleneck due to small unbatched requests, leading to low GPU utilization and higher cost even though the surrounding compute scales efficiently.

Configure a SageMaker real time endpoint with larger instance types and enable request level parallelism by submitting multiple concurrent mini batches across several threads. Rely on endpoint invocation concurrency to simulate high throughput behavior without adopting full batch transform or asynchronous inference - Submitting concurrent mini batches still results in many small inference calls, which does not maximize GPU utilization or eliminate per request overhead. Real time endpoints also enforce concurrency and latency constraints that make them unsuitable for large volume batch jobs, causing inconsistent throughput and higher costs under load.

A financial services company is rolling out dozens of foundation models for different risk scoring and customer analytics use cases. The head of model risk management has asked you to ensure that every model promotion through the CI/CD pipeline automatically produces an up to date, regulator ready model card that captures intended use, limitations, key metrics, and risk ratings without manual edits.

As a GenAI developer, what should you design so that programmatic model card generation is embedded as a mandatory step in the deployment workflow?

Configure the CI/CD pipeline to run SageMaker Processing jobs that export model evaluation metrics and store them in Amazon S3, then manually trigger model card creation from the SageMaker console. Use CloudWatch Events to notify reviewers whenever new metrics are uploaded

Correct answer
Integrate the SageMaker Model Card APIs into the CI/CD pipeline so that deployment stages automatically call create_model_card and update_model_card with metadata extracted from training and evaluation jobs. Configure the pipeline to block model promotion until the generated model card artifacts are validated and stored in the model registry

Create a Lambda function that runs after each deployment to read evaluation metrics from Amazon S3 and send a summary to the compliance team, who then use the SageMaker console to create model cards manually. Configure Amazon SNS notifications so that the Lambda function alerts reviewers whenever a new model version is promoted

Add a non blocking stage to the CI/CD pipeline that calls SageMaker Model Card APIs to create or update model cards using default templates without validating captured metadata. Allow the pipeline to continue promoting the model to production even if the model card creation step fails or produces incomplete documentation

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Integrate the SageMaker Model Card APIs into the CI/CD pipeline so that deployment stages automatically call create_model_card and update_model_card with metadata extracted from training and evaluation jobs. Configure the pipeline to block model promotion until the generated model card artifacts are validated and stored in the model registry

SageMaker model cards enable you to standardize how models are documented, thereby achieving visibility into the lifecycle of a model, from designing, building, training, and evaluation. Model cards are intended to be a single source of truth for business and technical metadata about the model that can reliably be used for auditing and documentation purposes. They provide a fact sheet of the model that is important for model governance.

Automating model card creation inside the CI/CD workflow ensures that all required documentation is consistently generated and updated before model promotion. By calling create_model_card and update_model_card programmatically, the pipeline enforces governance standards and removes manual steps that can introduce compliance gaps. Embedding model card validation as a blocking stage ensures that every deployment is accompanied by a complete and regulator ready document. This allows model risk teams to maintain traceability and consistent oversight across all foundation models.

How to use Amazon SageMaker Model Cards to improve model governance:  via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/use-amazon-sagemaker-model-cards-sharing-to-improve-model-governance/

Incorrect options:

Create a Lambda function that runs after each deployment to read evaluation metrics from Amazon S3 and send a summary to the compliance team, who then use the SageMaker console to create model cards manually. Configure Amazon SNS notifications so that the Lambda function alerts reviewers whenever a new model version is promoted - Emailing metrics to compliance teams shifts responsibility to manual processes that cannot guarantee timely or consistent model card creation. Governance requirements for regulated environments call for automated, enforceable steps rather than manual reviews triggered by SNS or email notifications.

Add a non blocking stage to the CI/CD pipeline that calls SageMaker Model Card APIs to create or update model cards using default templates without validating captured metadata. Allow the pipeline to continue promoting the model to production even if the model card creation step fails or produces incomplete documentation - Calling SageMaker Model Card APIs in a non blocking stage does not enforce governance because models can still be promoted even when model card creation fails or produces incomplete content. Without validation and a hard gate in the pipeline, the organization risks having production models that lack accurate or current documentation when regulators request evidence.

Configure the CI/CD pipeline to run SageMaker Processing jobs that export model evaluation metrics and store them in Amazon S3, then manually trigger model card creation from the SageMaker console. Use CloudWatch Events to notify reviewers whenever new metrics are uploaded - Running SageMaker Processing jobs to export metrics does not create or update model cards programmatically, and requiring manual creation through the console introduces compliance risks. Even with CloudWatch notifications, this approach does not ensure that every promotion includes a complete and validated model card.

Implement custom ETL pipelines to chunk documents and maintain vector embeddings inside the RDS database - This architecture allows combining relational metadata and document storage, but it shifts responsibility for chunking, embedding generation, and vector index maintenance to the development team. Since the question clearly states that the company wants to avoid managing vector infrastructure, RDS pgvector is not a suitable choice.

A global healthcare analytics company operates a clinical summarization system that currently runs in a single geographic region. New regulatory and availability requirements mandate that the system must remain fully functional even if one region experiences a prolonged outage, while also ensuring that user requests are routed according to regional compliance rules. You are responsible for designing a multi Region architecture that supports active active or active passive deployments, performs automated health checks, and redirects traffic safely during failures.

How should you architect the multi Region integration and routing strategy to meet these resilience requirements?

Run the Bedrock workload in one AWS Region and enable cross Region replication for data, while continuing to direct all inference requests through a single Route 53 simple record. Allow DNS caching to manage failover behavior without using health checks or routing policies

Create separate Bedrock endpoints in multiple AWS Regions but configure Route 53 with weighted routing that always favors the primary Region regardless of health status. Allow traffic to shift back only after administrators manually update routing weights following an outage.

Deploy the Bedrock workflow in two AWS Regions but front both services with a single Route 53 record that uses simple routing and has no health checks enabled. Leverage application clients to detect endpoint failures and manually shift requests to the secondary Region

Correct answer
Deploy the Bedrock based inference workflow in two AWS Regions and expose each through separate regional endpoints registered in Amazon Route 53 using failover or latency based routing. Configure Route 53 health checks to monitor each endpoint and automatically redirect traffic to the healthy Region during outages

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Deploy the Bedrock based inference workflow in two AWS Regions and expose each through separate regional endpoints registered in Amazon Route 53 using failover or latency based routing. Configure Route 53 health checks to monitor each endpoint and automatically redirect traffic to the healthy Region during outages

Deploying regional Bedrock endpoints behind Route 53 failover or latency based routing provides a robust multi Region pattern that supports regulatory compliance and uninterrupted clinical access. Route 53 health checks continuously monitor endpoint health so that requests seamlessly shift to the healthy Region during prolonged outages. This approach ensures predictable routing behavior, automatic failover, and geographic control while maintaining low latency and high availability. It meets both the regulatory requirement for region specific routing and the operational need for business continuity.

Incorrect options:

Deploy the Bedrock workflow in two AWS Regions but front both services with a single Route 53 record that uses simple routing and has no health checks enabled. Leverage application clients to detect endpoint failures and manually shift requests to the secondary Region - A single Route 53 record without routing policies or health checks cannot provide automated failover across Regions, forcing clients to handle failure detection themselves. This design violates continuity requirements and introduces unpredictable behavior during regional outages.

Create separate Bedrock endpoints in multiple AWS Regions but configure Route 53 with weighted routing that always favors the primary Region regardless of health status. Allow traffic to shift back only after administrators manually update routing weights following an outage. - Weighted routing that always prefers a primary Region cannot detect outages and will continue sending traffic to an unhealthy endpoint until weights are manually updated. This approach does not fulfill the requirement for automated failover or region specific routing controls.

Run the Bedrock workload in one AWS Region and enable cross Region replication for data, while continuing to direct all inference requests through a single Route 53 simple record. Allow DNS caching to manage failover behavior without using health checks or routing policies - Running inference in only one Region with simple DNS routing prevents traffic from shifting away from the failed Region and does not satisfy multi Region resilience needs. Replicating data does not enable automatic failover when the inference endpoint becomes unavailable.

A healthcare startup is building a clinical summarization assistant that doctors use to generate concise and detailed reports from unstructured notes and lab values. The assistant needs to support different personas such as doctors, nurses, and pharmacists so that each persona can receive a tailored summary with the appropriate level of clinical detail. The system must also handle sensitive PHI by performing local redaction before AI processing, and it must be able to stream responses back to the application with minimal latency while doctors are with patients. The company wants to avoid heavy infrastructure and prefers a fully managed orchestration layer that can evolve as new personas and workflows are added.

Which solution should the GenAI architect choose to meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Expose an Amazon API Gateway REST API that fronts an AWS Lambda ingestion function, perform PHI redaction inside the Lambda function, and then invoke an Amazon Bedrock Flow that orchestrates persona specific prompts, optional retrieval steps, and summarization with streaming responses using the Amazon Bedrock Converse API

Deploy a containerized microservice on Amazon ECS that performs PHI redaction, persona based routing, and direct Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel calls, and expose it behind an Application Load Balancer. Implement a custom WebSocket server in the container to send streaming responses to the clinical web application

Connect the application directly to an Amazon Bedrock Converse API endpoint from the frontend, send raw clinical notes without server side preprocessing, and rely on the model system prompt to ignore PHI fields. Use client side JavaScript to render incremental tokens to simulate streaming behavior

Use AWS Step Functions as the central orchestrator to call a Lambda redaction function, a Lambda prompt assembly function, and then an Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API call. Configure API Gateway to trigger the Step Functions workflow and return the final response

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Expose an Amazon API Gateway REST API that fronts an AWS Lambda ingestion function, perform PHI redaction inside the Lambda function, and then invoke an Amazon Bedrock Flow that orchestrates persona specific prompts, optional retrieval steps, and summarization with streaming responses using the Amazon Bedrock Converse API

This option aligns with the requirement to perform PHI redaction locally within a controlled backend boundary before any text is sent to a foundation model. API Gateway combined with a Lambda ingestion function provides a lightweight and serverless edge for receiving clinical text from the frontend, applying redaction logic, and validating requests. After redaction, Amazon Bedrock Flows can orchestrate persona aware prompts, RAG steps if needed, and summarization in a fully managed orchestration environment that does not require the team to maintain workflow engines or container clusters.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows.html

Using the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with streaming through the Flow output allows the assistant to send partial responses back through API Gateway so that doctors see summaries in near real time. Bedrock Flows also make it easier to add or modify personas later without redeploying application logic because the orchestration graph and model calls are centrally managed in the Bedrock control plane. This combination meets the startup’s preference for a fully managed orchestration layer, keeps PHI handling within Lambda under the startup’s control, and still delivers low latency streaming behavior suitable for interactive clinical workflows.

 via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows.html

Incorrect options:

Use AWS Step Functions as the central orchestrator to call a Lambda redaction function, a Lambda prompt assembly function, and then an Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API call. Configure API Gateway to trigger the Step Functions workflow and return the final response - Step Functions can orchestrate multiple Lambda functions and Bedrock calls, but it is optimized for durable, stateful workflows rather than low latency interactive streaming. The response to the client is only available once the workflow completes, which conflicts with the requirement to stream responses back to clinicians as they are generated. In addition, the team would need to manage and version the Step Functions state machine and its error handling logic directly, which increases operational overhead relative to using Bedrock Flows for GenAI specific orchestration.

Connect the application directly to an Amazon Bedrock Converse API endpoint from the frontend, send raw clinical notes without server side preprocessing, and rely on the model system prompt to ignore PHI fields. Use client side JavaScript to render incremental tokens to simulate streaming behavior - Calling the Converse API directly from the frontend and relying solely on system prompts to ignore PHI is not sufficient for healthcare privacy and compliance. PHI would still transit the network and be processed by the model, which violates the requirement that redaction must occur before AI processing. Client side JavaScript based streaming is also not a substitute for a managed backend pipeline where access control, auditing, and logging can be enforced.

Deploy a containerized microservice on Amazon ECS that performs PHI redaction, persona based routing, and direct Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel calls, and expose it behind an Application Load Balancer. Implement a custom WebSocket server in the container to send streaming responses to the clinical web application - While ECS and an Application Load Balancer can support custom microservices and WebSocket servers, this design introduces heavier infrastructure than the startup wants to manage. The team would need to operate container clusters, handle auto scaling policies, patch base images, and maintain a custom streaming protocol. This conflicts with the preference for a fully managed orchestration layer and adds DevOps complexity that is unnecessary when Bedrock Flows and serverless integrations can provide similar capabilities with much less overhead.

How should you identify and correct embedding drift so that search results consistently reflect the most up to date knowledge?

Perform a partial refresh by re-embedding only the segments related to newly added troubleshooting steps while leaving legacy embeddings in place. Validate retrieval quality using targeted tests rather than performing a full corpus re-embedding

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases but retain the mixed set of legacy and new embeddings while applying metadata filters that boost recently updated articles. Depend on Bedrock model based re-ranking to adjust for inconsistencies between the different embedding generations

Correct answer
Rebuild the entire vector store using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a single Titan Embeddings model and uniform preprocessing rules to eliminate version mismatches. Run retrieval relevance checks and drift evaluation tests to confirm that all vectors are aligned with the updated corpus

Re-embed only the documents that changed in the recent update cycle and preserve all older vectors generated with the previous embedding model. Modify OpenSearch ANN search settings to reduce stale recommendations without altering the embedding workflow

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Rebuild the entire vector store using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a single Titan Embeddings model and uniform preprocessing rules to eliminate version mismatches. Run retrieval relevance checks and drift evaluation tests to confirm that all vectors are aligned with the updated corpus

Re-embedding the entire corpus with a single Amazon Titan Embeddings model and a consistent preprocessing pipeline eliminates the root cause of drift, which is the mixing of vectors from different models and tokenization strategies. When all embeddings live in the same semantic space, similarity search behaves predictably and the knowledge assistant is much more likely to prioritize the updated troubleshooting content over stale material. Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides a managed RAG workflow that takes care of chunking, embedding, and storage in a vector store, while letting you choose a consistent embedding model such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings.

After re-embedding, you can run evaluation workflows that analyze retrieval relevance and measure how often updated documents appear in the top results. AWS guidance on RAG evaluation and embedding quality encourages systematic testing of retrieval results whenever you change embedding models or pipelines, so a full refresh combined with evaluation is a best practice rather than a one off fix.

Here is a deep-dive into vector data stores using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases:  via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/dive-deep-into-vector-data-stores-using-amazon-bedrock-knowledge-bases/

 via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/dive-deep-into-vector-data-stores-using-amazon-bedrock-knowledge-bases/

Incorrect options:

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases but retain the mixed set of legacy and new embeddings while applying metadata filters that boost recently updated articles. Depend on Bedrock model based re-ranking to adjust for inconsistencies between the different embedding generations - Keeping a mixed population of embeddings produced by different models and preprocessors leaves the semantic space fragmented, so nearest neighbor search can still prefer stale vectors even if you apply metadata filters or re ranking. Re-ranking and filtering are useful for tuning relevance within a consistent embedding space, but they do not repair fundamental incompatibilities between vector representations generated with different models or tokenization strategies. AWS guidance on Bedrock Knowledge Bases and vector stores emphasizes consistent embedding strategy and refresh workflows as key factors for accurate retrieval in RAG applications.

Re-embed only the documents that changed in the recent update cycle and preserve all older vectors generated with the previous embedding model. Modify OpenSearch ANN search settings to reduce stale recommendations without altering the embedding workflow - Refreshing only a subset of documents while leaving the majority of vectors on an older embedding model keeps two incompatible vector distributions in the same index, which maintains the drift problem instead of resolving it. Tuning ANN algorithms, distance metrics, or index parameters in Amazon OpenSearch Service improves performance and scalability, but does not fix semantic mismatches between embeddings generated by different models.

Perform a partial refresh by re-embedding only the segments related to newly added troubleshooting steps while leaving legacy embeddings in place. Validate retrieval quality using targeted tests rather than performing a full corpus re-embedding - A partial refresh that only re-embeds segments tied to new troubleshooting steps still leaves many related documents and older content represented by legacy embeddings, which can cause the similarity search to pull outdated material that appears closer in the old semantic space. Targeted tests might show apparent improvements on a narrow subset of queries, but they can easily miss broader drift effects that occur when users phrase questions differently or search across adjacent topics. AWS prescriptive guidance on RAG and embeddings stresses that when you change the embedding model or preprocessing pipeline, a comprehensive re embedding of the corpus combined with systematic evaluation is the reliable way to eliminate stale or inconsistent retrieval behavior.

Use AWS Step functions to enforce multi-stage approval workflows across business units, combine Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for topic blocking and injection resistance, and integrate Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval with citation metadata. Which orchestration approach would you recommend to coordinate this end to end custom GenAI training and deployment workflow?

Correct answer
Build an Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that defines the required steps. Configure the pipeline to trigger on the relevant events and roll back to an approved model version when evaluation metrics degrade

Leverage AWS CodePipeline to detect changes in a source repository and run CodeBuild jobs that call SageMaker APIs for training and deployment. Implement evaluation, metric comparison, and rollback behavior entirely in custom shell scripts inside the build stages

Schedule a SageMaker notebook instance to run a Jupyter notebook that reads new data, starts a training job, computes metrics, and directly updates the production endpoint. Store the active model information in a JSON file in S3 and overwrite it whenever a new model trains

Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate Lambda functions that submit SageMaker training jobs, run evaluation scripts, and update endpoints while storing model versions in a DynamoDB table. Configure an EventBridge rule to start the state machine whenever new training data arrives in S3

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Build an Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that defines the required steps. Configure the pipeline to trigger on the relevant events and roll back to an approved model version when evaluation metrics degrade

This solution uses Amazon SageMaker Pipelines as the primary orchestration layer for the end to end GenAI lifecycle. SageMaker Pipelines lets you define a directed acyclic graph of steps, including processing jobs for data preparation, SageMaker training jobs, model evaluation steps, conditional branches based on metrics, and integration with the SageMaker Model Registry to register candidate models. These steps run as a managed workflow that you can visualize, audit, and parameterize, and the pipeline definition itself is versionable through infrastructure as code.

The pipeline can then deploy approved model versions to SageMaker endpoints and record lineage information, which supports rollback and reproducibility. You can trigger the pipeline from CI or CD systems such as CodePipeline or from data events via the SageMaker SDK, so new datasets or configuration changes automatically re run the same orchestrated workflow. Conditional steps can compare new evaluation metrics against baselines and either promote the model to production or keep an earlier registry version active, which provides a structured mechanism for automated rollback when metrics regress.

Amazon SageMaker Pipelines:  via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/pipelines.html

Incorrect options:

Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate Lambda functions that submit SageMaker training jobs, run evaluation scripts, and update endpoints while storing model versions in a DynamoDB table. Configure an EventBridge rule to start the state machine whenever new training data arrives in S3 - This option uses AWS Step Functions with Lambda and custom model version tracking in DynamoDB, which can coordinate calls to SageMaker but does not natively support ML specific lifecycle capabilities. The team would have to implement their own model registry semantics, lineage tracking, approval workflow, and rollback logic instead of using the built in features of SageMaker Pipelines and the Model Registry that are designed for end to end ML orchestration.

Schedule a SageMaker notebook instance to run a Jupyter notebook that reads new data, starts a training job, computes metrics, and directly updates the production endpoint. Store the active model information in a JSON file in S3 and overwrite it whenever a new model trains - This option relies on a scheduled SageMaker notebook instance and a Jupyter notebook script as the orchestration mechanism, which is suitable for experimentation but weak for production grade pipelines. Notebooks make it harder to enforce consistent versioning, approvals, and rollback, and storing active model metadata only in an S3 JSON file provides less structure than a dedicated model registry or MLOps workflow.

Leverage AWS CodePipeline to detect changes in a source repository and run CodeBuild jobs that call SageMaker APIs for training and deployment. Implement evaluation, metric comparison, and rollback behavior entirely in custom shell scripts inside the build stages - This option uses AWS CodePipeline and CodeBuild as the primary orchestrator, embedding training, evaluation, and rollback logic in custom shell scripts. While CI or CD tools can trigger ML workflows, implementing all lifecycle behavior in scripts reduces transparency, makes the workflow harder to inspect and reuse, and does not take advantage of SageMaker specific constructs like Pipelines and the Model Registry that support model centric governance and rollback.

A large enterprise has centralized all foundation model inference inside a dedicated AI platform account that runs Amazon Bedrock models behind a controlled access layer. Individual business units maintain their own Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector collections and Aurora PostgreSQL clusters with the pgvector extension in separate AWS accounts. The enterprise must preserve strict cross account security boundaries, minimize operational overhead, and still support efficient vector similarity search for retrieval augmented generation.

What is the most effective way to design this cross account retrieval architecture?

Correct answer
Expose the business unit vector indexes through cross account IAM permissions supported by OpenSearch Serverless or Aurora pgvector and connect the AI platform account using AWS PrivateLink for secure, private retrieval. Then allow the Bedrock based assistant to issue vector similarity queries on demand while the data remains in the owner accounts

Ingest all business unit documents into a consolidated Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base inside the AI platform and let Bedrock generate new embeddings for all content. Then remove the need for cross account connectivity entirely by relying only on the consolidated Knowledge Base for retrieval

Export all embeddings and source metadata from each business unit into Amazon S3 in the AI platform account and rebuild new OpenSearch Serverless vector collections centrally. Then schedule periodic Lambda sync jobs to refresh the centralized collections as new documents arrive

Build a single Amazon API Gateway endpoint in the AI platform account that proxies requests to all business unit indexes across accounts. Then require each FM application to pass an index identifier so the gateway can forward the query to the correct backend

Overall explanation
Correct option:

Expose the business unit vector indexes through cross account IAM permissions supported by OpenSearch Serverless or Aurora pgvector and connect the AI platform account using AWS PrivateLink for secure, private retrieval. Then allow the Bedrock based assistant to issue vector similarity queries on demand while the data remains in the owner accounts

This approach uses AWS PrivateLink and cross account IAM permissions to let the AI platform query remote vector indexes without duplicating data or violating account level separation. OpenSearch Serverless supports cross account access using the assume role option, and Aurora pgvector supports cross account retrieval through secure VPC connectivity and IAM authentication when combined with controlled API exposure.

This design aligns with the requirements for secure multi account retrieval, optimal vector search performance, and minimal data movement. It preserves data ownership within each business unit while enabling efficient vector similarity search for retrieval augmented generation in the Bedrock environment.

Incorrect options:

Export all embeddings and source metadata from each business unit into Amazon S3 in the AI platform account and rebuild new OpenSearch Serverless vector collections centrally. This design also introduces synchronization delays and violates best practices for minimizing data movement across accounts.

Build a single Amazon API Gateway endpoint in the AI platform account that proxies requests to all business unit indexes across accounts. Then require each FM application to pass an index identifier so the gateway can forward the query to the correct backend - Using a central API Gateway proxy introduces a single point of routing, weakens fine grained access control, and forces request level filtering to determine the correct index. This breaks isolation guarantees across business units and increases operational overhead.

Ingest all business unit documents into a consolidated Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base inside the AI platform and let Bedrock generate new embeddings for all content. Then remove the need for cross account connectivity entirely by relying only on the consolidated Knowledge Base for retrieval - Reingesting all business unit documents into a consolidated Bedrock Knowledge Base forces a full re-embedding of content, increases duplication, and breaks the design principle of keeping vector stores close to their owners. It removes autonomy from the business units and complicates governance for large multi account environments.

Incorrect. KMS encryption and scoped IAM permissions are important security controls for storage and access, but they do not remove PII from text that is sent to the FM. This approach can still expose raw client identifiers during inference and does not provide response-side masking.
Correct selection
Add a Lambda preprocessing step that calls Amazon Comprehend PII detection and replaces detected spans with stable placeholders before invoking Amazon Bedrock.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Comprehend can detect common PII entity types and return the character offsets needed for application code to mask or replace values before sending text to a model. Stable placeholders preserve useful context, such as participant roles and repeated references, without exposing the original sensitive values.
Run Amazon Macie discovery on transcript buckets and send only objects without sensitive data findings to Amazon Bedrock.
Explanation
Incorrect. Macie is useful for discovering sensitive data in Amazon S3, but bucket discovery alone is not an inline masking control for each inference request. Because the transcripts often contain PII, filtering out every object with findings would also reduce application utility rather than preserving context through anonymization.
Add prompt instructions that tell the FM to omit PII and set deterministic inference parameters for every transcript summary request.
Explanation
Incorrect. Prompt instructions can guide the model, and deterministic settings can reduce output variability, but they are not a reliable privacy boundary. The raw sensitive values would still be included in the prompt, and the model might still reproduce them.
Overall explanation
Privacy-focused generative AI systems usually need controls both before inference and around inference. Amazon Comprehend PII detection identifies PII entity types in text and provides offsets, which lets a Lambda function replace sensitive spans with placeholders such as <CLIENT_NAME_1> or <ACCOUNT_ID_1> before the prompt is sent to Amazon Bedrock. See Detecting PII entities for how Comprehend supports this pattern.

Amazon Bedrock guardrails add a managed policy layer for prompts and model responses. Sensitive information filters can help detect and mask or block supported PII, and custom regex patterns can cover organization-specific identifiers such as account-number formats. See Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock and Sensitive information filters for the relevant capabilities.

Encryption, IAM scoping, and data discovery are still valuable, but they solve different parts of the privacy problem. They protect stored data and access paths, while preprocessing and guardrails reduce the chance that sensitive values enter the prompt or appear in the generated output. Prompt-only controls are an anti-pattern for privacy boundaries because they rely on model behavior rather than deterministic filtering and policy enforcement.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 2
Skipped
A university admissions office is preparing to release an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base assistant that answers questions about application deadlines, scholarship rules, and residency requirements. The team has an S3 prompt dataset in JSON Lines format with 700 prompts, including reference responses for single-turn retrieval tests and several four-turn conversations for answer-quality tests. The release gate must separately measure retrieval quality, generated answer quality, safety risks, and subjective usefulness, while avoiding custom evaluation pipelines. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Correct answer
Split the dataset by evaluation purpose. Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation with retrieval metrics on single-turn prompts, run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation with response metrics on conversations, and run a human-worker model evaluation job for subjective review.
Explanation
This approach uses the managed Amazon Bedrock evaluation modes that align to the required perspectives. Retrieve-only evaluation measures retrieved context, retrieve-and-generate evaluation measures generated responses, and a human-worker model evaluation job captures subjective usefulness without building a custom pipeline.
Run one retrieve-only RAG evaluation against the full dataset. Select response-quality and safety metrics for all prompts, then send low-scoring conversations to admissions staff for manual review outside the evaluation job.
Explanation
Retrieve-only RAG evaluation is for evaluating retrieved data, and retrieve-only prompt datasets support only a single turn. Response-quality metrics such as correctness, helpfulness, harmfulness, and refusal are associated with retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation, not retrieve-only jobs.
Run one retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation against the full dataset. Select context relevance, context coverage, and response-quality metrics, then use the generated metric scores as the only release gate.
Explanation
Retrieve-and-generate evaluation can assess generated responses and supports multi-turn conversations, but the documented retrieve-only metrics include context relevance and context coverage. This option also omits the required subjective usefulness perspective from human evaluation.
Run one LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation with a generator model and a separate evaluator model. Provide the Knowledge Base responses as bring-your-own inference data and use the judge scores for retrieval, response, and human-quality gates.
Explanation
LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation is useful for scoring generated responses with a separate evaluator model, and it can evaluate supplied inference response data. It does not replace a RAG retrieve-only evaluation for separately measuring retrieved context quality, and it does not provide human subjective review.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock evaluations are designed to support several complementary assessment perspectives rather than forcing every quality signal into one job type. The managed evaluation capabilities include automatic model evaluation, human-worker model evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation, and RAG or knowledge-base evaluation, as described in Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources.

For a RAG assistant, the important distinction is whether the team is testing retrieval, generation, or both. A retrieve-only RAG evaluation measures the retrieved data from a Knowledge Base or external RAG source. A retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation measures both retrieved data and generated answers, including supported response-quality and safety metrics, as covered in Evaluate a RAG application or Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base.

The dataset constraints also matter. RAG evaluation prompt datasets must be stored in Amazon S3 as .jsonl files, each line must be a valid JSON object, and an evaluation job can include up to 1000 prompts. Retrieve-only evaluations support only a single turn, while retrieve-and-generate jobs support up to five turns per conversation, which is why splitting the dataset by evaluation purpose is the clean managed approach. See Requirements for RAG evaluation prompt datasets.

The metric families are not interchangeable. Retrieve-only metrics include Builtin.ContextRelevance and Builtin.ContextCoverage, with context coverage requiring ground-truth reference responses in the prompt dataset. Retrieve-and-generate evaluations use response-oriented metrics such as correctness, completeness, helpfulness, logical coherence, faithfulness, harmfulness, stereotyping, and refusal, as documented in RAG evaluation metrics. LLM-as-a-judge is valuable when a separate evaluator model scores generated responses, but by itself it does not provide the separate retrieval-quality and human-subjective perspectives required here. The model roles for that mode are described in Model evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 3
Skipped
A regional credit union's member services team runs a live chat assistant on Amazon Bedrock by using Amazon Nova Pro through a supported cross-Region inference profile in a US Region. The team wants lower latency for interactive requests, must keep the same FM and application integration, and has not approved changing Amazon Bedrock inference service tiers or buying reserved capacity. If feature-specific acceleration quota is reached, the team prefers Bedrock to attempt normal processing rather than failing solely for that reason. Which request-level change best meets these requirements?

Correct answer
Set performanceConfig.latency to optimized on each supported inference request, and inspect the response and CloudTrail to confirm the served configuration.
Explanation
Correct. This requests the Bedrock preview latency optimization path per inference call for supported models and inference profiles, without creating a custom model or changing service tiers. If the latency-optimized quota is reached, Bedrock attempts to serve the request with Standard latency, and the actually served configuration can be checked in the response and CloudTrail.
Leave performanceConfig.latency at standard on each supported inference request, and enable response streaming to return generated tokens progressively.
Explanation
Incorrect. Streaming can improve perceived responsiveness because users can see tokens as they are generated, but it does not request the documented optimized latency configuration. If performanceConfig.latency is standard or is not specified, Bedrock uses the Standard latency setting.
Set maxTokens lower on each supported inference request, and inspect token count metrics to confirm shorter generated responses.
Explanation
Incorrect. Limiting generated output can reduce total generation work and may help control cost or end-to-end response length. It does not request the latency-optimized inference path or provide the documented fallback behavior for the latency-optimized quota.
Set performanceConfig.latency to optimized on the first request in each chat session, and inspect session history to confirm later turns inherit the configuration.
Explanation
Incorrect. Latency optimization is requested per inference call, so setting it only once does not reliably apply it to later requests. The scenario requires lower latency for interactive requests generally, which means each supported request must include the correct latency configuration.
Overall explanation
For supported Amazon Bedrock models and inference profiles, the request-level control for the preview latency optimization feature is performanceConfig.latency. Setting it to optimized asks Bedrock to use the optimized path for that call, while leaving it unset defaults to standard.

The per-call nature of this setting matters for chat applications because each turn is a separate inference request. Setting the value only once for a session is not the same as including it on every supported request that needs optimized latency.

The fallback behavior is important for resilient user experiences. If a request reaches the latency-optimized usage quota, Bedrock attempts to serve the request with Standard latency and charges it at Standard latency rates, and the served configuration is visible in the API response and in AWS CloudTrail.

Techniques such as response streaming and output length controls can still improve user experience or cost efficiency, but they solve different problems. They do not activate the documented latency optimization feature for the supported model and inference profile. For more details, see Optimize inference latency for foundation models in Amazon Bedrock and Optimize cost and performance using Amazon Bedrock inference service tiers.

Amazon Bedrock provides streaming inference through operations such as ConverseStream and InvokeModelWithResponseStream, but the target model must support streaming. With ConverseStream, the application receives named events such as messageStart, contentBlockDelta, messageStop, and error events, so application code must parse the event stream and emit only the appropriate incremental content to the client. See the Amazon Bedrock ConverseStream API reference. API…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 4
Skipped
A live sports analytics startup is adding an AI commentary assistant to its web application. The browser client uses server-sent events over HTTPS and must display partial generated commentary as soon as the foundation model produces it. The backend is implemented with AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway, and the team wants to use a common messages-based request format across supported Amazon Bedrock chat models. The team does not want to manage persistent WebSocket connections. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Configure an API Gateway HTTP API Lambda proxy integration for the streaming endpoint and return server-sent event data from Lambda.
Explanation
This is incorrect because API Gateway response streaming is documented for REST APIs, not HTTP APIs. Although HTTP APIs are suitable for many Lambda-backed workloads, they do not meet this specific response streaming requirement.
Correct selection
Invoke Amazon Bedrock by using ConverseStream, parse contentBlockDelta events, and forward incremental content to the client stream.
Explanation
This is correct because ConverseStream provides a consistent messages-based API for models that support streaming. The incremental generated content is delivered in named stream events, with contentBlockDelta carrying partial content that the application can forward.
Configure an API Gateway REST API Lambda proxy integration with the default BUFFERED transfer mode for the streaming endpoint.
Explanation
This is incorrect because the default response transfer mode is BUFFERED, which waits for the integration response instead of streaming chunks incrementally. Lambda can consume Bedrock streaming events, but API Gateway must use STREAM mode to pass them through progressively.
Invoke Amazon Bedrock by using Converse, return the full Lambda result, and rely on API Gateway to split the response into chunks.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Converse is not the streaming operation and does not provide partial model output as it is generated. API Gateway streaming can deliver chunks from the integration, but it cannot create incremental model tokens from a fully buffered Bedrock response.
Correct selection
Configure an API Gateway REST API Lambda proxy integration with response transfer mode set to STREAM for the streaming endpoint.
Explanation
This is correct because API Gateway response streaming is a REST API feature and supports Lambda proxy integrations. Setting the response transfer mode to STREAM allows incremental response delivery instead of buffering the full response.
Overall explanation
For a browser experience based on server-sent events or HTTP chunked delivery, the system needs streaming at two layers: the model invocation layer and the API delivery layer. Amazon Bedrock provides streaming inference through operations such as ConverseStream and InvokeModelWithResponseStream, but the target model must support streaming. With ConverseStream, the application receives named events such as messageStart, contentBlockDelta, messageStop, and error events, so application code must parse the event stream and emit only the appropriate incremental content to the client. See the Amazon Bedrock ConverseStream API reference.

API Gateway can expose this type of real-time interaction over HTTPS without requiring WebSocket connection management, but the documented response streaming feature applies to REST APIs with supported proxy integrations. The transfer mode must be set to STREAM; otherwise, the default BUFFERED behavior waits for the integration response before returning data to the client. The API Gateway documentation specifically describes response streaming for generative AI and server-sent event style use cases, including Lambda proxy integrations. See API Gateway response streaming and Lambda proxy integration response streaming requirements.

The buffered alternatives fail because they do not preserve incremental model output end to end. Calling a nonstreaming Bedrock operation and then enabling streaming at API Gateway only streams whatever the Lambda function chooses to send, after the model response has already been received. Similarly, choosing an API Gateway HTTP API does not satisfy the documented REST API response streaming requirement. Leaving a REST API integration in BUFFERED mode is also insufficient because the endpoint does not deliver the Lambda stream incrementally to the client.

Security scanning is also part of the Amazon Q Developer developer experience, so developers can identify certain code vulnerabilities without leaving the IDE workflow. Project rules let teams provide repository-specific guidance so generated suggestions can better align with local conventions, which is useful for GenAI applications that need consistent Bedrock client patterns, prompt handling, and error handling.

Amazon Q Developer customizations can be valuable when an organization wants suggestions tailored to private code, but they require administrative setup and rollout, which is not the lowest-overhead starting point for this sprint. Amazon Q Business is aimed at enterprise knowledge assistance and task automation, not IDE-native code completions and developer security scans. **Quick lesson:** The strongest design separates two safety concerns that are easy to confuse: token-level redaction and policy enforcement. Lambda pre and post processors can remove or mask sensitive tokens before content is logged and after the model responds, using deterministic patterns or services such as Amazon Comprehend for PII detection. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then provide managed controls for denied topics, content filters, word filters, sensitive information filters, and contextual grounding checks that can be applied to prompts and responses. For audit readiness, the system should retain evidence that is useful but not unnecessarily sensitive.…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 8
Skipped
A property insurance carrier's claims governance team runs an API Gateway endpoint that invokes Amazon Bedrock through AWS Lambda to draft claim correspondence. The team must support quarterly safety audits and regulatory evidence reviews. The design must not retain raw PII in logs or audit stores, must capture redacted prompt and response evidence, must apply centrally managed policy filters to both user input and model output, and must automatically route suspected violations for compliance review with minimal custom ML work. Which implementation best meets these requirements?

Add API Gateway request validators that reject malformed payloads, tune Amazon Bedrock inference parameters during invocation, write full interaction records to CloudWatch Logs and S3, and route timeout events through EventBridge to a Step Functions compliance workflow.
Explanation
API Gateway request validation is useful for enforcing request shape, but it does not identify PII or semantic policy violations in model content. Inference parameters do not provide centrally managed safety filtering, and retaining full interaction records violates the requirement to avoid raw PII in logs and audit stores.
Add Lambda pre and post processors that hash complete messages, apply prompt instructions during invocation, write hashed interaction records to CloudWatch Logs and S3, and route low confidence events through EventBridge to a Step Functions compliance workflow.
Explanation
Hashing complete messages protects the original text, but it does not preserve redacted prompt and response evidence that reviewers can inspect during an audit. Prompt instructions can guide model behavior, but they are not a centrally managed policy enforcement layer comparable to Bedrock Guardrails.
Correct answer
Add Lambda pre and post processors that redact sensitive tokens, apply an Amazon Bedrock guardrail during invocation, write redacted interaction records to CloudWatch Logs and S3, and route violation events through EventBridge to a Step Functions compliance workflow.
Explanation
This approach combines custom token-level redaction with managed Bedrock safety controls for both prompts and responses. Storing only redacted prompt and response evidence supports audits while EventBridge and Step Functions provide an automated review path for suspected violations.
Add Amazon Macie jobs that classify the audit bucket, apply an Amazon Bedrock guardrail during invocation, write raw interaction records to CloudWatch Logs and S3, and route Macie findings through EventBridge to a Step Functions compliance workflow.
Explanation
Macie can discover sensitive data in S3, but this design stores raw interaction records before detection occurs. That fails the requirement to avoid retaining raw PII and does not provide inline token-level redaction before logging.
Overall explanation
The strongest design separates two safety concerns that are easy to confuse: token-level redaction and policy enforcement. Lambda pre and post processors can remove or mask sensitive tokens before content is logged and after the model responds, using deterministic patterns or services such as Amazon Comprehend for PII detection. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then provide managed controls for denied topics, content filters, word filters, sensitive information filters, and contextual grounding checks that can be applied to prompts and responses.

For audit readiness, the system should retain evidence that is useful but not unnecessarily sensitive. Redacted prompt and response records in CloudWatch Logs and S3 can support investigations and regression analysis without preserving raw PII. EventBridge and Step Functions are a good fit for routing violations into a human compliance workflow because they decouple detection from review and make the remediation path explicit and repeatable.

API Gateway validation, prompt instructions, inference parameter tuning, and Macie scans can all be useful in a broader governance program, but they do not satisfy the full set of requirements here. API validation checks schema rather than content safety, prompt instructions are not a managed enforcement boundary, and Macie is primarily a data discovery control after data is stored. CloudTrail can complement this design by recording Bedrock API activity for audit trails, but it is not a substitute for redacted application-level prompt and response logging.

Relevant documentation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, Detecting PII entities with Amazon Comprehend, What is Amazon CloudWatch Logs?, What is Amazon EventBridge?, and Logging Amazon Bedrock API calls with AWS CloudTrail.

Question 9
