A regional credit union's digital banking team is deploying an Amazon Bedrock assistant that answers member questions. The assistant must block harmful user prompts and harmful model responses, refuse a small set of prohibited financial advice themes, block several hundred exact one-to-three word internal campaign codes, and mask PII in text responses. The same safety policy must also be used to review prewritten notification text from a rules engine before the text is sent, without invoking a foundation model. Which design will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom moderation logic?

Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters and custom word filters. Log model inputs and outputs to CloudWatch Logs and mask PII in a downstream review workflow.
Explanation
Incorrect. This approach does not use sensitive information filters to mask PII before text is returned, and logging is not a preventive control. It also does not provide independent pre-send guardrail evaluation for text that did not come from model inference.
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters, custom word filters, and sensitive information filters. Invoke the model for rules-engine text with a moderation prompt before sending notifications.
Explanation
Incorrect. This approach omits denied topics, which are needed for the prohibited financial advice themes. It also invokes a foundation model for rules-engine text even though ApplyGuardrail can evaluate text independently without model inference.
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters, denied topics for campaign codes, and sensitive information filters. Specify the guardrail during model inference and call ApplyGuardrail for rules-engine text.
Explanation
Incorrect. Denied topics are intended for contextual topics or themes, not exact words, phrases, or entity matching. The campaign codes are exact one-to-three word phrases, so custom word filters are the appropriate guardrail component.
Correct answer
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters, denied topics, custom word filters, and sensitive information filters. Specify the guardrail during model inference and call ApplyGuardrail for rules-engine text.
Explanation
Correct. Bedrock guardrails can evaluate both user inputs and model responses by using a guardrail ID and version during inference, and ApplyGuardrail can evaluate text without invoking a foundation model. Content filters, denied topics, word filters, and sensitive information filters align with the harmful content, theme refusal, exact phrase blocking, and PII masking requirements.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are designed as configurable safeguards that can be applied to user inputs and model responses during inference, or applied independently to text by using ApplyGuardrail. This makes them a good fit when the same policy must protect live model interactions and non-model text, such as notification copy generated by a rules engine. See Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and Use the ApplyGuardrail API.

The important design choice is to map each safety requirement to the correct guardrail component. Content filters address predefined harmful-content categories, including hate, insults, sexual content, violence, misconduct, and prompt attacks. Denied topics are for broader contextual themes, while word filters are for exact words or phrases, and sensitive information filters can block or mask detected PII in text outputs.

A common anti-pattern is trying to use denied topics as a general exact-match list for words, entities, or codes. AWS explicitly distinguishes denied topics from word filters and sensitive information filters, so using the wrong component can leave gaps or make the policy harder to manage. The relevant component behavior is documented in Guardrail components, Denied topics, Word filters, and Sensitive information filters.

Guardrails reduce custom moderation logic, but they are not a reason to ignore boundaries. Sensitive information filtering is probabilistic and context dependent, applies to text output, and does not cover every possible place sensitive values could appear, such as some trace or logging contexts if invocation logging is enabled. Engineers should pair guardrails with logging controls, least-privilege access, and careful review of what operational data is retained.

Question 10

An energy trading desk runs several Amazon Bedrock based assistants that use both streaming and nonstreaming runtime APIs. Product owners need a managed reporting view that compares model usage, latency, token consumption, throttling, and errors by model, and includes cost attribution through supported stakeholder dimensions. The operations team also needs detailed request and response records for troubleshooting selected incidents. The reporting design must minimize custom metric ingestion and must keep detailed log destinations within each workload account and Region. Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Use CloudWatch generative AI observability for Bedrock model invocation dashboards, and enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs or S3 in each account and Region.
Explanation
This uses the managed Model Invocations dashboard for Bedrock inference metrics such as invocations, tokens, latency, errors, and throttles. Enabling model invocation logging provides request, response, and metadata visibility within documented destination limits, with CloudWatch Logs or S3 as supported same-account, same-Region destinations.
Create CloudWatch dashboards from the AWS/Bedrock Invocations metric, and use that metric as the denominator for all errors, throttles, and latency percentiles.
Explanation
The Invocations metric counts only successful requests, so it is not a complete denominator for total request attempts. Throttles and other invocation errors are tracked separately, and treating successful invocations as total traffic can understate reliability issues.
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to S3 buckets in each account and Region, and build custom cross-account model comparison dashboards from those logs.
Explanation
This keeps the invocation log destinations within each workload account and Region, so it can satisfy the detailed logging constraint. However, using invocation logs as the primary source for comparison dashboards requires custom aggregation and reporting work instead of using the managed CloudWatch generative AI observability view.
Create CloudWatch dashboards from EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage, and use that metric as the primary source for quota planning and throttling risk reports.
Explanation
EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage is documented as an approximation and is not intended to be the sole indicator for quota use or capacity planning. It does not reflect reservation-based token consumption that is used for throttling decisions.
Overall explanation
CloudWatch generative AI observability provides a managed Model Invocations dashboard for Amazon Bedrock inference, which is well suited for stakeholder reporting because it already aggregates operational indicators such as invocation volume, token usage, latency percentiles, error rates, and throttling events. It also supports cost attribution through documented stakeholder dimensions such as application, user role, or specific user, so the reporting design should avoid claiming billed cost attribution specifically by model when the requirement is model-oriented operational comparison. See Monitor generative AI applications with Amazon CloudWatch.

For incident investigation, aggregate metrics are not enough. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging can capture request data, response data, and metadata for supported model invocation calls, but it is disabled by default. The supported destinations are CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3, and the destination resources must be in the same account and Region as the Bedrock workload. CloudWatch Logs has documented size and content considerations for captured input and output bodies, so S3 is the appropriate supported destination when larger JSON bodies or binary payload handling is required. See Monitor model invocation using invocation logging.

When interpreting Bedrock runtime metrics, reporting systems need to preserve the metric semantics. Invocations counts successful requests to the documented runtime APIs, while throttled requests are represented by InvocationThrottles and errors are tracked separately. Likewise, InvocationLatency measures the time until the last token is received, while TimeToFirstToken applies only to streaming APIs, so dashboards should not present these metrics as interchangeable. See Monitor runtime metrics for Amazon Bedrock.

Question 11
Skipped
A national museum consortium is building a semantic search capability for digitized exhibit descriptions, curator notes, and acquisition records by using Amazon Bedrock embeddings. The records are stored in Amazon S3 and are ingested by an existing AWS Lambda based pipeline before being written to a vector database. The vector database schema is configured for normalized floating-point vectors and section-level metadata. A pilot evaluation showed that 256-dimensional vectors did not meet the recall target for domain-specific terminology, but 512-dimensional vectors met the target while reducing storage compared with 1,024-dimensional vectors. Some source records are long, but each logical section is below the Titan Text Embeddings V2 input limit. Which ingestion configuration will meet these requirements with the LEAST unnecessary vector storage?

Configure the ingestion Lambda function to submit each complete record, call amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 with inputText and dimensions 1024, and store normalized float vectors with document metadata in the vector database.
Explanation
This configuration uses a valid model and vector type, but it keeps the default 1,024-dimensional output and therefore does not minimize vector storage. Submitting complete records also weakens section-level retrieval because the embedding represents broader document content rather than the logical sections used for citations.
Correct answer
Configure the ingestion Lambda function to split records into logical sections, call amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 with inputText and dimensions 512, and store normalized float vectors with section metadata in the vector database.
Explanation
This configuration uses the documented Titan Text Embeddings V2 model ID and selects the smallest dimensionality that the pilot showed meets the recall target. Splitting records into logical sections supports retrieval at the required section level, and storing float vectors matches the existing vector database schema.
Configure the ingestion Lambda function to split records into logical sections, call amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 with inputText, maxTokenCount, and topP, and store returned float vectors with section metadata in the vector database.
Explanation
This configuration uses a good chunking approach, but it applies text-generation inference parameters to an embedding model. Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports embedding-specific request fields such as inputText, normalize, dimensions, and embeddingTypes, not maxTokenCount or topP.
Configure the ingestion Lambda function to split records into logical sections, call amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 with inputText and embeddingTypes ["binary"], and store the legacy embedding field with section metadata in the vector database.
Explanation
This configuration does not match the existing floating-point vector schema because it requests only binary embeddings. In addition, when Titan Text Embeddings V2 is requested with only binary embedding output, the legacy embedding field is not included in the response.
Overall explanation
Titan Text Embeddings V2 is used to convert text into vector representations that a separate vector database can index and search. The documented model ID is amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0, and its output dimensionality can be configured as 1024, 512, or 256. In this scenario, the pilot result makes 512 the best tradeoff because it is the smallest size that met the recall target, which reduces storage compared with the default 1,024-dimensional vectors.

For retrieval use cases, AWS recommends segmenting documents into logical chunks such as paragraphs or sections even when the model can accept a long input. Chunking aligns the embedding with the retrievable unit, which helps the vector database return focused context and preserve section-level metadata for citations or filtering.

Embedding models do not perform similarity search by themselves. They return vectors, while the vector database performs indexing, similarity computation, filtering, and retrieval. The request should use embedding parameters such as inputText and dimensions, not text-generation parameters such as topP or maxTokenCount.

For more detail, see Amazon Titan Text Embeddings models and Amazon Titan Text Embeddings model parameters.

A lightweight router in the API layer, such as an AWS Lambda function, can classify requests by length, retrieved context count, confidence score, user intent, or other application signals, then call a smaller Amazon Bedrock model for simple cases and escalate to a larger model only when needed. This pattern is often called model cascading or dynamic routing. It trades a small amount of routing logic for lower average cost and latency, while preserving quality for…

Question 12
Skipped
A university library's digital collections team runs a public Q&A and summarization API on Amazon Bedrock. The application retrieves source passages from a knowledge base, then invokes the same high-capability FM for every request through an existing serverless API layer. Request profiling shows that most traffic consists of simple bibliographic lookups and short passage summaries, while a smaller portion requires multi-step reasoning across several retrieved sources. The team must reduce inference cost and median latency, preserve response quality for the complex requests, and avoid managing model hosting infrastructure. Which approach will BEST meet these requirements?

Purchase provisioned throughput for the current Bedrock FM and route all requests to the provisioned model ARN through the existing API layer.
Explanation
Incorrect. Provisioned throughput can provide predictable capacity for a specific model, but it does not change the fact that every request uses the largest model. This can help throughput consistency, but it does not directly reduce per-request model cost for routine work.
Enable Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the shared system prompt and continue routing every request to the current high-capability FM.
Explanation
Incorrect. Prompt caching can reduce latency and token processing cost when supported models reuse a stable prompt prefix. It does not address the main inefficiency of using a high-capability model for simple requests that a smaller model can handle.
Deploy the two FMs to a SageMaker multi-model endpoint and route requests through Lambda based on the same complexity criteria.
Explanation
Incorrect. A multi-model endpoint can consolidate hosting for multiple models, but it introduces model hosting, endpoint scaling, and container operational concerns. The scenario requires avoiding managed infrastructure responsibilities while continuing to use managed FM inference.
Correct answer
Implement a Lambda-based complexity router that invokes a smaller Bedrock FM for routine requests and invokes the larger FM only for low-confidence or complex requests.
Explanation
Correct. A routing layer can match model capability to request complexity, which reduces cost and latency for routine requests while retaining the larger model for cases that need deeper reasoning. Using Amazon Bedrock models keeps inference managed and avoids operating custom hosting infrastructure.
Overall explanation
The useful mental model is to separate request complexity from model capability. If most requests are routine, using the most capable model for every call is an expensive default. A lightweight router in the API layer, such as an AWS Lambda function, can classify requests by length, retrieved context count, confidence score, user intent, or other application signals, then call a smaller Amazon Bedrock model for simple cases and escalate to a larger model only when needed.

This pattern is often called model cascading or dynamic routing. It trades a small amount of routing logic for lower average cost and latency, while preserving quality for difficult requests. Amazon Bedrock remains the managed inference plane, so the team does not need to package models, operate endpoints, or tune instance scaling. See the Amazon Bedrock runtime API operations in Amazon Bedrock API Reference and the AWS Lambda service model in What is AWS Lambda?.

Provisioned throughput is useful when an application needs predictable throughput for a chosen Bedrock model, but it is associated with model capacity rather than request-level capability selection. Prompt caching can help when requests share a stable prefix, but it still sends all requests to the same large model. SageMaker multi-model endpoints are valid for some custom hosting scenarios, but they add endpoint and container management responsibilities that are unnecessary when managed Bedrock models satisfy the workload.

A live sports analytics platform uses Amazon Bedrock through the standard bedrock-runtime endpoint to generate real-time game summaries. The application uses both Converse and ConverseStream. Some audit samples include JSON prompt and response bodies that can exceed 100 KB. The platform team must monitor token usage, invocation latency, streaming responsiveness, and token burst anomalies without relying on static thresholds. The team also must retain detailed invocation records for supported model calls in the same account and Region. Which monitoring design will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Track runtime metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace, create CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms on token metrics or metric math, and enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 with optional CloudWatch Logs.
Explanation
This approach uses the documented CloudWatch namespace and runtime metrics for standard bedrock-runtime operations. Amazon S3 is required for large JSON bodies or binary payloads, while CloudWatch anomaly detection can identify unusual token patterns without fixed thresholds.
Track runtime metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace, create CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms primarily from EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage, and enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 with optional CloudWatch Logs.
Explanation
The namespace and logging destination can be appropriate, and CloudWatch anomaly detection avoids a fixed threshold. However, EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage is an approximation that should not be used as the primary signal for quota use or capacity planning, so token metrics or metric math are better suited for token burst monitoring.
Track runtime metrics in the AWS/BedrockMantle namespace, create CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms on TotalInputTokens, and enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 with optional CloudWatch Logs.
Explanation
The AWS/BedrockMantle namespace applies to OpenAI-compatible traffic through the bedrock-mantle endpoint, not standard bedrock-runtime Converse and ConverseStream calls. Bedrock-mantle also does not publish equivalents for InvocationLatency and TimeToFirstToken, which are required in the scenario.
Track runtime metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace, create CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms on token metrics, and enable model invocation logging only to CloudWatch Logs for all prompt and response bodies.
Explanation
The runtime metrics and anomaly detection parts are aligned with the requirements, but CloudWatch Logs alone is insufficient for large invocation payloads. Bedrock model invocation logging stores JSON bodies larger than 100 KB as separate S3 objects, so S3 must be configured when large prompt or response bodies must be retained.
Overall explanation
For standard Amazon Bedrock runtime calls such as Converse, ConverseStream, InvokeModel, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream, runtime metrics are published in the AWS/Bedrock CloudWatch namespace. Useful metrics for this scenario include InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, InvocationLatency, and TimeToFirstToken, with TimeToFirstToken applying to streaming operations. See Monitor Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics.

CloudWatch anomaly detection is a good fit for token burst detection because it builds an expected-value band from historical metric behavior instead of requiring a fixed static threshold. It can also be applied to metric math expressions, which lets teams monitor derived indicators such as combined input and output token patterns. See Using CloudWatch anomaly detection.

Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging is disabled by default and must be configured for each account and Region where supported runtime calls are made. Logs can be delivered to Amazon S3 and CloudWatch Logs, but large JSON bodies greater than 100 KB and binary data are stored in S3, so CloudWatch Logs alone does not satisfy a large-payload audit requirement. See Log Amazon Bedrock model invocation information.

It is also important not to confuse metric families. The AWS/BedrockMantle namespace is for OpenAI-compatible Bedrock traffic through the bedrock-mantle endpoint, not for the standard bedrock-runtime endpoint used by Converse and ConverseStream. AWS also documents EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage as an approximation, not an authoritative basis for quota or capacity planning, because Bedrock token quota accounting uses reservation and burndown behavior rather than simply adding input and output tokens. See Monitor OpenAI-compatible metrics and Runtime quotas and token burndown.

Which implementation will best meet these requirements?

Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are designed to apply safety policies to generative AI inputs and outputs, including content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information controls, and prompt attack protections. The ApplyGuardrail API can evaluate application text independently of a foundation model invocation, which makes it suitable for a preflight moderation gate when the raw prompt should be rejected before inference starts. See Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and Use the ApplyGuardrail API with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

A synchronous AWS Lambda step in front of the model is a practical place to combine managed safety evaluation with organization-specific controls, such as prohibited phrase lists stored in DynamoDB. Lambda can return deterministic rejection messages immediately and can record only safe audit fields, such as tenant ID, decision, policy version, timestamp, and a request hash. For the Lambda execution model, see What is AWS Lambda?.

The other approaches are close but miss important constraints. Putting the check inside an agent action group starts orchestration before the custom policy gate runs. Using another FM as the first classifier still exposes the unsafe prompt to a model. WAF and API Gateway validators are valuable perimeter controls, but they are not substitutes for semantic foundation model safety controls.

Use the supported EU Geographic Cross-Region system-defined inference profile, or create an application inference profile from it, invoke the profile as the model identifier, and allow all destination Regions in the profile through SCPs.
Explanation
Correct. Geographic Cross-Region Inference can route requests to supported Regions within a defined geography, such as the EU, and is designed to use compute across Regions for bursts. Applications invoke Cross-Region Inference by specifying the inference profile as the model identifier, and SCPs must allow all destination Regions in that profile.
Configure custom application routing to invoke the same model directly in multiple supported EU Regions, update the signing and endpoint logic, and allow those EU Regions through SCPs.
Explanation
Incorrect. Multi-Region direct invocation can be a valid resilience pattern when the application manages routing, retries, and regional endpoint behavior. However, it requires more application changes and operational logic than using the Bedrock-managed Cross-Region Inference profile that the model already supports.
Invoke the model directly in the current EU Region, add Step Functions retry handling, and return a queued status when regional invocation continues to fail.
Explanation
Incorrect. Retries and graceful degradation can improve resilience for transient failures, but they do not add access to compute in other Regions during a regional disruption or burst. The application would still depend on direct invocation in the same Region.
Use a Global Cross-Region system-defined inference profile, or create an application inference profile from it, invoke the profile as the model identifier, and allow aws:RequestedRegion unspecified through SCPs.
Explanation
Incorrect. Global Cross-Region Inference can use supported commercial AWS Regions worldwide, which does not satisfy a requirement to keep processing within the EU geography. The SCP handling described is relevant to global profiles, but the routing boundary is too broad for this scenario.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region Inference is the managed Bedrock mechanism for routing model requests across multiple AWS Regions by using an inference profile. The application does not call a separate regional endpoint directly for each destination Region. Instead, it specifies the inference profile as the modelId or model identifier for supported Bedrock runtime operations, and Bedrock can route the request to an eligible destination Region.

For a workload that must remain in the EU, a Geographic Cross-Region Inference profile is the right boundary because it keeps processing within a geography such as US, EU, or APAC. AWS provides system-defined inference profiles, and an application can use a supported system-defined profile directly or use an application inference profile that is created from it. A global profile is useful when worldwide supported commercial Regions are acceptable, but it is not appropriate when the stated compliance boundary is the EU geography.

SCPs are an important operational detail. For geographic profiles, AWS documents that the organization must allow all destination Regions in the inference profile. For global profiles, AWS documents a different SCP requirement involving aws:RequestedRegion with the value unspecified, which is why applying the global profile pattern would not meet the EU-only processing requirement.

Custom routing across multiple EU Regions can improve resilience, but it shifts routing, endpoint selection, retry behavior, and operational ownership into the application. Step Functions retries and queued fallback responses remain useful graceful degradation patterns, but by themselves they do not expand Bedrock model processing capacity across Regions. See Increase throughput with cross-Region inference.

Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom orchestration?

Correct answer

This uses the managed RAG operation that combines retrieval with model invocation, so the application can receive a generated response with citations. The query transformation configuration with QUERY_DECOMPOSITION is the documented way to split a complex prompt into smaller sub-queries for RetrieveAndGenerate.

Explanation

Configure AgenticRetrieveStream with generateResponse enabled, and point it at the existing custom vector-search knowledge base to return the final deduplicated result.
Explanation
AgenticRetrieveStream can plan, retrieve iteratively, evaluate sufficiency, and return deduplicated results with trace events. However, it currently requires a fully managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, so it does not preserve the existing custom vector-search knowledge base.
Configure Retrieve with a higher vectorSearchConfiguration.numberOfResults, and pass the returned chunks to InvokeModel for answer generation.
Explanation

Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides different query-time operations with different responsibilities. Retrieve returns relevant source chunks or images, while RetrieveAndGenerate runs the managed RAG pipeline by combining retrieval with model invocation and returning a generated response with citations. For a scenario that needs a generated answer and citations, RetrieveAndGenerate is the better fit than stitching together Retrieve and InvokeModel yourself. See the AWS overview of Knowledge Bases retrieval operations at Retrieve data and generate AI responses with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

For complex, multipart prompts, Amazon Bedrock documents query decomposition as an orchestration-time query transformation for RetrieveAndGenerate. The configuration uses orchestrationConfiguration.queryTransformationConfiguration with type set to QUERY_DECOMPOSITION, which lets the service split a complex prompt into smaller sub-queries and retrieve from multiple sources. Retrieval breadth can be tuned with KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration.numberOfResults, which controls how many source chunks are retrieved and has a documented range of 1 through 100. The relevant configuration details are in Configure and customize queries and response generation and KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration.

AgenticRetrieveStream is a powerful alternative for agentic retrieval, including planning, iterative retrieval, sufficiency evaluation, trace events, and optional response generation. The key constraint is that AWS currently documents it as requiring a fully managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, so it is not the least-disruptive choice when the existing design uses a custom vector-search knowledge base. Step Functions and Lambda can build a custom decomposition pipeline, including Lambda-based rewriting and service API calls, but that trades away the managed Knowledge Bases query transformation; Step Functions optimized Bedrock integrations are documented for InvokeModel and CreateModelCustomizationJob, not Knowledge Bases RetrieveAndGenerate. These tradeoffs are described in Agentic retrieval in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Call Amazon Bedrock with Step Functions, and Invoke AWS Lambda with Step Functions.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 18
Skipped
A construction materials laboratory's standards team is building a RAG assistant by using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for text-only testing standards stored in Amazon S3. Analysts ask narrowly scoped questions about test procedures, but the answer often needs definitions and exceptions that appear elsewhere in the same section. The team is creating the data source now, wants Bedrock-managed ingestion, wants precise matching on short passages, and wants the response context to include surrounding section material without maintaining custom preprocessing code. Which document segmentation approach should the team implement?

Configure the data source with FIXED_SIZE chunking, using 300-token chunks and configured overlap to include nearby text.
Explanation
Fixed-size chunking with overlap can be useful for predictable and simple segmentation. It is less suitable here because arbitrary token windows can still separate a procedure from definitions or exceptions that are several paragraphs away.
Correct answer
Configure the data source with HIERARCHICAL chunking, using smaller child chunks for matching and larger parent chunks for returned context.
Explanation
This is correct because hierarchical chunking is designed for cases where retrieval should match fine-grained text while providing a larger surrounding chunk as context. The team is creating the data source now, which is important because the chunking strategy must be chosen when the data source is connected.
Configure the data source with NONE chunking, using each uploaded standard as a single chunk for broad contextual retrieval.
Explanation
No chunking treats each document or file as a single source chunk, which can provide broad context but reduces retrieval precision for narrowly scoped questions. AWS also recommends preprocessing or splitting files yourself when using no chunking, which conflicts with the goal of avoiding custom preprocessing.
Configure the data source with SEMANTIC chunking, using FM-based boundaries and returned semantic chunks as the only context.
Explanation
Semantic chunking can improve chunk boundaries by grouping text according to meaning instead of only token counts. However, it does not specifically provide the parent-child retrieval pattern needed to return broader section context after matching a short passage.
Overall explanation
In Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion, source content is split into chunks, the chunks are converted to embeddings, and those embeddings are written to a vector index while maintaining a mapping to the original document. For text data sources, the documented chunking strategies include FIXED_SIZE, NONE, HIERARCHICAL, and SEMANTIC, as described in the ChunkingConfiguration API reference.

The key design tradeoff is retrieval precision versus context completeness. Small chunks tend to match narrowly scoped questions well, but they can omit definitions, caveats, and exceptions that are nearby but not inside the same chunk. Hierarchical chunking addresses that pattern by allowing a smaller child chunk to drive the match while a larger parent chunk supplies broader context to the generation step.

Semantic chunking is a strong option when the main problem is poor boundaries from fixed token splitting, but it does not by itself create the same parent-child context expansion behavior. Fixed-size chunking is simpler and can use required settings such as maxTokens and overlapPercentage, but overlap is still a blunt instrument when related material may be several paragraphs away, as shown in the FixedSizeChunkingConfiguration API reference.

Because Amazon Bedrock requires the chunking strategy to be selected when the data source is connected, teams should decide this before ingestion rather than assuming they can tune it later. The customization workflow documents that the chunking configuration is set in vectorIngestionConfiguration.chunkingConfiguration during data source creation and that the strategy cannot be changed after connecting the data source, as explained in Customize ingestion for a data source. General chunking behavior and the implications of no chunking are covered in How content chunking works for knowledge bases.

Call the Amazon Bedrock runtime with a JSON object containing inputText, textGenerationConfig, concatenated chat history, and embedded instruction text.
Explanation
This resembles a model-specific text generation format rather than a general dialog request structure. It can be appropriate for certain text models, but it does not provide a portable role-based conversation format across supported chat models.

Explanation
This can work for Anthropic Claude models through model-specific invocation, but it preserves provider-specific request formatting. It does not best meet the requirement to reduce transformations while evaluating several supported chat models.

Correct answer
Call the Amazon Bedrock runtime with a messages array, role-based content blocks, a separate system instruction, and common inference parameters.
Explanation
This is correct because the Amazon Bedrock Converse API uses a consistent message structure for supported conversational models. It represents turns with roles and content blocks, allows system instructions separately, and reduces provider-specific request formatting.
Overall explanation
For dialog applications on Amazon Bedrock, the most portable request shape is the Converse API. It accepts a messages list that contains user and assistant turns, supports content blocks, and provides a separate place for system instructions and common inference settings. This gives the application a stable conversation abstraction instead of forcing each application path to know the exact JSON schema for each model provider.

The tradeoff is that InvokeModel remains useful when an application needs a model-specific capability or a provider-specific request body that is not exposed through the common interface. However, using provider payloads, legacy prompt delimiters, or text-generation-only structures makes the application responsible for translating conversations into each model's required schema. That is exactly the operational burden the scenario is trying to avoid.

See the Amazon Bedrock documentation for the Converse API and the API reference for Converse. For comparison, model-specific invocation uses InvokeModel, where the request body depends on the selected model.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 20
Skipped
A legal aid network's intake automation team is building an Amazon Bedrock application that evaluates client eligibility across multiple programs. Some eligibility checks are independent, but each evaluation can require several sequential tool calls, such as checking residency, income limits, and case deadlines. The next tool call must depend on the previous tool result. The team needs a bounded workflow that records each model decision and tool observation for audit review, retries transient tool failures, and minimizes custom orchestration code. Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Create an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that invokes the FM, evaluates structured action outputs with Choice states, calls Lambda tool functions, configures Retry policies, appends observations to state, and stops on a final answer or step limit.

Explanation
This approach implements a ReAct-style loop in a managed workflow while keeping each model decision and tool observation visible in execution history. Standard workflows support durable orchestration, retries, branching, and explicit termination conditions without requiring a custom state engine.
Create an Amazon Bedrock agent with Lambda action groups for each check, enable agent tracing, describe the tool parameters, and instruct the agent to produce a final JSON eligibility decision.
Explanation
Bedrock Agents can invoke Lambda action groups and provide traces that show orchestration steps, which makes this a close alternative for agentic tool use. However, this option relies more on agent orchestration and prompt instructions than on a deterministic bounded workflow with explicit Step Functions retries and stop conditions.
Create an AWS Step Functions Express workflow that invokes the FM, evaluates structured action outputs with Choice states, calls Lambda tool functions, configures Retry policies, and writes observations to CloudWatch Logs.
Explanation
Express workflows support branching, service integrations, retries, and logging, so this is a plausible orchestration design for high-volume short workflows. However, Standard workflows are better aligned to audit review because they maintain durable execution history for individual workflow executions.
Create an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that groups eligibility checks in a Parallel state, invokes Lambda tool functions for each branch, aggregates outputs, and calls the FM once to produce the final decision.
Explanation
A Parallel state is useful for checks that are truly independent, and Standard workflows provide strong orchestration and audit capabilities. However, this design does not satisfy cases where the next tool call must be selected from the previous tool observation in an iterative loop.
Overall explanation
For structured problem solving that resembles ReAct, the application needs an explicit loop: ask the FM what action to take, validate that action, call the tool, feed the observation back into the next FM call, and repeat until the model emits a final answer or the workflow reaches a guard condition. AWS Step Functions Standard workflows are a strong fit because they provide managed state, branching with Choice states, retries with Retry, failure handling with Catch, and execution history that can be reviewed later.

The important design choice is to keep the control flow outside the model. The FM can decide the next action in a structured response, but Step Functions should enforce the step counter, validate the action shape, route to the correct Lambda tool, and stop the loop. This creates a practical boundary between probabilistic reasoning and deterministic orchestration.

A Parallel state is appropriate when checks are independent, but it is not sufficient for a dependency chain where later actions are chosen from earlier observations. Express workflows can use many of the same state types and integrations, and they can emit logs to CloudWatch Logs, but Standard workflows are the better fit when durable per-execution history is a central audit requirement. Bedrock Agents are useful for tool use with action groups and tracing, but they do not replace explicit workflow-level controls when the application must enforce bounded iteration and deterministic retry behavior.

For more information, see What is AWS Step Functions?, Standard vs. Express Workflows, Parallel workflow state, and How Amazon Bedrock Agents work.

An industrial robotics vendor's field-service AI team uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for a troubleshooting assistant. The team configured a custom knowledge base backed by Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. The vector store has embeddings, a filterable raw-text field, and metadata for product line and firmware major version. Service tickets contain exact fault codes plus natural-language symptoms. The current retrieval step often returns semantically similar content from the wrong firmware line and sometimes misses chunks that contain the exact fault code. The application must select context chunks quickly before a separate model invocation. Which approach will best improve retrieval relevance while meeting these constraints?

Call RetrieveAndGenerate with vectorSearchConfiguration, set overrideSearchType to HYBRID, enable textual reranking, and return the cited source chunks from the generated response.
Explanation
Incorrect. RetrieveAndGenerate performs retrieval and then invokes a model to generate an answer with citations. The application needs to select context chunks quickly before a separate model invocation, so adding generation at this stage does not meet the workflow constraint.
Correct answer
Call Retrieve with vectorSearchConfiguration, set overrideSearchType to HYBRID, tune numberOfResults, and apply one andAll RetrievalFilter for product line and firmware metadata.
Explanation
Correct. The knowledge base is custom, so vectorSearchConfiguration is the correct retrieval configuration field. Hybrid search can combine vector similarity with raw-text matching for exact fault codes, and a single andAll filter can constrain retrieval to the applicable metadata values.
Call Retrieve with vectorSearchConfiguration, set overrideSearchType to SEMANTIC, increase numberOfResults toward 100, and apply one orAll RetrievalFilter for product line and firmware metadata.
Explanation
Incorrect. SEMANTIC search uses vector embeddings only, so it does not address the missed exact fault-code matches as directly as hybrid search. Increasing the result count can add work and noise, and an orAll filter would broaden the metadata match instead of limiting results to the intended product and firmware combination.
Call Retrieve with managedSearchConfiguration, keep the default hybrid behavior and MANAGED reranking, tune numberOfResults, and filter by product line and firmware metadata.
Explanation
Incorrect. managedSearchConfiguration applies to fully managed knowledge bases, not custom knowledge bases. Although managed knowledge bases use hybrid search and managed reranking by default, using that configuration field does not match the stated knowledge base type.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases separate retrieval from generation. Retrieve returns relevant source chunks or images, while RetrieveAndGenerate retrieves and then invokes a model to produce an answer with citations, as described in Retrieve data and generate AI responses with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

For a custom knowledge base, retrieval tuning belongs under vectorSearchConfiguration. When the vector store supports it, overrideSearchType can be set to HYBRID so retrieval uses both embeddings and raw text, which is useful when a query contains a mix of exact identifiers and semantic descriptions. The documented hybrid-search support and numberOfResults range are covered in Configure and customize queries and response generation.

Metadata filtering is also important for speed and relevance because it reduces the candidate set before the selected chunks are used as model context. The filter object is a union, so a request should use one top-level filter member, such as andAll with child filters for product line and firmware version, rather than multiple top-level filters. The filter structure and supported operators are documented in RetrievalFilter.

Overall explanation
AWS Well-Architected Tool is designed to make architecture reviews consistent. It lets teams define workloads, answer lens questions, document decisions, capture notes, and receive improvement plans, which is different from provisioning infrastructure. The service is useful here because the airline needs repeatable assessment artifacts across deployment scenarios, not another CI/CD or infrastructure deployment mechanism. See AWS Well-Architected Tool introduction.

Lenses are the unit of standardization in AWS WA Tool. The official Generative AI lens is a Lens Catalog lens maintained by AWS and is intended for generative AI workload best practices, while a custom lens can capture organization-specific pillars, questions, best practices, and improvement plan links. This combination lets a platform team use AWS-maintained guidance and still enforce internal review criteria. See Lenses in AWS WA Tool, Lens Catalog, and Custom lenses.

Custom lens lifecycle details matter in a multi-account standardization program. A custom lens is defined in JSON, starts in DRAFT status, and must be published before it can be applied to workloads or shared with other AWS accounts. Major custom lens versions represent substantial changes and are not automatically applied to workloads, while minor versions are automatically applied, so versioning should be planned intentionally. See Create a custom lens and Publish and update a custom lens.

Retrieve can return content, document identifiers, locations, metadata, and optional relevance scores, while JSON Schema validation can enforce the required response contract before the application returns the answer.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases should be treated as a retrieval mechanism for grounding, not as a built-in truth oracle. The application can use Retrieve to obtain source evidence, then perform its own claim-to-evidence comparison, semantic similarity check, or reviewer workflow before returning the answer. The documented response can include retrieval content, document identifiers, locations, metadata, and an optional relevance score, which is useful as an evidence-ranking signal but should not be misrepresented as factual certainty. See Retrieve API reference and Retrieve data and generate responses from a knowledge base.

The managed knowledge base detail matters because RetrieveAndGenerate has a documented limitation for managed knowledge bases, where the API reference says to use AgenticRetrieveStream or Retrieve instead. Citations from RetrieveAndGenerate are also not the same as retrieval scores, because citation objects contain generated response spans and retrieved references, while the documented relevance score is part of KnowledgeBaseRetrievalResult returned by Retrieve. The search configuration is another subtle boundary: fully managed knowledge bases use managed search configuration and always use hybrid search, while semantic versus hybrid override applies to eligible custom or vector knowledge bases. Question 24
Skipped
An online grocery chain's store operations platform team is adding an FM agent that can check inventory substitutions. The existing tool logic is a stateless AWS Lambda function that validates SKU and store IDs, then calls internal APIs. The function currently receives API Gateway JSON, dispatches by an unprefixed tool name, and returns a JSON object. The team wants MCP-compatible tool access through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, minimal infrastructure, and no multi-turn tool state. Which implementation should the team choose?

Package the logic as an AgentCore Runtime MCP server. Run stateless streamable HTTP on 0.0.0.0:8000/mcp, proxy MCP RPC messages through InvokeAgentRuntime, and adapt the handler inside the container.
Explanation
AgentCore Runtime can run MCP server containers with stateless streamable HTTP, so this is a technically viable MCP deployment pattern. It still adds a containerized Runtime deployment and MCP server contract for a lightweight stateless Lambda use case that Gateway can expose directly.
Deploy a custom MCP server on Amazon ECS Fargate. Publish the image to Amazon ECR, place it behind an ALB and Cognito, and register the server as an MCP target in Gateway.
Explanation
An ECS Fargate architecture is a valid pattern for containerized custom MCP servers, especially for more complex tools. It adds more infrastructure than needed for a stateless Lambda function that can be exposed directly through a Gateway Lambda target.
Expose the function through an AgentCore Gateway HTTP target. Keep the API Gateway event contract, dispatch from the unprefixed tool name in the request body, and rely on direct forwarding for MCP discovery.
Explanation
HTTP targets are direct forwarding targets and are not the same as Lambda targets that define tools through a ToolDefinition. Keeping the existing API Gateway event contract also ignores the documented Gateway Lambda event and context schema.
Correct answer
Add the function as an AgentCore Gateway Lambda target. Provide a ToolDefinition, update the handler for Gateway event properties, handle the prefixed tool name from context, and return valid JSON.
Explanation
This approach uses the documented Gateway Lambda target path for exposing custom code as an MCP-compatible tool. The handler must adapt to the Gateway event and context shape, including the prefixed tool name format, and must return JSON the gateway can parse.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is the integration layer that can turn Lambda functions, APIs, and existing services into MCP-compatible tools for agents. For a lightweight stateless tool that already exists as Lambda code, the lowest-overhead design is to add the function as a Gateway Lambda target and define the tool contract with a ToolDefinition, including the required name, description, and inputSchema.

The important implementation detail is that Gateway does not pass an arbitrary MCP JSON-RPC envelope to the Lambda handler. The Lambda receives an event object whose properties come from the tool input schema, while metadata such as bedrockAgentCoreToolName is in the Lambda context, and documented tool names use a target-name prefix. See Add Lambda function targets to a gateway.

HTTP targets and Runtime targets are useful in other integration patterns, but they are forwarding patterns rather than the best fit for directly adapting existing stateless Lambda tool code. The Gateway target behavior is described in Supported targets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, and Runtime MCP server deployment has its own container contract, documented in Host MCP servers with AgentCore Runtime. ECS Fargate is appropriate when the tool needs a full custom MCP server with more operational controls, but it does not minimize infrastructure for this Lambda-based requirement.

**Quick lesson:** For content handling issues, the first step is to distinguish input budget problems from generation quality problems. Amazon Bedrock CountTokens is designed for this preflight diagnostic: it estimates the input tokens that the same request would use for inference, and tokenization is model-specific. That makes it a better control point than character counts, byte counts, or a locally guessed tokenizer. See the Amazon Bedrock Runtime API reference for CountTokens. After measuring the real input size, the application still needs a strategy for deciding what content earns space in the prompt. Fixed-order truncation is a common anti-pattern…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 25
Skipped
A national insurance carrier's claims automation team uses Amazon Bedrock to evaluate complex claim files. Each request includes system instructions, retrieved policy clauses, claim notes, adjuster comments, and the user's question. For large claims, reviewers find that the model sometimes ignores important notes that appear late in the assembled prompt. The current implementation estimates input size by character count and removes the oldest retrieved chunks when the estimate exceeds an internal threshold. The team must keep the same foundation model and reduce omissions caused by incomplete prompt processing. Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

Use a local tokenizer to estimate model input size, and continue dropping the oldest retrieved chunks when the local estimate crosses the threshold.
Explanation
Incorrect. Tokenization varies by model, so local estimates can diverge from what the Bedrock model will actually count. Continuing to drop chunks by age also fails to address whether the removed or retained content is necessary for the claim decision.
Correct selection
Replace fixed-order truncation with dynamic chunk selection that prioritizes semantically relevant claim notes and policy clauses within the measured token budget.
Explanation
Correct. Removing the oldest chunks is a brittle strategy because age does not indicate relevance to the current question. Dynamic chunking and selection can preserve the most useful context while staying within the token budget identified during preflight checks.
Enable prompt caching for the static instructions, and rely on the cache checkpoint to prevent retrieved claim notes from being omitted.
Explanation
Incorrect. Prompt caching can improve latency and cost for repeated static prompt prefixes, but it does not make an overlarge request fit the model context window. The application still needs to measure and manage the dynamic claim notes and retrieved policy context.
Increase the maxTokens setting for responses, and keep the current prompt assembly and retrieval truncation behavior unchanged.
Explanation
Incorrect. The maxTokens setting controls how much output the model can generate, not how much input context can be processed. If the problem is missing input content, increasing the response allowance does not make late prompt sections more likely to be considered.
Correct selection
Call Amazon Bedrock CountTokens with the same model request before inference, and use the result to reshape or reject prompts that exceed the available input budget.
Explanation
Correct. CountTokens estimates the input tokens for the same Amazon Bedrock request that would be used for inference, which is more reliable than character counting because tokenization is model-specific. Using the result before invocation helps the application decide whether to prune, summarize, or ask for a smaller input before important content is silently omitted.
Overall explanation
For content handling issues, the first step is to distinguish input budget problems from generation quality problems. Amazon Bedrock CountTokens is designed for this preflight diagnostic: it estimates the input tokens that the same request would use for inference, and tokenization is model-specific. That makes it a better control point than character counts, byte counts, or a locally guessed tokenizer. See the Amazon Bedrock Runtime API reference for CountTokens.

After measuring the real input size, the application still needs a strategy for deciding what content earns space in the prompt. Fixed-order truncation is a common anti-pattern because it optimizes for prompt length without preserving evidence needed to answer the current question. A better approach is to assemble context dynamically, using relevance, metadata, summarization, or chunking strategy changes so the highest-value claim notes and policy clauses remain inside the measured budget. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports configurable chunking approaches for RAG data preparation, described in Chunking options for knowledge bases.

The distractors focus on adjacent features that are useful for other problems but do not resolve incomplete input processing. Increasing maxTokens helps only when the answer is being cut short. Prompt caching can reduce repeated prefix processing cost and latency, but it is not a context window expansion mechanism. Observability and retries are valuable, but the remediation for omitted prompt content is to measure the request accurately and make better context selection decisions before invoking the model.

Question 26
Skipped
An aerospace parts distributor's AI reliability team runs several Amazon Bedrock applications that use the Converse and InvokeModel APIs for supplier Q&A. After a prompt template change, users report occasional hallucinated part substitutions and inconsistent answers for the same golden test prompts. Which approach will meet these requirements?

Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket in a logging account, then run golden dataset comparisons against the captured records.
Explanation
Model invocation logging destinations must be in the same AWS account and Region as the invocations being logged. A centralized logging account might be useful for other audit pipelines, but it does not satisfy this feature's destination requirements.
Configure AWS CloudTrail data analysis for Amazon Bedrock API activity, then run golden dataset comparisons against the recorded invocation events.
Explanation
CloudTrail is useful for API auditing, but it is not the right primary source for capturing model request and response payloads for response diffing. The troubleshooting requirement needs the content of supported model invocations, not only an audit trail of API activity.
Correct answer
Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to Amazon S3 in the same account and Region, then run golden dataset comparisons against the captured request and response records.
Explanation
This approach captures request data, response data, and metadata for supported Amazon Bedrock runtime calls such as Converse and InvokeModel. Storing the records in the same account and Region satisfies the logging destination constraint and provides artifacts for hallucination detection and output diffing.
Route the application through the Amazon Bedrock Responses API, then enable model invocation logging to capture the generated responses for comparison.
Explanation
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging applies to supported calls through the bedrock-runtime endpoint, including Converse and InvokeModel. Calls through other endpoints, such as the Responses API on bedrock-mantle, are not captured by this logging feature.
Overall explanation
GenAI troubleshooting often needs observability artifacts that traditional ML monitoring does not provide. For hallucination analysis and response consistency testing, teams need to compare the actual prompt, retrieved or injected context, model response, and related metadata against a golden dataset or prior known-good outputs.

Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging is designed for this kind of operational investigation. It can capture request data, response data, and metadata for supported calls, and it can deliver those records to Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3. The destination must be in the same account and Region, and logging is disabled by default, so it must be explicitly configured. See Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.

The endpoint boundary matters. The feature logs calls through the bedrock-runtime endpoint for supported operations such as Converse, ConverseStream, InvokeModel, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream. A framework that depends on unsupported endpoints or relies only on API audit events will not provide the same prompt and response records needed for hallucination triage, output diffing, and prompt regression analysis.

The test harness can orchestrate managed Amazon Bedrock APIs, but the team wants to avoid building a custom retrieval or logging pipeline. Which implementation will best meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Call Retrieve for the Knowledge Base, pass returned chunks with source identifiers to Converse, enable model invocation logging to same-account, same-Region S3 or CloudWatch Logs, add cohort IDs in requestMetadata, and compare client-side latency with AWS/Bedrock token metrics.
Explanation
This uses the managed Knowledge Bases retrieval API for source chunks and a supported bedrock-runtime API for generation. Converse calls can be captured by model invocation logging, requestMetadata is the caller-supplied field for cohort tags, and AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics include token counts for supported runtime APIs.
Call RetrieveAndGenerate for the Knowledge Base, enable model invocation logging to same-account, same-Region S3 or CloudWatch Logs, add cohort IDs in requestMetadata, and compare AWS/Bedrock runtime token and latency metrics.
Explanation
RetrieveAndGenerate is the managed Knowledge Bases path for combining retrieval and generation with citations. However, the supplied documentation grounds model invocation logging, requestMetadata, and AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics in supported bedrock-runtime model invocation APIs, not as direct request-level logging controls for RetrieveAndGenerate.
Call Retrieve for the Knowledge Base, invoke a Prompt management prompt through InvokeModel, include chunks and cohort payloads in body, enable model invocation logging, and compare successful Invocations as all attempts.
Explanation
Retrieve can supply relevant source chunks, and InvokeModel is a supported runtime API for model invocation logging. However, when a Prompt management prompt is specified in modelId, the body should be omitted because it is ignored if included, and Invocations counts successful requests only rather than all attempts.
Call Retrieve for the Knowledge Base, pass returned chunks with source identifiers to ConverseStream, enable model invocation logging to same-account, same-Region S3 or CloudWatch Logs, add cohort IDs in requestMetadata, and use TimeToFirstToken as the end-to-end latency measure.
Explanation
Retrieve plus ConverseStream can be a valid managed retrieval and streaming generation design, and ConverseStream is a supported runtime API for invocation logging. The weakness is using TimeToFirstToken as the end-to-end latency measure, because it measures only first-token latency for streaming responses rather than latency through the last token.
Overall explanation
The cleanest POC design separates managed retrieval from a model invocation API path that is explicitly documented for logging and runtime metrics. Retrieve returns relevant source chunks or images from a Knowledge Base, while RetrieveAndGenerate is the managed API that combines retrieval with generation and citations. Because the POC also needs request-level prompt and response samples with cohort tagging, using Retrieve followed by Converse keeps the generation call on a documented bedrock-runtime API path. See Query a knowledge base and generate responses based off the retrieved data and Amazon Bedrock API choices.

Model invocation logging is disabled by default, and it can capture supported bedrock-runtime calls such as Converse, ConverseStream, InvokeModel, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream. Amazon Bedrock populates log-entry fields automatically except optional requestMetadata, which is the appropriate place to attach cohort identifiers. Supported log destinations are Amazon S3, CloudWatch Logs, or both, and the destination resources must be in the same account and Region. See Log Amazon Bedrock model invocation activity.

For measurements, Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics are published in the AWS/Bedrock namespace for supported runtime APIs and include metrics such as InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, InvocationLatency, throttles, and errors. InvocationLatency is measured until the last token is received, while TimeToFirstToken applies only to streaming APIs and is not a full response latency measure. For a two-call RAG harness, client-side timing can capture end-to-end elapsed time, while Bedrock metrics provide comparable model invocation and token-use data. See Monitor Amazon Bedrock with Amazon CloudWatch.

The tempting managed RetrieveAndGenerate design is strong for Knowledge Base citations, but the provided documentation does not support treating model invocation logging and requestMetadata as direct request-level logging controls for that API. The Prompt management distractor fails because when a prompt is supplied in modelId, the body field should be omitted. The streaming distractor uses a supported logging path, but it chooses the wrong latency metric for end-to-end POC comparison. The documented InvokeModel request and modelId behavior are covered in Run inference with Amazon Bedrock models.

Question 28
Skipped
A cross-border law firm's e-discovery platform team runs document search and redaction systems in an on-premises data center because case evidence cannot be replicated into AWS. The application is allowed to send selected prompt excerpts to Amazon Bedrock in an approved AWS Region for summarization. The data center already has private connectivity to a VPC in that Region. The team must invoke models without routing API traffic over the public internet and must minimize custom networking components. Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Deploy an HTTPS proxy in the connected VPC, configure on-premises DNS to resolve the Bedrock runtime hostname to the proxy, allow private client access to the proxy, and have the proxy call the regional runtime endpoint.
Explanation
Incorrect. This can centralize egress through a private path from the data center to the VPC, but it adds a custom networking component that the scenario asks to minimize. Unless the proxy also uses the Bedrock runtime interface endpoint, its outbound call still depends on the regular regional service endpoint path.
Advertise the connected VPC CIDR to the data center, forward on-premises DNS queries to Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint IPs, use IAM policies for required Runtime API actions, and keep the application calling the regional runtime hostname.
Explanation
Incorrect. Private connectivity to a VPC and IAM authorization do not, by themselves, create a private path to the Bedrock runtime service. Without the Bedrock runtime interface endpoint and appropriate private DNS resolution, the regional service hostname is not reached through PrivateLink.
Correct answer
Create an interface VPC endpoint for the Amazon Bedrock runtime service in the connected VPC, enable private DNS, forward on-premises DNS queries to Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint IPs, and apply an endpoint policy for required Runtime API actions.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock private access uses interface VPC endpoints that are powered by AWS PrivateLink, and Bedrock Runtime APIs such as InvokeModel or Converse can use the Bedrock runtime endpoint. Enabling private DNS and forwarding on-premises name resolution to Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint IP addresses lets SDK calls use private endpoint addresses without adding a custom proxy layer.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for the Amazon Bedrock control service in the connected VPC, enable private DNS, forward on-premises DNS queries to Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint IPs, and apply an endpoint policy for required Runtime API actions.
Explanation
Incorrect. The Bedrock control service endpoint is for management APIs, not Bedrock Runtime APIs such as InvokeModel or Converse. Private DNS and endpoint policies do not make a control-plane endpoint handle runtime invocations.
Overall explanation
For private Amazon Bedrock access from a VPC, use an interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink. The service selection matters for the intended call path: Bedrock Runtime APIs such as InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, Converse, and ConverseStream use the Bedrock runtime endpoint, while Bedrock management operations use a different endpoint service.

In a hybrid architecture, the on-premises environment can keep regulated evidence in place and send only approved prompt excerpts across existing private connectivity into the VPC. To make standard SDK calls resolve to private endpoint addresses from the data center, enable private DNS for the interface endpoint and forward the relevant on-premises DNS queries to Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint IP addresses, rather than forwarding directly to the VPC resolver address.

Private routing to the VPC is not sufficient without the required runtime interface endpoint, because AWS service hostnames do not automatically become PrivateLink targets. A proxy can be made to work, but it adds operational overhead and does not inherently provide PrivateLink-based access to Bedrock. See Use Amazon Bedrock with interface VPC endpoints.

A knowledge base can use an Amazon S3 data source, apply a supported embedding model, store embeddings in a supported vector store, and expose retrieval through Bedrock APIs such as Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate. The office must enforce a baseline set of content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters, and contextual grounding checks on Bedrock model inference calls for accounts in selected OUs. Application teams must not be required to update every inference request, but they may apply stricter safeguards for specific applications. The organization already uses CloudTrail for API audit events. Which governance implementation will meet these requirements?

Create one versioned Bedrock guardrail in the management account, add a guardrail resource-based policy for member accounts, and attach one AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policy across both Regions.
Explanation
Incorrect. Amazon Bedrock policy enforcement is Region-specific and requires separate guardrails for each Region where the controls must apply. A single guardrail and policy configuration cannot satisfy a two-Region enforcement requirement.
Create account-level Bedrock guardrail enforcements in member accounts with IaC, delegate version updates to application teams, and standardize the baseline safeguards across accounts.
Explanation
Incorrect. Account-level enforcement is a supported guardrail enforcement layer, and IaC can make rollout more consistent across member accounts. However, this does not provide centralized OU-scoped governance through AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policies, and delegating version updates to teams weakens consistent oversight across Regions.
Correct answer
Create versioned Bedrock guardrails in the management account in each required Region, add guardrail resource-based policies for member accounts, and attach AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policies to the target OUs.
Explanation
Correct. AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policies enforce safeguards from a guardrail in the management account across selected roots, OUs, or accounts for Bedrock model inference calls. Because enforcement is Region-specific and requires a specific guardrail version, separate versioned guardrails and appropriate resource-based policies are needed for each Region.
Create enforced Bedrock guardrails that include the automated reasoning policy, attach AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policies to the target OUs, and rely on application guardrails for unsupported calls.
Explanation
Incorrect. AWS explicitly states not to include the automated reasoning policy in an enforced guardrail because that safeguard is unsupported for guardrail enforcements and can cause runtime failures. Adding application guardrails does not make an unsupported organization-level enforcement configuration valid.
Overall explanation
AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policies are designed for exactly this kind of centralized runtime governance. They let an organization enforce safeguards from Amazon Bedrock Guardrails across a root, OU, or individual account for Amazon Bedrock model inference calls, without requiring every application team to pass a guardrail on every request. See Amazon Bedrock policies.

The important operational detail is that these policies reference a specific guardrail version created in the management account and are Region-specific. For a two-Region deployment, the governance team needs a versioned guardrail in each Region and must attach the appropriate organization policy to the intended OUs. Member accounts also need access to apply the centrally managed guardrail, which is why the guardrail resource-based policy and identity permission model matter. See Resource-based policies for guardrails.

Bedrock guardrail enforcement has multiple layers: organization-level enforcement, account-level enforcement, and application or request-specific guardrails. When more than one guardrail applies, the effective controls are the union of the guardrails, with the most restrictive overlapping controls taking precedence. This means the central baseline can coexist with stricter application guardrails, rather than forcing a lowest-common-denominator policy. See Guardrail enforcements.

Governance designs should also avoid unsupported safeguards in enforced guardrails. Current enforced guardrail safeguards include content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters, and contextual grounding checks, but AWS warns not to include the automated reasoning policy in an enforced guardrail. CloudTrail provides API audit events, but runtime blocking of model behavior requires guardrail enforcement rather than audit logging alone. See Logging Amazon Bedrock API calls with AWS CloudTrail.

Question 32
Skipped
A pharmaceutical safety surveillance group's GenAI team maintains an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG assistant over adverse-event procedures. After changing chunking rules and metadata filters, the team must validate whether retrieved context has improved before changing prompts or foundation models. The validation must isolate retrieval from answer generation, compare relevance and coverage across a fixed prompt dataset, and preserve enough per-result data to analyze ranking and latency. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Create a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock over the benchmark dataset and review Builtin.ContextRelevance and Builtin.ContextCoverage.
Explanation
A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job evaluates the retrieved data rather than the generated answer. ContextRelevance and ContextCoverage directly align with testing whether the retrieved passages are relevant to each question and whether they cover the needed context.
Increase numberOfResults beyond 100 for each query, collect the complete candidate set, and treat returned parent and child chunks as fixed-size ranking samples.
Explanation
numberOfResults has a documented valid range of 1 to 100, so values beyond that range are not a valid way to expand the candidate set. The actual number of returned results can also be lower than the requested maximum, including when hierarchical chunking replaces child chunks with parent chunks.
Correct selection
Invoke Retrieve for each benchmark prompt, configure numberOfResults within the supported range, and persist retrievalResults content, metadata, location, score, and elapsed request time.
Explanation
This isolates the retriever because Retrieve queries the knowledge base and returns source results without invoking a foundation model to generate an answer. The response includes a score field that can be used for ranking analysis, and the test harness can record elapsed request time for retrieval latency analysis.
Invoke RetrieveAndGenerate for each benchmark prompt, collect generated citations, and compare citation content as the raw retriever output for per-result ranking analysis.
Explanation
RetrieveAndGenerate combines retrieval with model invocation, so its output is affected by the generation step and is not an isolated retriever test. The citation references returned by RetrieveAndGenerate do not expose the same retrieval score field that Retrieve returns for ranking analysis.
Create a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job over the same dataset and use generated response quality as the primary retriever optimization signal.
Explanation
A retrieve-and-generate evaluation is useful for end-to-end RAG quality, but it evaluates both the retrieved data and the generated response. Using generated response quality as the primary signal would confound retriever behavior with prompt and model behavior.
Overall explanation
For retrieval quality testing, the most important design choice is separating the retriever from the generator. The Retrieve API is the right tool for this isolation because it queries an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and returns source results in retrievalResults without asking a model to synthesize an answer. AWS documents that those results include fields such as content, metadata, location, and score, which makes the response suitable for analyzing ranking behavior across a benchmark prompt set. See Retrieve data and generate AI responses with knowledge bases and Test knowledge base retrieval.

Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluations complement an API-level harness by providing managed evaluation jobs. A retrieve-only RAG evaluation focuses on the retrieved data, and the built-in metrics for that job type are Builtin.ContextRelevance and Builtin.ContextCoverage, which map directly to whether the retrieved context is relevant and sufficiently covers the question. RetrieveAndGenerate and retrieve-and-generate evaluations are valuable later for end-to-end RAG validation, but they include model generation, so they are not the best primary mechanism for isolating raw retrieval behavior. The retrieval configuration also matters: Bedrock returns up to five results by default, and numberOfResults is a maximum in the valid range of 1 to 100, not a guarantee of a fixed result count. See Evaluate RAG applications and Configure and customize queries and response generation.
