### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 27
Skipped
A maritime logistics provider's operations automation team runs a synchronous GenAI assistant behind Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The assistant answers container status questions, extracts a few fields from shipping emails, and drafts exception analyses for delayed shipments. API profiling shows that most requests are deterministic extraction or single-record lookup tasks after internal API calls, while a smaller set requires synthesis across shipment history, contracts, and customer-specific rules. The team must reduce inference cost and median latency without reducing quality for exception analyses. The routing decision must consider request type, internal API result confidence, and whether contract language is referenced. The team cannot fine-tune models or manage inference servers. Which deployment approach will BEST meet these requirements?

Enable prompt caching for shared instructions on the current larger Bedrock model and prune dynamic context for lookup tasks before invoking the same model.
Explanation
Incorrect. Prompt caching can reduce latency and cost when a supported model repeatedly uses the same static prompt prefix. It does not choose a lower-cost model for routine work, and dynamic lookup results and contract-specific context still require normal inference on the larger model.
Deploy a smaller model and the current larger model to SageMaker real-time endpoints and use auto scaling policies to maintain endpoint capacity as request volume changes.
Explanation
Incorrect. SageMaker real-time endpoints can host models with more deployment control, but this adds model hosting and endpoint operations that the team wants to avoid. Auto scaling policies help maintain capacity as load changes, but they do not by themselves implement routing based on request complexity, confidence, or contract-reference signals.
Correct answer
Implement a Lambda or Amazon Bedrock Flows cascade that invokes a smaller Bedrock model for routine tasks and escalates low-confidence or complex requests to the current larger model.
Explanation
Correct. This approach matches model capability to task complexity while keeping inference on managed Amazon Bedrock APIs. Using application-specific confidence and request metadata allows the system to preserve quality for complex exception analyses while reducing cost and latency for routine requests.
Move all traffic to provisioned throughput for the current larger Bedrock model and tune response token limits for routine tasks before returning synchronous API responses.
Explanation
Incorrect. Provisioned throughput can improve predictable capacity for a selected model, but it does not change the fact that every request uses the larger model. Token limits can reduce output cost, but they do not address the main inefficiency of using high-capability inference for simple extraction and lookup tasks.
Overall explanation
The strongest design is a model cascade: use a less expensive, lower-latency model for tasks that do not require deep reasoning, then escalate to a more capable model only when the request characteristics justify it. Because the team already has API Gateway and Lambda in the path, Lambda can evaluate request type, internal API confidence, and contract-related flags before calling InvokeModel on the appropriate Amazon Bedrock model. Amazon Bedrock Flows can also express multi-step orchestration patterns when the team wants a managed workflow for prompts, model calls, and conditional branching.

This pattern is different from simply improving the current model's capacity or prompt efficiency. Provisioned throughput is useful when an application needs more predictable throughput for a specific model, but it does not reduce the cost of sending simple requests to an unnecessarily capable model. Prompt caching is useful for repeated static prompt prefixes, but it is not a substitute for selecting a cheaper model when the task itself is simple. SageMaker endpoints can be appropriate when a team needs custom hosting control, but they introduce endpoint management and scaling operations that are unnecessary when the requirement is to keep API-based managed inference.

For implementation details, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation for submitting single prompts with InvokeModel, Amazon Bedrock Flows, and Provisioned Throughput for Amazon Bedrock.

A university medical library's digital collections team is building an ingestion workflow for an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG assistant. Which workflow will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

Use AWS Step Functions to invoke Amazon Textract for scanned PDFs and photographs, Amazon Transcribe with custom vocabulary for audio, Amazon Comprehend to flag transcript PII for review, and SageMaker Processing to standardize CSV data into JSON artifacts in S3.
Explanation
Amazon Comprehend can analyze transcript text for PII, but flagging PII for review does not satisfy the requirement to redact PII from audio transcripts before indexing. This workflow also relies on a less direct document and image extraction path than Bedrock Data Automation for producing structured multimodal artifacts.
Use AWS Step Functions to invoke SageMaker Processing custom containers for scanned PDF OCR, photograph captioning, audio transcription, and CSV conversion, and store container outputs as JSON and Markdown artifacts in S3.
Explanation
This approach can be engineered to work, but it moves OCR, image understanding, ASR, and packaging into custom containers that the team must build and maintain. The requirement favors managed extraction and avoiding hosted custom extraction models, so this adds avoidable operational overhead.
Correct answer
Use AWS Step Functions to invoke Amazon Bedrock Data Automation blueprints for scanned PDFs and photographs, Amazon Transcribe with custom vocabulary and PII redaction for audio, and SageMaker Processing to standardize CSV data into JSON and Markdown artifacts in S3.
Explanation
This workflow uses managed, modality-specific services for document, image, audio, and tabular inputs. Bedrock Data Automation can extract structured outputs from multimodal assets, Transcribe provides audio-specific controls such as custom vocabulary and PII redaction, and SageMaker Processing can run repeatable normalization jobs without hosting custom extraction models.
Use AWS Step Functions to invoke a Bedrock multimodal model for scanned PDFs, photographs, audio, and CSV rows, request JSON and Markdown in the prompt, and store the model responses as the only intermediate artifacts in S3.
Explanation
Prompting a general multimodal foundation model can be useful for ad hoc analysis, but it does not provide the same managed controls for audio transcription, custom vocabulary, and transcript PII redaction. It also makes schema consistency depend primarily on prompt adherence, which is weaker than using specialized extraction services for recurring ingestion.
Overall explanation
Complex multimodal ingestion pipelines work best when each modality is handled by a service designed for that modality, then converted into a common representation for retrieval. Amazon Bedrock Data Automation is designed to extract structured information from unstructured multimodal content and can produce outputs such as JSON, HTML, Markdown, and CSV that are easier to review and transform before indexing. Amazon Transcribe is the right fit for the English oral histories because it provides speech-to-text features such as custom vocabularies for domain terms and PII redaction in transcripts.

SageMaker Processing is appropriate for repeatable data transformation jobs, such as normalizing CSV finding aids or merging extracted artifacts into canonical JSON and Markdown files in Amazon S3. Sending every asset directly to a general FM is a common anti-pattern for ingestion, because it overuses the model as an OCR, ASR, and schema enforcement engine instead of using managed extraction services. The durable S3 artifacts also create an inspection point before the data is synchronized into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, which is important for compliance and quality control.

Relevant documentation: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation, Custom vocabularies in Amazon Transcribe, Redacting PII in Amazon Transcribe, and Process data with SageMaker Processing.

Amazon Bedrock evaluations support several modes, including automatic model evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, human-worker evaluation, and RAG or knowledge-base evaluation, as described in Evaluate model and RAG source performance. ### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 29
Skipped
An insurance claims operations team is preparing a generative AI assistant that answers questions from policy documents and drafts claim-handling guidance. The release gate will run from a CI/CD pipeline through Amazon Bedrock evaluation APIs. The team has 1,600 anonymized prompt examples in Amazon S3, including single-turn policy lookup questions and several six-turn claim conversations. Claims specialists can review a sample of generated answers each week. The team must separately assess retrieved context quality, generated answer quality, safety risks, and subjective usefulness while minimizing custom evaluation code. Which TWO actions should the team take to meet these requirements?

Correct selection
Partition the prompt data into S3 JSON Lines files of 1,000 prompts or fewer, with single-turn records for retrieval tests and conversations capped at five turns for generation tests.
Explanation
This is correct because Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluation prompt datasets must be JSON Lines files in S3 and each evaluation job supports up to 1,000 prompts. Retrieve-only evaluation supports only a single turn, while retrieve-and-generate jobs support conversations with up to five turns.
Configure EvaluationDatasetMetricConfig with CitationPrecision and CitationCoverage for retrieve-and-generate jobs, and use those API metric values as release-blocking controls.
Explanation
This is incorrect for an API-driven release gate because the EvaluationDatasetMetricConfig API reference does not list CitationPrecision or CitationCoverage as valid retrieve-and-generate knowledge-base metric names. The implementation should use metric names that are valid for the API being called.
Submit the complete prompt history as one S3 JSON Lines file to a retrieve-and-generate job, and use the job output as the only release gate.
Explanation
This is incorrect because a single evaluation job supports up to 1,000 prompts, and the six-turn conversations exceed the retrieve-and-generate conversation limit. A single retrieve-and-generate job also does not separately evaluate retrieval-only quality or incorporate human review.
Run one retrieve-only RAG evaluation against the Knowledge Base, and use Correctness, Faithfulness, Harmfulness, and Refusal to assess contexts and final answers.
Explanation
This is incorrect because retrieve-only RAG evaluation is for evaluating retrieved data, not generated responses. The documented retrieve-only metrics are ContextRelevance and ContextCoverage, and ContextCoverage requires ground truth in the prompt dataset.
Correct selection
Run Bedrock RAG evaluation jobs for retrieval and retrieve-and-generate assessment, and run LLM-as-a-judge plus human-worker evaluations for sampled generated responses.
Explanation
This is correct because Amazon Bedrock evaluations support RAG evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation, and human-worker model evaluation. Combining these modes lets the team assess retrieved context, generated answers, safety dimensions, and subjective usefulness without building a custom evaluation pipeline.
Overall explanation
A comprehensive FM output assessment should treat evaluation as a set of complementary measurements rather than a single score. Amazon Bedrock evaluations support several modes, including automatic model evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, human-worker evaluation, and RAG or knowledge-base evaluation, as described in Evaluate model and RAG source performance.

For RAG systems, Bedrock separates retrieve-only evaluation from retrieve-and-generate evaluation. Retrieve-only jobs focus on the quality of retrieved context, while retrieve-and-generate jobs evaluate both retrieval and generated answers, as covered in Evaluate a knowledge base or RAG source. The dataset constraints matter operationally: prompt datasets must be JSON Lines files in S3, have a .jsonl extension, contain valid JSON objects per line, and stay within the documented prompt and conversation-turn limits in Prompt datasets for knowledge base evaluation.

The metric set also depends on the job type. Retrieve-only evaluation uses context-focused metrics such as Builtin.ContextRelevance and Builtin.ContextCoverage, with ground truth required for coverage, while retrieve-and-generate evaluation supports answer-quality and safety-oriented metrics documented in Retrieve and retrieve-and-generate evaluation metrics. When a CI/CD gate calls the API directly, use the valid metric names from EvaluationDatasetMetricConfig, because API valid values are the authoritative contract for request parameters.

Question 30
Skipped
An online education platform’s AI platform team manages a domain-specific tutoring assistant on Amazon SageMaker AI. Major releases are delivered as trained model artifacts with inference code, and specialty updates are delivered as LoRA adapter bundles in .tar.gz files in Amazon S3. The base foundation model for specialty updates already runs as a base inference component on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The team must version major releases, require approval before production deployment, reuse the running base model for LoRA updates, and rely on SageMaker AI MLOps project template behavior for rollback after a production version is rejected. Which TWO actions should the team include in the deployment and lifecycle design? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Register each major release in a Model (Package) Group with create_model_package, approve the deployable version, and reject an approved version to trigger template rollback.
Explanation
This action uses the SageMaker Model Registry as the versioned lifecycle control point for major releases. Versioned model packages must be approved before deployment, and SageMaker AI MLOps project templates can initiate deployment of the latest still-approved version when an approved version is later rejected.
Register each major release as a Marketplace model package, attach it to a Model (Package) Group, and promote it by assigning package versions.
Explanation
Marketplace model packages are a different type of model package and are not versionable entities associated with Model Groups. The correct versioned registry path uses model packages inside a Model (Package) Group, with versions added as new packages are registered.
Correct selection
Create adapter inference components for specialty LoRA bundles, referencing the base inference component and each .tar.gz artifact location in Amazon S3.
Explanation
This action uses the documented SageMaker AI mechanism for LoRA adapter deployment. Adapter inference components let the team attach LoRA artifacts to an existing base inference component instead of hosting a separate full model copy for each specialty update.
Change failed candidates from PendingManualApproval to Rejected, and rely on the project template to deploy the latest approved production version.
Explanation
Changing a model package from PendingManualApproval to Rejected does not initiate the rollback behavior described for SageMaker AI MLOps project templates. The documented rollback behavior occurs when an already approved version is changed from Approved to Rejected.
Deploy specialty LoRA bundles on separate real-time endpoints, hosting a full base model copy and routing requests to endpoints by subject.
Explanation
Separate endpoints can be used for real-time inference, but this approach does not meet the requirement to reuse the running base model for LoRA updates. It increases operational overhead and duplicates the base model deployment that adapter inference components are designed to avoid.
Overall explanation
SageMaker Model Registry provides the lifecycle structure for versioned model releases. A Model (Package) Group contains model packages, and each package in the group represents a numeric version of a trained model, starting at 1 and incrementing as new versions are added. Registering a version is a registry operation, commonly done with create_model_package, not the same operation as deploying an endpoint. See Register and deploy models with Model Registry and Register a model version.

Approval status is part of the production control plane. For versioned model packages, the deployable version must have ModelApprovalStatus set to Approved. With SageMaker AI-provided MLOps project templates, approval transitions are not all equivalent: moving PendingManualApproval or Rejected to Approved can initiate deployment of that version, while moving Approved to Rejected can initiate deployment of the latest version that still has Approved status. See CreateModelPackage and Update the approval status of a model.

For LoRA deployment, SageMaker AI has a separate mechanism: adapter inference components. The base foundation model must already be deployed as a base inference component on a SageMaker AI endpoint, and the LoRA adapter artifacts must be stored as a .tar.gz file in Amazon S3. The adapter inference component references both the base inference component and the adapter artifact location, which lets the team deploy specialty behavior without standing up a complete duplicate base model for each update. See Deploy adapters with inference components.

Marketplace model packages and separate full-model endpoints are close enough to sound plausible, but they miss the specific lifecycle and efficiency requirements. Marketplace packages are not the versioned Model Group entities needed for release governance, and separate endpoints duplicate the base foundation model instead of using the LoRA adapter deployment path. For deployment from approved registry versions, SageMaker AI supports SDK and Boto3 paths such as deploying by model package ARN, as described in Deploy a model from the registry.

Set Amazon Bedrock latency-optimized inference for supported calls, keep the approved model in the current Region, and track time-to-first-token during surge windows.
Explanation
This is incorrect because latency-optimized inference is intended to improve response latency characteristics for supported models, not to reserve additional invocation throughput. It may improve perceived responsiveness, but it does not directly address throttling caused by insufficient model capacity.
Configure Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for reusable briefing instructions, keep the dynamic forecast content in each request, and monitor cache activity during surge windows.
Explanation
This is incorrect because prompt caching can reduce repeated processing for a static prompt prefix where the feature is supported. It can improve latency and cost for suitable prompts, but it does not provide reserved throughput for a predictable surge of model invocations.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput is the best fit when a workload has predictable demand and needs more consistent throughput for the same supported model. The team reserves model capacity, sizes it from observed request and token patterns, and invokes the provisioned model ARN through the Bedrock runtime API. This keeps the operational model close to the existing design while addressing the actual bottleneck, which is model invocation capacity.

Capacity planning for generative AI should use both request volume and token volume, because long prompts and long completions consume more model work than short interactions. CloudWatch usage, error, and latency trends help determine whether provisioned capacity is right-sized and whether the surge pattern justifies reserved capacity instead of on-demand invocation. See Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock and Monitor Amazon Bedrock with Amazon CloudWatch.

On-demand quota increases, performanceConfig latency optimization, and prompt caching are all plausible Bedrock optimization tools, but they solve different problems. Quota increases can help when account-level limits are the constraint, but they do not reserve capacity for a known surge. Latency-optimized inference targets responsiveness metrics, and prompt caching reduces repeated work for static prompt prefixes, but neither is a substitute for provisioned model throughput. For related tradeoffs, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock, Optimize latency for foundation models in Amazon Bedrock, and Prompt caching for model inference in Amazon Bedrock.

An agricultural commodities exchange's risk technology team is deploying a generative AI assistant that drafts market surveillance alerts. Regulatory reviewers require repeatable evidence of model purpose, risk rating, evaluation observations, approval state, data source attribution, and transformations applied to reference datasets. The deployment pipeline releases models from SageMaker Model Registry packages and from vendors outside SageMaker AI, and the team wants exportable audit artifacts without maintaining manual spreadsheets. Which TWO actions should the team include in the compliance framework? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Use AWS Glue crawlers and ETL jobs with Data Catalog tables to capture dataset metadata and transformation records, and reference catalog identifiers in release evidence for provenance.
Explanation
This is correct because the AWS Glue Data Catalog is a centralized metadata repository for dataset location, schema, and related metadata. AWS documentation also states that it maintains records of transformations and operations on data, which supports lineage, auditing, compliance, and provenance.
Correct selection
Create SageMaker Model Cards through APIs or the AWS CLI for each release, populate governed fields from pipeline metadata, update cards as artifacts change, and export reviewed cards.
Explanation
This is correct because SageMaker Model Cards support governance documentation such as intended use, risk rating, evaluation details, observations, and recommendations. They can be created programmatically, exported, and versioned when most edits are made, which supports repeatable audit evidence without a manual spreadsheet.
Create model cards from Model Registry packages and external-model records, accept imported or supplied fields as complete evidence, and export the cards for review packages.
Explanation
This is incorrect because a model card created from a Model Registry package can include missing or inaccurate imported information, and AWS says the card must be edited. Model cards can also document external models, but externally supplied fields still need governance review rather than being accepted as complete evidence automatically.
Encode lineage by applying AWS Glue tags to crawlers, jobs, and databases for every upstream file and transform, then use tag reports as the compliance record.
Explanation
This is incorrect because AWS Glue tags are resource labels used for organization, access control, and cost accounting, not arbitrary data-lineage records. Tags are useful for categorizing supported resources, but they are limited in number and do not replace catalog metadata and transformation history.
Set SageMaker model-card status to Archived after deployment, treat the archived state as approval evidence, and store all source attribution in model-card tags.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Archived is a valid SageMaker model-card status, but it is not the same as an approval state for review evidence. Model-card tags are optional and limited, and they are not the right place to store comprehensive source attribution or transformation history.
Overall explanation
A strong compliance framework separates model governance evidence from data provenance evidence. SageMaker Model Cards are designed to document model details such as intended use, risk rating, training and evaluation information, observations, and recommendations, and they can be created and managed programmatically through APIs such as CreateModelCard. See Amazon SageMaker Model Cards and Use APIs to manage model cards.

Model cards make governance evidence repeatable, but they do not automatically prove regulatory compliance. When a card is created from a SageMaker Model Registry model package, SageMaker can import some package data, but AWS warns that the resulting card can contain missing or inaccurate information that must be reviewed and edited. This matters when an organization uses both registry packages and models hosted or registered outside SageMaker AI, as described in Create a model card.

The AWS Glue Data Catalog addresses the data side of the audit requirement. Crawlers can scan data sources, infer schema, and create or update catalog tables, while Glue ETL jobs use those tables as sources and targets. AWS documentation states that the Data Catalog maintains records of transformations and operations performed on data, which supports lineage, provenance, auditing, and compliance, as covered in AWS Glue Data Catalog and crawlers.

Using a real status for the wrong governance meaning, treating automatically imported registry metadata as complete, or substituting tags for lineage weakens the framework. The CreateModelCard API defines valid statuses such as Draft, PendingReview, Approved, and Archived, but Archived means no more updates should be made and does not by itself establish review approval. Tags are useful labels, but they are not comprehensive lineage records and are constrained by the resources and limits documented for the service. See CreateModelCard.

A maritime logistics platform team runs a shipment-planning assistant by using the Amazon Bedrock ConverseStream API. The assistant can request tools for vessel schedules, port restrictions, and weather risk, but the tool APIs run inside the application VPC. The team needs an operational framework that measures tool call frequency, tool failures, and tool latency alongside token usage, model latency, throttles, and streaming responsiveness. The framework must support anomaly baselines by customer and workflow, and auditors require model invocation logs in the same account and Region. Which approach will meet these requirements?

Keep client-side tool execution, enable model invocation logging only, infer tool utilization from ModelInvocationLog token fields, and use AWS/Bedrock InvocationLatency metrics for tool latency baselines.
Explanation
Model invocation logs and runtime metrics provide model-level observability, but they do not measure the execution time or failure rate of application-owned tools. Inferring per-tool utilization from token counts and invocation latency would miss tool-specific behavior and would create unreliable baselines.

Explanation

EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage is documented as an approximation that should not be the sole capacity signal, and TimeToFirstToken measures streaming model responsiveness rather than per-tool utilization.
Move the tools to server-side tool use on the Responses API, rely on Bedrock to invoke each tool, and use model invocation logging to capture customer and workflow baselines.
Explanation
Server-side tool use changes the execution model and is currently documented for the Responses API, not the Converse API workflow described in the scenario. Model invocation logging for Amazon Bedrock captures supported bedrock-runtime operations and does not currently capture calls through other endpoints such as the Responses API on bedrock-mantle.
Correct answer
Keep client-side tool execution, add customer and workflow values to requestMetadata, instrument each ToolUseBlock and tool result in the application, and combine invocation logs with AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics.
Explanation
This approach matches how client-side tool use works with ConverseStream: the model requests a tool, and the application executes it. The application can measure tool duration and failures, while requestMetadata, invocation logs, and CloudWatch runtime metrics provide correlation for customer, workflow, tokens, latency, throttles, and streaming responsiveness.
Overall explanation
With Amazon Bedrock client-side tool use, the model can decide that a tool is needed, but the application remains responsible for executing the tool and returning the result. That means tool-level performance, such as duration, failures, retries, and downstream status, must be captured by the application around each requested ToolUseBlock, including its name, input, and toolUseId. See Call a tool with Amazon Bedrock models and ToolUseBlock.

The Converse and ConverseStream APIs provide the model-side operational signals needed to correlate tool behavior with foundation model behavior. For streaming responses, messageStop carries stopReason, and the final metadata event contains usage and metrics; the runtime endpoint also publishes CloudWatch metrics such as Invocations, InvocationLatency, InvocationThrottles, InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, and TimeToFirstToken. These metrics are documented in Carry out a conversation with the Converse API operations and Monitor Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics.

requestMetadata is the right correlation hook for baselines by customer and workflow because Amazon Bedrock describes it as metadata that can be filtered when using invocation logs. Model invocation logging is disabled by default, and when enabled it can send supported runtime invocation logs to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3 in the same account and Region. The important tradeoff is that Bedrock logs and CloudWatch metrics provide model invocation visibility, while application instrumentation provides the missing tool execution visibility; a robust tool performance framework needs both. See Log Amazon Bedrock model invocation activity.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 34
Skipped
A regional public transit authority's safety analytics team runs a RAG assistant that uses Amazon OpenSearch Service as the vector store for rail maintenance manuals, bus operator procedures, procurement policies, and safety bulletins. The application currently stores all embeddings in one k-NN index with a domain metadata field and uses a domain post-filter after each vector query. Each request already contains the domain selected by the user interface. During peak periods, some searches return fewer than the requested top 10 chunks after filtering, and node-level metrics show uneven load after the cluster was resized from 6 to 8 data nodes. The team must improve semantic retrieval latency and domain relevance without replacing OpenSearch Service or changing the embedding model. Which architecture change will best meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Create a separate k-NN index for each domain, route each query to the selected domain index, and reindex with primary shard counts planned around the data-node count.
Explanation
This routes vector search to the relevant corpus before candidate retrieval, which avoids relying on a post-filter to remove unrelated domains after the k-NN query. Planning shard counts against the data-node count also addresses the uneven distribution risk that can create hot nodes after a cluster resize.
Keep one shared k-NN index, add a stricter domain post-filter to each query, and increase k until each filtered response usually contains 10 chunks.
Explanation
Post-filters are applied after the k-NN query and can reduce the final number of hits below k, so increasing k is only a workaround that adds more search work. This approach still searches across unrelated domains and does not address the shard distribution issue after the node-count change.
Create a separate k-NN index for each domain, send every query to all domain indices with _msearch, and merge the ranked results in application code.
Explanation
The _msearch API can batch multiple vector searches into a single request, which can help high query volume use cases. However, broadcasting every request to all domain indices ignores the known domain selection, increases unnecessary fanout, and can add merge complexity without improving domain targeting.
Keep one shared k-NN index, increase the number of primary shards aggressively, and rely on automatic shard distribution to rebalance query load.
Explanation
More primary shards can increase parallelism in some cases, but excessive sharding is a common OpenSearch anti-pattern because shards consume heap and CPU resources. This approach also keeps unrelated domains in the same candidate pool and does not use the domain information available before search.
Overall explanation
For a RAG vector store that already knows the request domain, a multi-index retrieval architecture is often better than a single broad index plus a post-filter. The application can route the query to the relevant domain-specific k-NN index before vector search, which reduces the candidate space and avoids retrieving semantically similar chunks from unrelated domains.

Amazon OpenSearch Service k-NN indexes store embeddings in knn_vector fields and require k-NN to be enabled for the index, as described in Vector search for Amazon OpenSearch Service. When the query uses filtering after k-NN, AWS documents that filtering can reduce the final returned result count, so k should not be treated as a guarantee of exactly that many final hits. The k-NN documentation also notes that size should be included because k is not a substitute for the overall response size, see k-nearest neighbor search in Amazon OpenSearch Service.

Sharding must be treated as a capacity and distribution decision, not as unlimited parallelism. AWS operational best practices explain that primary shards are distributed across data nodes and recommend choosing shard counts with the data-node count in mind to avoid hot nodes, see Operational best practices for Amazon OpenSearch Service. Excessive sharding can increase heap pressure and coordination overhead, so the better design is targeted routing plus planned shard counts, not simply adding shards or increasing k.

Question 35
Skipped
A property insurance carrier's claims automation team uses Amazon Bedrock prompts to draft claim summaries. Recent prompt edits improved summaries for auto claims but caused inconsistent outputs for property claims and liability claims. The team has six prompt templates, each with about 80 SME-reviewed evaluation samples. The team must use the samples to systematically refine the prompts, compare original and optimized behavior across three candidate FMs, and avoid building a custom evaluation service. Which approach will meet these requirements?

Run simple prompt optimization with OptimizePrompt separately for each template and target model. Use the optimized prompt events from each run, then manually compare the rewritten prompts against the evaluation samples.
Explanation
Incorrect. Simple prompt optimization is a fast heuristic rewrite for a single short prompt and one target model. It does not use evaluation data or support multiple models, so it does not meet the requirement for systematic sample-based refinement across three FMs.
Save each revised template as a DRAFT prompt in Prompt management. Use the prompt-version JSON comparison view, then select the version with the smallest configuration differences for release.
Explanation
Incorrect. Prompt-version comparison shows JSON differences between prompt versions and helps audit what changed. It does not evaluate response quality, consistency, or behavior against SME-reviewed samples, so selecting the smallest diff is an anti-pattern for quality validation.
Correct answer
Create an Advanced Prompt Optimization job with a JSONL dataset for the six templates and their samples. Use an LLM-as-a-judge rubric across the three target models, then review the original and optimized results.

Explanation
Correct. Advanced Prompt Optimization is designed for evaluation-driven prompt optimization and can compare original and optimized prompts across multiple models. The stated number of templates, samples, and models fits the documented limits, and an LLM-as-a-judge rubric avoids building a custom evaluator.
Create managed prompt variants in Prompt builder for each template. Use Compare variants with test variables for the claim inputs, then save the best variant as the working draft for later release.
Explanation
Incorrect. Prompt builder can compare variants interactively with test variables, but it is not the best fit for optimizing six templates against 80 samples each across three models. It is useful for authoring and side-by-side testing, not for evaluation-driven optimization at this scale.
Overall explanation
Advanced Prompt Optimization is the best fit when prompt quality problems require systematic refinement against evaluation data rather than another round of ad hoc prompt edits. It supports evaluation-driven optimization, can compare original and optimized prompts across up to five models, and accepts up to ten prompt templates per job with up to 100 evaluation samples per prompt template, as described in Optimize prompts with Advanced Prompt Optimization.

The scenario fits those constraints: six templates, about 80 samples per template, and three candidate FMs. The JSONL input format also aligns with prompt templates that use variables, because the documented input requires fields such as templateId, promptTemplate, and evaluationSamples, and variable names must match the {{variableName}} placeholders, as shown in Advanced Prompt Optimization input dataset.

Simple prompt optimization is intentionally lighter weight. It is a heuristic rewrite of a single short prompt for one model, works best for prompts around 1K tokens or less, and explicitly does not use evaluation data or support multiple models, as documented in Optimize prompts in Amazon Bedrock.

Prompt management remains valuable for creating, testing, saving, reusing, and versioning prompts, and Prompt builder can compare variants with test variables, as described in Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock and Create prompts in Prompt management. However, those tools do not replace an evaluation-driven optimization job when the requirement is to use a sample set systematically across multiple models. Version JSON comparison, described in Deploy prompts in Prompt management, is useful for auditing configuration changes, not for proving response quality improvements.

Question 36
Skipped
A biotech patent research group is running a 4-week proof of concept for an Amazon Bedrock assistant that drafts prior-art search summaries for internal analysts. The team must compare several chat-capable foundation models before selecting one, minimize per-model client code, measure latency, throttling, and token usage from managed telemetry, and quantify answer quality on a held-out prompt dataset before requesting production funding. Which combination of actions will best validate feasibility, performance characteristics, and business value with the least custom implementation? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Run Bedrock model evaluation jobs against the held-out prompt dataset, using one task type per job and the evaluation method that matches the scoring need.
Explanation
Correct. Bedrock evaluations support automatic, human-based, and judge-model approaches for assessing model outputs. A model evaluation job has one task type, so separate jobs should be used if the PoC needs to evaluate different task categories.
Rely on default model invocation logging for prompt samples, and compare Invocations with submitted attempts to infer throttling.
Explanation
Incorrect. Model invocation logging is disabled by default, so prompt and response samples are not captured unless logging is explicitly configured. The Invocations metric counts successful requests only, while throttled requests and other invocation errors are tracked separately.
Build the PoC harness on InvokeModel for the chat workflow, and reuse the same request body across all candidate models to simplify comparisons.
Explanation
Incorrect. InvokeModel is valid for direct single-model inference control, but its request body is model-specific. Reusing one request body across different model providers is not a reliable way to compare chat-capable models.
Run StartAsyncInvoke for the chat workflow, and retrieve each result later to compare interactive responsiveness across candidate models.
Explanation
Incorrect. StartAsyncInvoke is documented for asynchronous generation that can be retrieved later, including video generation use cases. That pattern does not directly measure the interactive responsiveness expected from a chat proof of concept.
Correct selection
Build the PoC harness on Converse or ConverseStream for the chat workflow, and collect AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics for latency, throttles, and token counts.
Explanation
Correct. Converse is intended for chat and helps reduce model-specific branching when comparing chat-capable models. The AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics include latency, throttling, and token-count metrics that are appropriate for a performance-focused proof of concept.
Overall explanation
A biotech patent research group is running a 4-week proof of concept for an Amazon Bedrock assistant that drafts prior-art search summaries for internal analysts. The team must compare several chat-capable foundation models before selecting one, minimize per-model client code, measure latency, throttling, and token usage from managed telemetry, and quantify answer quality on a held-out prompt dataset before requesting production funding.

Which combination of actions will best validate feasibility, performance characteristics, and business value with the least custom implementation? (Select TWO.)

Converse is the better abstraction when the PoC needs a chat workflow and wants less model-specific request handling. AWS describes Converse as a way to build multi-turn conversational applications and standardize across models, while InvokeModel gives direct request and response control with model-specific request bodies. See Amazon Bedrock API choices and Run inference with Amazon Bedrock models.

For performance validation, the PoC should use CloudWatch runtime metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace rather than relying only on application-side timing. Metrics such as InvocationLatency, InvocationThrottles, InputTokenCount, and OutputTokenCount provide a managed view of behavior across test runs, and TimeToFirstToken applies when streaming APIs are used. The Invocations metric counts successful requests only, so it should not be treated as a count of all attempts or as a throttling proxy, as described in Monitor Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics.

For business-value validation, Bedrock evaluations are a stronger proof point than ad hoc inspection because they provide a documented mechanism for scoring model outputs. Evaluation jobs can use automatic scoring, human workers, or a judge model depending on whether the team needs computed metrics, subjective review, or LLM-as-judge explanations. AWS documents that each model evaluation job uses one task type, so a PoC that mixes question answering, summarization, and classification should plan separate jobs, as covered in Evaluate models and knowledge bases in Amazon Bedrock and Model evaluation task types.

Model invocation logging can be useful for human review, but it is not automatic. If the team wants prompt and response samples, it must explicitly enable logging to supported destinations such as Amazon S3, CloudWatch Logs, or both, with destination resources in the same account and Region. That behavior is documented in Log Amazon Bedrock model invocation activity.

**Quick lesson:** The safest integration pattern is to separate retrieval from generation. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provide distinct APIs for this purpose: Retrieve returns the most relevant source chunks or images, while RetrieveAndGenerate combines retrieval with an FM invocation to produce a natural-language answer. When multiple assistants need different models, prompts, formatting rules, or citation logic, Retrieve is the better shared interface because it returns evidence rather than a completed answer. ### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 37
Skipped
A medical device manufacturer's field support platform team is standardizing a RAG retrieval layer over Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Several internal assistants will call the same retrieval capability through tool or function interfaces, but each assistant must choose its own FM, prompt template, response formatting, and citation handling after retrieval. The vector store backing each knowledge base might change over time, so the interface must avoid search settings that are not portable across knowledge base configurations. Which design will meet these requirements with the LEAST integration risk?

Correct answer
Create an application-owned search tool with a JSON parameter schema. Execute the tool in client code by calling Retrieve, then pass the returned chunks to the selected FM.
Explanation
This design exposes retrieval through a consistent tool interface while keeping generation under the caller's control. Retrieve returns relevant source chunks or images, so the application can use the FM, prompt template, formatting, and citation logic that each assistant requires.
Create a reusable retrieval tool that always sets overrideSearchType to HYBRID. Execute the tool against every knowledge base and pass the results to the selected FM.
Explanation
A reusable retrieval tool is a reasonable pattern, but always forcing HYBRID is not portable across knowledge base configurations. For custom knowledge bases, overrideSearchType HYBRID can be specified only with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store that has a filterable text field; other vector store configurations require SEMANTIC or use different managed retrieval semantics.
Create an application-owned answer tool with a JSON parameter schema. Execute the tool in client code by calling RetrieveAndGenerate, then return the generated answer to callers.
Explanation
RetrieveAndGenerate can be parameterized with model and generation settings, including a prompt template. However, this proposed shared answer tool centralizes generation in the retrieval layer and returns a finished answer, which conflicts with the requirement for each assistant to perform its own generation and citation handling after retrieval.
Create an agent action group for vector search with an OpenAPI schema and a function schema. Configure the model to invoke the knowledge base operation directly.
Explanation
Bedrock Agent action groups use either an OpenAPI schema or a function schema for an action group, not both. Bedrock tool use also does not mean the model directly executes arbitrary tools, because execution is handled by application code or supported server-side mechanisms.
Overall explanation
The safest integration pattern is to separate retrieval from generation. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provide distinct APIs for this purpose: Retrieve returns the most relevant source chunks or images, while RetrieveAndGenerate combines retrieval with an FM invocation to produce a natural-language answer. When multiple assistants need different models, prompts, formatting rules, or citation logic, Retrieve is the better shared interface because it returns evidence rather than a completed answer. See Query a knowledge base and retrieve data from it.

RetrieveAndGenerate is still a valid Knowledge Bases API for many RAG applications, and it can accept model and generation configuration parameters. The issue in this scenario is not that the API can never be customized, it is that a shared answer-producing tool would make generation part of the common retrieval layer. That design creates tighter coupling for assistants that are supposed to own their own FM selection, prompt templates, formatting, and citation behavior. See RetrieveAndGenerate.

Tool and function interfaces are useful because they create a stable contract between the orchestrator and the retrieval implementation. In Amazon Bedrock tool use, the model can decide that a tool is needed, but tool execution is performed by application code for client-side tool use, or by supported server-side mechanisms such as a registered Lambda function or AgentCore Gateway. That means the application can expose a normalized searchKnowledgeBase operation while still controlling exactly how the Knowledge Bases API is called. See Tool use in Amazon Bedrock.

The design should also avoid assuming that every knowledge base supports the same search controls. overrideSearchType is not a universal switch for hybrid retrieval, because for custom knowledge bases, HYBRID can be specified only when using an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store that has a filterable text field. Other vector store configurations are limited to SEMANTIC search for vectorSearchConfiguration, while managed knowledge bases use managedSearchConfiguration and different retrieval semantics. See KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration and Query a knowledge base and retrieve data.

Correct selection
Apply the Generative AI Lens from the Lens Catalog to each AWS WA Tool workload and use its questions, best practices, notes, and improvement plan during reviews.
Explanation
This is correct because the Generative AI Lens is an AWS-maintained Lens Catalog lens for generative AI workloads. AWS WA Tool lenses provide a consistent assessment structure with questions, best practices, notes, and improvement plans.
Configure AWS WA Tool improvement plans to deploy standard prompt catalogs, guardrail resources, and conversational interface components during each workload review.
Explanation
This is incorrect because AWS WA Tool provides an assessment and improvement-planning process, not an application infrastructure deployment engine. Deployment should remain in the separate CI/CD pipeline while AWS WA Tool standardizes review artifacts.
Create one custom lens that copies the Generative AI Lens review content, designate it as the AWS-maintained baseline, and apply only that custom lens to each workload.
Explanation
This is incorrect because custom lenses are user-defined and are not AWS official content. The official AWS-maintained generative AI guidance should come from the Lens Catalog Generative AI Lens, not from a copied custom lens.
Import a custom lens JSON document for restaurant-specific controls, keep the lens in DRAFT status, share it with the required AWS accounts, and use workload notes to track progress.
Explanation
This is incorrect because a newly imported or created custom lens remains in DRAFT status until it is published. A DRAFT custom lens cannot be applied to workloads or shared with other AWS accounts.
Overall explanation
AWS Well-Architected Tool is designed to standardize architecture assessment, not to provision application resources. It helps teams document decisions, evaluate workloads against best practices, and generate improvement recommendations through a consistent review process. For this scenario, that makes it appropriate for governance artifacts and progress tracking while the existing CI/CD pipeline remains responsible for deploying prompts, guardrails, knowledge bases, and application components.

Lenses are the mechanism that make AWS WA Tool useful for repeatable reviews. The official Lens Catalog includes the Generative AI lens, which AWS describes as best practices for architecting generative AI workloads on AWS. Applying that lens gives teams AWS-maintained generative AI review content without having to recreate or maintain it themselves.

When an organization needs its own additional review criteria, a custom lens is the right extension point. Custom lenses are JSON documents that can define pillars, questions, best practices, and improvement plan links, and they can be shared with other AWS accounts after publication. The publish step matters because a newly created or imported custom lens remains in DRAFT status until it is published, so a draft lens cannot satisfy a multi-account workload review requirement.

The mental model is to separate assessment standards from deployment automation. AWS WA Tool and lenses define how workloads are measured and improved, while infrastructure as code and CI/CD systems implement the technical changes. For more detail, see the AWS WA Tool introduction, lens behavior, and custom lens documentation: AWS Well-Architected Tool, Lenses, Custom lenses, and Creating a custom lens.

Question 39
Skipped
A regional law firm's litigation technology team is building a RAG assistant for attorneys. The ingestion pipeline stores brief passages in a vector store. At query time, an AWS Lambda function must call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly with InvokeModel to generate an Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 vector for the attorney's question, then call Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet to answer from retrieved passages. The team currently sends raw text strings as request bodies and receives validation errors from both calls. The team's architecture requires direct model invocation and cannot switch to a managed abstraction. Which TWO changes should the team make to format the inference requests correctly? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Serialize the Claude 3.5 Sonnet request as JSON that includes anthropic_version, max_tokens, and a messages array with user content blocks containing the retrieved context and question.
Explanation
This is correct because Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock uses the Anthropic Messages API format when invoked directly. The request must include the Bedrock Anthropic API version, output token control, and a role-based messages array with content blocks.
Serialize the Claude 3.5 Sonnet request as JSON that places the complete prompt in prompt using Human: and Assistant: delimiters with max_tokens_to_sample.
Explanation
This is incorrect because that prompt-completion format applies to older Anthropic text completion style requests, not Claude 3.5 Sonnet Messages API requests on Amazon Bedrock. Claude 3.5 Sonnet expects messages, content blocks, and max_tokens rather than prompt and max_tokens_to_sample.
Correct selection
Serialize the Titan Text Embeddings V2 request as JSON that places the query text in inputText and includes supported embedding options only when needed.
Explanation
This is correct because Titan Text Embeddings models in Amazon Bedrock expect a model-specific JSON request body rather than a raw string. For Titan Text Embeddings V2, the input text is supplied in inputText, with optional supported fields such as embedding dimensions or normalization when applicable.
Serialize both Bedrock Runtime requests as JSON that places the text under inputText and passes generation settings under textGenerationConfig.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Amazon Bedrock Runtime does not provide a single generic request body that works for every model invoked with InvokeModel. The inputText field is appropriate for Titan Text Embeddings V2, but Claude 3.5 Sonnet requires the Anthropic Messages API shape rather than textGenerationConfig.
Serialize the Titan Text Embeddings V2 request as JSON that places the query text in a messages array with role user and content type text.
Explanation
This is incorrect because the role-based messages format is used by chat-style model APIs, not by Titan Text Embeddings V2. An embeddings request needs the model's embedding input schema, so using messages would fail validation for this model.
Overall explanation
When using Amazon Bedrock Runtime with InvokeModel, the HTTP operation is common, but the JSON body is not universal. Bedrock passes the request body to the selected model family, so each model's documented schema must be followed. The contentType is typically application/json, but the decisive issue in this scenario is the body schema for each model.

For Titan Text Embeddings V2, the request body supplies text through inputText, with optional supported embedding controls such as dimensions or normalization depending on the use case. For Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet, direct invocation uses the Anthropic Messages API shape, including anthropic_version, max_tokens, and a messages array whose content blocks carry the retrieved context and user question. Mixing these schemas is a common integration anti-pattern: a chat messages body is not an embeddings request, and an older prompt-completion body is not a Claude Messages request. See the Amazon Bedrock documentation for InvokeModel, Titan Text Embeddings model parameters, and Anthropic Claude Messages API parameters.

Question 40
Skipped
A regional airline's crew operations team uses an Amazon Bedrock custom knowledge base backed by Amazon OpenSearch Serverless to retrieve policy snippets before a separate Amazon Bedrock model call. The source documents are in Amazon S3 and include associated metadata files for fleet type, airport region, and policy effective date. The current vector index uses the nmslib engine and stores embeddings but does not store raw document text as a filterable field. Queries often mix exact policy codes with natural-language questions, and the retrieval step must reduce irrelevant chunks without adding another model call in the request path. Which approach will best improve retrieval relevance and speed while meeting these constraints?

Keep the current vector index and configure implicitFilterConfiguration with a Claude model. Call Retrieve with SEMANTIC search and generated metadata filters.
Explanation
Incorrect. Implicit metadata filtering uses a model to generate filters from the query, which adds a model-based preprocessing step to the request path. Semantic-only search also does not take advantage of exact policy codes in raw text.
Keep the OpenSearch Serverless index on the nmslib engine and add equals filters. Call Retrieve with vectorSearchConfiguration filters and HYBRID search.
Explanation
Incorrect. For Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector stores, AWS documents that metadata filtering requires a faiss vector index. Keeping the nmslib index would not satisfy the filtering requirement that is central to reducing irrelevant chunks.
Move the knowledge base to a fully managed configuration and set managedSearchConfiguration. Call Retrieve with semantic search and a larger numberOfResults value.
Explanation
Incorrect. Fully managed knowledge bases use managedSearchConfiguration, but they always use hybrid search and do not offer semantic-only search. Increasing the number of retrieved results can increase context volume and does not address the need to filter by fleet, region, and policy metadata.
Correct answer
Rebuild the OpenSearch Serverless index with the faiss engine and a filterable text field. Call Retrieve with vectorSearchConfiguration metadata filters and HYBRID search.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector indexes must use the faiss engine for metadata filtering in Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and hybrid search requires a supported store with a filterable text field. Using Retrieve keeps the step focused on returning source chunks before the separate model invocation.
Overall explanation
For a custom Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base, the retrieval configuration for vector search belongs under vectorSearchConfiguration, and overrideSearchType can be set to HYBRID or SEMANTIC. Hybrid search is useful when queries combine exact identifiers, such as policy codes, with semantic wording because it searches both embeddings and raw text when the vector store supports it and has a filterable text field, as described in Configure and customize queries and response generation.

Metadata filtering is the speed and relevance lever in this scenario because it prunes the candidate set before chunks are supplied as FM context. For Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector stores, AWS documents that the vector index must use the faiss engine for metadata filtering, and S3 data sources require associated metadata JSON files to use filters. The filter structure is a union type, so a request uses one top-level RetrievalFilter member, such as an andAll expression that combines multiple child filters, as documented in RetrievalFilter.

Retrieve is the appropriate API when the application only needs relevant source chunks before a separate model invocation. RetrieveAndGenerate would combine retrieval with model generation, which is not needed here, while implicit filtering can be valuable but uses a model-generated preprocessing step that conflicts with the stated request-path constraint. The distinction among Retrieve, RetrieveAndGenerate, and agentic retrieval is summarized in Retrieve data and generate AI responses with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

Question 41
Skipped
A tax-preparation software provider's compliance automation team is building a bulk review system for taxpayer letters. A Standard AWS Step Functions state machine uses a Map state to process each letter independently. Each Map item must run a guardrail precheck on the letter, call an FM through AWS Lambda only when the precheck passes, run a guardrail postcheck on the draft, and then write either the accepted draft or a review record. Some valid FM calls take up to 90 seconds. If one FM call stalls, only that letter should be sent to review and the remaining Map items should continue. The security team also requires a control that prevents application roles from invoking Amazon Bedrock unless the approved guardrail is included in the inference request. Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT and source OUTPUT inside each Map item. Invoke Bedrock from Lambda with configured Lambda and Task timeouts, catch per-item timeout failures, and use Guardrails CloudWatch metrics to enforce approved guardrail usage.
Explanation
This validates input and output and can isolate stalled items when the catch is placed inside each Map item. However, Guardrails CloudWatch metrics provide operational visibility, not an authorization control, so they cannot prevent application roles from invoking Bedrock without the approved guardrail.
Call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT and source OUTPUT inside each Map item. Invoke Bedrock from a Step Functions HTTP Task with TimeoutSeconds set above 90 seconds, catch per-item timeout failures, and add an explicit Deny with bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier.
Explanation
This uses the right guardrail placement and an IAM guardrail condition, but the HTTP Task integration has a hard maximum duration of 60 seconds. Because valid FM calls can take up to 90 seconds, this approach can fail valid work even when TimeoutSeconds is set higher.
Call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT and source OUTPUT inside each Map item. Invoke Bedrock from Lambda with configured Lambda and Task timeouts, catch timeout failures on the Map state, and add an explicit Deny with bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier.
Explanation
This includes the correct guardrail checks and IAM enforcement, and it sets explicit timeouts. However, catching the failure at the Map state handles the Map failure path as a whole, rather than routing only the failed letter from within the item workflow while allowing the other items to proceed normally.
Correct answer
Call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT and source OUTPUT inside each Map item. Invoke Bedrock from Lambda with configured Lambda and Task timeouts, catch per-item timeout failures inside the Map item, and add an explicit Deny with bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier.
Explanation
This validates both user text and generated drafts by using ApplyGuardrail independently of model invocation. Placing the timeout handling inside each Map item isolates a stalled FM call to that item, while the explicit Deny with bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier prevents inference calls that omit the approved guardrail.
Overall explanation
ApplyGuardrail is designed to be used independently of foundation model invocation, which makes it suitable for both sides of this workflow. The workflow can call ApplyGuardrail with source set to INPUT before invoking the model and with source set to OUTPUT after the draft is generated. This lets the application reject unsafe input before inference and inspect generated content before returning or storing it. See Use the ApplyGuardrail API with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

For a Map-based workflow, the placement of error handling matters as much as the timeout values. A Step Functions Task state has a very large default timeout, so the workflow should set task timeouts intentionally and coordinate them with the Lambda function timeout. To send only the stalled letter to review, the timeout catch path must be inside the per-item processing logic, not only on the Map state as a whole. Step Functions task timeouts and error handling behavior are described in Task workflow state and Handling errors in Step Functions workflows.

The HTTP Task distractor is close because it also uses prechecks, postchecks, timeout handling, and IAM enforcement. The subtle limit is that a Step Functions HTTP Task has a hard maximum duration of 60 seconds, even if TimeoutSeconds is configured with a larger value. That makes it unsuitable when valid FM calls can take up to 90 seconds.

IAM enforcement is separate from workflow validation. Amazon Bedrock supports the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key for inference APIs, and an explicit Deny is the appropriate control to block inference requests that do not use the approved guardrail. Guardrails CloudWatch metrics, documented under the AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails namespace, are useful for monitoring but cannot serve as an authorization boundary. See Enforce use of a guardrail during model inference and Monitor Amazon Bedrock Guardrails using CloudWatch metrics.

Question 42

A university registrar's digital services team is standardizing an Amazon Bedrock advising assistant that is used by several web and mobile applications. The team needs centrally managed role instructions, prompted JSON response guidelines, runtime values for term, program, and student question, an immutable production configuration, and safeguards that evaluate both user input and generated responses. The static instruction portion should be eligible for Amazon Bedrock Prompt management prompt caching where supported. The applications already use the Converse API. Which implementation will meet these requirements with the LEAST application-side prompt logic?

Create a CHAT prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt management with role instructions, JSON response rules, and variables such as {{term}} and {{program}}. Create a prompt version, invoke Converse with the base model ID, render the template into messages and system fields, and attach the guardrail with guardrailConfig.
Explanation
Incorrect. When invoking a managed prompt through Converse, the versioned prompt ARN is used as modelId and the application supplies values through promptVariables. The application should not send messages or system for that managed prompt because those are defined in the prompt template.
Create a CHAT prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt management with role instructions, JSON response rules, and variables such as {{term}} and {{program}}. Save and test the DRAFT prompt, invoke it with Converse by using the DRAFT prompt ARN as modelId, pass promptVariables, and attach the guardrail with guardrailConfig.
Explanation
Incorrect. A draft is mutable and is appropriate for authoring and testing, not for an immutable production configuration. The production deployment should use a prompt version, which is a point in time snapshot of the prompt and its configurations.
Create a TEXT prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt management with role instructions, JSON response rules, and variables such as {{term}} and {{program}}. Create a prompt version, invoke it with Converse by using the versioned prompt ARN as modelId, pass promptVariables, enable prompt caching, and attach the guardrail with guardrailConfig.
Explanation
Incorrect. Although Prompt management supports TEXT templates, variables, prompt versions, and guardrails with Converse, Prompt management prompt caching requires the CHAT template type. This approach applies the safeguard requirement, but it does not satisfy the requirement for the static instruction portion to be eligible for that caching feature.
Correct answer
Create a CHAT prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt management with role instructions, JSON response rules, and variables such as {{term}} and {{program}}. Create a prompt version, invoke it with Converse by using the versioned prompt ARN as modelId, pass promptVariables, and attach the guardrail with guardrailConfig.
Explanation
Correct. A CHAT prompt supports managed prompt templates for Converse-compatible models and is required for Prompt management prompt caching. A prompt version provides a stable production artifact, promptVariables supply runtime values, and guardrailConfig applies the guardrail during Converse inference.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Prompt management is designed to centralize prompt authoring, testing, versioning, and reuse, including templates with variables such as {{term}}. A prompt variant can define the message, model, and inference configuration, and a production release should use a prompt version rather than a mutable draft, as described in Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock and Deploy prompts in Amazon Bedrock.

For a managed prompt invoked through Converse, the application uses the versioned prompt ARN as modelId and supplies runtime values in promptVariables. The managed prompt already contains the template messages and system instructions, so sending separate messages or system fields shifts prompt assembly back into application code and conflicts with the managed prompt invocation pattern shown in Code examples for Prompt management.

The template type matters because CHAT templates are compatible with Converse-capable models, and Prompt management prompt caching requires the CHAT template type. A TEXT prompt can be useful in other cases, but it does not meet the caching-related constraint in this scenario, as documented in Create prompts in Prompt management.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails complements the instruction framework by enforcing responsible AI safeguards during inference. With the Converse API, the application attaches a guardrail by using guardrailConfig, and guardrails can evaluate user inputs and model responses for configured safeguards such as content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters, and grounding checks, as covered in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and Use a guardrail.

The API does not return redacted text by itself, so the Lambda function or another preprocessing component must perform the actual transformation. Question 43
Skipped
A municipal social services agency's casework platform uses Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API to draft eligibility explanations and to emit tool_use requests that update a case management system. Residents can enter names, phone numbers, national identifiers, and case details in free-form text. The agency requires that raw PII is removed before any foundation model invocation, that no raw Bedrock request or response payloads are captured in Bedrock invocation logging, that Bedrock enforces zero durable retention of FM request and response data, and that sanitized audit records in a versioning-enabled S3 bucket are deleted completely after 90 days. Which implementation best meets these requirements?

Mask input and output by using Bedrock Guardrails sensitive information filters; set Responses API store=false; enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs with KMS encryption; validate tool_use parameters in the tool service; use S3 Lifecycle Expiration and NoncurrentVersionExpiration.
Explanation
Incorrect. Guardrails masking does not ensure that raw input is absent from Bedrock model invocation logs, because the logged input field can contain the original unmodified request when logging is enabled. Setting store=false on the Responses API is not equivalent to Bedrock zero data retention, and validating tool_use parameters only inside the tool service does not filter what the model emits.
Scan the audit bucket by using Macie automated sensitive data discovery; set Bedrock data retention to provider_data_share; leave model invocation logging disabled; apply Guardrails to text plus custom redaction for tool_use parameters; use S3 Lifecycle Expiration and NoncurrentVersionExpiration.
Explanation
Incorrect. Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3 and is not a live prompt redaction mechanism before foundation model invocation. The provider_data_share retention mode is not zero data retention, so it does not meet a requirement to avoid durable request and response retention or provider sharing.
Redact input in Lambda by using Comprehend DetectPiiEntities offsets before invoking Bedrock; set Bedrock data retention to inherit; keep model invocation logging disabled; apply Guardrails to text and tool_use outputs; use S3 Lifecycle Expiration and NoncurrentVersionExpiration.
Explanation
Incorrect. The inherit retention mode depends on the inherited effective policy and does not by itself enforce zero data retention. Bedrock Guardrails sensitive information filters inspect prompts and text responses, but the documented filter does not detect PII in tool_use or function-call output parameters.
Correct answer
Redact input in Lambda by using Comprehend DetectPiiEntities offsets before invoking Bedrock; set Bedrock data retention to none; keep model invocation logging disabled; apply Guardrails to text plus custom redaction for tool_use parameters; use S3 Lifecycle Expiration and NoncurrentVersionExpiration.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities returns entity types and character offsets, so application logic can redact sensitive spans before the text reaches the foundation model. Bedrock zero data retention requires an effective retention mode of none, Guardrails sensitive information filters cover text but not tool_use parameters, and versioned S3 buckets need both current and noncurrent version expiration.
Overall explanation
Privacy-preserving FM interaction design has to protect data at several boundaries, not only at the final response. Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities is appropriate before invocation because it identifies PII entities and returns offsets that an application can use to redact or replace sensitive spans before sending text to the model, as described in DetectPiiEntities. The API does not return redacted text by itself, so the Lambda function or another preprocessing component must perform the actual transformation.

For Bedrock, zero data retention is a separate control from response storage flags. The none retention mode means no request or response data is written to durable storage by AWS or shared with the model provider, and Bedrock blocks requests for models that require retention, as described in Amazon Bedrock data retention. Bedrock also documents that model providers do not automatically receive customer prompts or completions through normal Bedrock operation, but customers remain responsible for security configuration and hosted content under the shared responsibility model in Data protection in Amazon Bedrock.

Guardrails are useful but must be applied with their documented boundaries in mind. Sensitive information filters can block or anonymize PII in prompts and text responses, but they do not detect PII in tool_use or function-call output parameters through supported APIs, as documented in Sensitive information filters. Also, if model invocation logging is enabled, Bedrock can collect request and response data for supported runtime operations, and the guardrails documentation warns that some log and trace fields can contain original PII values, so keeping Bedrock invocation logging disabled and writing only sanitized application logs is the safer design for this requirement, consistent with Model invocation logging.

Finally, retention in a versioning-enabled S3 audit bucket requires lifecycle rules that handle both current and noncurrent versions. An ordinary expiration rule for the current version can add a delete marker in a versioned bucket, while older versions remain unless NoncurrentVersionExpiration is configured, as explained in Elements to describe lifecycle actions.

Question 44
