A retail pharmacy's clinical communications team uses Amazon Bedrock Prompt management for an outreach assistant. The team maintains five candidate prompt configurations as separate release candidates across releases and must run a fixed regression suite of edge cases before promotion. The release process must preserve the approved prompt text and inference configuration for rollback, support automation rather than visual review, and publish pass or fail results to CloudWatch. Which approach will best meet these requirements?

Evaluate the three highest-priority candidate configurations with Prompt builder comparison, run Lambda checks against the selected draft, create a prompt version for that draft, and publish summarized outcomes to CloudWatch.
Explanation
This narrows validation to three candidates, while the team maintains five candidates and needs fixed regression coverage across releases. Prompt builder comparison is useful for interactive testing, but the documented console comparison supports adding up to three variants, so it is not the right control plane for a five-candidate regression gate.
Update the draft prompt for each candidate, run a Lambda regression script through InvokeModelWithResponseStream for all supported text models, validate responses, and overwrite the draft after tests pass.
Explanation
A draft is mutable and does not provide the same snapshot semantics as a prompt version. Prompt management prompts can be used with InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream only when the prompt configuration specifies Anthropic Claude or Meta Llama, so this does not work for all supported text models.
Create separate Prompt management prompts for each candidate, run a scheduled Lambda regression job, write pass or fail events to CloudWatch Logs, and copy the winning text into the production prompt.
Explanation
This automates testing and can record outcomes, but copying only the winning text into production does not preserve the associated inference configuration as a release artifact. Separate prompts can support experimentation, but rollback should rely on version snapshots rather than reconstructing production prompt state.
Correct answer
Create prompt versions for release candidates, run a Step Functions regression workflow that invokes the prompts through the Converse API, validate responses with Lambda, and emit test outcomes to CloudWatch.
Explanation
Correct. Prompt versions create snapshots of the prompt and configuration, which supports controlled promotion and rollback. A Step Functions workflow with Lambda validation provides an automated release gate, and CloudWatch can capture the resulting regression signals.
Overall explanation
Prompt management is useful for prompt QA because it lets teams create, edit, save, test, and reuse prompts while keeping related configuration with the prompt. It supports variables and variants for experimentation, but the console comparison experience is not a substitute for a scalable regression gate because the documented comparison UI supports adding up to three variants. See Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock and Create prompts in Prompt management.

For a release process, the key distinction is between a mutable draft and a version. Saving creates or updates the draft, while creating a version creates a snapshot of the prompt and its configuration, with versions created incrementally starting at 1. That snapshot behavior is what makes the prompt suitable for promotion, rollback, and repeatable QA. See Deploy prompts in Prompt management and Create a prompt version.

The automated workflow can use Step Functions to coordinate the fixed regression suite, Lambda to validate expected output properties such as schema conformance or prohibited response patterns, and CloudWatch to capture pass or fail results for monitoring. Using the Converse API aligns with the documented Prompt management support model for supported text models. By contrast, relying on InvokeModel or InvokeModelWithResponseStream for Prompt management prompts is limited to configurations that specify Anthropic Claude or Meta Llama models, as described in Supported models and Regions for Prompt management.

Question 45
Skipped
An airline catering provider's menu-planning team maintains versioned Amazon Bedrock Prompt management prompts. The team already compares prompt variants in the console before creating prompt versions. The team needs to add troubleshooting controls that expose the actual request and response payloads for failed invocations and detect response format drift with minimal custom telemetry. The solution does not use Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents. Which combination of actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

Use AWS/Bedrock CloudWatch metrics such as InputTokenCount and InvocationLatency to inspect the prompt text and response bodies for failed requests.
Explanation
Incorrect. CloudWatch metrics for Amazon Bedrock runtime are useful for trends, latency, throttling, errors, and token usage. They do not provide prompt text or response bodies, so they cannot support content-level troubleshooting of prompt confusion.
Correct selection
Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging for bedrock-runtime calls to CloudWatch Logs, and configure Amazon S3 large-data delivery in the same account and Region.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging can capture request data, response data, and metadata for supported bedrock-runtime calls such as Converse. CloudWatch Logs can contain JSON bodies up to the documented size limit, and configuring Amazon S3 large-data delivery helps preserve larger bodies in the same account and Region.
Add Lambda application logs for prompt variable keys, request IDs, and parser exceptions, and rely on those logs instead of Bedrock model invocation logging.
Explanation
Incorrect. Lambda application logs can help correlate failures with application behavior, but they do not automatically provide Bedrock runtime request and response payload logging. This approach also shifts payload capture into custom code, which does not meet the requirement for minimal custom telemetry.
Correct selection
Configure structured outputs for the Converse request by using outputConfig.textFormat with a supported JSON Schema subset for the response contract.
Explanation
Correct. Structured outputs constrain model responses to a JSON schema, which directly addresses downstream failures caused by response shape drift. The schema must use supported JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 features, because unsupported features cause immediate validation errors.
Invoke the managed prompt ARN with Converse while supplying system, inferenceConfig, messages, and promptVariables to override the prompt template.
Explanation
Incorrect. When invoking a managed prompt with Converse or ConverseStream, fields such as system and inferenceConfig cannot be included. If messages are included, they are appended after the prompt's messages rather than replacing the prompt template, which can make prompt confusion worse.
Overall explanation
For content-level prompt troubleshooting, Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging is the most direct control because it records supported bedrock-runtime invocations, including request and response data and invocation metadata. The logging feature is disabled by default, and CloudWatch Logs records JSON bodies only up to the documented limit, so configuring an Amazon S3 destination for larger data is important when prompts or contexts can be large. See Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.

Structured outputs address a different failure mode: the model may produce semantically plausible text that does not satisfy the application contract. With Converse APIs, outputConfig.textFormat can constrain the response to a supported JSON schema, which makes format drift detectable instead of letting malformed responses reach a parser later. The schema must stay within the supported subset, because unsupported JSON Schema features can cause immediate 400 errors, as described in Structured outputs.

CloudWatch metrics such as token counts, invocation latency, throttles, and client or server errors help identify operational trends, but they are not prompt-content logs. Managed prompts also have specific invocation rules: when the prompt ARN is supplied as modelId, the application passes promptVariables, and the prompt template already defines the prompt content. The restrictions for managed prompts and the role of prompt versions are covered in Test a prompt, while runtime metrics are covered in Monitor Amazon Bedrock runtime using CloudWatch metrics. Lambda application logs can be useful for correlation, but relying on them instead of Bedrock model invocation logging would require custom payload capture and would not provide the managed Bedrock runtime logging control needed here.

A seaport terminal operator's berth-planning team runs an internal web application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The security team requires the endpoint to be reachable only from the VPC, clients must not receive AWS credentials, malformed JSON should be rejected before compute is invoked when possible, and request rates must be throttled to stay within downstream model capacity. Which architecture will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom integration code?

Correct answer
Expose an API Gateway private REST API through an interface VPC endpoint. Configure a resource policy, request validation, throttling, and a Lambda proxy integration that calls the metadata service and Amazon Bedrock Runtime.
Explanation
Correct. A private REST API can be invoked only through an interface VPC endpoint and can use a resource policy to restrict access further. API Gateway request validation and throttling reduce custom code, while Lambda is the right integration point for calling the internal microservice and Amazon Bedrock synchronously.
Expose an API Gateway HTTP API with a VPC link. Configure a JWT authorizer, route throttling, and a Lambda integration that calls the metadata service and Amazon Bedrock Runtime.
Explanation
A VPC link for an HTTP API is used to connect API Gateway to private integration targets, not to make the API itself private to VPC callers. This also does not provide the same REST API request model validation capability needed to reject malformed JSON before compute is invoked.

However, a direct service integration does not provide the custom orchestration needed to retrieve vessel metadata from an internal HTTPS microservice before constructing the Bedrock request.

Explanation
A regional REST API can support validation, throttling, and Lambda integration, but it creates a public API endpoint unless additional controls are added. This does not satisfy the requirement that the endpoint be reachable only from the VPC.
Overall explanation
For a synchronous GenAI enhancement inside an existing private application, API Gateway private REST APIs are a strong fit because callers access the API through an interface VPC endpoint instead of a public internet endpoint. API Gateway can enforce a resource policy, validate request bodies against a model, and apply throttling before requests reach downstream compute, reducing the amount of custom defensive code needed in the integration layer.

Lambda is the practical adapter when the request must be enriched with data from an internal microservice before invoking a foundation model. The function can call the vessel metadata service, construct the prompt or model payload, invoke InvokeModel on Amazon Bedrock Runtime, and return the generated brief through the same request path. A regional public API misses the private-only endpoint requirement, an HTTP API VPC link solves a different problem, and a direct Bedrock integration lacks the orchestration step required by the scenario.

Relevant documentation: Private REST APIs in API Gateway, Request validation for REST APIs in API Gateway, Usage plans and API keys for REST APIs, Set up Lambda proxy integrations in API Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock Runtime InvokeModel.

Question 47
Skipped
A renewable energy grid operator's maintenance analytics team is building a generative AI assistant that drafts incident handoff notes from technician reports. Reports arrive as emails and web forms in plain text. The same turbine model, substation, dates, and measurements appear in inconsistent aliases, date formats, capitalization, and units. The team must preserve the original reports, improve FM response consistency before generation, and provide structured fields to a workflow engine. The solution must avoid custom model training and must not require technicians to change how they submit reports. Which TWO steps should the team implement?

Increase the chunk size and embedding dimensions for each report, and rely on semantic retrieval to include more raw context.
Explanation
Incorrect. Larger chunks or higher-dimensional embeddings may affect retrieval behavior and storage cost, but they do not standardize inconsistent source text. Providing more raw context can still leave the FM to resolve conflicting aliases, formats, and units at generation time.
Correct selection
Run Amazon Comprehend entity detection and key phrase extraction on each report, and store extracted values as metadata and prompt variables.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Comprehend can extract entities such as dates, locations, organizations, quantities, and key phrases from unstructured text without training a custom model. Persisting those extracted values gives the application stable fields that can be used in prompts, filters, and downstream workflow logic.
Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to mask PII and block denied topics for each report, and use the filtered text as the canonical record.
Explanation
Incorrect. Bedrock Guardrails are designed for safety controls such as content filtering, denied topics, PII handling, and grounding checks. They do not normalize aliases, convert units, or produce the structured incident fields required by the workflow.
Correct selection
Invoke an AWS Lambda preprocessing function to standardize aliases, dates, units, capitalization, and delimiters into a canonical JSON record.
Explanation
Correct. Lambda is appropriate for deterministic normalization logic, such as applying alias maps, converting units, and emitting a fixed JSON structure. This keeps the original report intact while giving the FM and workflow engine a consistent representation.
Lower the model temperature and top_p for the generation request, and ask the FM to infer a consistent schema from raw text.
Explanation
Incorrect. Lower sampling parameters can make generation less random, but they do not improve the quality or consistency of the input data. Asking the FM to infer structure from raw text also delays normalization until generation and is less reliable than creating validated fields first.
Overall explanation
For inconsistent operational text, a strong pattern is to separate extraction, normalization, and generation. Amazon Comprehend can identify entities and key phrases in plain text, which turns free-form reports into structured signals that are easier to reference in prompts and downstream workflows. See Detect entities and Detect key phrases.

AWS Lambda is a good fit for deterministic transformations that should not depend on an FM's probabilistic behavior, such as alias lookup, date parsing, unit conversion, casing cleanup, and JSON construction. This preserves the original report as the source of record while creating a canonical representation for the FM. Lambda is commonly used to run event-driven preprocessing logic, as described in What is AWS Lambda?.

Guardrails, larger embeddings, and lower temperature can each be useful in the right place, but they solve different problems. Bedrock Guardrails help apply safety and compliance controls, not general data normalization, as described in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Retrieval tuning and generation parameter tuning may improve retrieval behavior or reduce randomness, but neither creates validated structured fields from messy source data.

Question 48
Skipped
An online brokerage's platform risk team is replacing voluntary guardrail usage with centralized controls for Amazon Bedrock. Several product accounts in AWS Organizations invoke Bedrock Runtime directly from services, and audit sampling found that some requests omit application guardrail identifiers. The production workload is approved in one AWS Region today, but the firm wants the same governance pattern whenever an additional Region is approved. The team must enforce centrally managed responsible AI safeguards for the designated accounts, allow trading and compliance applications to add stricter request-level controls, and retain detailed request and response evidence for supported Bedrock Runtime invocations. Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

Configure account-level enforced guardrails in every member account and require each application to include the selected guardrail ID and version. Use AWS CloudTrail events as the only source for prompts, completions, and token usage evidence.
Explanation
Incorrect. Account-level and request-specific guardrails can be useful, but requiring every application call to supply a guardrail does not provide centralized governance from AWS Organizations. CloudTrail provides API audit events, but model invocation logging is the separate Bedrock feature that captures detailed request and response data for supported runtime invocations.
Add an automated reasoning policy to the centrally approved guardrails and attach organization-level enforcement policies to the relevant accounts. Use application-specific guardrails only for exceptions that should relax the baseline controls.
Explanation
Incorrect. Automated reasoning policies are not supported in enforced guardrails, and AWS warns that including them can cause runtime failures. Application-specific guardrails are combined with enforced guardrails by union semantics, so they can add stricter controls but cannot relax the baseline.
Correct selection
Create centrally approved guardrails in the management account for each required Region and publish fixed guardrail versions. Attach AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policies to the target OUs or accounts that reference those regional versions.
Explanation
Correct. AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policies are designed to enforce Amazon Bedrock Guardrails safeguards at the root, OU, or account scope for Bedrock model inference calls. These policies are Region-specific and require a specific guardrail version, so each approved Region needs its own versioned guardrail reference.
Create one centrally approved guardrail in the management account and attach one AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policy to all target OUs. Reference the guardrail's draft version and use the same guardrail ARN for every approved Region.
Explanation
Incorrect. Amazon Bedrock policies are Region-specific and require separate guardrails for each AWS Region where the controls are enforced. A single regional guardrail reference and draft-based governance do not provide the versioned, regional enforcement model required for this scenario.
Correct selection
Configure resource-based policies on the centrally approved guardrails for the member accounts and grant invoking roles permission to apply guardrails. Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging in each workload account and Region to same-account, same-Region destinations.
Explanation
Correct. Organization-level enforcement uses guardrails that exist in the organization administrator or management account, so member accounts need access through guardrail resource-based policies and callers need identity permission to apply the guardrail. Model invocation logging is the Bedrock capability for capturing request data, response data, and metadata for supported runtime calls, and it is enabled per account and Region.
Overall explanation
AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policies are the central governance mechanism for applying Amazon Bedrock Guardrails across a root, OU, or account scope for model inference calls. The policy references a guardrail in the management account, but policies require a specific guardrail version and are Region-specific, so workloads in each approved Region need an appropriate versioned regional guardrail reference. See Amazon Bedrock policies in AWS Organizations.

Bedrock guardrail enforcement is layered: organization-level, account-level, and application or request-specific guardrails can all apply. The effective control is the union of applicable guardrails, with the most restrictive overlapping control taking precedence, so application teams can add stricter controls but cannot weaken the centrally enforced baseline. Enforced guardrails must also avoid unsupported safeguards such as automated reasoning policies, as described in Guardrail enforcements.

Because the enforced guardrail resides in the organization administrator or management account, member accounts need access through a guardrail resource-based policy, and invoking principals need identity permissions such as bedrock:ApplyGuardrail, as described in Resource-based policies for guardrails. For governance evidence, model invocation logging is separate from CloudTrail and can capture detailed request data, response data, and metadata for supported Bedrock Runtime calls when enabled with same-account, same-Region destinations. CloudTrail remains important for API auditability, but it is not a substitute for Bedrock model invocation logs, as documented in Model invocation logging and Log Amazon Bedrock API calls with AWS CloudTrail.

Question 49

An online education provider's tutoring platform invokes Amazon Bedrock by using ConverseStream for chat and InvokeModel for image-based feedback in two AWS Regions. The teams want to avoid building a custom request logger, and all logging destinations must remain in the workload account and Region where each invocation occurs. Which observability design meets these requirements?

Correct answer

Send tenant and lesson identifiers as requestMetadata on ConverseStream calls and as the request metadata header on InvokeModel calls. Create CloudWatch dashboards from AWS/Bedrock runtime and delivery metrics.
Explanation
This design uses the managed Bedrock invocation logging capability in the same account and Region as the invocations. S3 delivery supports large JSON bodies and binary image data, while request metadata provides caller-supplied tenant and lesson fields for filtering forensic records.
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging in each workload Region with CloudWatch Logs delivery only. Send tenant and lesson identifiers as requestMetadata on ConverseStream calls and as the request metadata header on InvokeModel calls. Create CloudWatch dashboards from AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics and inline log bodies.
Explanation
CloudWatch Logs delivery can capture supported inline JSON bodies only within the documented inline size behavior. Large request or response bodies and binary image outputs require S3 delivery, so this design does not meet the stated payload requirements.
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging in each workload Region with CloudWatch Logs and S3 delivery. Send tenant and lesson identifiers as the request metadata header on all Bedrock runtime calls. Create CloudWatch dashboards from AWS/Bedrock runtime and delivery metrics.
Explanation
The metadata mechanism differs by operation family. Converse and ConverseStream use the request-body requestMetadata field, while InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream use the request metadata HTTP header.
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging in each workload Region with CloudWatch Logs and S3 delivery. Send tenant and lesson identifiers as requestMetadata on ConverseStream calls and as the request metadata header on InvokeModel calls. Build centralized dashboards from aggregated invocation log records only.
Explanation
Writing invocation logs locally avoids the regional delivery problem, and the log records can support forensic filtering by caller-supplied metadata. However, invocation log records are not a substitute for the documented AWS/Bedrock runtime and delivery metrics needed for latency, throttling, prompt caching, and delivery health dashboards.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging is the managed feature intended for forensic visibility into supported runtime calls. It is disabled by default and is configured per AWS account and per Region, with delivery to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or both in the same account and Region. Because the workload includes payloads larger than 100 KB and binary image responses, S3 delivery is needed for the data that cannot be delivered inline to CloudWatch Logs. See Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.

For business-level traceability, Bedrock supports per-request metadata on individual runtime inference calls. The correct mechanism depends on the API: Converse and ConverseStream use the requestMetadata request-body field, while InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream use the X-Amzn-Bedrock-Request-Metadata HTTP header. The metadata is recorded only when invocation logging is enabled in the Region where the call is made, and it is subject to documented limits. See Track Amazon Bedrock model invocation using invocation tagging.

Operational dashboards should use the AWS/Bedrock CloudWatch metrics that the Bedrock runtime publishes, such as invocation counts, latency, throttles, token counts, time to first token for streaming calls, prompt cache token metrics, and model invocation log delivery success or failure metrics. This separates aggregate service health monitoring from detailed forensic records, which is a practical observability pattern for FM applications. See Monitor Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics with Amazon CloudWatch.

Question 50
Skipped
A pharmaceutical research platform team exposes a generative AI endpoint through an Amazon API Gateway REST API and AWS Lambda. The Lambda function calls Amazon Bedrock to summarize investigator notes for internal users. During bursts at shift changes, some requests receive throttling or timeout errors from downstream services. The users need synchronous responses when the system is healthy, but the application must degrade gracefully during sustained downstream failures. The team also needs trace visibility across the API layer, Lambda function, and downstream AWS SDK calls. Which implementation will meet these requirements with the MOST resilient operational design?

Configure Lambda reserved concurrency as the primary rate control, use fixed-interval retries for Bedrock calls, add a fallback that invokes the same model in another Region, and enable CloudWatch metrics without distributed tracing.
Explanation
Reserved concurrency can protect a Lambda function, but it is a coarse control and does not replace API-level throttling for clients. Fixed-interval retries can synchronize retry storms, and a cross-Region fallback can add complexity without providing the required distributed trace visibility.
Configure API Gateway throttling above peak client demand, use immediate retries in Lambda for Bedrock errors, add a longer Lambda timeout for all requests, and enable CloudWatch Logs only for the Lambda function.
Explanation
Setting throttling above peak demand does not protect the downstream model invocation path from bursts. Immediate retries and longer timeouts can amplify congestion during throttling events, and Lambda logs alone do not provide trace visibility across service boundaries.
Configure API Gateway caching for prompt requests, use client-side retries from each application, add a secondary Lambda function for manual replay, and enable AWS X-Ray active tracing only on the REST API stage.
Explanation
API Gateway caching is not a general resilience mechanism for non-deterministic prompt responses and does not address downstream throttling reliably. Pushing retry behavior to clients creates inconsistent retry patterns, and tracing only the REST API stage leaves a visibility gap in Lambda and downstream calls.
Correct answer
Configure API Gateway throttling to match downstream capacity, use AWS SDK exponential backoff retries in Lambda, return a cached fallback after a failure threshold, and enable X-Ray active tracing for the REST API stage and Lambda with X-Ray SDK instrumentation of the Lambda AWS SDK client.
Explanation
This approach limits request rate before downstream capacity is exceeded, retries transient failures with backoff, and provides a graceful fallback when failures persist. Enabling X-Ray active tracing for the REST API stage and Lambda, plus instrumenting the Lambda AWS SDK client, provides trace visibility into downstream SDK calls as subsegments.
Overall explanation
Resilient FM systems usually combine backpressure, bounded retries, graceful degradation, and observability. API Gateway throttling and usage controls help shape incoming traffic before it reaches Lambda and the model invocation path. The AWS SDK retry modes use exponential backoff patterns for retryable failures, which is safer than tight retry loops because it gives the downstream service time to recover.

A fallback response should be treated as a degradation path, not as a way to hide all errors. For example, a cached summary template, a previously generated result, or a message that asks the user to retry later can preserve user experience during sustained failures without continuing to overload the model. The key is to trigger the fallback after bounded retries or a circuit-breaker style failure threshold, rather than retrying indefinitely.

AWS X-Ray complements CloudWatch Logs and metrics by showing request traces across supported services. For API Gateway, active tracing is documented for REST APIs, so specifying the REST API endpoint type matters when the design relies on API-layer X-Ray traces. Active tracing for Lambda provides function-level trace data, and instrumenting the Lambda AWS SDK client with the X-Ray SDK lets downstream AWS SDK calls appear as subsegments so engineers can locate whether latency or errors are occurring in the API layer, function code, or model invocation path. See the AWS documentation for Throttle API requests for better throughput, Retry behavior, Amazon API Gateway and AWS X-Ray, and Patching libraries.

Question 51
Skipped
A regional credit union's compliance automation team is adding an analyst-facing review panel to a loan-dispute assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock for multi-turn conversations. Analysts want to see model-generated reasoning when the selected model provides it, but security policy forbids exposing provider-redacted reasoning content. The application already applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to user inputs and model responses, and follow-up turns must continue reliably after an analyst reviews the conversation. The team accepts extra latency only for cases routed to this review panel. Which implementation will provide the required transparency while preserving supported multi-turn behavior?

Route review-panel requests through Converse with Guardrails enabled, display reasoning blocks after guardrail filtering, create a new conversation state after each analyst review, and resend only the current prompt.
Explanation
Bedrock Guardrails help filter inputs and model responses, but the documentation excludes reasoning content blocks from that guardrail filtering. Starting a new conversation with only the current prompt also fails the requirement to continue the reviewed multi-turn conversation reliably.
Route review-panel requests through RetrieveAndGenerate, display citations entries as the reasoning trace, pass retrieved references as the next turn's prior messages, and ignore Converse reasoning fields.
Explanation
Knowledge Base citations provide source attribution for generated response parts and retrieved references, not the model's reasoning trace. Retrieved references do not replace Converse message history or reasoning signatures for multi-turn reasoning-capable conversations.
Route review-panel requests through Converse, decode reasoningContent.redactedContent into display text when reasoningText is absent, omit reasoning signatures from saved history, and replay only user-visible messages.
Explanation
The redactedContent member is provider-encrypted reasoning content that is redacted for safety reasons, not a fallback explanation for analysts. Omitting signatures and the prior message history can break supported multi-turn Converse behavior when reasoning signatures are involved.
Correct answer
Route review-panel requests to a reasoning-capable model through Converse, render returned reasoningContent.reasoningText when present, preserve the returned signature with the full message history, and hide redactedContent.
Explanation
This uses the documented Converse reasoning field and handles the ReasoningContentBlock union correctly. Preserving the reasoning signature with the previous messages supports later multi-turn Converse requests and avoids treating provider-redacted reasoning as displayable text.
Overall explanation
Transparent FM output design should distinguish between model reasoning, source attribution, and safety filtering. For reasoning-capable models, the Amazon Bedrock Converse API can return reasoningContent, and streaming calls can emit partial reasoning content in content block deltas, as described in Carry out a conversation with the Converse API operations.

The reasoning block must be handled carefully because ReasoningContentBlock is a union: it can contain either reasoningText or redactedContent, but not both. The redactedContent value is base64-encoded reasoning content encrypted by the model provider for safety reasons, so an application should not treat it as user-facing explanatory text. See ReasoningContentBlock for the documented structure.

Multi-turn behavior is another important constraint. When reasoningText.signature is returned, Bedrock documents that the signature is a tamper safeguard and that later Converse requests must include the signature and all previous messages. Dropping hidden or non-user-visible parts of the conversation transcript can cause later requests to fail or lose continuity.

Guardrails and citations solve different transparency and governance problems. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails explicitly excludes reasoning content blocks from guardrail filtering, and RetrieveAndGenerate returns citations for source attribution rather than model reasoning. Also, model reasoning is best reserved for cases that need it because AWS notes that reasoning is useful for complex tasks but can add latency and output-token overhead in Reasoning models in Amazon Bedrock.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 52
Skipped
A renewable energy grid operator's operations platform team is building an Amazon Bedrock agent that helps dispatchers inspect turbine status and open maintenance work orders in an internal CMMS. In integration tests, the agent usually chooses the correct tool, but it occasionally sends plant codes in an unsupported format, uses priority values that the CMMS does not accept, or creates descriptions that exceed the CMMS field limit. The team wants to keep managed agent orchestration, make the tool contract reusable for future agents, and prevent invalid write operations from reaching the CMMS. Which TWO actions should the team take to improve tool reliability while meeting these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Add detailed prompt instructions that list valid plant codes, priority values, and description limits, and rely on the agent to self-correct invalid tool arguments.
Explanation
This is incorrect because prompt instructions can improve model behavior but are not a deterministic validation boundary. The requirement is to prevent invalid write operations from reaching the CMMS, which requires executable validation logic rather than relying only on model compliance.
Subscribe CloudWatch Logs to a Lambda function that detects validation failures after invocation and submits corrected CMMS requests using parsed trace details.
Explanation
This is incorrect because log processing is an after-the-fact observability pattern, not a safe control point for preventing invalid mutations. Replaying corrected requests from logs also creates reliability and idempotency risks, especially for write operations.
Correct selection
Implement the action group Lambda handler to normalize and validate parameters, enforce backend limits, and return structured errors before calling the CMMS.
Explanation
This is correct because a Lambda action group handler is the right place to apply deterministic validation and error handling before invoking the downstream system. The model can still produce imperfect arguments, so backend-facing code must enforce limits and return predictable responses.
Configure an API Gateway request validator on the InvokeAgent client API, using the same JSON schema to reject requests that include invalid maintenance fields.
Explanation
This is incorrect because an API Gateway validator in front of the client request validates the user-facing API payload, not the internal parameters that the agent later generates for a tool call. The invalid values in this scenario are produced during orchestration, so validation must occur at the tool integration boundary.
Correct selection
Define each maintenance operation in an OpenAPI schema in Amazon S3, including required fields, types, parameter descriptions with valid value guidance, and response shapes for the Bedrock action group.
Explanation
This is correct because Bedrock agent action groups can use an OpenAPI schema to describe the tools that the agent can call. A precise schema gives the model a reusable, standardized contract for operation names, parameters, request bodies, and expected responses. Valid values can be documented in descriptions for model guidance, while deterministic enforcement belongs in the handler.
Overall explanation
For Bedrock agents, the durable way to integrate tools is to give the agent a precise tool contract and then enforce that contract in code. An action group can be defined with an OpenAPI schema stored in Amazon S3, which helps the agent understand available operations, parameter names, required fields, types, parameter descriptions, and response formats. The schema guides tool use, but supported schema features should not be treated as a complete enforcement layer for every backend rule. See the AWS documentation for Add an action group to your agent in Amazon Bedrock.

The schema improves tool selection and argument construction, but it does not replace deterministic validation. A Lambda action group handler should normalize inputs, check values such as plant codes and priorities, enforce length limits, apply idempotency safeguards where needed, and return a structured error response instead of calling the downstream CMMS when validation fails. AWS documents the event and response pattern for this integration in AWS Lambda functions for Amazon Bedrock agent action groups.

Prompt-only controls are useful as guidance, but they are not a reliable enforcement layer because foundation model outputs are probabilistic. API Gateway request validation can protect a public client API, but it does not validate parameters that the agent generates internally for an action group. CloudWatch log processing is valuable for troubleshooting and audit workflows, but using logs to repair or replay write operations is an anti-pattern when the requirement is to block invalid operations before they affect the backend.

Question 53
Skipped
A digital media streaming service's personalization science team is selecting among three Amazon Bedrock text models for a production synopsis generator. The team has 750 representative prompts prepared in Amazon S3. The 750 prompts are stored in S3 as a valid JSON Lines (.jsonl) custom prompt dataset for the summarization task. The team wants an automated, repeatable first-pass evaluation before any human preference study. The evaluation must use the same dataset and the same summarization task definition for each model, save results for analysis, and avoid building a custom evaluator service. Which approach will meet these requirements?

Create three automatic model evaluation jobs with CreateEvaluationJob, one for each model or inference profile. Use the built-in summarization prompt dataset, the same task type, and S3 output configurations with an evaluation role.
Explanation
This approach remains automated and uses the correct one-job-per-model structure, but it does not use the team's prepared representative dataset. Built-in prompt datasets for automatic evaluation are randomly down sampled to 100 prompts, so they would not satisfy the requirement to evaluate the same 750-prompt dataset.
Create one automatic model evaluation job with CreateEvaluationJob that lists all three models or inference profiles. Use the same S3 .jsonl prompt dataset, the summarization task type, and one S3 output configuration with an evaluation role.
Explanation
This approach would be attractive because it appears to centralize the comparison, but it does not match how automated model evaluation jobs are constrained. For model evaluation jobs, automated jobs support a single model or inference profile, so one job cannot evaluate all three models together.
Correct answer
Create three automatic model evaluation jobs with CreateEvaluationJob, one for each model or inference profile. Use the same S3 .jsonl prompt dataset, the same summarization task type, and S3 output configurations with an evaluation role.
Explanation
This approach fits the automated first-pass requirement and respects the limit that an automated model evaluation job supports one model or inference profile. A 750-prompt custom dataset is within the documented limit for automatic evaluation jobs, and using the same dataset and task type keeps the comparison controlled.
Create three automatic model evaluation jobs with CreateEvaluationJob, one for each model or inference profile. Configure multiple task types in each job, use the same S3 .jsonl prompt dataset, and write results to S3.
Explanation
Running one automated job per model is the right overall structure, but configuring multiple task types in the same model evaluation job is not supported. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs allow one task type per job, so the summarization task must be kept as the single task type for this controlled comparison.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock model evaluations are designed for this kind of systematic comparison without building a custom scoring pipeline. The key design constraint is that an automatic model evaluation job evaluates one selected model or inference profile, so comparing three candidates requires three separate jobs that share the same prompt dataset and task type. The CreateEvaluationJob API also requires evaluation configuration, output data configuration, and a role ARN, which is why the evaluation role and S3 output location are part of the correct implementation.

The custom dataset is also important. Built-in automatic evaluation datasets are down sampled to 100 prompts, while a custom prompt dataset for automatic evaluation can contain up to 1,000 prompts, must be stored in Amazon S3, and must use JSON Lines with a .jsonl extension. A 750-prompt representative dataset is therefore appropriate for an automatic evaluation job, and reusing it across the three jobs helps isolate model behavior from dataset variation.

Human-based evaluations remain valuable later, especially for subjective preference, tone, and user experience judgments. They are not the best first step here because the team requested an automated screening run over its prepared prompt set before moving to a preference study. For more detail, see Evaluate models and RAG systems using Amazon Bedrock Evaluations, CreateEvaluationJob, Create an automatic model evaluation job, and Prompt datasets for model evaluation jobs.

A nationwide legal aid network's intake automation team uses an Amazon Bedrock model to generate short case summaries from client intake notes. Which approach best meets these requirements?

Explanation
Checking the total prompt count and aggregate scores is not enough to enforce full benchmark coverage. Automated evaluation reports can show fewer model responses than total prompts, and only model responses are used in metric calculations.
Create an automatic ModelEvaluation job from the custom S3 .jsonl dataset, provide two inference profiles for baseline and candidate models, poll ListEvaluationJobs with nextToken until terminal status, and fail the gate on comparison regressions.
Explanation
Automatic model evaluation jobs support one model or inference profile in the inference configuration. Comparing two models or inference profiles in a single evaluation job is supported for human-worker model evaluation jobs, which is a different evaluation approach.
Create an automatic RagEvaluation job from the custom S3 .jsonl dataset, provide roleArn and outputDataConfig.s3Uri, poll ListEvaluationJobs with nextToken until terminal status, and fail the gate on missing responses or metric regressions.
Explanation
A RAG evaluation is for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation sources or systems, not for directly regression testing a model on a summarization benchmark. The scenario requires a model evaluation job because the release gate is measuring generated summaries from a Bedrock model against a fixed prompt dataset.
Correct answer
Create an automatic ModelEvaluation job from the custom S3 .jsonl dataset, provide roleArn and outputDataConfig.s3Uri, poll ListEvaluationJobs with nextToken until terminal status, and fail the gate on missing responses or metric regressions.
Explanation
This approach uses an unattended automatic model evaluation with the required S3 dataset and S3 output location. It accounts for asynchronous job creation, pagination when enumerating jobs, and the need to inspect response coverage before trusting aggregate metric results.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Evaluations is appropriate for this release quality gate because automatic evaluation jobs can run programmatically and write auditable results to Amazon S3. The CreateEvaluationJob API accepts the job and returns HTTP 202 with a jobArn, so the pipeline must wait for a terminal job status instead of treating job creation as a completed evaluation. The API also requires a roleArn and outputDataConfig.s3Uri, which are necessary for Bedrock to perform the evaluation and store results. See CreateEvaluationJob and Evaluate models and RAG systems.

For a fixed regression benchmark, a custom automatic evaluation dataset must be stored in Amazon S3 as a .jsonl file and can contain up to 1,000 prompts per automatic evaluation job, so the 900-prompt dataset fits within the documented limit. Evaluation outputs are stored as .jsonl files in the configured S3 location, which gives the team an auditable artifact for each deployment decision. See Use custom prompt datasets and Model evaluation job results in Amazon S3.

The details that make this a reliable CI/CD gate are the evaluation type, the inference configuration, and the interpretation of results. ModelEvaluation is the correct application type for testing a model on summarization prompts, and an automatic model evaluation job supports one model or inference profile rather than a two-model comparison. Automated reports distinguish total prompts from prompts that received model responses, and Bedrock calculates metrics only from model responses, so the pipeline should inspect the S3 output and fail the gate if response coverage or metric thresholds miss the baseline. See Programmatic model evaluation reports and ListEvaluationJobs.

Question 55
Skipped
A legal publishing firm's knowledge engineering team is preparing a large archive of court opinions and editorial summaries for FM-based question answering. The archive is already registered as tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and the team wants to validate completeness, schema consistency, and basic content constraints before the documents are used for embeddings. The team does not have an existing AWS Glue ETL job for this dataset. The team wants AWS to recommend an initial set of validation rules, run those rules repeatedly on the cataloged data, publish operational signals to Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon EventBridge, and store validation results in Amazon S3. The team does not need row-level failed-record identification. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom code?

Explanation
A Lambda-based validator could be made to publish metrics, events, and reports, but it requires custom implementation of the rule engine and scheduling logic. This is an anti-pattern for the stated goal because AWS Glue Data Quality already provides managed DQDL-based validation for cataloged datasets.
Add AWS Glue Data Quality transforms to a new AWS Glue ETL job, use rule recommendations to bootstrap DQDL rules, schedule recurring job runs, and publish results to CloudWatch, EventBridge, and Amazon S3.
Explanation
AWS Glue Data Quality in ETL jobs is useful when validation must occur inside a pipeline before loading data. However, rule recommendations are not supported for the ETL job entry point, so this does not satisfy the requirement to have AWS recommend the initial rules.
Correct answer
Create AWS Glue Data Quality rulesets from the Data Catalog tables, use rule recommendations to bootstrap DQDL rules, schedule recurring evaluations, and publish results to CloudWatch, EventBridge, and Amazon S3.
Explanation
This option matches a cataloged dataset that does not already have an ETL job. AWS Glue Data Quality for the Data Catalog supports rule recommendations, DQDL rules, recurring evaluations, CloudWatch and EventBridge integration, and writing results to Amazon S3.
Profile the cataloged data in SageMaker Data Wrangler, export transformation steps for recurring validation, emit custom metrics to CloudWatch, and write validation reports to Amazon S3 by using a processing workflow.
Explanation
SageMaker Data Wrangler can help inspect and prepare data, but this option requires more custom workflow construction for recurring data quality operations and event signaling. It also does not use AWS Glue Data Quality rule recommendations for cataloged datasets.
Overall explanation
For data that is already represented as tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, the lowest-code path is to use AWS Glue Data Quality directly from the catalog. This entry point is designed for cataloged datasets and can help create an initial ruleset through rule recommendations, then run DQDL-based evaluations over time. See AWS Glue Data Quality.

The key distinction is the entry point. Data quality checks in AWS Glue ETL jobs are better when validation must occur proactively inside a transformation or loading pipeline, especially when you need ETL-specific capabilities such as identifying failed records or dynamic rules. In this scenario, there is no existing ETL pipeline, the data is already cataloged, and the team specifically wants rule recommendations, which points to Data Catalog data quality rather than ETL job data quality.

SageMaker Data Wrangler and custom Lambda validation can both participate in data preparation workflows, but they add implementation burden when the requirement is managed DQDL rules, scheduled evaluations, and AWS-native operational outputs. For FM consumption, validation should catch missing fields, malformed metadata, and content constraints before embedding or retrieval workflows consume the data, while also producing auditable signals through CloudWatch, EventBridge, and S3 results.

Question 56
Skipped
A pharmaceutical benefits manager's digital servicing team is adding a single-turn RAG question-answering feature for members who ask about drug coverage and prior authorization requirements. Internal responsible AI policy requires the system to avoid clinical advice topics, mask member identifiers in prompts and responses, reject answers that are not supported by retrieved plan documents, reject answers that conflict with machine-readable coverage rules, and keep documentation of the approved FM's intended use and limitations. Enforcement must occur before the API returns a response, with minimal custom compliance logic. Which design will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with denied topics, sensitive information filters, contextual grounding checks, and Automated Reasoning checks. Maintain model-card documentation, and use a Lambda response gate to reject results that fail configured checks.
Explanation
Correct. Bedrock Guardrails provide managed controls for restricted topics, PII handling, contextual grounding, and policy reasoning checks, which minimizes custom enforcement code. Lambda can keep the compliance decision in the server-side request path before the API returns a member-facing answer.
Configure a Lambda response gate that uses Amazon Comprehend entity detection, regular expressions, and a coverage-rule engine. Maintain model-card documentation, and reject responses that match restricted-topic or identifier patterns.
Explanation
Incorrect. A Lambda-only gate can support custom redaction and rule checks, but it increases custom compliance logic and does not provide managed contextual grounding for RAG answers. Pattern and entity checks are useful supplemental controls, but they are not equivalent to Guardrails topic, PII, grounding, and policy checks.
Configure Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs with reference contexts and coverage-rule examples. Maintain model-card documentation, and use a Lambda response gate to allow only prompts and models from the latest approved evaluation set.
Explanation
Incorrect. Evaluation jobs can produce governance evidence for a prompt or model version, but they do not validate each generated answer at runtime. A cached approval set for prompts and models can reduce deployment risk, but it cannot prove that a specific response is grounded or consistent with current coverage rules.
Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with denied topics, sensitive information filters, and contextual grounding checks. Maintain model-card documentation, and use a Lambda response gate to reject results that fail grounding or topic checks.
Explanation
Incorrect. This design provides runtime controls for topic restrictions, PII handling, and RAG grounding, but it does not validate the answer against the machine-readable coverage rules. Without an Automated Reasoning check or equivalent policy validation in the request path, conflicting coverage answers can still pass.
Overall explanation
For a policy-compliant RAG application, the strongest design separates runtime enforcement from general prompt guidance and offline evaluation. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be attached to model use to apply managed safety controls such as denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters, contextual grounding, and other checks depending on the configured guardrail capabilities.

Contextual grounding is especially relevant to single-turn RAG question answering because it compares generated answers with grounding sources and the user query, helping identify responses that are not sufficiently supported by retrieved context. See Detect hallucinations using contextual grounding check. For machine-readable policy constraints, Automated Reasoning checks can evaluate whether model output satisfies encoded rules, and a server-side Lambda gate can accept only responses whose configured guardrail outcomes satisfy policy, such as an Automated Reasoning result of valid and grounding checks within configured thresholds.

Model-card documentation complements enforcement by recording the FM's intended use, limitations, evaluation findings, and risk considerations for reviewers. Amazon SageMaker Model Cards illustrate this governance pattern, but documentation alone does not prevent a noncompliant answer from reaching a user. Offline evaluations, prompt approvals, custom pattern matching, and Lambda-only checks can all improve governance, but they do not replace managed per-response controls when the policy requires topic, privacy, grounding, and coverage-rule enforcement before the API returns.

A global shipping line's regulatory compliance team is building an Amazon Bedrock assistant that answers questions about customs procedures from a custom vector knowledge base. The team must implement an accuracy verification step before showing an answer to users. The verifier must inspect source chunks and source metadata, use a relevance signal for each retrieved chunk, and reject answers that do not match a required JSON structure. The team does not want to rely on the knowledge base as an intrinsic truth-checking service. Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Call the RetrieveAndGenerate API, require citations for every sentence, and use the returned retrievedReferences content as the required JSON contract.
Explanation

The retrievedReferences contain cited content, location, and metadata, but this does not replace explicit output validation against the required schema.
Call the Retrieve API with numberOfResults set to 100, accept any answer with matching metadata, and treat high relevance scores as factual confidence.
Explanation
Retrieve can return retrieval results with relevance scores, and numberOfResults can raise the maximum number of results. However, numberOfResults is a maximum rather than a guarantee, and the retrieval score indicates relevance to the query, not whether a generated claim is factually true.
Call the RetrieveAndGenerate API, require citations in the generated answer, and compare each claim to retrievedReferences content and metadata.
Explanation
RetrieveAndGenerate can generate a natural-language answer with citations to retrieved references, and those references can include cited content and metadata. However, this response structure does not provide the per-result relevance score required by the verifier, and citations do not replace explicit JSON Schema validation.
Correct answer
Call the Retrieve API, validate the model output against a JSON Schema, and compare each claim to the returned content, metadata, documentId, and relevance score.
Explanation
This approach uses Retrieve for retrieval evidence, including source content, metadata, documentId, and the optional score that represents relevance to the query. JSON Schema validation and claim comparison are application-level verification controls that reduce unsupported responses without treating the knowledge base as a truth checker.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases helps ground responses by retrieving relevant source material, but it should not be modeled as an automatic truth oracle. The Retrieve operation is the better fit when the application needs to inspect evidence directly, because it returns retrievalResults that can include source content, documentId, location, metadata, and an optional score representing relevance to the query. See Retrieve and Query a knowledge base.

The important design distinction is that relevance is not factuality. A high retrieval score can help prioritize which chunks to check, but the application still needs verification logic that compares generated claims against the retrieved evidence and rejects unsupported claims. A JSON Schema validator complements retrieval by enforcing the response contract, while the source chunks and metadata support claim-level review and auditability.

RetrieveAndGenerate is useful when the application wants Bedrock to generate an answer with citations, but its citation structure is not the same as Retrieve results. The documented Citation object contains a generated response segment and retrievedReferences, and RetrievedReference contains cited content, location, and metadata, while the documented relevance score is part of KnowledgeBaseRetrievalResult returned by Retrieve. See Citation and RetrieveAndGenerate.

A Lambda wrapper can run deterministic pattern checks and Amazon Comprehend PII detection before evidence is written, then call Amazon Bedrock with Guardrails or use the guardrail evaluation API so both the incoming prompt and generated response are checked against centrally managed safety policies.

The application calls InvokeFlow with one JSON payload that contains an incident object, an array of rule excerpts, and a requested tone. The flow already contains one flow input node and a final flow output node. The workflow must run an evidence-summary prompt first, pass that summary into a ruling-draft prompt, and let production mobile clients continue using a stable workflow reference while analysts keep editing the draft flow. Early tests fail when the whole request is connected to every prompt variable. Which TWO changes should the team make to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Create separate flow input nodes for incident, rules, and tone, and connect each input node directly to the matching Prompt node variable.
Explanation
This is incorrect because an Amazon Bedrock flow has exactly one flow input node and begins with that node. The supported pattern is to send one content payload to InvokeFlow and use node input expressions to select the parts needed by later nodes.
Correct selection
Map the input node document into Prompt node inputs by using expressions, and pass the evidence prompt modelCompletion into the ruling prompt.
Explanation
This is correct because a flow input node outputs the InvokeFlow content as document, and node inputs can use expressions to extract the needed parts of upstream input. The evidence Prompt node output is modelCompletion, which is a String that can be passed to a downstream prompt variable for the next generation step.
Invoke the editable flow draft directly from the mobile application, and use a naming convention to identify the production-ready draft.
Explanation
This is incorrect because direct production use of an editable draft does not provide the stable deployment boundary described for Amazon Bedrock Flows. AWS documents publishing immutable flow versions and invoking them through aliases for deployment.
Connect the evidence Prompt node output to a downstream Object input, and rely on runtime validation to parse the generated text into fields.
Explanation
This is incorrect because a Prompt node's documented output is modelCompletion of type String. Amazon Bedrock validates node input and output data types at runtime, so generated text should not be treated as an Object merely because it resembles structured content.
Correct selection
Publish a tested immutable flow version and invoke the workflow from production clients through an alias that targets that version.
Explanation
This is correct because Amazon Bedrock Flows deployment is based on immutable versions and aliases. Using an alias gives production clients a stable reference while the editable draft can continue to change until the next tested version is promoted.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Flows models a workflow as nodes and connections. The flow starts with exactly one flow input node, which takes the content from the InvokeFlow request and makes it available as document. Later node inputs use expressions to extract specific values from upstream inputs, and Amazon Bedrock validates the configured input and output data types at runtime, as described in Amazon Bedrock Flows node types.

For a sequential prompt chain, the important mental model is that each Prompt node is a typed workflow component, not an untyped text box. A Prompt node can fill prompt variables from its inputs, and its documented output is modelCompletion with type String. That makes it appropriate to pass a generated evidence summary into another prompt, but not to pretend the generated text is automatically a typed Object unless the workflow includes an explicit step that produces the required type.

Deployment is a separate concern from draft workflow editing. Amazon Bedrock Flows uses published immutable flow versions and aliases for invocation, which lets production callers use a stable reference while authors continue iterating on the draft. AWS describes this deployment model in Amazon Bedrock Flows.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 60
Skipped
A biotech research institute's compliance engineering team is deploying an internal literature review assistant. The application invokes Amazon Bedrock FMs directly by using Converse and InvokeModel from compute resources in private VPC subnets, and it reads source documents from S3 locations registered in Lake Formation. Security requires inference traffic to stay off the public internet, access to be limited to approved principals and approved model ARNs, Lake Formation table permissions to be enforced rather than bypassed by broad IAM compatibility settings, and model inputs and outputs to be retained for review in the deployment account and Region. Which configuration will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Create an interface VPC endpoint for com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime, attach a restrictive endpoint policy, grant Bedrock invocation through identity-based IAM policies scoped to approved model ARNs, remove IAMAllowedPrincipals or use Lake Formation hybrid access for governed tables, and enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs or S3 in the same account and Region.
Explanation
Correct. The runtime endpoint is the endpoint used for Converse and InvokeModel, and a custom endpoint policy plus identity-based IAM policies provides network and authorization controls. Revoking broad IAMAllowedPrincipals access or using hybrid access lets Lake Formation enforce fine-grained permissions, and model invocation logging is the Bedrock feature that records inputs and outputs to supported same-account, same-Region destinations.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock, keep the default endpoint policy, grant Bedrock invocation through identity-based IAM policies scoped to approved model ARNs, leave IAMAllowedPrincipals with Super for governed tables, and use CloudTrail management events as the record of prompts and responses.
Explanation
Incorrect. The bedrock endpoint is for control plane API traffic, so it does not cover runtime inference APIs such as Converse and InvokeModel. The default endpoint policy allows full Bedrock access through the endpoint, IAMAllowedPrincipals with Super can bypass Lake Formation governance expectations, and CloudTrail API events are not the Bedrock feature for retaining prompt and response content.
Create interface VPC endpoints for com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agent-runtime and com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agent, attach a restrictive endpoint policy, grant Bedrock invocation through identity-based IAM policies scoped to approved model ARNs, revoke broad Lake Formation grants, and use CloudWatch Bedrock runtime metrics to reconstruct prompt and response content.
Explanation
Incorrect. Agent runtime endpoints are not the endpoint services for direct foundation model runtime APIs in this scenario. CloudWatch runtime metrics are useful for counts, latency, errors, throttles, and token usage, but they do not reconstruct model input and output content for compliance review.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime, attach the default endpoint policy, grant Bedrock invocation through identity-based IAM policies with a wildcard resource scope, grant Lake Formation permissions without changing compatibility defaults, and enable Bedrock model invocation logging to a central S3 bucket in a separate security account.
Explanation
Incorrect. The runtime endpoint is appropriate, but the default endpoint policy and wildcard IAM resource scope do not limit access to approved model ARNs as required. Keeping Lake Formation compatibility defaults can weaken fine-grained governance, and model invocation logging destinations must be in the same account and Region.
Overall explanation
For direct FM invocation from VPC workloads, Amazon Bedrock uses interface VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink. The endpoint suffix matters: com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime is the relevant service name for runtime calls such as Converse and InvokeModel, while the control plane and agent endpoints cover different API families. See Use interface VPC endpoints with Amazon Bedrock.

A VPC endpoint creates private connectivity, but it is not by itself an authorization boundary because the default endpoint policy allows full Bedrock access through the endpoint. Bedrock access should be constrained with a custom endpoint policy and identity-based IAM policies scoped to the required actions and resources, because Bedrock does not support resource-based policies; the IAM behavior is documented in How Amazon Bedrock works with IAM and the model invocation deny examples are in Amazon Bedrock identity-based policy examples.

Lake Formation also has a two-layer model: principals need both IAM permissions and Lake Formation permissions, and the default IAMAllowedPrincipals Super grant can make access behave like IAM-only compatibility mode unless revoked or handled with hybrid access. For compliance retention, enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or both in the same account and Region, rather than relying on CloudWatch metrics or CloudTrail events to preserve request and response bodies. Relevant docs are Lake Formation permissions reference, Log model invocation data, and Monitor Bedrock runtime metrics.

Question 61
Skipped
A maritime logistics operator's port automation team is building a generative AI assistant on Amazon Bedrock. The assistant uses RAG over partner-uploaded manifests and can call backend tools to create berth-change requests. Security testing finds two adversarial patterns: direct jailbreak prompts in chat messages and prompt-injection instructions hidden inside uploaded documents. The team must add managed runtime detection where possible and must run repeatable adversarial tests before each release. The team cannot train or host a custom safety model. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Configure AWS WAF managed rule groups on API Gateway. Tune SQL injection and cross-site scripting rules to inspect request bodies for jailbreak text.
Explanation
This option is incorrect because AWS WAF is designed to protect web applications from common HTTP-layer attacks, not to semantically classify natural-language jailbreak attempts. WAF can be useful at the API edge, but it does not address hidden prompt-injection instructions in RAG context.
Correct selection
Add an automated adversarial test workflow that replays jailbreak prompts and poisoned-document samples through ApplyGuardrail and the application path before release.
Explanation
This option is correct because a repeatable workflow can test known jailbreak and prompt-injection cases before deployment. Using ApplyGuardrail independently and testing the full application path helps catch both policy configuration gaps and orchestration gaps.
Analyze AWS CloudTrail records for Amazon Bedrock API activity after release. Block IAM principals that generated suspicious invocation patterns.
Explanation
This option is incorrect because CloudTrail is primarily an audit mechanism for recording API activity, not a managed runtime classifier for adversarial prompt content. IAM controls are essential for least privilege, but IAM policies do not evaluate the semantic intent of prompt text.
Run Amazon Macie discovery jobs on the manifest bucket. Use the sensitive data findings to quarantine files that contain adversarial instructions.
Explanation
This option is incorrect because Amazon Macie is a data security and DLP service for discovering sensitive data, such as credentials or personal information. Macie findings do not provide prompt-injection or jailbreak intent detection for uploaded documents.
Correct selection
Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with prompt attack, denied topic, and harmful content filters. Apply the guardrail to chat requests and model responses.
Explanation
This option is correct because Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides managed filtering for inputs and outputs, including content filters and prompt attack detection. It reduces the need to build and operate a custom safety classifier, while still requiring proper authorization for any backend tool calls.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is the managed control that best fits runtime protection against unsafe model interactions. Guardrails can evaluate model inputs and outputs for configured policies, including content filtering, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information handling, and prompt attack filtering where supported, as described in Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and Content filters for Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

For prompt injection hidden in retrieved documents, the important mental model is that the application should not blindly place untrusted retrieved text into the model context. The ApplyGuardrail operation can be used outside a direct model invocation to evaluate content before or after it flows through the application, which makes it useful for checking retrieved chunks, tool inputs, or generated responses, as shown in ApplyGuardrail.

Automated adversarial testing complements runtime controls because jailbreak and prompt-injection defenses are configuration-sensitive and application-specific. A workflow built with services such as AWS Step Functions and Lambda can replay a curated corpus of malicious prompts and poisoned-document fixtures, record results, and fail a release when expected guardrail interventions do not occur, using the orchestration concepts in What is AWS Step Functions?.

Edge and governance controls still matter, but they solve different problems. AWS WAF helps with HTTP-layer threats, Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data, and CloudTrail provides auditability, but none of those services is a substitute for semantic prompt-attack filtering and pre-release adversarial regression testing.
