Question 62
Skipped
A private equity firm's research engineering team is replacing a keyword-only search portal with an Amazon Bedrock RAG assistant for investment committee memos, earnings-call transcripts, and SEC filing excerpts stored in Amazon S3. Analysts need semantic retrieval for narrative text, but they also need ticker symbols, clause IDs, and product codes to influence matching when the vector store supports that capability. The security team will allow either the team's approved OpenSearch Service managed clusters or another documented Bedrock Knowledge Bases vector-store integration. The application must use Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval and citations rather than a custom retriever. Which TWO implementation steps should the team include?

Configure OpenSearch managed-cluster indexes with the nmslib engine, matching embedding dimensions, raw-text fields, and Bedrock metadata fields for each topic.
Explanation
This is incorrect. The surrounding index design is close, because Bedrock Knowledge Bases needs compatible dimensions plus mapped text and metadata fields. However, AWS documents that nmslib is not supported for the vector used for search in the Bedrock Knowledge Bases setup for OpenSearch Service managed clusters.
Create a Knowledge Base backed by S3 Vectors using binary embeddings, large parent-chunk metadata, and metadata keys for every source attribute.
Explanation
This is incorrect. S3 Vectors is a documented Bedrock Knowledge Bases vector-store option, but Amazon S3 Vectors supports floating-point embeddings, not binary embeddings. Bedrock Knowledge Bases also documents metadata limits for S3 Vectors, and hierarchical chunking is not recommended with an S3 vector bucket when high token counts can exceed metadata-size limits.
Configure Bedrock retrieval to use HYBRID for every vector store, and request more than 100 results to compensate for parent replacement.
Explanation
This is incorrect. Hybrid retrieval is not universal, because it depends on documented vector-store support and a filterable text field. The KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration API also limits numberOfResults to the documented range, so requesting more than 100 results is not valid.
Correct selection
Configure Bedrock retrieval to use HYBRID only for supported RDS, OpenSearch Serverless, or MongoDB vector stores with a filterable text field, and use SEMANTIC otherwise.
Explanation
This is correct. Hybrid search can combine vector similarity with lexical matching, which helps with ticker symbols, clause IDs, and product codes when the vector-store integration supports it. Bedrock Knowledge Bases currently documents hybrid retrieval for Amazon RDS, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, and MongoDB vector stores with a filterable text field, so other store types, including OpenSearch Service managed clusters, should use semantic search.
Correct selection
Create a customer-managed Knowledge Base backed by OpenSearch vector indexes, and configure supported vector search, matching dimensions, raw-text fields, and Bedrock metadata fields.
Explanation
This is correct. A customer-managed Knowledge Base lets the team keep control of the vector store while using Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval and citations. The OpenSearch index must be configured with compatible vector search settings, embedding dimensions that match the selected embedding model, and the text and metadata fields that Bedrock maps during retrieval.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is a RAG integration point, not a model-training mechanism. It connects to data sources, retrieves relevant information at query time, and can use retrieved content to generate grounded responses with citations, as described in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

For an architecture that keeps Bedrock Knowledge Bases in the retrieval path while allowing the team to manage its own vector layer, a customer-managed Knowledge Base backed by OpenSearch is a valid pattern. The vector index must be compatible with Bedrock's expectations, including matching embedding dimensions and the required raw text and metadata mappings. AWS documents setup requirements and caveats for supported vector stores in Set up a vector store for your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and the supported creation paths in Create a knowledge base.

Hybrid search is useful when identifiers and exact terms matter alongside semantic similarity, but it is conditional rather than guaranteed for every vector store. In KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration, overrideSearchType can be set to HYBRID or SEMANTIC, but AWS documents hybrid search only for supported vector-store configurations that contain a filterable text field. Current Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation identifies Amazon RDS, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, and MongoDB vector stores for hybrid retrieval, while OpenSearch Service managed clusters remain valid Bedrock Knowledge Bases vector stores but are not currently documented for hybrid retrieval. The same API also documents the valid numberOfResults range, as shown in KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration.

Several plausible alternatives fail on documented limits. OpenSearch managed clusters cannot use nmslib for the Bedrock Knowledge Bases search vector setup. S3 Vectors can be a valid vector-store path, but Bedrock Knowledge Bases documents floating-point embeddings and metadata limits for that integration, and Chunking options for Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases cautions against hierarchical chunking with an S3 vector bucket when high token counts can exceed metadata-size limits.

Question 63
Skipped
A civil engineering consultancy's urban analytics team is extending an FM agent with tools for parcel zoning checks and traffic simulation. The toolset is already implemented as a containerized MCP server that uses native GIS libraries, can run multi-step tool invocations with progress notifications, and must run in the team's VPC behind existing ALB, WAF, CloudWatch logging, Secrets Manager, and Parameter Store controls. The team also has existing MCP-aware clients that expect normal MCP tool access. Which implementation will best satisfy these requirements?

Correct answer
Deploy the MCP server image as an Amazon ECS on Fargate service in the VPC, front it with the existing ALB and WAF controls, and use the server's MCP endpoint from MCP clients.
Explanation
Correct. AWS guidance for containerized custom MCP servers describes an ECS/Fargate architecture with images in Amazon ECR, private VPC placement, load balancing, WAF, CloudWatch logs, Secrets Manager, and Parameter Store. This approach preserves the MCP server model for complex custom tools and aligns with the stated networking and security controls.
Deploy the MCP server image to AgentCore Runtime, expose the MCP endpoint at the existing container path, and keep stateless_http=True for all tool invocations.
Explanation
Incorrect. AgentCore Runtime can deploy and run MCP server containers, but the documented container contract requires the MCP server to be available at 0.0.0.0:8000/mcp and to use streamable HTTP transport. Stateless MCP is the default for basic servers, but stateful MCP is used when the server needs features such as progress notifications or session context across requests.
Register the container endpoint as an AgentCore Gateway HTTP target, place it behind the existing ALB and WAF controls, and use Gateway aggregation for a consolidated tools/list.
Explanation
Incorrect. AgentCore Gateway HTTP targets send traffic directly and do not provide MCP aggregation or protocol translation. Aggregation into a consolidated tools/list is documented for MCP targets, not HTTP targets.
Expose the GIS functions as AgentCore Gateway Lambda targets, define each tool with inputSchema and outputSchema, and send MCP JSON-RPC payloads through the Lambda event.
Explanation
Incorrect. Lambda targets are useful for custom code behind Gateway tool invocations, but Gateway passes an event object containing properties from the tool inputSchema, not an arbitrary MCP JSON-RPC envelope. This also does not fit the requirement for an already containerized MCP server with multi-step stateful behavior and progress notifications.
Overall explanation
For complex custom toolsets that already exist as a containerized MCP server, the most direct fit is to host that server as an application workload. AWS guidance for deploying MCP servers on AWS describes an Amazon ECS on Fargate pattern with container images in Amazon ECR, private VPC placement, ALB or CloudFront fronting layers, AWS WAF, CloudWatch logs, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Cognito OAuth, and DynamoDB-backed session or token mappings. See Deploying Model Context Protocol servers on AWS.

AgentCore Gateway is useful when converting APIs, Lambda functions, and services into MCP-compatible tools, or when connecting pre-existing MCP servers through Gateway endpoints. However, its target types matter. MCP targets support aggregation, where Gateway acts like one virtual MCP server and consolidates capabilities into tools/list, while HTTP targets forward traffic directly without aggregation or protocol translation. See Supported targets in AgentCore Gateway and What is Amazon Bedrock AgentCore?.

Lambda targets are a strong pattern for lightweight tool implementation, but the Lambda integration has a specific Gateway event and context schema. Gateway passes a map of properties from the tool inputSchema, and Lambda must return valid JSON that Gateway can parse. It is not a generic way to pass arbitrary MCP JSON-RPC envelopes into an existing MCP server, as described in Add a Lambda function target to AgentCore Gateway.

AgentCore Runtime can run MCP server containers, but its documented contract is specific to Runtime deployments, including serving the MCP endpoint at 0.0.0.0:8000/mcp with streamable HTTP transport. Stateless MCP is the default and recommended mode for basic Runtime MCP servers, but stateful MCP is used when the server needs features such as progress notifications, elicitation, sampling, or session context across requests. The scenario emphasizes an existing enterprise ECS/Fargate deployment pattern with VPC, ALB, WAF, logging, and secrets controls, so hosting the custom MCP server as an ECS/Fargate service is the best match. See Host MCP servers with AgentCore Runtime.

Question 64
Skipped
A travel marketplace's partner-integrations team is adding a generative AI assistant that converts pasted hotel webhook payloads and support notes into itinerary-change summaries. The public API uses Amazon API Gateway, an AWS Lambda integration, and Amazon Bedrock. Partner messages sometimes contain loyalty account identifiers, payment references, and API secrets. The assistant must keep sensitive values out of model prompts when possible, enforce misuse and content policies on model inputs and outputs, and return only JSON that matches the contract consumed by a mobile workflow. The team wants layered controls with managed AWS services and minimal custom ML work. Which TWO steps should the team implement? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Add a preprocessing Lambda step that uses Amazon Comprehend PII detection and deterministic pattern matching to redact sensitive values before invoking Amazon Bedrock.
Explanation
Correct. This adds an inline control before inference, which reduces the chance that sensitive values are included in the prompt sent to the FM. Comprehend provides managed PII detection, while deterministic patterns are appropriate for known partner secret formats and account identifier patterns.
Run Amazon Macie discovery jobs on archived transcript buckets and send EventBridge alerts when stored partner messages contain sensitive data.
Explanation
Incorrect. Macie can help discover sensitive data that has already been stored in Amazon S3, which is useful for governance and remediation workflows. It is not an inline control that redacts live prompts before inference or validates generated JSON before the API response is returned.
Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails sensitive information filters and instruct the model to always emit the required JSON response shape.
Explanation
Incorrect. Guardrails are an important managed safety layer, but prompt instructions are not a deterministic contract for machine-consumed JSON. This approach lacks a separate pre-inference redaction step for known proprietary patterns and lacks post-inference schema validation before returning output.
Correct selection
Apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to runtime calls and have Lambda validate or filter the generated JSON before API Gateway returns the response.
Explanation
Correct. Bedrock Guardrails provide managed policy enforcement for model inputs and outputs, including content and sensitive information controls. Lambda validation adds a deterministic post-inference layer for schema conformance and response filtering before the client receives the result.
Use API Gateway request validation with JSON Schema and AWS WAF regex pattern sets to reject malformed requests and likely secret formats.
Explanation
Incorrect. API Gateway request validation and WAF regex rules can reduce malformed traffic and catch some predictable patterns at the perimeter. They do not provide model-aware prompt and response policy enforcement, and they are not sufficient for generated JSON validation after the FM responds.
Overall explanation
Layered FM safety works best when different controls protect different stages of the request path. Amazon Comprehend can detect PII in text, which makes it useful in an inline preprocessing Lambda function before the request reaches Amazon Bedrock, as described in Detecting PII entities. Deterministic pattern matching complements managed PII detection because partner API secrets, payment reference formats, and proprietary identifiers might not map cleanly to a generic entity type.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides managed policy enforcement for inputs and outputs, including content filters, denied topics, word filters, and sensitive information filters, as covered in Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock. A Lambda postprocessor then provides deterministic application control, such as parsing the model output and validating that it conforms to the JSON schema expected by the mobile workflow. API Gateway request validation, documented in Request validation for REST APIs in API Gateway, is useful for checking the incoming payload shape but does not understand free-form text safety or validate generated model output. Macie discovery and WAF regex rules can support broader security programs, but they do not replace inline pre-inference redaction, runtime guardrails, and post-inference response validation.

Question 65
Skipped
A video game studio's community safety team is building an Amazon Bedrock assistant that drafts replies to player reports. The assistant must inspect both the report text and the draft reply. For draft replies, the team wants the most conservative blocking for Hate, Insults, Violence, and Misconduct, but wants to block Sexual content only when the classification confidence is highest because plot descriptions often contain benign romance. For report text, the team wants the most conservative protection against prompt attacks. The team wants to avoid maintaining a separate moderation model or custom classifier. Which guardrail configuration best meets these requirements?

Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with the default blocked message. Define denied topics for Hate, Insults, Violence, Misconduct, and Sexual content, set input Prompt Attack to HIGH, and specify the guardrail ID and version during inference.
Explanation
Denied topics are intended for contextual themes, not for applying the predefined harmful-content categories with confidence-based filter strengths. This approach also cannot express the requirement to treat Sexual content differently by classification confidence.
Correct answer
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with the default blocked message. Set response content filters to HIGH for Hate, Insults, Violence, and Misconduct, set response Sexual to LOW, set input Prompt Attack to HIGH, and specify the guardrail ID and version during inference.
Explanation
This configuration uses the built-in content filter categories that match the required harmful-content classes. A HIGH filter strength blocks content classified at LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH confidence, while a LOW filter strength blocks only content classified at HIGH confidence.
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with the default blocked message. Set response content filters to MEDIUM for Hate, Insults, Violence, and Misconduct, set response Sexual to HIGH, set input Prompt Attack to HIGH, and specify the guardrail ID and version during inference.
Explanation
This configuration reverses part of the required confidence behavior. MEDIUM would not apply the most conservative blocking for the specified response categories, and HIGH for Sexual would block more than only the highest-confidence classifications.
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with the default blocked message. Set input content filters to HIGH for Hate, Insults, Violence, Misconduct, and Prompt Attack, set response Sexual to LOW, and specify the guardrail ID and version during inference.
Explanation
This configuration focuses the major harmful-content filters on user input rather than on generated replies. It would not provide the required conservative response-side blocking for Hate, Insults, Violence, and Misconduct.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be attached to model invocations by specifying a guardrail ID and version, which lets the same configured safeguards evaluate user inputs and model responses during inference. The content filter safeguard includes predefined categories such as Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, Misconduct, and Prompt Attack, so it is the right fit when the requirement is harmful-content moderation rather than exact-word blocking or PII handling. See Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and Content filters overview.

The important nuance is how LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH filter strengths behave. A HIGH strength is the most conservative setting because it blocks content classified with LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH confidence, while LOW blocks only content classified with HIGH confidence. That means the response filters that must be most conservative should use HIGH, while the Sexual response filter should use LOW to avoid blocking lower-confidence cases.

Denied topics would be a poor fit for this scenario because they are designed for contextual topics or themes, not for representing the predefined harmful-content categories with confidence thresholds. Word filters and sensitive information filters solve different problems: exact words or phrases, and PII or other sensitive entities. For denied topic limits and intended use, see Denied topics filters.

Question 67

A medical device manufacturer's postmarket surveillance team is replacing manual triage for incoming device complaint narratives. The application must classify complaints, draft standardized JSON summaries, and escalate potential adverse events. Most complaints are routine and should use a low-cost model, but any complaint flagged as adverse must be reviewed by two different FMs in parallel. A deterministic business rule must compare their risk scores, attach reviewer rationales, and route the case to a human queue when they disagree. The team needs explicit retries, timeouts, and execution history for each complaint, and does not want to train or fine-tune models. Which implementation will best meet these requirements?

Build an Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing layer that selects lower-cost or higher-capability models, invokes two reviewer model calls from Lambda, and uses a Lambda postprocessor to compare scores and prepare escalation records.
Explanation
Intelligent prompt routing can help optimize model choice for cost and capability, and Lambda can compare outputs from multiple model calls. However, this Lambda-centered approach does not provide workflow-level execution history, explicit branch retries, per-step timeouts, or guaranteed parallel orchestration semantics.
Build an Amazon Bedrock Flow that uses condition nodes after triage, calls separate prompt nodes for review, invokes a Lambda node to combine scores, and uses the flow output as the human escalation record.
Explanation
This is a plausible prompt orchestration approach, but it is not the best fit for the stated operational controls. The scenario emphasizes durable workflow execution history, explicit retry and timeout handling, and parallel reviewer execution, which are core Step Functions capabilities.
Correct answer
Build an AWS Step Functions state machine that calls Amazon Bedrock from Lambda tasks, uses Choice routing after triage, runs two reviewer tasks in a Parallel state, and invokes a Lambda function to aggregate scores and enqueue human escalations.
Explanation
This is correct because Step Functions provides explicit workflow control, execution history, retries, timeouts, and parallel branches. Lambda can invoke Bedrock models and implement the deterministic aggregation logic that compares scores and routes disagreements to a human queue.
Build an Amazon Bedrock agent that exposes classifier, reviewer, and escalation action groups, enables trace collection, configures return control for tool calls, and lets the agent orchestrate the review steps from complaint instructions.
Explanation
Agents are useful when an FM should plan tool use from natural language instructions, and tracing can show reasoning and tool calls. This scenario needs deterministic routing, guaranteed parallel reviewer branches, and workflow-level retry behavior rather than agent-selected orchestration.
Overall explanation
The strongest design separates model selection, parallel model review, and deterministic aggregation into explicit workflow steps. AWS Step Functions is designed for this kind of coordination because a state machine can use branching logic, parallel states, retry policies, timeout settings, and execution history for each complaint. Lambda functions can encapsulate the Bedrock calls and the business rule that compares reviewer scores before placing a case onto a human review queue.

Amazon Bedrock Flows is useful for chaining prompts, models, conditions, and supported integration nodes, but the scenario is asking for workflow-grade operational controls as much as prompt orchestration. Bedrock agents are better when the model should decide which tools to use, which is less appropriate when regulated adverse-event handling requires deterministic branching. Intelligent prompt routing helps with cost and latency by selecting an appropriate model, but it does not replace a durable workflow engine for coordinating parallel review, retries, timeouts, and auditable adjudication.

For the relevant AWS mechanics, see the Step Functions Parallel workflow state, Step Functions error handling in Step Functions, Amazon Bedrock run inference, and Amazon Bedrock Flows documentation.

**Quick lesson:** For an automated deployment quality gate, Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs are a better fit than ad hoc log analysis or human review. The CreateEvaluationJob API starts an asynchronous evaluation and requires configuration such as roleArn and an S3 output location, but a successful response only confirms that the job was accepted. The pipeline still needs to wait for terminal status and inspect the generated report artifacts before making a release decision. See CreateEvaluationJob. Automatic model evaluations have two details that matter for regression testing. AWS documents one task type per model evaluation job, and custom automatic…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 68
Skipped
An industrial equipment manufacturer's service engineering team uses Amazon Bedrock to generate two outputs for technician tickets: a short incident summary and a routing category. Before each release, the team runs an unattended regression gate in a deployment pipeline. The benchmark contains 1,600 prompts with reference responses and optional category tags in Amazon S3. The team must measure built-in automatic evaluation metrics for both summarization and classification, preserve auditable results, and avoid passing a release when the model fails to return responses for part of the benchmark. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Call CreateEvaluationJob for separate automatic ModelEvaluation jobs by task type, using S3 JSON Lines datasets with a .jsonl extension and no more than 1,000 prompts per job.
Explanation
This is correct because automatic model evaluation jobs support one task type per job, so summarization and classification must be evaluated separately. Custom prompt datasets for automatic evaluation must be in Amazon S3 as JSON Lines files with a .jsonl extension, and each automatic evaluation job can include up to 1,000 prompts.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs and S3, then calculate regression pass or fail decisions from logged prompts, responses, and token metrics.
Explanation
This is incorrect because model invocation logging is configured separately from evaluation jobs and does not provide the built-in automatic evaluation metrics requested. Logs can help with troubleshooting, but they are not a substitute for systematic evaluation jobs with persisted evaluation outputs.
Submit one automatic ModelEvaluation job that includes both task types and all 1,600 prompts, then use category-level scores to approve or reject the release.
Explanation
This is incorrect because AWS documents one task type per automatic model evaluation job. It also exceeds the documented limit of up to 1,000 prompts for a custom prompt dataset in a single automatic evaluation job.
Run one human-worker ModelEvaluation job with the baseline and candidate models, then approve the release when CreateEvaluationJob returns an HTTP 202 jobArn.
Explanation
This is incorrect because a human-worker evaluation does not meet the requirement for an unattended regression gate. In addition, an HTTP 202 response with a job ARN means the evaluation job was accepted, not that the evaluation has completed or passed.
Correct selection
Track evaluation job completion with status-aware pagination, read the S3 .jsonl result files, and fail the release on score regression or insufficient response coverage.
Explanation
This is correct because CreateEvaluationJob starts the work asynchronously and returns a job ARN, not completed evaluation results. Automated reports include the total prompts and the number of prompts that received responses, and only returned model responses are used in metric calculations.
Overall explanation
For an automated deployment quality gate, Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs are a better fit than ad hoc log analysis or human review. The CreateEvaluationJob API starts an asynchronous evaluation and requires configuration such as roleArn and an S3 output location, but a successful response only confirms that the job was accepted. The pipeline still needs to wait for terminal status and inspect the generated report artifacts before making a release decision. See CreateEvaluationJob.

Automatic model evaluations have two details that matter for regression testing. AWS documents one task type per model evaluation job, and custom automatic evaluation datasets must be stored in Amazon S3 as JSON Lines files with a .jsonl extension and can contain up to 1,000 prompts per job. A benchmark that covers summarization and classification across 1,600 prompts therefore needs to be partitioned across multiple jobs rather than submitted as one oversized, multi-task job. See Model evaluation task types and Prompt datasets for model evaluation jobs.

A robust gate also checks whether the evaluation is representative, not just whether the average metric looks acceptable. Bedrock evaluation results are written to S3 as .jsonl files, and automated reports show both total prompts and prompts that received responses. Because metric calculations use only model responses, missing responses can make a regression result misleading unless the gate explicitly checks response coverage. See Model evaluation job report files in Amazon S3 and Programmatic model evaluation reports.

**Quick lesson:** The design needs an enterprise-friendly boundary for a legacy system, plus an asynchronous buffer between webhook intake and foundation model inference. The ingestion Lambda can accept and normalize the webhook quickly, send a message to SQS, and return an acknowledgment while a separate Lambda consumer drains the queue…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 70
Skipped
A municipal water utility's operations center is adding an Amazon Bedrock ticket-summarization capability to a legacy outage-management application. The legacy application can send HTTPS webhooks, but it cannot use AWS SDKs or AWS credentials. The application must receive an acknowledgment within 2 seconds, while summary generation can take up to 1 minute. During severe weather, webhook volume can spike sharply. The operations center wants retryable processing, loose coupling from Amazon Bedrock latency, and the ability to retain failed requests for later inspection. Which integration approach will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

Expose an API Gateway REST API that invokes Lambda to validate the webhook, start a Step Functions Standard workflow, return an acknowledgment, and invoke Amazon Bedrock from a single workflow task.
Explanation
Incorrect. Step Functions can provide retries and orchestration, but a one-task workflow per webhook adds cost and state-management overhead that is unnecessary for this simple asynchronous integration. It also does not provide the same natural queue backlog and worker-draining model as SQS for severe-weather bursts.
Correct answer
Expose an API Gateway REST API that invokes Lambda to validate the webhook, enqueue the ticket in Amazon SQS with a DLQ, return an acknowledgment, and use a Lambda consumer to invoke Amazon Bedrock.
Explanation
Correct. API Gateway provides an HTTPS entry point for the legacy application without requiring AWS credentials on the client. SQS buffers spikes, decouples webhook acknowledgment from Bedrock latency, supports retryable consumption, and can move failed messages to a dead-letter queue for later inspection.
Expose an API Gateway REST API that invokes Lambda to validate the webhook, publish the ticket to Amazon SNS with a subscription DLQ, return an acknowledgment, and invoke Amazon Bedrock from a Lambda subscriber.
Explanation
Incorrect. SNS is useful for fanout, but it is not the best fit when the main requirement is durable buffering and controlled draining of a bursty workload into a downstream model invocation path. A direct Lambda subscription can create pressure on the Bedrock integration during spikes, while SQS is purpose-built for queue-based backpressure.
Expose an API Gateway REST API that invokes Lambda to validate the webhook, call Amazon Bedrock during the request, return the generated summary, and configure Lambda retries for failures.
Explanation
Incorrect. Calling Amazon Bedrock synchronously inside the webhook request couples the legacy application to model latency and can exceed the 2-second acknowledgment requirement. Lambda retries do not provide the same durable backlog and failure inspection pattern for accepted webhook work as an SQS queue with a DLQ.
Overall explanation
The design needs an enterprise-friendly boundary for a legacy system, plus an asynchronous buffer between webhook intake and foundation model inference. Amazon API Gateway is a good front door because it exposes an HTTPS API and can integrate with Lambda for request validation, transformation, and acknowledgment without requiring the caller to use AWS credentials. See What is Amazon API Gateway?.

Amazon SQS is the key integration component for loose coupling in this scenario. The ingestion Lambda can accept and normalize the webhook quickly, send a message to SQS, and return an acknowledgment while a separate Lambda consumer drains the queue and calls Amazon Bedrock. Lambda event source mappings for SQS support retry-oriented processing, and failed messages can be isolated with an SQS dead-letter queue. See Using Lambda with Amazon SQS and Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS.

The synchronous API-to-Bedrock option is a common anti-pattern for webhook integrations because the external system becomes dependent on model response time and transient model throttling. SNS and Step Functions are valid integration services, but they optimize for different problems: SNS for pub/sub fanout, and Step Functions for multi-step orchestration. For burst absorption, simple retryable work queues, and cost-effective worker-based processing before calling InvokeModel, SQS plus Lambda is the strongest fit. Bedrock model invocation patterns are described in Run inference with Amazon Bedrock models.

**Quick lesson:** For this workload, the key design constraint is not just semantic search, it is semantic search inside the same transactional and authorization boundary as the existing learning platform data. Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension lets the team store embeddings in PostgreSQL tables and run vector similarity queries alongside normal SQL predicates and joins, which is a good fit when entitlement decisions depend on relational data that changes with the content. Using pgvector but filtering authorization only after nearest-neighbor retrieval is a subtle failure mode. The application might discard unauthorized chunks after the vector…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 71
Skipped
A subscription-based online learning platform's AI team is adding semantic retrieval to a tutoring assistant that uses a foundation model. Lesson transcripts, course metadata, enrollment records, license terms, and regional embargo rules are already stored in an Aurora PostgreSQL database. Before any retrieved transcript chunk can be sent to the model, the application must enforce authorization by using SQL joins across these existing tables. Transcript edits, embedding updates, and access-control metadata changes must be committed through the same application transaction. The first release cannot introduce a separate search service. Which implementation should the team choose?

Correct answer
Enable the pgvector extension on Aurora PostgreSQL, store transcript embeddings with the lesson rows, and query vectors with the existing entitlement joins.
Explanation
This meets the requirement to keep embeddings and authorization data in the same Aurora PostgreSQL database. The application can combine vector similarity search with SQL joins and use normal database transactions for transcript, embedding, and metadata changes.
Create an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base backed by Aurora PostgreSQL, ingest transcript exports, and apply metadata filters during retrieval.
Explanation
Bedrock Knowledge Bases can use Aurora PostgreSQL as a vector store, but the retrieval path uses the Knowledge Bases abstraction rather than arbitrary live SQL joins across existing entitlement tables. The ingestion workflow also separates vector updates from the same application transaction that updates the source records.
Create a separate Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with pgvector, stream transcript chunks asynchronously, and query copied entitlement metadata during retrieval.
Explanation
This keeps the design in the PostgreSQL family, but it separates embedding and entitlement updates from the source transaction. Asynchronous synchronization can expose stale transcript chunks or stale access-control metadata during retrieval.
Enable the pgvector extension on Aurora PostgreSQL, retrieve nearest transcript chunks first, and apply entitlement checks in application code.
Explanation
This uses Aurora and pgvector, but it changes the authorization boundary by filtering after retrieval instead of using SQL joins as part of the retrieval query. It can also return an incomplete authorized result set if the nearest chunks are mostly unauthorized and are discarded after the vector search.
Overall explanation
For this workload, the key design constraint is not just semantic search, it is semantic search inside the same transactional and authorization boundary as the existing learning platform data. Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension lets the team store embeddings in PostgreSQL tables and run vector similarity queries alongside normal SQL predicates and joins, which is a good fit when entitlement decisions depend on relational data that changes with the content.

Using pgvector but filtering authorization only after nearest-neighbor retrieval is a subtle failure mode. The application might discard unauthorized chunks after the vector query and miss relevant authorized chunks that would have ranked lower globally, while also moving the enforcement point out of the database query that already understands enrollment, licensing, and embargo rules.

A separate Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with asynchronously copied data can look attractive because it preserves PostgreSQL and avoids a dedicated search service, but it no longer provides the same write transaction for transcripts, embeddings, and access-control metadata. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can reduce operational overhead for RAG and can use Aurora PostgreSQL as a vector store, but they are better suited when retrieval can be expressed through the Knowledge Bases retrieval model and metadata filters instead of live relational joins over the application schema.

Relevant AWS documentation includes Using Aurora PostgreSQL as a vector database with pgvector, Set up a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock, and Create a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock.

Skipped
A precision agriculture equipment manufacturer's field-support platform team is designing a troubleshooting assistant on Amazon Bedrock. The team must programmatically validate model capabilities before finalizing the architecture. Which TWO design decisions should the team include? (Select TWO.)

Use bedrock-runtime InvokeModel for chat orchestration, and normalize each model response in the application to preserve a unified multi-turn format.
Explanation
This is incorrect because InvokeModel gives direct access to model-native request and response formats. It can be useful when an application needs model-specific controls, but it does not meet the requirement to avoid separate model-native request builders.
Correct selection
Use bedrock-runtime Converse or ConverseStream for chat orchestration, and validate candidate base models with ListFoundationModels or GetFoundationModel before selection.
Explanation
This is correct because Converse and ConverseStream provide the AWS-native standardized interface for conversational use cases. ListFoundationModels and GetFoundationModel are Amazon Bedrock control plane model discovery APIs that can be used before runtime invocation to inspect model capabilities before choosing models.
Create a cross-Region inference profile for the custom model, and pass its inference profile ID as modelId to provide dedicated production capacity.
Explanation
This is incorrect because inference profiles are routing and usage-tracking constructs, not dedicated capacity purchases. AWS documents that inference profiles currently do not support Provisioned Throughput, so this would not satisfy the dedicated capacity requirement.
Use bedrock-mantle Chat Completions for AWS SDK chat orchestration, and list models through bedrock-runtime ListFoundationModels for all endpoints.
Explanation
This is incorrect because bedrock-mantle is for OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible APIs, while the scenario calls for AWS SDK based orchestration. Model discovery differs by endpoint family, so Amazon Bedrock control plane discovery APIs should not be treated as universal discovery for bedrock-mantle endpoints.
Correct selection
Create Provisioned Throughput for the custom model, and pass the returned provisionedModelArn as the modelId for premium inference requests.
Explanation
This is correct because the premium path requires dedicated production capacity, which is the purpose of Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock. The returned provisioned model ARN is the identifier that must be used as the modelId when invoking that provisioned deployment.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock architecture decisions include both the model and the runtime interface. For AWS-native conversational applications that need a common multi-turn structure across supported models, Converse and ConverseStream are the standardized APIs. InvokeModel remains valuable when direct model-native request and response formats are required, but that flexibility shifts more compatibility work into the application. See Amazon Bedrock API endpoints.

Model discovery should be part of the design before runtime invocation. ListFoundationModels and GetFoundationModel are Amazon Bedrock control plane model discovery APIs that expose information such as model IDs, supported modalities and features, and deprecation status. AWS also documents separate discovery behavior for OpenAI-compatible APIs, which is why a design should not assume that one discovery mechanism applies to every endpoint family. See Get information about Amazon Bedrock models.

The premium path has a different architectural concern: deployment capacity. Because the premium path requires dedicated production capacity, the appropriate Bedrock deployment choice is Provisioned Throughput, and the application uses the returned provisionedModelArn as the modelId. Inference profiles solve a different problem, routing and tracking usage across one or more Regions, and AWS states that inference profiles currently do not support Provisioned Throughput. See Amazon Bedrock model IDs, CreateProvisionedModelThroughput, and Inference profiles for Amazon Bedrock.

Set `service_tier` to `priority` on nightly summary calls and keep rider chat calls on the Standard service tier.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Priority provides faster response times at a price premium, which does not fit a nightly job that can wait. Leaving rider chat on Standard also fails to use the documented low-latency request control for the supported chat model.
Correct selection
Set `service_tier` to `flex` on nightly summary calls that can tolerate delayed processing for discounted execution.
Explanation
This is correct because Flex is intended for workloads that can tolerate longer processing times in exchange for discounted processing. The nightly summaries are not read until the next morning, so they match the cost and latency tradeoff of the Flex service tier.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock exposes two separate request-level control planes that are easy to confuse. Latency Optimized Inference is selected with performanceConfig.latency, where valid values are standard and optimized, and omitted requests default to standard. It is documented as a preview feature for specific models and inference profiles, including the stated Claude 3.5 Haiku profile, so it is the appropriate fit for the rider chat path. See Optimize latency for inference with Amazon Bedrock.

Inference service tiers are a different control from performanceConfig.latency. Bedrock documents Reserved, Priority, Standard, and Flex tiers, with request values such as priority, default, and flex. Priority is for faster processing at a premium, while Flex is for workloads that can tolerate longer processing and provides discounted processing. That makes Flex the better match for nightly summaries, while latency optimization is the better match for interactive rider chat. See Inference service tiers in Amazon Bedrock.

Question 74
Skipped
A pharmaceutical regulatory affairs team is building a GenAI workflow to draft responses to agency information requests. Each request follows a fixed process: normalize the intake JSON, invoke two Amazon Bedrock prompt-based checks in parallel, merge the findings, revise the draft up to three times if either check fails, and then wait for an assigned reviewer to approve or reject the response. Reviewer decisions can take up to 7 days. The team needs deterministic transitions, durable state, and an auditable execution history for every branch and reviewer handoff while minimizing custom state-management code. Which implementation will best meet these requirements?

Create a Strands Agents application with AWS Agent Squad routing, persist workflow state in DynamoDB, and call Bedrock models and reviewer APIs from specialized worker agents.
Explanation
Incorrect. Strands Agents and Agent Squad can implement specialized agent routing and multi-agent applications, and DynamoDB can store application state. This approach requires more custom orchestration, state handling, and audit logic than using a managed workflow service designed for durable approvals.
Create an Amazon Bedrock Flow that uses prompt, condition, and Lambda nodes, implements the bounded revision counter in Lambda, and invokes the flow for each response request.
Explanation
Incorrect. Bedrock Flows can chain prompts and models, use condition logic, and invoke Lambda nodes, so they are viable for parts of the GenAI prompt workflow. However, the several-day reviewer handoff and strong end-to-end audit and callback-control requirements fit Step Functions Standard workflows better than a flow execution with custom state logic.
Create an Amazon Bedrock agent with action groups for checking, revision, and approval, enable agent tracing, and let the agent choose the next tool from request context.
Explanation
Incorrect. Bedrock agents are useful when an FM should plan, select tools, and invoke action groups based on a user request. This scenario describes a fixed regulated workflow, so autonomous tool selection is less appropriate than deterministic orchestration with explicit state transitions.
Correct answer
Create an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that uses Lambda and Amazon Bedrock integrations, Parallel and Choice states, bounded revision paths, and a task-token callback for reviewer approval.
Explanation
Correct. Step Functions Standard workflows provide durable state, deterministic transitions, execution history, parallel branching, choice logic, retries, and callback patterns for long-running human approvals. The task-token callback pattern is well suited when an external reviewer action must resume the workflow days later.
Overall explanation
AWS Step Functions Standard workflows are the best fit when a GenAI application needs a deterministic, long-running business process around model calls. The workflow can use Parallel states for independent checks, Choice states for branching, retry and catch behavior for failure handling, and an execution history that records state transitions and inputs and outputs according to the logging configuration. Standard workflows are designed for durable orchestration, including executions that can run far longer than a human review cycle.

The reviewer step is the decisive constraint. Step Functions supports the callback with task token integration pattern, where the workflow pauses until an external system calls back with success or failure. This pattern is commonly used for human approval workflows because the approval interface, such as an API Gateway and Lambda endpoint, can send the token back to Step Functions only when the reviewer makes a decision. See Wait for a Callback with the Task Token and Standard vs. Express Workflows.

Amazon Bedrock Flows are valuable for managed prompt chaining and GenAI logic, including prompt nodes, condition nodes, Lambda nodes, and connections between nodes. They are not the best end-to-end control plane for a regulated several-day reviewer handoff that needs established callback semantics and deterministic auditability across the whole business process. Bedrock Flows documentation is available at Automate workflows with Amazon Bedrock Flows.

Amazon Bedrock agents and agent frameworks such as Strands Agents are stronger fits when the application benefits from planning, tool use, and dynamic delegation. In this scenario, the path is already known, and the organization needs durable control over every state transition rather than an autonomous planner deciding what to do next. Bedrock agent concepts are described in Automate tasks in your application using conversational agents.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 75
Skipped
An aerospace maintenance consortium's knowledge platform team uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to augment answers from a proprietary maintenance-record system that exposes changes through an internal event stream. The knowledge base data source is configured as a custom data source. Each event identifies whether a record was created, amended, or retired. The team must keep retrieval results current within minutes, avoid scanning unchanged records, and use supported Bedrock Knowledge Bases maintenance operations. Which design best meets these requirements?

Process each change event by calling StartIngestionJob with the knowledgeBaseId and dataSourceId and polling GetIngestionJob until completion.
Explanation
This is a supported normal synchronization pattern, but it is not the best fit for targeted event-driven updates from a custom data source. StartIngestionJob performs a data source sync, which can skip unchanged documents incrementally, but the scenario requires avoiding scans of unchanged records.
Process each change event by updating the underlying vector store entries directly and storing deletion state in a DynamoDB tracking table.
Explanation
This bypasses the Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion layer that manages parsing, chunking, embedding, and indexing for the configured data source. Maintaining parallel deletion state outside the knowledge base can leave retrieval behavior inconsistent with the source of truth.
Process each change event by rewriting the source record and relying on Knowledge Bases retrieval requests to detect the latest source version.
Explanation
Changing source records alone does not update a Bedrock knowledge base. The documentation states that adding, modifying, or removing files from a data source requires a sync or an applicable direct ingestion operation before the vector store reflects the changes.
Correct answer
Process each change event by calling IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments for created or amended records and DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments for retired records.
Explanation
This is correct because direct ingestion operations are supported for custom data sources and can apply targeted document additions, updates, and deletions without running a sync job. This design uses the change event payload to update only the affected documents, which aligns with the requirement to avoid scanning unchanged records.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases separates the source of truth from the indexed representation used at retrieval time. During ingestion, Bedrock parses source content, chunks it, converts it into embeddings with the configured embedding model, and writes the resulting representation to the configured vector store. Source changes do not automatically appear in retrieval results just because the upstream system changed.

For a regular data source sync, the documented operation is StartIngestionJob, followed by GetIngestionJob until the job reaches COMPLETE. That workflow is incremental, so unchanged documents can be skipped while new, changed, and deleted documents are handled appropriately. However, it is still a sync workflow for the data source, not the most targeted design when the application already receives per-document change events.

For custom data sources, Bedrock supports direct document maintenance through KnowledgeBaseDocuments operations such as adding, updating, and deleting documents without using an ingestion job. That makes event-driven maintenance a better match for systems that already know exactly which record changed. The tradeoff is that the application must reliably translate its change events into the correct Bedrock document operations, but it avoids unnecessary source scanning and keeps the vector store aligned with the upstream record lifecycle.

See the Amazon Bedrock documentation on syncing and ingesting data in Sync your data sources with your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and the API reference for StartIngestionJob. The ingestion job object and its status values are described in IngestionJob.

Question 1
Skipped
A telehealth provider's clinical search team manages Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for several product lines. The product lines currently use a mix of RDS, MongoDB Atlas, Pinecone, and S3_VECTORS storage configurations for standard float embeddings. A new cost-reduction program will introduce binary vector embeddings only for supported workloads, and teams can choose embedding models independently during migrations. The platform team needs an automated release guardrail that prevents unsupported migrations, keeps nonbinary workloads on their current stores, and favors serverless operations unless an exception accepts cluster administration. Which approach will meet these requirements?

Enable binary embeddings on OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS by default and OPENSEARCH_MANAGED_CLUSTER by exception after validating embedding dimensions only, and leave RDS, MONGO_DB_ATLAS, PINECONE, and S3_VECTORS storage configurations on float embeddings.
Explanation
This plan chooses the correct storage targets for binary vectors and aligns with the serverless preference. It is incomplete because matching dimensions alone does not verify that the selected embedding model supports the BINARY embedding data type.
Enable binary embeddings when the selected embedding model supports BINARY across OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS, RDS, and MONGO_DB_ATLAS after verifying embedding dimensions, and leave Pinecone and S3_VECTORS storage configurations on float embeddings.
Explanation
Validating that the embedding model supports BINARY is necessary, which makes this plan plausible. However, RDS and MongoDB Atlas are not documented as storage targets that support binary vectors for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Enable binary embeddings for every valid StorageConfiguration type after validating type names, model identifiers, field mappings, and tenant routing, and roll back only if ingestion or retrieval tests fail.
Explanation
Validating type names, model identifiers, and mappings is useful operational hygiene. However, it does not enforce the documented binary-vector support boundaries, and waiting for ingestion or retrieval tests to fail is a reactive anti-pattern.
Correct answer
Implement a release policy that enables binary embeddings only when the selected embedding model supports BINARY and the storage target is OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS by default, allows OPENSEARCH_MANAGED_CLUSTER only through an exception, and leaves other valid storage targets on float embeddings.
Explanation
This approach encodes both required compatibility checks before allowing a binary-vector migration. It also preserves serverless operations as the default while avoiding unnecessary migrations for workloads that continue to use standard float embeddings.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases support a defined set of StorageConfiguration.type values: OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS, PINECONE, REDIS_ENTERPRISE_CLOUD, RDS, MONGO_DB_ATLAS, NEPTUNE_ANALYTICS, OPENSEARCH_MANAGED_CLUSTER, and S3_VECTORS. A storage target being valid for a knowledge base does not mean it supports every embedding data type. The API reference lists the supported storage configuration values in StorageConfiguration.

For binary vector embeddings, the release guardrail must check two compatibility boundaries: whether the selected embedding model supports the BINARY embedding data type, and whether the storage target supports storing binary vectors. AWS documents binary vector storage support for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and Amazon OpenSearch Managed clusters, not for RDS, MongoDB Atlas, Pinecone, S3_VECTORS, or Redis Enterprise Cloud. The knowledge base setup guidance describes the vector index requirements and binary vector support constraints in Set up a vector index for your knowledge base.

From an operational management perspective, this is best handled as a predeployment policy rather than as a rollback after failed ingestion or retrieval. Choosing OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS as the default satisfies the serverless operations preference, while allowing OPENSEARCH_MANAGED_CLUSTER by exception recognizes that it is compatible but adds cluster administration responsibilities. Keeping nonbinary workloads on their existing valid stores reduces migration risk and avoids changing systems that do not need binary embeddings.

The programmatic fit comes from the SageMaker model-card APIs, including CreateModelCard, UpdateModelCard, DescribeModelCard, and ListModelCardVersions. With low-level APIs, the Content must conform to the model-card JSON schema and be provided as a string, and ModelCardStatus supports the documented states Draft, PendingReview, Approved, and Archived. A key design point is that SageMaker Model Cards can be created for SageMaker-hosted models, Model Registry model packages, models hosted or registered outside SageMaker AI, or even without associating a model. That makes them suitable for a mixed FM deployment estate without forcing artificial SageMaker model records. A civil engineering firm's standards team uses a fully managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for a building-code assistant. The knowledge base has filterable metadata attributes for jurisdiction and edition on each source document. User queries often combine exact section identifiers with natural-language descriptions. The current implementation requests 40 chunks for every query and performs custom reranking in an AWS Lambda function, which increases latency and sometimes includes irrelevant excerpts from other jurisdictions. Which approach will best improve retrieval relevance and speed while preserving the existing generation flow?

Call RetrieveAndGenerate with managedSearchConfiguration, set numberOfResults closer to the displayed excerpt count, apply an andAll filter for jurisdiction and edition, and reuse its citations.
Explanation
This is incorrect because RetrieveAndGenerate retrieves context and invokes a model to generate an answer. The application already has a separate generation step with a custom prompt, so adding generation during retrieval changes the flow and adds unnecessary model work.
Call Retrieve with vectorSearchConfiguration, set overrideSearchType to HYBRID, apply an andAll filter for jurisdiction and edition, and remove Lambda reranking.
Explanation
This is incorrect because vectorSearchConfiguration and overrideSearchType apply to custom knowledge bases, not fully managed knowledge bases. Fully managed knowledge bases use managedSearchConfiguration and do not expose a semantic-only versus hybrid override.
Call Retrieve with managedSearchConfiguration, set numberOfResults closer to the displayed excerpt count, apply an orAll filter for jurisdiction and edition, and remove Lambda reranking.
Explanation
This is incorrect because an orAll filter is less selective for this use case and can match documents from the right edition but the wrong jurisdiction, or the right jurisdiction but the wrong edition. The retrieval path is otherwise appropriate, but the filter logic does not best address the cross-jurisdiction relevance problem.
Correct answer
Call Retrieve with managedSearchConfiguration, set numberOfResults closer to the displayed excerpt count, apply an andAll filter for jurisdiction and edition, and remove Lambda reranking.
Explanation
This is correct because fully managed knowledge bases use managedSearchConfiguration, and managed retrieval uses hybrid search with managed reranking enabled by default unless changed. Reducing numberOfResults and applying supported metadata filters narrows the candidate set before context augmentation, which can improve relevance and reduce downstream work.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases separate retrieval from generation. Retrieve returns relevant source chunks for applications that want to supply their own downstream prompt, while RetrieveAndGenerate also invokes a model and returns a generated answer with citations, as described in Query a knowledge base.

For a fully managed knowledge base, the retrieval configuration must use managedSearchConfiguration. AWS documents that managed knowledge bases always use hybrid search, and managed reranking is enabled by default unless it is configured differently, in Test knowledge base retrieval.

The practical optimization is to reduce unnecessary candidates and filter earlier. numberOfResults is configurable, and metadata filters such as an andAll combination of jurisdiction and edition can constrain the retrieval set before the chunks are passed to the model, as covered in Configure and customize queries and response generation and RetrievalFilter. Using orAll is a subtle but important near miss because it broadens the match and can preserve the same kind of irrelevant cross-jurisdiction results the team is trying to reduce.

Explanation
This uses a plausible AppConfig retrieval pattern, but it mishandles Converse parameters. Common inference parameters belong in inferenceConfig, while provider-specific request fields must be sent through additionalModelRequestFields.

This centralizes routing configuration and avoids embedding model IDs in code. It incorrectly assumes that every configured model can use Converse, but API compatibility is model-specific and must be represented in the routing logic or configuration.
Correct answer
Use an AWS AppConfig hosted freeform configuration profile keyed by stage, tenant, and task. Add the AppConfig Agent Lambda extension layer to each function, read the local endpoint, select the configured modelId or inference profile, and call Bedrock Converse only for entries marked compatible.
Explanation
This externalizes routing and rollout data in AppConfig so the Lambda functions do not need code changes when model selections change. The AppConfig Agent Lambda extension provides a runtime-agnostic local retrieval path, and Converse gives a unified message interface for models that support it.
Use an AWS AppConfig hosted freeform configuration profile keyed by stage, tenant, and task. Add the AppConfig Agent Lambda extension layer to each function, read the local endpoint, select the configured modelId or inference profile, and call Bedrock InvokeModel with one shared JSON body.
Explanation
This uses an appropriate shared configuration source and local retrieval pattern. It falls short because InvokeModel uses model-specific request and response formats, so one shared JSON body across providers is not a valid portability assumption.
Overall explanation
The key architectural move is to keep routing policy outside the Lambda code and make every function consume the same deployed configuration. AWS AppConfig supports hosted freeform configuration, which fits a document containing stage, tenant, task, weight, modelId, inference profile, and compatibility metadata. For Lambda, the AppConfig Agent extension can be added as a layer and lets the function read configuration from http://localhost:2772/..., avoiding direct configuration-store calls in each handler.

For model portability, Amazon Bedrock's Converse API is the right message-oriented interface when the selected model supports it. The selected model or inference profile is still chosen at runtime with modelId, but switching that value alone does not guarantee API compatibility. A robust routing document should therefore identify which configured targets are Converse-compatible instead of assuming every Bedrock model can use the same runtime API.

InvokeModel remains useful when direct model-native control is needed, but it uses model-specific request and response formats. Converse also has boundaries: common settings go in inferenceConfig, provider-specific request fields go in additionalModelRequestFields, and response field paths are only for requesting model-native response fields. See AWS AppConfig feature flags and freeform configuration, AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension, Amazon Bedrock API options, Bedrock inference parameters and modelId, Converse API inference configuration, and model API compatibility.

Explanation
This preserves client-side tool execution, where the application, not Amazon Bedrock, runs the tools and can measure real tool latency and failures. requestMetadata is designed to appear in invocation logs for filtering, and AWS/Bedrock plus Converse response metrics provide model-side tokens, latency, errors, throttles, and streaming responsiveness.

Explanation
ToolUseBlock identifies the requested tool and its input, but it does not measure execution after the application calls the internal API. Model invocation logs can include request data, response data, and requestMetadata, but they do not replace instrumentation of client-side tool outcomes.
Overall explanation
In client-side tool use, the model can request a tool, but the application code runs the tool and sends the result back to the model, as described in Amazon Bedrock tool use. That means a useful tool performance framework needs two telemetry planes: Bedrock model-runtime telemetry and application-side tool-executor telemetry.

The application should record the actual tool call count, tool name, toolUseId, agent or workflow, success or failure, and latency around the internal API call. The Converse request can include requestMetadata, which is specifically intended for filtering invocation logs, and Converse or ConverseStream responses expose usage and latency data as documented in Conversation inference. The AWS/Bedrock namespace adds service-level metrics such as invocations, invocation latency, client and server errors, throttles, token counts, and TimeToFirstToken for streaming operations, as shown in Monitor runtime metrics for Amazon Bedrock.

Model invocation logging is valuable for audit and correlation, but it is disabled by default and applies to supported bedrock-runtime operations such as Converse and ConverseStream, with CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3 destinations in the same account and Region. The logging behavior and log fields, including caller-supplied requestMetadata, are covered in Model invocation logging. It does not cause Amazon Bedrock to execute client-side tools or measure the latency of internal tool APIs, so relying on Bedrock logs alone leaves a critical observability gap.

A regional bank's contact-center AI team is choosing between two Amazon Bedrock FM configurations for a customer email response generator. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom development?

Configure CORS on the S3 output bucket, then create a human-based model evaluation job that includes both FM configurations and writes results to the bucket.
Explanation
This approach matches the need for subjective side-by-side ratings because human-based Amazon Bedrock evaluation jobs can compare two models or inference profiles. CORS is required on the S3 output bucket for human-based evaluation jobs, so configuring it addresses the stated bucket gap.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock evaluations support both automatic evaluation and human-based evaluation. Automatic jobs produce computed scores and are a good fit for repeatable metrics, while human-based jobs are designed for human ratings and preferences, which is important when the deciding criteria include subjective qualities such as tone, empathy, and brand alignment. See Evaluate models and RAG sources using Amazon Bedrock Evaluations.

The key constraint is that the team wants one side-by-side comparison of two FM configurations. The CreateEvaluationJob API documentation states that automated model evaluation jobs support a single model or inference profile, while model evaluation jobs using human workers support two models or inference profiles. The same API also requires job configuration such as evaluationConfig, outputDataConfig, and roleArn; for this scenario, the S3 output destination is part of the evaluation system rather than a custom reporting pipeline. See CreateEvaluationJob.

CORS is the subtle operational requirement in this scenario. AWS states that CORS configuration is not required for automated model evaluation jobs or LLM-as-a-judge jobs, but it is required on the S3 output bucket for human-based evaluation jobs. Configuring CORS on the output bucket and then running a human-based model evaluation job satisfies the subjective comparison requirement without building a custom evaluator application.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 7
Skipped
A university registrar's AI services team is building an internal advising assistant by using Amazon Bedrock Agents. The assistant can look up degree requirements and submit course-substitution requests to a student information system. Integration tests show that the agent usually selects the correct submission tool, but it sometimes sends department codes that are not in the catalog, omits an advisor approval ID for graduate students, or retries after a timeout and creates duplicate submissions. The team wants to keep managed agent planning, make the tool contract reusable for future advising agents, and prevent invalid or duplicate writes from reaching the student information system. Which TWO actions should the team take to improve tool reliability while meeting these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Define the action group contract with an OpenAPI schema in Amazon S3 that specifies operations, required fields, parameter descriptions, and allowed values.
Explanation
This is correct because an Amazon Bedrock agent action group can use an OpenAPI schema to describe the tools that the agent may invoke. A precise schema improves tool selection and argument construction, and the same contract can be reused across future agents.
Correct selection
Implement a Lambda action group handler that validates cross-field rules, checks idempotency before writes, and returns structured errors for rejected requests.
Explanation
This is correct because a Lambda handler is the right place to enforce business rules that the schema alone should not be trusted to guarantee. Idempotency checks and structured error handling prevent duplicate or invalid writes from reaching the downstream system.
Proxy the student information system through API Gateway request validation and use the Lambda function only to forward accepted requests.
Explanation
This is incorrect because API Gateway request validation can check basic request shape, but it is not sufficient for the stated cross-field rule and idempotency requirements. A thin proxy Lambda still leaves key reliability controls outside the agent action handler.
Add few-shot examples to the agent instructions that show valid department codes, graduate approval cases, and timeout retry behavior.
Explanation
This is incorrect because prompt examples can improve model behavior but do not create a reliable enforcement boundary. The foundation model can still generate missing or invalid parameters, and prompt instructions do not prevent duplicate writes during retries.
Enable long-term memory for the agent to store previous advising context, department preferences, and advisor approval IDs across sessions.
Explanation
This is incorrect because memory is designed to preserve context and user preferences, not to validate tool calls or enforce write safety. Remembered data can also be stale or unrelated to the current request, so it should not replace explicit validation.
Overall explanation
For an Amazon Bedrock agent, an action group gives the foundation model a tool contract that describes which operations exist and what inputs they expect. Defining that contract with an OpenAPI schema helps the agent plan tool use and generate more consistent parameters, especially when operations have similar names or constrained values. AWS documents this pattern for action groups in Add an action group to your agent in Amazon Bedrock.

The schema is not a substitute for application-side controls. A Lambda action group handler should treat model-generated parameters as untrusted input, validate business rules such as conditional approval requirements, enforce idempotency for write operations, and convert downstream failures into predictable responses. AWS describes how Lambda functions are used with Bedrock agent action groups in Define AWS Lambda functions for agent action groups.

Prompt examples, memory, and API Gateway validation can be useful supporting tools, but they do not fully satisfy the reliability boundary in this scenario. API Gateway request validation can validate request parameters and payloads at an API layer, as described in Request validation for REST APIs in API Gateway, but it does not replace domain validation and idempotency inside the tool implementation. The mental model is to use the schema to guide tool use and Lambda to enforce correctness before side effects occur.

In this design, one rule starts a Lambda-based GenAI integration for approved records, and the Lambda function publishes a second event such as descriptionGenerated after it calls Amazon Bedrock. That keeps generation centralized while allowing new downstream applications to subscribe without changing the curator application or the summarizer. See Amazon EventBridge rules and Amazon EventBridge targets. Failure handling has two different layers. EventBridge target retry…

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 8
Skipped
A national museum consortium operates a collection-management application that publishes objectStatusChanged events to a custom Amazon EventBridge event bus when curators approve new exhibit records. The consortium wants to add GenAI-generated exhibit descriptions by using Amazon Bedrock. The generation step completes in less than 3 minutes and should be centralized so downstream consumers do not each invoke Bedrock for the same approved record. Multiple existing applications must consume the generated description, including a public website, an accessibility review workflow, and a translation workflow. New consumers should be added without changing the curator application or the GenAI integration. Failed event deliveries and Lambda execution failures must be captured for later investigation. Which architecture will meet these requirements with the LEAST integration coupling?

Create an API Gateway endpoint that the curator application calls for approved records. Invoke a Lambda summarizer synchronously and return the generated description to the caller.
Explanation
This design changes the integration contract from event-driven publishing to synchronous API invocation. It also makes the curator application part of the GenAI request path, which increases coupling and does not help independent consumers subscribe to generated descriptions.
Correct answer
Create an EventBridge rule for approved records that invokes a Lambda summarizer. Publish a descriptionGenerated event to EventBridge. Configure EventBridge target DLQ handling and a Lambda on-failure destination.
Explanation
This approach keeps the curator application, the GenAI summarizer, and downstream consumers loosely coupled through events. The Lambda function can perform the Bedrock invocation centrally, then publish a new event that independent consumers can subscribe to with their own rules. EventBridge DLQ handling captures target delivery failures, while the Lambda on-failure destination captures asynchronous function execution failures.
Create an EventBridge rule for approved records that invokes a Lambda summarizer. Call each downstream application from the summarizer and configure Lambda asynchronous failure handling.
Explanation
This can invoke Bedrock centrally, but it couples the summarizer to every downstream application. Adding a new consumer would require changing the Lambda function or its configuration, which violates the requirement for independent consumer onboarding.
Create an EventBridge rule for approved records that targets an SNS topic. Subscribe one Lambda function per downstream application and invoke Bedrock inside each subscriber.
Explanation
SNS fan-out can decouple consumers, but this design causes each subscriber to invoke Bedrock independently. That does not satisfy the requirement to centralize generation for each approved record and can produce inconsistent descriptions across consumers.
Overall explanation
Amazon EventBridge is designed for event-driven integration where one producer emits a business event and multiple consumers react through independently managed rules. In this design, one rule starts a Lambda-based GenAI integration for approved records, and the Lambda function publishes a second event such as descriptionGenerated after it calls Amazon Bedrock. That keeps generation centralized while allowing new downstream applications to subscribe without changing the curator application or the summarizer. See Amazon EventBridge rules and Amazon EventBridge targets.

Failure handling has two different layers. EventBridge target retry policies and dead-letter queues help capture events that EventBridge cannot deliver to a target, for example because the target cannot be invoked successfully. After Lambda accepts an asynchronous invocation, function execution errors are handled by Lambda asynchronous invocation behavior, so a Lambda on-failure destination or Lambda dead-letter queue is needed to retain failed execution records for investigation. See Using dead-letter queues with EventBridge, Invoking Lambda functions asynchronously, and Capturing records of asynchronous invocations.

The main tradeoff is where coupling is placed. Having the summarizer call every downstream system directly centralizes consumer knowledge in the GenAI component, while having every subscriber invoke Bedrock preserves fan-out but duplicates generation work. A synchronous API path can be appropriate when a caller needs an immediate response, but it is not the best fit when an existing application already emits domain events and consumers need to evolve independently. EventBridge and Lambda provide at-least-once processing semantics, so if the business later requires duplicate suppression for generated descriptions, the Lambda workflow should add an idempotency check such as a conditional write keyed by record ID.
