### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 40
Skipped
A museum consortium's digital preservation team is building an artifact-cataloging workflow. An AWS Lambda function reads a JPEG image from Amazon S3 and a short curator note, then invokes Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock by using InvokeModel. The workflow must avoid a separate OCR or image-captioning service, must keep direct runtime API calls, and must provide both the image and the note to the model in the same inference request. The current request body puts the image bytes and the note in separate top-level JSON fields, and the call fails request validation. Which change should the team make?

Send an InvokeModel request with a JSON body that includes model parameters, a top-level prompt string, and inline base64 image data in a separate field.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Claude 3 multimodal requests on Bedrock do not accept arbitrary top-level fields for image bytes. The image must be placed in the provider-defined message content structure, not beside a legacy-style prompt string.
Send an InvokeModel request with a JSON body that includes model parameters, a user message, and a vector embedding generated from the image bytes.
Explanation
This is incorrect because an embedding vector is not the same as providing the image as multimodal input to Claude. It also adds an extra inference step and removes visual details that the selected model can process directly when the request is formatted correctly.
Correct answer
Send an InvokeModel request with a JSON body that includes model parameters, a user message, and content blocks for the instruction text and base64-encoded image data.
Explanation
This is correct because Anthropic Claude 3 models on Amazon Bedrock use a model-specific messages payload for direct InvokeModel calls. Multimodal input is represented as content blocks within a message, with text and image blocks formatted according to the model provider's schema.
Send an InvokeModel request with a JSON body that includes model parameters, a user message, and an S3 object URI for the image inside the instruction text.
Explanation
This is incorrect because placing an S3 URI in the prompt does not provide the image pixels to the model for direct inference. The model receives the request payload, not permission to fetch arbitrary S3 objects referenced in natural language.
Overall explanation
When an application uses Amazon Bedrock Runtime with InvokeModel, the body must match the selected model provider's inference schema. For Anthropic Claude 3 multimodal inference, the request is not a generic JSON object with arbitrary fields. It uses a messages-style structure that includes required model parameters and message content blocks, where text and images are represented as separate typed blocks.

The practical mental model is that InvokeModel is a transport API, while the model family defines the payload contract. Bedrock validates the body against that contract before sending it to the model, so fields that seem reasonable to an application developer, such as imageBytes or s3Uri, will fail or will be treated only as text if they are not part of the provider schema. For direct multimodal calls, the application typically reads the S3 object, encodes the image data as required by the model schema, and places it in the image content block with the accompanying instruction text.

Using an S3 URI in the prompt is useful only as text unless another service or tool retrieves the object and supplies its contents. Similarly, generating an embedding can support retrieval or similarity search, but it is not a substitute for providing visual input to a vision-capable model. See the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API reference and the Anthropic Claude messages API in Amazon Bedrock documentation for the model-specific request structure.

Question 41

A film post-production studio's rights-management engineering team is building an internal assistant that summarizes contract clauses by using Amazon Bedrock. The workflow must reject disallowed user text before any model invocation, validate generated text before returning it, and send a request to human review if a model call stalls. Some valid model calls take 75 to 100 seconds, and the full remediation workflow can run for 8 minutes. The security team also requires application roles to be blocked from invoking Bedrock unless the approved guardrail identifier and version are supplied with the inference request. Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Configure an Express Step Functions workflow that applies the guardrail with source INPUT and branches on GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED, invokes Bedrock through Lambda with a 900-second Lambda timeout, catches States.Timeout for review, applies the guardrail with source OUTPUT, and enforces access with a permissions boundary.
Explanation
Express workflows have a maximum execution duration of 5 minutes, so an 8-minute remediation workflow can exceed the service limit. A permissions boundary is not the documented request-level control for requiring a specific Bedrock guardrail on inference calls.
Configure a Standard Step Functions workflow that applies the guardrail with source INPUT and branches on GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED, invokes Bedrock through an HTTP Task with TimeoutSeconds set to 180, catches States.Timeout for review, applies the guardrail with source OUTPUT, and enforces bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier with an explicit Deny.
Explanation
This approach includes both the pre-inference and post-inference guardrail checks, but the Bedrock call is placed behind an HTTP Task. An HTTP Task in Step Functions has a hard maximum duration of 60 seconds, even if a larger TimeoutSeconds value is configured, so valid 75 to 100 second calls can fail.
Correct answer
Configure a Standard Step Functions workflow that applies the guardrail with source INPUT and branches on GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED, invokes Bedrock through Lambda with aligned Lambda and Task timeouts, catches States.Timeout for review, applies the guardrail with source OUTPUT, and enforces bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier with an explicit Deny.
Explanation
This approach validates input before the model call and validates output after the model call by using ApplyGuardrail independently of inference. Standard workflows can run for the 8-minute remediation window, and explicit Task and Lambda timeouts provide predictable failure handling that can be caught and routed to review.
Configure a Standard Step Functions workflow that applies the guardrail with source INPUT and branches on GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED, invokes Bedrock through Lambda with a 900-second Lambda timeout, uses CloudWatch guardrail metrics to stop stalled work, applies the guardrail with source OUTPUT, and enforces access with identity Allow policies.
Explanation
A Lambda timeout alone does not set the Step Functions Task timeout, and a Task timeout is not short by default. CloudWatch guardrail metrics are useful for monitoring, but they are not a workflow control mechanism, and identity Allow policies do not require the approved guardrail when other permissions might also allow invocation.
Overall explanation
ApplyGuardrail is useful here because it can assess text independently from foundation-model invocation, so a workflow can validate the user prompt before calling the model and validate the model response before returning it. The documented source values let the workflow distinguish prompt assessment with INPUT from response assessment with OUTPUT, and the workflow can branch on GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED when a guardrail action occurs. See Use the ApplyGuardrail API with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

Step Functions and Lambda timeouts are separate safeguards. A Lambda function can be configured up to 900 seconds, but a Step Functions Task state should also set an explicit TimeoutSeconds because the default is very large, and a Catch handler can route States.Timeout to human review. The 75 to 100 second valid calls also make an HTTP Task a poor fit because HTTP Tasks have a hard 60-second maximum, as described in Task workflow state, Handling errors in Step Functions workflows, and Configure Lambda function timeout.

A Standard workflow fits the 8-minute remediation path, while Express workflows are limited to 5 minutes, according to Step Functions service quotas. To prevent bypass, IAM should enforce the approved guardrail during inference with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key and an explicit deny, which blocks requests that use another guardrail or omit the required guardrail despite other permissions. See Require users to specify a guardrail in model inference calls. CloudWatch guardrail metrics are valuable for monitoring behavior, but they are not a substitute for explicit workflow timeouts or IAM request controls, as described in Monitor Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with Amazon CloudWatch; Step Functions CloudWatch metrics are also documented as best effort in Monitor Step Functions with CloudWatch metrics.

### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 42
Skipped
A maritime insurance consortium's claims automation team uses Amazon Bedrock in us-west-2 to draft catastrophe claim summaries. The application invokes a provisioned throughput ARN for a selected foundation model to cover predictable daily traffic. During hurricanes, unpredictable request spikes exceed the committed capacity and cause user-visible failures. The team must continue using the existing committed capacity for normal traffic, must not buy additional committed capacity for rare events, and is approved to process requests in any supported commercial AWS Region. The selected foundation model has a Global Cross-Region inference profile, and the team wants the overflow path to use the broadest documented regional pool available for the model. Which solution will improve continuity during these spikes while meeting the stated constraints?

Correct answer
Keep the provisioned throughput ARN for baseline traffic, and route overflow invocations to the Global Cross-Region inference profile by setting the profile as the model identifier.
Explanation
This approach preserves the existing provisioned throughput path for predictable demand while using Cross-Region Inference only for unplanned overflow. Cross-Region Inference is invoked by specifying an inference profile as the model identifier, and Global profiles can route to supported commercial Regions worldwide.
Keep the provisioned throughput ARN for baseline traffic, and route overflow invocations to a Geographic Cross-Region inference profile for the source geography.
Explanation
This uses a documented Cross-Region Inference pattern, but a Geographic profile keeps processing within a specific geography such as US, EU, or APAC. The scenario asks for the broadest documented regional pool available for the model, which is the Global profile when worldwide commercial Region processing is approved.
Keep the provisioned throughput ARN for baseline traffic, and retry overflow invocations against the same ARN with exponential backoff and jitter.
Explanation
This uses a real resiliency technique that can help with short transient failures, but it remains constrained by the same committed capacity. It does not use the approved Global Cross-Region inference profile, and inference profiles currently do not support Provisioned Throughput.
Keep the provisioned throughput ARN for baseline traffic, and route overflow invocations to direct on-demand model identifiers in selected commercial Regions.
Explanation
This can look like a reasonable custom failover design, but it bypasses the selected model's documented Global Cross-Region inference profile. The application would own regional selection and availability handling instead of invoking the Bedrock profile that is designed for managed cross-Region routing.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region Inference is designed for burst handling by using inference profiles that define a foundation model and the Regions where requests can be routed. An application invokes the profile by passing the inference profile as the modelId, rather than by calling a specific regional model identifier directly. For workloads with approval to use supported commercial Regions worldwide, a Global Cross-Region inference profile is the documented profile type that can use supported commercial AWS Regions globally.

The important design nuance is that Cross-Region Inference is not a provisioned throughput failover mechanism. The documentation states that inference profiles currently do not support Provisioned Throughput, so the resilient design is to keep the existing provisioned throughput ARN for predictable baseline traffic and send only overflow, fallback, or degraded-mode traffic through the profile. This preserves the committed capacity investment while adding a separate on-demand burst path.

A Geographic profile can be appropriate when processing must stay within a geography, but it is narrower than a Global profile and does not match a requirement to use the broadest supported commercial Region pool. A retry-only strategy with exponential backoff can reduce the effect of brief throttling, but it cannot add capacity when the same provisioned throughput ARN is already saturated. Direct regional on-demand model invocation can be built as custom application logic, but it does not use the selected model's managed Global Cross-Region inference profile.

For more details, see Increase throughput with cross-Region inference.

This is correct because Prompt builder can compare up to three variants, and a variant can include the prompt message, model, and inference configuration. Using the same test variables makes the comparison controlled while staying within the managed Bedrock workflow.
Create a single Prompt builder comparison with the production version and all three candidates, then select the best of the four returned outputs.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Prompt builder comparison supports adding up to three variants. The production snapshot should be inspected through prompt version comparison, not combined with three draft alternatives in a four-way variant run.
Invoke the managed prompt through Converse with promptVariables plus system and inferenceConfig overrides, then compare outputs from the regression runs.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Converse requests that use a Prompt management prompt cannot include system or inferenceConfig fields. Those settings belong in the managed prompt and its variants, while variable values are supplied through promptVariables.
Run simple prompt optimization for each candidate with the regression samples and target all three models, then choose the highest scoring optimized prompt.
Explanation
This is incorrect because simple prompt optimization is a fast heuristic rewrite for a single short prompt and one target model. It does not use evaluation data and does not support comparing multiple models.
Correct selection
Use Prompt management version comparison to compare the production version with the current draft JSON, then inspect the highlighted template and configuration differences.
Explanation
This is correct because a production version is a snapshot of a prompt and its configurations at a point in time. Prompt management provides a version comparison view that shows two prompt-version JSON objects side by side and highlights fields that exist in only one version.
Overall explanation
Prompt management is useful for more than storing prompt text. A managed prompt can capture the prompt content, model choice, and inference configuration, so troubleshooting response quality must include both wording changes and configuration changes. AWS documents Prompt management as the Bedrock feature for creating, editing, saving, testing, and reusing prompts, including variants that can include the model and inference configuration: Amazon Bedrock Prompt management.

For a controlled comparison of alternatives, Prompt builder supports comparing up to three variants with the same test variable values, then saving one result as the working draft. That fits this scenario because the team has exactly three candidate variants and wants to compare wording, model, and inference settings without building a custom testing harness. See Create prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt management.

For regression troubleshooting, the production version matters because it is a snapshot of the prompt and its configurations at a point in time. Prompt management includes a version comparison tool that displays two prompt-version JSON objects side by side and highlights fields present in only one version, which helps isolate whether a behavior change came from instructions, variables, model selection, or inference configuration. See Deploy prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt management.

The distractors reflect common anti-patterns. Simple prompt optimization can be helpful for quickly rewriting a short single prompt, but it does not use evaluation data and does not support multiple models, so it is not the right systematic comparison method here: Optimize prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt management. Similarly, when invoking a managed prompt with Converse or ConverseStream, fields such as system and inferenceConfig cannot be included in the request, and variable values should be supplied through promptVariables: Test prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt management.

The key reporting nuance is latency semantics. InvocationLatency measures the time from when the request is sent until the last token is received, so it is a completion-latency metric. TimeToFirstToken applies only to streaming APIs such as ConverseStream and InvokeModelWithResponseStream, making it the right metric for user complaints about how long a streaming chat takes to begin responding.

Question 45
Skipped
A maritime insurance underwriter's GenAI team runs an Amazon Bedrock RAG assistant that answers coverage questions from a shared policy corpus. Adjusters often ask the same business question with different wording, and the corpus is published with a new version identifier whenever policies change. The team must reduce expensive generation calls and improve p95 response time, but cached answers can be reused only when the prior request is a high-confidence match for the current question and the same corpus version. Which caching design will best meet these requirements?

Configure CloudFront to cache assistant responses by normalized query string and corpus version, use short TTLs, and forward cache misses to API Gateway.
Explanation
Incorrect. Edge caching can reduce latency for exact cache keys, especially for cacheable HTTP responses, but it does not identify paraphrases with the same intent. Short TTLs also do not provide a confidence threshold for answer reuse.
Correct answer
Generate an embedding for each normalized question, search a MemoryDB vector index for a thresholded cache hit scoped by corpus version, and invoke Amazon Bedrock on misses.
Explanation
Correct. This design supports reuse across differently worded questions by comparing vector similarity rather than exact text. Scoping entries by corpus version prevents returning answers generated from outdated policy content.
Enable Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for static instructions and policy boilerplate, reuse cached prompt prefixes, and invoke Amazon Bedrock for every adjusted question.
Explanation
Incorrect. Prompt caching can reduce latency and token-processing cost for a repeated static prefix, but it does not reuse completed answers. The requirement is to avoid unnecessary generation calls when a high-confidence prior answer is available.
Create a deterministic hash of each normalized question, store generated answers in DynamoDB with a TTL scoped by corpus version, and invoke Amazon Bedrock on hash misses.
Explanation
Incorrect. Deterministic hashing is effective for exact or near-exact repeated requests after normalization, but it will miss most paraphrased questions. The TTL and version scope help freshness, but they do not solve the similarity matching requirement.
Overall explanation
For this workload, the important distinction is between exact-match caching and similarity-based caching. A deterministic hash, API cache, or edge cache is useful when repeated requests produce the same cache key, but it does not understand that two differently worded questions can ask the same thing. A semantic cache stores an embedding for a prior question and retrieves candidates by vector similarity, then uses a carefully chosen threshold to decide whether to return the cached response or call the generative model.

Amazon MemoryDB supports vector search, which makes it a suitable low-latency store for embeddings and cached responses when the application needs fast similarity lookup, as described in Vector search in MemoryDB. The cache entry should include operational metadata such as the policy corpus version, tenant or authorization scope when applicable, and creation time so that a similar query does not receive a stale or unauthorized answer. Amazon Bedrock prompt caching is a different optimization: it can cache reusable prompt prefixes, such as system instructions or stable examples, but the model is still invoked for the request, as described in Prompt caching for faster model inference. The mental model is that prompt caching reduces repeated prompt processing, while semantic response caching avoids selected generation calls entirely when the application can safely reuse a prior result.

A legal aid nonprofit's intake automation team is building an Amazon Bedrock agent that triages tenant-support requests. The agent returns a natural-language answer to the applicant and can also emit tool_use function-call parameters for an internal scheduling tool. The team must block unsafe content in both prompts and natural-language responses, mask PII in text responses, and prevent unredacted PII from being stored in model invocation logs or passed in tool-call parameters. The team prefers managed safety controls when they are supported and wants the least custom moderation code that still satisfies these constraints. Which design best meets these requirements?

Configure an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters and sensitive information filters for prompt and response text. Rely on guardrail PII masking for tool_use parameters and encrypt model invocation logs.
Explanation
Incorrect. Encryption of logs protects stored data from unauthorized access, but it does not prevent unredacted PII from being stored or visible to authorized readers. Sensitive information filters do not detect PII in tool_use function-call output parameters, so relying on guardrail masking for tool parameters misses a stated requirement.
Configure an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters and custom word filters for prompt and response text. Add known PII terms through supported text APIs and retain guardrail trace matches.
Explanation
Incorrect. Word filters are exact-match controls for words or phrases, so they are not a reliable replacement for PII handling in dynamic text and tool parameters. Guardrail trace match fields can contain original PII values, so retaining those matches can preserve sensitive values that the design is trying to avoid storing.
Configure an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters and denied topics for prompt and response text. Model PII categories as denied topics and restrict access to encrypted invocation logs.
Explanation
Incorrect. Denied topics are intended for contextual topics or themes, not individual words, entity types, or PII detection. Restricting access to encrypted logs is a useful security control, but it does not prevent unredacted PII from being stored in model invocation logs.
Correct answer
Configure an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with content filters and sensitive information filters for prompt and response text. Add application-side redaction for tool_use parameters and avoid raw model invocation logging.
Explanation
Correct. Amazon Bedrock guardrails can apply content filters and sensitive information filters to user inputs and model responses, including masking PII in supported text outputs. Sensitive information filters do not inspect tool_use function-call output parameters, and model invocation logs can contain original request data, so application-side redaction and avoiding raw invocation logs cover the documented gaps.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are the managed control for applying safeguards during inference or independently with ApplyGuardrail, as described in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. A guardrail can evaluate user input and model responses with content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters, contextual grounding checks, and Automated Reasoning checks, as shown in Guardrail components.

For this scenario, content filters are the right managed mechanism for harmful categories, and sensitive information filters can block or anonymize PII in supported text outputs. The important boundary is that sensitive information filters support only text output and do not detect PII in tool_use function-call output parameters, which is why redaction or validation in application code is still required for tool calls, as documented in Sensitive information filters. The same page notes that trace match fields and model invocation logs can contain original PII values when logging is enabled, so a safety design should not persist raw invocations for sensitive content. Denied topics are for contextual themes, not individual words or entity types, and Word filters are exact-match controls, so they are not substitutes for PII handling across dynamic tool parameters.

Explanation
This uses the documented Amazon Bedrock latency optimization control for the supported interactive model path without changing the model integration. Flex is the appropriate service tier for work that can tolerate longer processing and is intended to provide discounted processing.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock separates two request-level controls that solve different parts of this scenario. Latency Optimized Inference is requested with performanceConfig.latency = optimized on supported models and inference profiles, while service tiers are selected separately with values such as priority, default, and flex.

For the dispatcher workflow, the team needs a request-level change that keeps the same Amazon Nova Pro integration and does not require a client-side streaming change. Because the model path is documented as supported, setting performanceConfig.latency to optimized is the targeted way to request lower latency for the interactive calls. If optimized quota is reached, Amazon Bedrock can serve the request with Standard latency, and the actual served latency configuration is visible in the API response and CloudTrail logs, as described in Optimize latency for Amazon Bedrock foundation models.

For the replay workload, the operational tradeoff is different: the process can wait longer, so cost reduction matters more than response time. service_tier = flex matches that shape because Flex is documented for workloads that can tolerate longer processing and provides discounted processing. Priority is the opposite tradeoff, faster response at a premium, and default explicitly selects Standard, as described in Amazon Bedrock inference service tiers.

An online continuing education provider's GenAI platform team is integrating Amazon Bedrock into two separate workflows. A Lambda backend powers an interactive tutor where learners must see partial answers as they are generated, and the team wants a consistent multi-turn message interface while it evaluates different supported chat models. A nightly Step Functions workflow launches long-form lesson summary generation for approved courses. The summaries do not need enrichment by existing workers, can be read from Amazon S3 after completion, and the team wants to avoid custom queue consumers and long-running Lambda invocations. The selected models support the required Bedrock invocation modes. Which implementation will best meet these requirements?

Use the Boto3 bedrock-runtime client to call invoke_model_with_response_stream from the Lambda tutor backend. Use a workflow Lambda task to call start_async_invoke with modelId, modelInput, and outputDataConfig, and store the returned invocationArn.
Explanation
This can stream responses, but InvokeModel request bodies are model-specific and do not provide the same standardized multi-turn message contract as Converse. It increases model-switching work for the chat path even though the asynchronous lesson path is appropriate.

Explanation
ConverseStream fits the interactive tutor requirement, but an SQS-backed Lambda consumer is a custom queue-processing path. SQS standard queues are useful when the application needs decoupled workers, but they can deliver duplicates and do not provide the Bedrock-managed output destination and invocation tracking requested here.
Use the Boto3 bedrock-runtime client to call converse from the Lambda tutor backend. Use a workflow Lambda task to call start_async_invoke with modelId, modelInput, and outputDataConfig, and store the returned invocationArn.
Explanation
Converse is the native multi-turn chat API, but the nonstreaming method does not provide partial response tokens as they are generated. The asynchronous lesson workflow is appropriate, but the chat path misses the streaming requirement.
Correct answer
Use the Boto3 bedrock-runtime client to call converse_stream from the Lambda tutor backend. Use a workflow Lambda task to call start_async_invoke with modelId, modelInput, and outputDataConfig, and store the returned invocationArn.
Explanation
This meets the interactive requirement because converse_stream exposes the streaming Converse operation through the Bedrock Runtime SDK while preserving a standardized multi-turn chat interface. StartAsyncInvoke starts a Bedrock-managed asynchronous invocation, stores output according to outputDataConfig, and returns an invocationArn that the workflow can track.
Overall explanation
Converse is the Bedrock API family designed for standardized chat interactions, while ConverseStream is the SDK operation to use when the application needs incremental response delivery. In contrast, InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream provide direct model access, but their request bodies are model-specific, which makes them less suitable when the application is trying to preserve a common multi-turn chat contract across supported chat models.

For the overnight workflow, StartAsyncInvoke is the Bedrock service-level asynchronous operation. The request includes modelId, modelInput, and outputDataConfig, and the service returns an invocationArn that the application can store for later status tracking. This avoids keeping a Lambda invocation open while the model runs and avoids building a separate queue consumer when no custom enrichment or queue-specific behavior is required.

Amazon SQS remains a valid pattern for asynchronous GenAI systems when the application needs custom workers, enrichment, retries, or orchestration around model invocation. However, SQS standard queues are at-least-once, so duplicate delivery is possible and application-level idempotency is still needed. In this scenario, the managed Bedrock asynchronous operation better matches the requested operational model.

Prepare a JSONL file with one evaluation sample per line. Repeat templateId and promptTemplate for each sample, use {variableName} placeholders, and rely on the job to group samples by templateId.
Explanation
Advanced Prompt Optimization expects one prompt template per JSONL line, not one evaluation sample per line. Text placeholders use double curly braces, so single curly braces would not match the documented placeholder syntax.
Prepare a JSONL file with one prompt template per line. Include both steeringCriteria and customLLMJConfig for each template, omit customEvaluationMetricLabel, and let the optimizer infer the grading label.

Prepare a single JSON document containing an array of all prompt templates. Set version to a current release date, combine all variable names in one inputVariables object, and attach the samples under each template.
Explanation
The input format is JSONL, with one prompt template on each line, rather than a single JSON array document. The version value is fixed in the documented schema, and combining multiple keys in one inputVariables object is identified as a common input mistake.
Overall explanation
Advanced Prompt Optimization is designed for an evaluation-based feedback loop: samples are injected into prompt-template variables, sent to target model(s), graded, analyzed, rewritten, and sent through the loop again. For this scenario, the team has representative evaluation samples and wants multi-model comparison, which fits the advanced workflow described in How Advanced Prompt Optimization works.

The input preparation details matter because the job consumes a strict JSONL format. The documented input schema requires one prompt template per line, a fixed version value of bedrock-2026-05-14, required fields such as templateId, promptTemplate, and evaluationSamples, and text placeholders such as {{variableName}} whose names match the inputVariables entries. The documented limits include up to 10 templates per job, 100 evaluation samples per template, and 5 models per job, so 6 templates, 80 samples each, and 3 models are within scope. Common schema mistakes, such as using single braces, putting multiple variable keys in one inputVariables object, or mixing incompatible evaluator settings, can cause an otherwise reasonable optimization design to fail input validation. See Prepare input for Advanced Prompt Optimization for the required fields, limits, and common mistakes.

Overall explanation
For FM-specific troubleshooting, the useful evidence is often the actual interaction content, not only aggregate latency or error metrics. In this scenario, the team needs to compare how two prompt versions behave for paired inputs, so the pipeline needs request data, response data, and invocation metadata that can be analyzed later for response consistency and formatting regressions.

Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging is designed for that capture path. It can log supported model runtime invocations to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and/or Amazon S3, and it is disabled by default, so it must be explicitly enabled in the relevant account and Region. The documented destination boundary matters because the log destination must be in the same AWS account and Region as the invocations.

The endpoint boundary is equally important. Bedrock model invocation logging captures supported calls through the bedrock-runtime endpoint, including Converse, ConverseStream, InvokeModel, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream. Calls through other endpoints, such as the Responses API on bedrock-mantle, are outside the documented capture scope.

CloudTrail remains valuable for governance and API auditing, but it is not a substitute for a specialized GenAI observability pipeline that needs prompt and response payloads for output diffing. See Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging for the documented capture scope, destinations, and endpoint limitations.

A national rail operator's passenger-support platform team is building an Amazon Bedrock assistant for station agents. Sessions can pause for up to 12 hours and resume from a different device. The solution must keep auditable server-side context and must not keep compute running while waiting for users. The team has an Amazon Comprehend custom classification endpoint for intent labels. Which implementation will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom orchestration code?

Explanation
This approach can preserve auditable context and avoid running compute while users are idle. However, the slot collection and turn transition logic is implemented in custom Lambda code, so Step Functions is not used for the multi-turn orchestration work.

Explanation
This approach uses durable server-side state and can pause workflow execution without keeping compute active. However, periodic rechecks add polling logic and user-visible delay compared with resuming the workflow directly when the next user message arrives.

Correct answer
Implement an API Gateway and Lambda front end that classifies messages with Amazon Comprehend, stores session state and task tokens in DynamoDB, and uses a Step Functions Standard workflow with callback tasks for clarification before invoking Amazon Bedrock.
Explanation
This approach separates short-lived request handling from long-lived conversation orchestration. Step Functions Standard workflows can wait for external callbacks without keeping Lambda running, and DynamoDB provides durable server-side state across devices.
Overall explanation
For interactive GenAI systems, a useful mental model is to separate turn ingestion, conversation state, and workflow control. API Gateway and Lambda are well suited to receiving each message, calling an Amazon Comprehend custom classification endpoint, and returning the next response quickly. DynamoDB is a strong fit for durable session records, collected fields, conversation metadata, and any task token needed to resume orchestration from a later user message.

AWS Step Functions Standard workflows are appropriate when the workflow must pause for human input without keeping compute resources active. The callback task pattern lets a workflow hand out a task token, wait while the user supplies missing information, and continue when another Lambda invocation calls back with the next message. This reduces custom state-management code in the application and avoids patterns such as polling loops or rebuilding the entire slot-filling state machine in Lambda.

Close alternatives can still be viable building blocks, but they do not best satisfy the least custom orchestration code requirement. Wait-state polling, DynamoDB-only state transitions, and EventBridge continuation handlers can all keep server-side state, but they push more branching, correlation, and resume logic into application code. Amazon Comprehend custom classification can provide intent labels that drive routing and prompt selection, but the classifier itself does not maintain conversational state. See the AWS documentation for waiting for a callback with a task token in Step Functions, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon Comprehend document classification.

Amazon Bedrock architecture decisions include both the model and the invocation mode. For bursty on-demand traffic that must remain within a geography, a geographic cross-Region inference profile is the better fit than a global profile because global profiles can use supported commercial AWS Regions worldwide. AWS also documents that requests can fail when IAM policies or SCPs do not allow all destination Regions in the selected profile, so the policy design must match the profile routing behavior.

For the custom model path, the stated requirement for stable high volume and dedicated Bedrock capacity points to Provisioned Throughput. Bedrock uses different modelId values depending on the invocation mode: a base model ID for base model invocation, an inference profile ID for cross-Region inference, and the returned provisionedModelArn for Provisioned Throughput. Overall explanation
Amazon AppFlow is designed for managed data movement between SaaS applications such as Salesforce and AWS destinations such as Amazon S3. In this scenario, it provides the enterprise data synchronization layer while avoiding custom connector code, OAuth refresh handling, and polling logic. See What is Amazon AppFlow?.

Landing synchronized records in Amazon S3 creates a durable integration boundary that other services can consume independently. S3 event notifications can publish object-created events to services such as Amazon SQS, which lets the ingestion process absorb bursts and retry independently of the SaaS source. See Amazon S3 event notifications and Amazon SQS dead-letter queues.

The Lambda consumer should treat Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion as an asynchronous downstream step, rather than part of the Salesforce synchronization path. This preserves loose coupling, gives the team a replay point for failed triggers, and keeps SaaS data extraction separate from FM retrieval indexing. For the ingestion API, see StartIngestionJob.

Step Functions Standard workflows provide durable state, branching, retries, and execution history while Lambda handles fraud scoring, policy checks, and ServiceNow integration.

Amazon Bedrock Data Automation is designed to extract structured data and generated artifacts from multimodal inputs such as documents, images, audio, and video. In this scenario, configured extraction blueprints let the insurer define the claim fields it needs without maintaining separate OCR, image-analysis, and parsing logic for each document type. See Amazon Bedrock Data Automation.

AWS Step Functions Standard workflows are the appropriate coordination layer when the business process has multiple dependent steps, conditional routing, approval paths, partner API retries, and an execution history that operations teams can inspect. A state machine can start after the EventBridge notification, run extraction, invoke Lambda functions for fraud scoring and policy checks, branch threshold exceptions to an approval path, and create the ServiceNow task only after the required checks are complete. Step Functions workflow types and service integrations are documented in Standard vs Express Workflows, Using AWS Step Functions with other services, and Invoke Lambda with Step Functions.

The important design tradeoff is separation of concerns. Bedrock Data Automation handles extraction, Step Functions handles orchestration and recovery, and Lambda handles custom business logic such as scoring APIs and ServiceNow updates. Alternatives that use short-duration Express workflows for human approvals, assemble lower-level extraction services, or place the whole workflow inside one Lambda function miss at least one stated constraint.

A global package delivery network's operations AI team uses Amazon Bedrock with Meta Llama 3.1 405B Instruct through a supported US cross-Region inference profile under a private arrangement that permits continued production use of this model version. The application supports a live exception-triage console. Profiling shows that adding all retrieved policy excerpts plus the requested explanation often makes the request total input plus maximum output about 12K tokens. Operators need faster responses during active incidents, the team must keep the same FM, and finance will not approve Reserved capacity or a Priority service tier premium. The team also wants to reduce prompt-size-related fallback to Standard latency. Which request design best meets these requirements?

Keep retrieved context unchanged and send each live request with service_tier set to flex, then rely on discounted processing for bursts and retry slow responses.
Explanation
This is incorrect. Flex is intended for workloads that can tolerate longer processing times in exchange for discounted processing, so it is not appropriate for an active incident console that needs faster responses. It also does not address the Llama 3.1 405B token-size condition that can cause latency-optimized requests to fall back to Standard latency.
Keep retrieved context unchanged and send each live request with performanceConfig.latency set to optimized, then inspect the served latency configuration in the response and CloudTrail logs.
Explanation
This is incorrect. Inspecting the served latency configuration improves observability, but it does not prevent large Llama 3.1 405B requests from falling back to Standard latency because of the documented token threshold. The design leaves the known prompt-size cause unresolved for the live path.
Prune retrieved context and cap response tokens to keep each live request within the supported total token size, then send calls with service_tier set to default and omit performanceConfig.latency.
Explanation
This is incorrect. Setting service_tier to default explicitly selects the Standard service tier, but service tiers are distinct from the performanceConfig.latency setting. Omitting performanceConfig.latency leaves the latency value at its default standard setting and does not request latency-optimized inference.
Correct answer
Prune retrieved context and cap response tokens to keep each live request within the supported total token size, then send calls with performanceConfig.latency set to optimized and leave service_tier unset.
Explanation
This is correct. For Meta Llama 3.1 405B Instruct, Amazon Bedrock documents fallback to Standard latency when latency-optimized requests exceed the supported total token size, so pruning and output limits address the stated prompt-size issue. Setting performanceConfig.latency to optimized requests latency optimization without selecting the Priority service tier or Reserved capacity.
Overall explanation
Latency Optimized Inference in Amazon Bedrock is requested on individual inference calls by setting performanceConfig.latency to optimized. If the parameter is not specified, requests default to standard, so using only service-tier controls does not request this feature. The documented behavior is described in Latency optimized inference in Amazon Bedrock.

The token-size detail matters because latency optimization is model and profile specific. For Meta Llama 3.1 405B Instruct, requests above the documented total input plus output token threshold fall back to Standard latency, so a responsive design must reduce retrieved context and cap output size before requesting optimized latency. This is a latency-cost tradeoff: the system gives the model less context, but it improves eligibility for the faster path and reduces token processing cost.

Service tiers solve a related but different problem. Amazon Bedrock service tiers use values such as priority, default, and flex, and are separate from performanceConfig.latency. Inference service tiers in Amazon Bedrock explains that Priority has a price premium and Flex is for workloads that can tolerate longer processing times, so neither is the best fit for this live, cost-constrained incident workflow.

Insert a Lambda privacy gate that calls Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities, redacts request text from returned offsets before Bedrock invocation, and blocks or redacts tool_use arguments before tool execution.
Explanation
This is correct because DetectPiiEntities identifies PII entity types and returns begin and end character offsets with confidence scores. The application must perform the redaction or blocking itself, and validating tool_use arguments separately addresses a path that Bedrock Guardrails sensitive information filters do not cover.
Configure Bedrock Guardrails sensitive information filters to anonymize prompts and responses, and rely on the guardrail to remove PII from text and tool_use output parameters.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Guardrails sensitive information filters inspect prompts and model responses for PII only for text output. The documented filter does not detect PII in tool_use or function-call output parameters through supported APIs, so this does not meet the tool execution requirement.
Use Amazon Macie discovery as a synchronous request filter by scanning each submitted transcript object, and invoke Bedrock only after the discovery result returns no PII.
Explanation
This is incorrect because Macie is for sensitive data discovery in S3, not live prompt filtering in the inference path. Automated discovery evaluates S3 bucket inventory on a periodic basis, and targeted jobs analyze selected S3 data rather than acting as a low-latency request validator.
Correct selection
Run Amazon Macie automated discovery or targeted discovery jobs with managed data identifiers on the S3 transcript bucket, and route findings to the security remediation workflow.
Explanation
This is correct because Macie is designed to discover, log, and report sensitive data in Amazon S3. Managed data identifiers provide built-in detection for categories of sensitive data such as credentials, financial information, PHI, and PII including passport numbers and driver license IDs.
Overall explanation
The live interaction path and the stored archive path need different privacy controls. Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities is suitable for the prompt-sized text segments because it returns detected entity metadata, including offsets, but it does not return already redacted text, so the application must apply the redaction or blocking logic before calling Bedrock. The same privacy gate should validate tool_use arguments before tool execution because Bedrock Guardrails sensitive information filters do not detect PII in function-call output parameters.

Amazon Macie is the right control for the S3 archive because it automates sensitive data discovery, logging, and reporting for S3 objects, and its managed data identifiers can detect specific sensitive data types such as passport numbers and driver license IDs. Macie should not be placed in the synchronous inference path because it is not a live prompt filter. The existing Bedrock settings are also important: Bedrock data retention mode none provides zero durable retention when supported, while Bedrock model invocation logging is disabled by default and should remain off when raw prompt and response payloads must not be captured.

Overall explanation
For managed Amazon S3 data sources in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, document metadata is supplied through an associated metadata file named like filename.extension.metadata.json, not through S3 object tags or ordinary S3 user-defined metadata headers. The S3 connector also supports a metadataFilesPrefix parameter so a pipeline can keep those metadata files in a separate prefix from the source documents, and each metadata file must be 10 KB or smaller. See Connect to an Amazon S3 data source for your knowledge base.

The metadata schema matters because the attribute key is what retrieval filters and reranking configurations can use. Bedrock Knowledge Bases metadata attributes support STRING, NUMBER, BOOLEAN, and STRING_LIST, so a timestamp intended for numeric range comparison should be represented as NUMBER, while a tag set should be represented as STRING_LIST. The schema behavior is described in MetadataAttributeSchema, and retrieval filters are configured under retrievalConfiguration.vectorSearchConfiguration.filter as described in KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration and RetrievalFilter.

Question 61
Skipped
A pharmaceutical manufacturing plant's reliability engineering team is building an assistant that triages robotic filling-line outages. For each incident, the FM must propose the next diagnostic action in structured JSON, call the selected internal diagnostic API, append the observation, and repeat until it produces a final recommendation or reaches six tool calls. If the recommendation includes a line restart or calibration change, the process must wait up to 4 hours for approval from a plant engineer. The team requires durable execution history, per-step retry with exponential backoff for API timeouts, bounded execution, and minimal custom orchestration code. Which implementation will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Implement a Standard AWS Step Functions state machine that invokes Amazon Bedrock for each reasoning turn, calls Lambda tool tasks, gates remediation with callback approval, and stops after a fixed iteration count.
Explanation
Correct. A Standard Step Functions workflow provides durable execution history, native retry and catch behavior, looping through Choice states and counters, and long-running callback approval with task tokens. This fits a ReAct-style pattern because the workflow can alternate between FM decisions and tool observations while enforcing an explicit stopping condition.
Implement an Amazon Bedrock Flow that invokes the selected model for each diagnostic step, calls Lambda function nodes, gates remediation with condition nodes, and routes remediation paths.
Explanation
Incorrect. Amazon Bedrock Flows can chain models, prompts, conditions, and function calls, so it is plausible for structured GenAI logic. However, the scenario needs long-running human approval, per-state retry behavior, and durable audit-oriented execution history, which are better matched by Step Functions.
Implement an Express AWS Step Functions workflow that invokes Amazon Bedrock for each reasoning turn, calls Lambda tool tasks, gates remediation with a wait state, and stops after a fixed iteration count.
Explanation
Incorrect. Express workflows are optimized for high-volume, short-duration workloads, not human approvals that can wait for hours. They also do not provide the same long-running callback pattern and durable execution model required for this incident workflow.
Implement a Lambda function that invokes Amazon Bedrock for each reasoning turn, calls diagnostic APIs, stores loop state in DynamoDB, sends approval messages, and retries failed calls in code.
Explanation
Incorrect. This design can be made to work, but it pushes loop control, retry logic, approval correlation, and state recovery into custom code. It does not minimize orchestration code and is more error-prone than using a workflow service built for durable state transitions.
Overall explanation
A ReAct-style implementation alternates between a model decision, an action, an observation, and another model decision. AWS Step Functions Standard workflows are a strong fit when that loop must be bounded, auditable, and resilient because the state machine owns the control flow rather than hiding it inside application code.

In this scenario, the FM can be invoked through an Amazon Bedrock service integration or an AWS SDK integration, and Lambda tasks can encapsulate the diagnostic APIs. Choice states and a loop counter can enforce the six-tool-call limit, while Retry and Catch blocks handle transient tool failures with backoff. For remediation approval, the callback task token pattern lets the workflow pause until an external engineer decision arrives, which is the right mental model for human-in-the-loop gates that may take hours.

Amazon Bedrock Flows are useful for chaining prompts, models, conditions, and function calls, but they are not a replacement for every durable workflow requirement. Express workflows and Lambda-only loops are also common near misses: they can orchestrate model calls, but they either target short-running high-throughput execution or require custom code for state, retries, and approval correlation.

For more information, see What is AWS Step Functions?, Call Amazon Bedrock with Step Functions, Error handling in Step Functions, and Wait for a callback with the task token.

When the desired retrieval unit is already defined by preprocessing, chunkingStrategy NONE tells Bedrock to treat each document or file as a single source chunk. AWS recommends doing your own preprocessing when you choose no chunking, which matches the one-notice-per-file design. See How Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases chunks content. ### Complete source detail (preserved)

Question 63
Skipped
A renewable energy cooperative's compliance team uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon S3 data source that contains text-only interconnection notices. The team connected the data source last week without specifying a chunking configuration. After testing, the team found that Bedrock split several short notices across chunks, causing retrieved context to omit exception clauses. The source documents have now been preprocessed so that each file contains exactly one complete notice. The team does not need page-number citations or filtering by page-number metadata. Which document segmentation approach should the team implement?

Update the existing data source to use chunkingStrategy NONE. Resync the same S3 prefix after replacing each object with a one-notice-per-file version.
Explanation
Treating each file as one chunk would match the desired segmentation behavior, but changing the chunking strategy on an already connected data source is not supported. Resyncing the original data source does not make Bedrock reinterpret it with a different chunking strategy.
Create a new data source that uses chunkingStrategy SEMANTIC. Sync the preprocessed notices and let Bedrock infer the notice boundaries during ingestion.
Explanation
Semantic chunking is intended to divide text based on semantic content rather than fixed token sizes. It is not the best fit when the application has already created authoritative file boundaries and requires each file to be treated as one chunk.
Correct answer
Create a new data source that uses chunkingStrategy NONE. Sync the preprocessed one-notice-per-file S3 prefix and retire the original data source.
Explanation
This approach uses the preprocessed files as the segmentation boundary, so each file is treated as a single text chunk. A new data source is required because the chunking strategy cannot be changed after the data source is connected.
Create a new data source that uses chunkingStrategy FIXED_SIZE. Set maxTokens to 300 and overlapPercentage to 20 for the preprocessed notices.
Explanation
Fixed-size chunking can be useful when similarly sized text windows are acceptable, but it does not express the requirement that each file remain a single complete notice. Even with overlap, Bedrock can split notices into multiple chunks based on the configured token window.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion splits source text into chunks, converts those chunks into embeddings, and writes the embeddings to a vector index while maintaining a mapping to the original document. When the desired retrieval unit is already defined by preprocessing, chunkingStrategy NONE tells Bedrock to treat each document or file as a single source chunk. AWS recommends doing your own preprocessing when you choose no chunking, which matches the one-notice-per-file design. See How Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases chunks content.

The subtle operational constraint is timing. Bedrock requires the chunking strategy to be selected when the data source is connected, and the documentation states that you cannot change the chunking strategy after connecting to the data source. Therefore, the practical path is to create a new data source with the required vectorIngestionConfiguration.chunkingConfiguration, sync the preprocessed prefix, and then retire the old data source after validation. See Customize ingestion for a data source and ChunkingConfiguration.

Fixed-size and semantic chunking are valid Bedrock strategies, but they optimize different tradeoffs. Fixed-size chunking creates token-window chunks with an overlap setting, which helps maintain continuity but does not preserve a file as a single unit. Semantic chunking can improve topic-aware segmentation, but it delegates boundaries to Bedrock rather than using the compliance team's explicit preprocessing. The caveat with no chunking is that page-number citation viewing and filtering by x-amz-bedrock-kb-document-page-number are not available, but the scenario explicitly does not require those capabilities.

Question 64
Skipped
A pharmaceutical manufacturing quality team is extending an FM-based deviation triage assistant. The team already has separate MCP servers for batch-record lookup, laboratory instrument status, and change-control ticket search. The assistant's MCP client must connect to a single endpoint and discover a merged tool catalog before invoking tools. The team does not want to rewrite the existing MCP servers or host new containers. Which implementation best meets these requirements?

Configure Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with each existing MCP server as an HTTP target, then route tool calls directly through the Gateway endpoint.
Explanation
Incorrect. HTTP targets are useful for sending traffic to HTTP services, but they do not provide MCP aggregation or protocol translation. This would not satisfy the requirement for one merged MCP tool catalog.
Create Lambda targets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as adapter tools that call the existing MCP servers, then maintain ToolDefinitions for each exposed tool.
Explanation
Incorrect. Lambda targets are appropriate for custom Lambda-backed tool implementations, with a ToolDefinition and a Gateway-specific event and context schema. This approach adds adapter code and manual tool definition maintenance instead of using Gateway's MCP target aggregation for existing MCP servers.
Correct answer
Configure Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with each existing MCP server as an MCP target, then connect the assistant's MCP client to the Gateway endpoint.
Explanation
Correct. AgentCore Gateway can connect pre-existing MCP servers and expose them through a Gateway endpoint. MCP targets operate in aggregation mode, so the gateway can present a consolidated tool catalog to the client.
Configure Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with each existing MCP server as a Runtime target, then route requests by path from the Gateway endpoint.
Explanation
Incorrect. Runtime targets forward requests and responses without aggregation or protocol translation. They are not equivalent to MCP targets when the client needs a consolidated MCP capability list.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is designed to turn APIs, Lambda functions, existing services, and existing MCP servers into MCP-compatible tools for agents. For a client that needs a single MCP endpoint with a merged tool catalog, the important distinction is the Gateway target type. MCP targets are aggregated by the gateway, which acts as one virtual MCP server and combines the attached MCP targets into a consolidated tools/list.

HTTP targets and Runtime targets are close alternatives, but they have different semantics. HTTP targets send traffic directly and do not perform MCP aggregation or protocol translation. Runtime targets also forward requests and responses without aggregation, use path-based routing, and are better suited when you want pass-through behavior rather than a unified MCP server abstraction.

Lambda targets are a good fit when the tool logic is implemented as custom Lambda code behind Gateway tool invocations. However, Lambda targets require a ToolDefinition with an input schema, and the Lambda function receives a Gateway-specific event object rather than an arbitrary MCP JSON-RPC envelope. In this scenario, building Lambda adapters around existing MCP servers would add code and schema maintenance, while attaching the servers as MCP targets uses the Gateway capability that directly matches the required single endpoint and merged tool discovery behavior.

For more details, see What is Amazon Bedrock AgentCore?, Supported targets in AgentCore Gateway, Use Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, and Add a Lambda function target to AgentCore Gateway.

Correct answer
Expose a retrieval service that calls Retrieve with managedSearchConfiguration for the managed knowledge base and returns normalized chunks and source metadata.
Explanation
This design separates retrieval from generation, so each assistant can choose its own FM, prompts, formatting, and citation handling. For managed knowledge bases, AWS documents the use of managedSearchConfiguration rather than vectorSearchConfiguration when querying retrieved content.
Expose a generation service that calls RetrieveAndGenerate for the managed knowledge base and returns generated answers and citations to each caller.
Explanation

Expose a retrieval tool definition that has the FM call Retrieve directly and relies on Bedrock guardrails to sanitize returned source references.
Explanation
In Bedrock tool use, the model decides when a tool is needed, but execution is performed by application code or by a supported server-side mechanism. Guardrails also do not sanitize Knowledge Base references retrieved at runtime, so this design does not provide a reliable standardized retrieval boundary.
Overall explanation
A shared RAG access layer should keep retrieval separate from generation when downstream applications need independent control over the FM, prompt template, response schema, and citation presentation. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides distinct retrieval APIs: Retrieve returns relevant source chunks or images, while RetrieveAndGenerate combines retrieval with model invocation to generate an answer. The documented way to decouple custom RAG orchestration is to call Retrieve directly, as described in Retrieve data and generate AI responses with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

Managed knowledge bases have their own retrieval configuration semantics. AWS documents that managed knowledge base retrieval uses managedSearchConfiguration, always uses hybrid search, and does not support semantic-only search, as described in Test and configure knowledge base retrieval. Using vectorSearchConfiguration with overrideSearchType is appropriate only for specific custom knowledge base configurations, such as an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store with a filterable text field, not as a portable setting for managed knowledge bases.

RetrieveAndGenerate is also the wrong abstraction for this scenario because it performs generation as part of the call and the API reference explicitly says it cannot be used with managed knowledge bases, as shown in RetrieveAndGenerate. Tool interfaces should expose an application-owned capability that executes retrieval and returns normalized data. Bedrock tool use does not mean the model directly executes arbitrary APIs, and guardrails apply to the input and generated model response rather than sanitizing retrieved Knowledge Base references at runtime, as described in Use tools with Amazon Bedrock models.

Use a Step Functions Standard Workflow with a Wait state loop. Have Lambda send the review request, check a DynamoDB decision item after each wait interval, and continue when the item changes.
Explanation
This avoids keeping a Lambda function open and can preserve execution history in a Standard Workflow. However, it adds polling delay, repeated state transitions, and extra coordination logic that the callback task-token pattern avoids.
Correct answer
Use a Step Functions Standard Workflow with a Lambda callback integration. Pass $$.Task.Token into the review request, and have an API Gateway backed Lambda function in the case-management account call SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure.
Explanation
This approach uses the callback task-token pattern so the workflow can wait durably without keeping Lambda code running. The callback is made by a principal in the same AWS account as the workflow, which is required for Step Functions task tokens.
Use a Step Functions Standard Workflow with a Lambda callback integration. Pass $$.Task.Token into the review request, and have the central platform account's API Lambda function call SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure directly.
Explanation
This uses the right waiting pattern, but the callback principal is in a different AWS account from the workflow. Step Functions task tokens must be returned by principals in the same AWS account, so this direct cross-account callback will not work.
Overall explanation
Long-running human review is a classic fit for the Step Functions callback task-token pattern. A state can invoke an integrated service with .waitForTaskToken, include $$.Task.Token in the payload sent to the reviewer workflow, and then wait until an external process calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure. The AWS human-approval tutorial demonstrates this pattern with API Gateway, Lambda, SNS, IAM roles, and a state machine that waits at a Lambda callback task: Tutorial: Create a human approval project.

The important design tradeoff is that Step Functions owns the durable wait, not Lambda. That lets the application preserve workflow state and audit history while avoiding a function that sleeps, polls, or remains open for days. A Standard Workflow with periodic checking can also avoid idle Lambda compute, but it is less direct because it introduces polling intervals, additional transitions, and extra decision-state management instead of resuming immediately when the reviewer responds.

For reviews that can take weeks, a Standard Workflow is the appropriate workflow type because it supports long-running, durable executions, whereas Express Workflows are intended for much shorter executions. The callback also has an account-boundary requirement. AWS documents that callback tokens are read from $$.Task.Token and that the external system must return the token by calling SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure; task tokens must be returned by principals in the same AWS account: Connect to resources using service integrations. If the review portal is fronted by a central account, the implementation must still arrange for the actual Step Functions callback to be made by an appropriate principal in the workflow account.

InvocationLatency measures the time from request until the last token is received, while TimeToFirstToken applies only to streaming APIs such as ConverseStream and InvokeModelWithResponseStream. Model invocation logging is a separate capability from metrics and must be explicitly enabled because it is disabled by default. It can send supported bedrock-runtime invocation records to Amazon S3, CloudWatch Logs, or both, with destination resources in the same account and Region, which fits a short review-oriented proof of concept without building a custom log collection pipeline. A pharmaceutical clinical operations team is building an autonomous assistant that coordinates protocol review, trial-site feasibility analysis, and regulatory checklist generation. The team wants to use open-source agent code, connect to internal tools that expose Model Context Protocol endpoints, preserve case context across multiple user turns, and run investigations that can last several hours without managing agent hosting infrastructure. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom state-management and hosting effort? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Deploy the Strands-based agent application to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, and invoke it with the same runtimeSessionId for each request in a case.
Explanation
This is correct because AgentCore Runtime is a secure, serverless hosting environment that works with Strands and other frameworks. Reusing the same runtimeSessionId across requests maintains conversation context, while a new case should use a new unique session ID.
Correct selection
Build the coordinator and specialist agents with Strands Agents by using its Graph or Workflow collaboration patterns, and connect internal tools through native MCP integration.
Explanation
This is correct because Strands Agents is documented as an open-source SDK initially released by AWS for autonomous agents, including multi-agent patterns such as Graph and Workflow. It also has native MCP integration, which matches the requirement to connect to tools that expose MCP endpoints.
Deploy each specialist agent as a separate AgentCore Runtime invocation, and generate a new runtimeSessionId for every user turn to ensure isolated case handling.
Explanation
This is incorrect because creating a new runtimeSessionId for every turn starts a separate conversation context rather than preserving state within the case. Isolation between cases is useful, but it should be achieved by using a unique session ID per case, not by changing it on every request.
Implement the multi-agent routing manually inside custom AgentCore Runtime code, and pass all conversation state in each InvokeAgentRuntime payload instead of reusing sessions.
Explanation
This is incorrect because it increases custom orchestration and state-management work when Strands already provides documented multi-agent collaboration patterns. Passing all state in every request also ignores the documented runtimeSessionId mechanism for maintaining conversation context.
Expose MCP tools as OpenAPI action group schemas in an Amazon Bedrock agent, and use AgentCore Runtime only as a stateless wrapper for the coordinator.
Explanation
This is incorrect because the scenario specifically requires tools that expose MCP endpoints, and the documented Strands and AgentCore Runtime capabilities support MCP directly. Using AgentCore Runtime as a stateless wrapper also fails to use runtime session state for multi-turn case context.
Overall explanation
Strands Agents fits the agent implementation requirement because it is documented as an open-source SDK initially released by AWS for autonomous AI agents, with a model-first approach, AWS service integration, native Model Context Protocol support, and multi-agent collaboration patterns such as Swarm, Graph, and Workflow. For a system that needs coordinator and specialist agents, these built-in patterns reduce the amount of custom routing and coordination code the team must maintain. See Strands Agents.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime fits the hosting requirement because it provides a secure, serverless environment for agent or tool code and is documented as framework-agnostic, including support for Strands. It is not limited to short chat calls: the runtime supports long-running workloads up to 8 hours and request payloads up to 100 MB, which is important for investigations that can span several hours. See Host agents and tools in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime.

State management hinges on the runtimeSessionId. When the application calls InvokeAgentRuntime with the same runtimeSessionId across related requests, AgentCore Runtime maintains conversation context for that session; when a new case begins, the application should use a new unique session ID. Generating a new session for every turn or passing all state manually in each payload discards the managed session model and adds avoidable complexity. See Invoke an AgentCore Runtime agent.

Skipped
A specialty food retailer's digital experience team is building a recipe assistant that accepts pantry photos converted to text labels, dietary restrictions, and shopping preferences. The assistant must first classify each request by complexity, route simple substitution questions to a smaller low-cost FM, route multi-course meal planning to a larger FM, and run allergen-sensitive responses through two different FMs before a deterministic policy check chooses the final JSON response. Product managers need to adjust routing conditions and prompt steps without redeploying the application, but developers can maintain a small amount of aggregation code. Which implementation will best meet these requirements?

Create an Amazon Bedrock Agent with action groups that invoke separate Lambda functions for each model selection and aggregation step.
Explanation
Agents are well suited when a foundation model needs to choose tools dynamically, but this scenario needs controlled branching that product managers can adjust as a workflow. Pushing routing and aggregation into action-group Lambda functions increases custom orchestration code and makes the route less transparent.
Correct answer
Create an Amazon Bedrock Flow with conditional branches to specialized prompt nodes and invoke an AWS Lambda node for deterministic aggregation.
Explanation
This approach uses a managed Bedrock orchestration workflow for prompt chaining and conditional routing while keeping only the deterministic aggregation logic in code. It supports coordinating multiple model calls and routing paths without requiring the application to implement a custom orchestration engine.
Create an Amazon Bedrock prompt router that sends each request to a lower-cost or higher-capability model and returns the selected model output.
Explanation
Prompt routing can help choose between models for cost and capability tradeoffs, but it is not a full workflow for multi-step branching, parallel review, and deterministic aggregation. It also does not provide the custom policy check needed to choose between allergen-sensitive model outputs.
Create an AWS Step Functions state machine with Lambda tasks that invoke each Bedrock model and apply all routing logic in code.
Explanation
Step Functions can coordinate retries and parallel work, and it can be used for Bedrock integrations through service integrations or Lambda. However, placing the model routing and prompt-step logic in Lambda does not satisfy the requirement for product managers to adjust the generative workflow without application redeployment.
Overall explanation
Amazon Bedrock Flows is designed for managed orchestration of generative AI workflows. A flow can connect prompt, model, condition, agent, knowledge base, and Lambda-related steps so that a request can be classified, routed, enriched, and post-processed without embedding the whole decision tree in application code. For this scenario, conditional branches handle the cost and capability split, while a small AWS Lambda function performs the deterministic aggregation and policy check that should not be left to a probabilistic model.

Agents are powerful when the model should decide which tool to use, but they are not the best fit when the application requires an explicit model coordination graph that non-developers can adjust. Step Functions is a strong general-purpose workflow service, especially for retries and auditability, but it would put more of the GenAI-specific routing and prompt logic into code unless the team builds additional tooling. Bedrock prompt routing helps optimize cost and latency by selecting among models, but it does not by itself implement multi-step prompt chains, parallel model review, or custom aggregation. See Amazon Bedrock Flows, Intelligent prompt routing in Amazon Bedrock, and What is AWS Lambda?.
